blocks.text: Every day you use and share creative work, music, videos, memes, photos, school assignments, apps, and games. All of these are examples of intellectual property (IP) ideas and creations that belong to someone. Just because something is easy to copy or download online does not mean it is free to use however you want.

You will explore what it means to own digital work and why copyrights, licenses, and credits matter. It's important to learn the difference between being inspired by someone's idea and stealing their work, and you'll see how plagiarism and piracy can affect creators, students, and even your own future opportunities.

You'll also practice making smarter choices about what you post, share, and reuse, especially on social media and in school projects, so that you can participate online in a way that is both ethical and respectful of others' rights.
Intellectual Property Theft online
Intellectual property theft online is when someone steals or uses another person's creative work without permission. This includes music, movies, books, artwork, software, designs, and logos.

Just because a file can be copied easily does not mean it is free to use. This kind of theft harms creators who depend on selling their work to make a living. If people steal their work instead of paying for it, creators lose money and opportunities, which can discourage them from creating new content.

There are also legal and personal risks for the person doing the stealing. Intellectual property theft can lead to serious consequences, such as lawsuits, fines, losing online accounts, or facing school discipline if it violates school policies. Downloading pirated content from untrusted websites can also expose your device to malware, viruses, and scams.

To avoid these problems, it is important to respect creators' rights: buy or stream content from legal sources, use free or open-licensed materials, and always give proper credit when using someone else's work. Respecting intellectual property online helps protect both creators and users.
Intellectual Property and Digital Ownership

In the digital world, creators and users both have rights. Digital rights are legal rights for people to use, access, and create digital information and content. Along with your right to find and access content, creators have rights that protect their work.
Intellectual property is a term for creations of the mind, such as writing, music, art, inventions, and brand symbols. There are several ways to protect intellectual property in law.
Digital Rights and Protections
The table below summarizes three common ways intellectual property is protected.
Type Definition

Copyright Protections granted by the federal government to creators, writers, and inventors. Copyright includes the rights to reproduce, display, make derivative works, and distribute the work by sale, rental, or lending. Copyright is automatically given to creators of original works; no application is necessary.

Trademark A trademark is a symbol for a company or institution that is used to identify them. Trademarks include logos, slogans, names of specific products, or other iconography tied to the company. A trademark must be registered and approved and must be able to uniquely identify the company (not be overly generic).

Holding a trademark allows a company or brand to prevent competitors from releasing products with names or logos that would confuse consumers into thinking they are purchasing from the original company.

Patent A patent is a special type of intellectual property protection for inventions and products. Patents must be submitted and approved. Having a patent can be used to prevent others from copying, selling, or using that particular invention without permission.
Understanding these protections helps you respect others’ creations and better protect your own creative work online.
Copyright Basics
Copyright and Licensing

A copyright is a legal protection that gives content creators the right to determine how their creations are used and reproduced. If everything is copyrighted, how can we use things created by other people? Typically, content is licensed by the copyright holder. A license can be an informal agreement or a detailed contract. In all cases, the copyright holder can specify terms of use for their content, granting specific permissions and listing specific conditions for using it.
Copyright and Intellectual Property
Term Description
Intellectual Property Intellectual property refers to works created from the creativity or intellect of the human mind. They are often protected by copyright.
Common examples include books, paintings, songs, poems, movies, and inventions.

Piracy Using somebody else's intellectual property without their consent in a way reserved for the copyright holder, such as downloading a movie without paying or selling a copy of a CD. Piracy is punishable by fines and, in serious cases, jail time.
License A contract that specifies who may use specific content, including information about specific permissions and conditions for using the media.

Permission A permission in a license refers to ways that licensed content may be used. For example, a license may grant permission for the content to be modified or to be used for commercial purposes.

Condition A condition in a license refers to specific things the license holder must do to use the content. For example, a license may require that the media be used with attribution to the original creator.
Attribution Giving credit to the copyright holder, often by name. For example: Photo by: Michael Olsen on unsplash.com
Term Description

Fair Use An exception to copyright law that allows short excerpts of a copyrighted work to be used for purposes that benefit the public, such as criticism, teaching, research, and news reporting. Fair use is not a guaranteed right; it is a legally defensible position.

Public Domain When a copyright expires, the work enters the public domain, meaning anyone can use it freely. Copyrights usually expire 70 years after the creator's death, or about 100 years after publication for works by companies or anonymous creators. Creators can also choose to donate their content to the public domain.
New creations based on public domain content are not automatically in the public domain. For example, the original Sherlock Holmes stories are public domain, but a new Sherlock Holmes movie is not.
Creative Commons Creative Commons is a copyright framework that offers several different licensing schemes so users can remix, reuse, or share creative works.
Users must give attribution to the owner and follow the terms of the specific license.

Content published online with a Creative Commons license may allow reuse for many purposes. A common condition is that the content cannot be used for commercial purposes, meaning it cannot be used to make money or sell products and services.

Proprietary Software Proprietary software is any software where the publisher retains intellectual property rights to the source code. Most software you buy is proprietary. Generally, the end user has the right to use the software, but does not have the right to make and distribute unauthorized copies.

Open-Source Software Software where anyone can inspect, enhance, and modify the source code is considered open source. Open-source software is often free and can have third-party add-ons to enhance the product. Common examples are GIMP and the Linux operating system.
Open source is not the same thing as a free license or open license, which is a license that allows others to reuse another creator’s work as they wish.
Plagiarism

Plagiarism is when you take someone else's words, ideas, images, or work and present them as if they were your own. This can happen when you copy and paste from a website into your assignment, use a friend's essay, or borrow sentences from an article and only change a few words. It also includes using music, art, or photos you did not create without giving credit.
Any time you use someone else's work without clearly saying where it came from, you are committing plagiarism.

Plagiarism is considered a serious form of cheating and dishonesty in school and beyond. When you plagiarize, you are not showing what you actually understand or can do; you are taking credit for someone else's effort. Schools and colleges expect students to be honest and to do their own work. That is why they often have strict rules and consequences for plagiarism, such as getting a zero on the assignment or facing disciplinary action. To avoid plagiarism, you should always put information into your own words and give proper credit to your sources.
Examples of different types of plagiarism:

items: Direct plagiarism: Word-for-word copying of someone else's work without using quotations or giving credit (attribution).
Self-plagiarism: Submitting work that includes past work of your own without permission or acknowledgment.
Mosaic plagiarism: Borrowing phrases or sentence structures from a source without quotation marks, even if some words are changed.
Accidental plagiarism: Forgetting to cite sources, misquoting a source, or unintentionally paraphrasing too closely. Accidental plagiarism can be just as serious as intentional plagiarism.

blocks.text: Copyright infringement is related but not the same as plagiarism. Copyright infringement happens when someone uses another person's protected work, such as music, movies, books, artwork, photos, or software, without permission or proper rights. Examples include downloading pirated movies, sharing a paid textbook PDF with friends, posting a full song in your video without permission, or copying artwork and claiming it as your own. Copyright laws are meant to protect creators so they can control how their work is used and be credited and paid fairly. Even if you find something easily online, that does not mean it is free to use in any way you want.

Some people think they can avoid copyright problems by adding a disclaimer such as “I'm not the creator of this movie and no copyright infringement is intended” before sharing a Hollywood movie on YouTube. This does not actually protect you from copyright infringement. It is similar to walking out of a store with unpaid food while saying, “I'm not the baker of this bread, and no theft is intended.” Clarifying that you are not the original creator may avoid plagiarism, but using someone else's media without a license or permission (except in fair use situations) is still copyright infringement.

Copyright infringement is typically not prosecuted as a criminal offense in the United States except for large-scale cases. However, copyright holders can sue for damages, and many individuals and companies are known for aggressively pursuing legal action when their copyrighted materials are used without a license.
Practical copyright ethics on social media

Practical copyright ethics on social media means thinking about whether you have the right to post or share something before you hit “upload” or “share.” Just because you find a picture, song, meme template, or video online does not mean it is free to use however you want. Most of that content is protected by copyright, which gives the creator control over how it is used.

When you repost someone's art without credit, use a full song in your video without permission, or upload a movie clip you did not create, you might be breaking copyright rules, even if you are not making money from it.

One simple way to be more ethical is to always credit the creator when you use their work. If you share a drawing, photo, or quote someone else made, tag them or mention their name and, when possible, link back to where you found it. However, giving credit alone does not always make it legally okay; you still need to make sure the creator allows their work to be reused. You can look for content labeled with Creative Commons licenses, “royalty-free” music or images, or use built-in music and sound libraries provided by the social media platform, since those are usually cleared for use there.

It is also smart to create and share more of your own original content. Take your own photos, make your own edits, record your own sounds, or design your own graphics instead of copying others. If you really want to use someone else's work, such as a clip from a show or a piece of music, use only short portions when it fits fair use (for example, for commentary or criticism), and still give credit. When in doubt, choose safer options or ask permission directly.
By following these practical habits, you show respect for creators, protect yourself from account strikes or takedowns, and help make social media a fair and honest place.

blocks.text: You are surrounded by media every day, videos, posts, news stories, memes, ads, and more.

Some of it is helpful and accurate, but some of it is misleading, biased, or created just to get a reaction. Learning to read media carefully is called media literacy, and it’s an important skill for making good decisions in your daily life.

You will see how your brain’s common biases can affect what you believe, and how to tell the difference between facts, opinions, and advertising. It's important to identify who created a piece of content, what their motives might be, and how techniques like clickbait, ragebait, and altered or AI-generated media are used to grab your attention.
By practicing media literacy, you can become a more thoughtful and careful consumer of information. This helps you decide what to trust, what to question, and what to ignore online and offline.
Common Biases in Human Psychology

Common biases in human psychology are mental shortcuts or habits in the way we think that can cause us to see information in a distorted way. One important bias is confirmation bias, which happens when we mostly pay attention to information that agrees with what we already believe and ignore anything that challenges us. For example, if you think a certain celebrity is amazing, you might only click on positive articles about them and dismiss any criticism as "haters." This makes it harder to see the full picture and can trap you in an echo chamber, especially online.

Another common bias is the bandwagon effect, which is when people start believing or doing something just because many others are doing it. On social media, this shows up in trends, viral posts, and "cancel culture." If a post has lots of likes, shares, or comments, you might assume it's true or worth supporting without really checking the facts. Similarly, halo effect bias happens when you assume that because someone is good at one thing, like being popular, attractive, or funny, they must be right or trustworthy about everything else, including serious topics like politics or health.

In media literacy, recognizing these biases matters because they affect how we interpret what we see online. Algorithms on apps and websites often feed us more of what we already agree with or enjoy, which strengthens our confirmation bias. To think more clearly, it helps to slow down and ask yourself: "Am I liking or sharing this just because it fits what I already think? Am I believing this because it's popular or because I've actually checked it?" By being aware of these common human biases, you can make more independent, informed choices about what to believe, who to trust, and what to share.
Identify Facts, Opinions, and Advertising

Being media literate means knowing how to tell the difference between facts, opinions, and advertising when you see them in news, social media, videos, and posts. A fact is something that can be proven true or false, like "The test is on Friday" or "Water freezes at 0°C." An opinion is what someone thinks or feels, such as "This movie is amazing" or "I hate math." Advertising is content created mainly to get you to buy something, support something, or change your behavior, even if it doesn't look like a traditional ad. Recognizing which is which helps you understand what you're really being told.

Facts are important because they give you solid information about the world. They are based on evidence, can be checked in reliable sources, and don't change just because someone doesn't like them. For example, "The school has 800 students" is a fact that can be confirmed by school records. When you see a statement online, ask yourself: "Can I verify this from a trustworthy source?" If the answer is yes, it's probably a fact. Being able to spot facts helps you make better decisions and avoid being misled by rumors or false information.

Opinions, on the other hand, are personal thoughts, feelings, or beliefs. They often use words like "best," "worst," "should," "love," or "hate." For instance, "The new school lunch is gross" or "This is the best video game ever" are opinions. They can be based on facts, but they are not facts themselves because different people can honestly disagree. In the media, opinions appear in comment sections, reviews, opinion articles, and influencer posts. When you recognize something as an opinion, you know it reflects how one person or group sees things, not necessarily how everyone does.

Advertising can be tricky because it doesn't always look like a typical commercial. Sometimes it's clearly labeled with words like "Ad," "Sponsored," or "Paid promotion," but other times it's hidden inside a YouTube video, Instagram post, or TikTok. A creator might talk about a product they were paid to promote or show a brand's logo a lot without saying it's an ad. To spot advertising, look for content that is strongly pushing you to buy, click, sign up, or "learn more," especially if it focuses on benefits and leaves out negatives. Understanding whether you're seeing facts, opinions, or advertising helps you think more clearly, question what you see, and become a smarter, more independent viewer.
Identify the Creator and their Motives

When you see any kind of media, a TikTok, YouTube video, news article, meme, or ad, one of the first questions you should ask is, "Who created this?" The creator could be a single person, a company, a news organization, a political group, or even a bot. Sometimes the creator is obvious, like a verified influencer or a well-known brand. Other times, it's hidden behind a username, a logo, or an anonymous account. Identifying the creator helps you understand how trustworthy the content might be and what kind of point of view it represents.

Once you have an idea of who made the content, the next question is, "Why did they make this?" This is about figuring out the creator's motives. Are they trying to inform you, like a news report explaining a current event? Are they trying to entertain you, like a funny skit or a meme?

Are they trying to persuade you, like a political post asking you to support a certain side? Or are they trying to sell you something, like an ad for a product or a "sponsored" video? Many pieces of media mix these motives, for example, a funny video that also promotes a brand.

Knowing the creator's motives helps you spot possible bias. Bias doesn't always mean lying; it can mean leaving out information, exaggerating certain details, or presenting only one side of a story. For example, a company's ad for its own product probably won't mention any flaws. A political group's post might highlight only the facts that support its position. An influencer who is being paid to promote a product might only talk about the good parts. When you understand what the creator wants from you, your money, your support, or your attention, you can judge the message more carefully.

To practice this skill, get in the habit of asking a few quick questions whenever you see media: Who made this? What do they want me to think, feel, or do? How are they trying to influence me through emotions, jokes, fear, or excitement? Are there any important viewpoints or facts that might be missing? By looking beyond the surface and paying attention to the creator and their motives, you become a more thoughtful, critical viewer. This helps you avoid being easily tricked or manipulated and makes you more in control of what you choose to believe and share.
Identifying Clickbait and Ragebait

Clickbait and ragebait are types of online content designed to grab your attention and make you click, often by playing with your emotions instead of giving you solid information. Clickbait usually uses dramatic headlines like "You Won't Believe What Happened Next!" or "This One Trick Will Change Your Life!" The goal is to make you so curious that you click, even if the article or video doesn't really deliver what the title promises. Sometimes, clickbait hides important details or exaggerates the story to get more views, likes, or ad money.

Ragebait is a more intense form of clickbait that tries to make you angry, shocked, or outraged so you'll react, comment, and share. Ragebait headlines might insult a group, twist a quote, or show only the most extreme part of a story: "This Teacher's Rule Will Make You Furious" or "You Won't Believe What These Teens Did!" The creators know that strong emotions, especially anger, make people more likely to spread the content without checking if it's fair, accurate, or missing important context. This can increase drama, arguments, and misinformation online.

To protect yourself from clickbait and ragebait, it helps to slow down and look for warning signs. Ask yourself: Does this headline sound too extreme or too good (or bad) to be true? Is it using lots of ALL CAPS, exclamation marks, or emotional words like "shocking," "disgusting," or "unbelievable"? Before you share, consider reading beyond the headline, checking the source, and seeing if other reliable outlets are reporting the same story. If a post seems designed only to make you feel angry or hyped up, be cautious. Recognizing clickbait and ragebait is a key media literacy skill that helps you stay in control instead of being manipulated by your emotions.
Identify Altered or Generated Media

In today's digital world, it's important to learn how to identify altered or generated media, images, videos, or audio that have been edited, faked, or created by AI. Altered media includes things like photos that have been heavily edited with filters, apps that change faces or bodies, or videos that have clips cut out to change the meaning. Generated media goes a step further and can include deepfakes (videos where someone's face or voice is replaced with another person's) or AI-generated images and audio that look and sound real, even though they never actually happened. These tools can be used for fun, but they can also spread lies, bullying, or misinformation.

To spot altered or generated media, look closely for clues. In images, check for strange lighting, blurry edges, weird fingers, mismatched earrings, or backgrounds that don't line up correctly; these can be signs of heavy editing or AI generation. In videos, watch for unnatural blinking, odd mouth movements, or audio that seems slightly out of sync with the person's lips. If a video or image makes a celebrity, teacher, or classmate look like they did something shocking or totally out of character, be extra careful. Ask yourself: "Where did this come from? Is it from a trusted source? Are other reliable places reporting the same thing?" Being media literate means not believing everything at first glance, especially when it comes to dramatic or emotional content. Before you react, share, or judge someone based on a picture or video, try to verify it. You can use reverse image search to see where an image first appeared, check fact-checking websites, or compare the content to coverage from trustworthy news sources. Remember that altered and generated media can harm reputations, fuel rumors, and influence opinions. By slowing down, looking for signs of editing, and checking the source, you protect yourself and others from being fooled or unfairly treated.

blocks.text: The internet connects billions of devices and people around the world. Every time you send a message, watch a video, join an online game, or search for information, you are using this massive global network. But what is the internet really, and how does it actually work behind the scenes?

Computer networks link devices together so they can share information. Web pages, websites, and web servers work together to store and deliver content. IP addresses and URLs act like digital addresses and directions, helping your device find exactly the right place on the web.
Understanding these basics turns the internet from something that feels like "magic" into a clear system of devices, connections, and rules that make online communication and information possible.

The Internet is a system of computer networks all over the world talking to each other, without any one person or group controlling it. Think of the Internet as a large highway that emails, videos, games, and all kinds of data travel over. Internet technology has made it possible for people to play games online, send emails, make video calls, chat, share files, and more. It connects millions of computers, websites, and servers. It's a network of networks.

Some form of Internet technology dates back to the late 1960s, and a United States government program by the Department of Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. It began as a way for researchers to share information more easily. Because computers at that time were large and immobile, taking up whole rooms in some cases, people had to either travel to the computer's location to see the data on that computer or have magnetic computer tapes sent through the postal service. This was not very secure or efficient. Over the next decade, more groups developed other small networks of computers, but each network was isolated from the others. They did not have a common language or set of protocols.
Protocols

In the early 1980s, the people behind the different networks agreed on one shared language, one that allowed all the networks to talk to each other and to share information. This shared language is called the Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol (T CP/IP), and it's still the way the Internet communicates today.

All the Internet-connected computers follow these rules to maintain quick communication, as well as the integrity of the data. Data integrity is the idea that data sent over the Internet is accurate, consistent, complete, and correct when it arrives at its destination. In other words, the data you receive is the same as the data you asked for. These protocols mean that when you get data from another computer on the Internet, that data hasn't changed while it traveled to you.
Internet Architecture

The Internet is a decentralized system, meaning that there isn't one group or person that holds all the information on the Internet or governs how the Internet runs. Instead, everything connected to the Internet, from your phone to a university computer, can all do the same things.

Every device can ask for information from others (or act as a client), and every device can share information with others (or act as a server). This is sometimes referred to as peer-to-peer architecture. Peer-to-peer architecture allows smaller groups to share information just as easily as groups with more computing power. Peer-to-peer architecture makes it easier to share files, stream video, and resist security threats.
Computer Networks and Connectivity
From One Device to a Network

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: Imagine a single computer sitting in a room with no cables, no Wi-Fi, and no way to connect to anything else. It can only use the information already stored on it. Now compare that to your experience today: you can message friends, stream videos, play online games, and look up information in seconds. The difference is computer networks.

A computer network is a group of devices linked together so they can share information. These devices can be desktop computers, laptops, tablets, phones, game consoles, smart TVs, and many others. Even devices like printers, security cameras, or smart thermostats can be part of a network.

A very small network might exist in a single room or home. Larger networks might connect an entire school or office building. These different networks can then link together to reach even more places.
Wired and Wireless Connectivity
For a network to work, devices need some way to send data between them. This is called connectivity. You can think of connectivity like the paths that connect houses in a neighborhood:

items: Wired connections are like solid roads. Devices use network cables to connect to the network. These cables carry electrical signals that represent data. Wired connections are usually very stable and fast, which is why they are common in offices, schools, and data centers.

Wireless connections are more like invisible paths through the air. Devices use radio waves, such as Wi-Fi or cellular signals, to communicate without needing a cable. Wireless connections make it easy to move around with phones, laptops, and tablets.

blocks.text: On a typical home network, both types of connectivity are often used at the same time. A router might connect to the internet using a cable from the wall, while phones and laptops connect to that router over Wi-Fi.
Small Networks, Big Networks

Networks can be built in many different sizes. A small home network might have just a few devices. A school might have hundreds of computers, printers, and tablets connected. Large companies and universities might have networks that span multiple buildings or campuses.

Even though the size and complexity can change, the basic idea is the same: connected devices can share data. A file saved on one computer can be opened on another. A printer in the hallway can be used by any computer on the network. A game server in one city can send updates to players in many different places.
When many of these smaller networks are linked together, information can travel a very long way from one neighborhood or school to the other side of the world.
Public and Private Networks
Not every network is open to everyone. Some networks are meant to be shared with the public, while others are meant to be kept private.

items: A public network is open for general use. The public internet is the largest example. Anyone with a connection can reach public websites, watch videos, or read online articles.

A private network belongs to a specific group, such as a company, school, or family. Devices inside the private network can usually reach the public internet, but outside devices cannot freely reach into the private network.

blocks.text: A useful analogy is a city with open streets and gated communities. The public roads are like the public internet; anyone can use them. A gated neighborhood is like a private network; only people with permission can enter. Devices such as routers and firewalls act like the gates and guards, controlling who can go in and out.
Some organizations build an intranet, which is like a private “mini-internet” inside the company.
It might use web pages, email, and internal chat tools, but only employees or authorized users can access it.
Clients, Servers, and Peers
When devices communicate on a network, they often take on different roles depending on what is happening.

items: A client is a device that requests information or services. For example, when you open a browser and type in the address of a website, your computer or phone is acting as a client.
A server is a device that responds to those requests and provides information, such as a website, a file, or a game update.

blocks.text: In many cases, the same device can act as both a client and a server at different times. A classroom computer might request a web page (client role) and also share a simple file with another student on the same network (server role).

When devices on a network share directly with each other instead of always going through a central server, this is often called a peer-to-peer connection. In a peer-to-peer group, each device, or “peer,” can both send and receive. This model is common in small file-sharing setups or when friends connect their devices for a shared activity.
Connectivity in Everyday Life
Computer networks and connectivity are part of many everyday activities, even when they are not obvious. A few examples include:

items: Saving a school project to cloud storage and opening it later on a different device
Joining an online game where players connect from many different locations
Using a messaging app to chat with family members in another city or country
Having a smart doorbell send video to your phone over your home network
Connecting a laptop to a school printer over the school’s internal network

blocks.text: In each case, devices rely on networks to move data from one place to another. Cables, wireless signals, public and private networks, and different device roles all work together so that information can travel quickly and reliably, often in just a fraction of a second.
Web Pages and Web Sites

It's pretty common to think that the Internet and the World Wide Web (W W W), or websites, are the same, but they're actually different things. The Internet is a huge network of computers all over the world. The Web, on the other hand, is a collection of interconnected files that use the Internet to share content such as text, graphics, audio, video, and more. If you imagine the Internet and the Web as a city, the Internet would be all the roads and highways that connect different neighborhoods. The Web would be the diners, movie theaters, coffee shops, and stores along the way.
Web Content

The World Wide Web was created to help organize information. A scientist named Tim Berners- Lee, who worked in a lab in Switzerland, noticed that big projects were making huge amounts of data, and that was stored in many different places. Sometimes, scientists even lost data because they could not find it. He suggested a way to link all the data together like a "web" using hypertext documents that could be stored on computers called servers. In 1990, he set up the very first web server and web page. By 1993, websites started to be available for everyone to use.

You can see the very first website ever created at https://info.cern.ch/ At its simplest, a website is a collection of pages that are all linked together and share information. Every webpage uses a special kind of code that decides how it looks or appears on your screen.

This special code is called HyperText Markup Language (HTML) . HTML is what organizes everything you see on a webpage, such as images, advertisements, and text. It also makes sure all the parts of the webpage work well together. Thanks to HTML, webpages can look the same and work properly no matter which browser you use to view them.
HTML is packed with details on all the different parts of a webpage and instructions on how to display them. It's a key part of making webpages work.
Protocols

HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) is the basis of the World Wide Web. This protocol, or set of rules, allows a web browser to communicate with a web server and request a website, transmit the website data, and load it on your browser for you to see.

There are many other protocols involved in directing traffic across the web. Some are concerned with email and other messages, others focus on transferring files, while still more protocols deal with discovering devices on local networks and improving communication.
Web Architecture

The World Wide Web was originally designed as a decentralized system. This means no single person, group, or organization owns or controls all the information. However, most Internet users use only certain social media or messaging applications today. These applications are owned by large corporations that are centralized and control all the content on their platforms.
This is why many feel the Internet is controlled by a few large companies.
The World Wide Web uses a design called client-server architecture to access and navigate information. A client, usually a person using a web browser, requests data from a web server.

The server returns the page with the information requested. You can select any links in that document to request more information from the original web server or possibly create a request to a different web server. These hyperlinks are the key to the World Wide Web.

The web server is equipped with powerful hardware, specialized software, and is expected to be running almost constantly. Servers have large amounts of memory, multiple CPUs, and large storage capacities. In addition to its power, the server will have better quality components than a traditional desktop, and more of them: servers typically have multiple hard drives and power supplies. All of these extras allow web servers to fulfill lots of requests in a short amount of time, and to stay available for nearly its whole lifespan.
IP Addresses and URLs
Finding Things on the Internet

When you want to call a friend, you probably tap their name in your contacts instead of typing their phone number every time. Your phone quietly looks up the number for you and dials it in the background. The Internet works in a very similar way.

When you want to visit a website, you type or tap a web address like comptia.com or click a link. Behind the scenes, your device has to find a specific computer somewhere on the Internet that can provide that site. To do that, it uses two key pieces:

items: IP addresses – the exact “numbers” that identify devices on the Internet.
URLs – the readable web addresses you use every day.

blocks.text: IP addresses and URLs work together so that you can use simple names, while your device uses precise numbers to reach the right place.
What Is an IP Address?

An IP address is a unique set of numbers that identifies a device on a network that uses the Internet Protocol (IP). You can think of it like a street address for a house. Without an address, the postal service would not know where to deliver a letter. Without an IP address, the Internet would not know where to send data.
IP addresses usually look like one of these:

items: IPv4 example: 192.168.1.10

blocks.text: You do not need to memorize these formats, but it helps to recognize that they are numbers, not words. When your device sends a request across the Internet, it includes both its own IP address (so the response can find its way back) and the destination IP address (so the data knows where to go).
What Is a URL?

A Uniform Resource Locator(URL) is the text address you type into your browser to reach a page or resource on the Web. It is designed to be easy for people to read and remember, like a contact name in your phone.
A typical URL such as https://www.example.com/page can be broken into parts:

items: Protocol - https:// tells the browser which set of rules to use when requesting the resource.
Domain name – www.example.com is the main name of the site, made of words and dots instead of numbers.
Path – /page points to a specific page or file on that site.

blocks.text: You can think of a URL like a full mailing address written in a friendly format. The domain name is like the name of the building, and the path is like the room or office number inside that building.
How URLs and IP Addresses Work Together
Computers and other devices communicate using numbers, but people usually prefer names.
URLs and IP addresses work together to make both sides happy.

When you enter a URL such as comptia.com , your device needs to find the IP address that matches that name. This process is like asking your phone to “Call Coach” and letting it look up the correct phone number behind the scenes.

Once the IP address is known, your device uses that number to send and receive data with the correct web server. You keep working with the simple URL, but the actual communication happens using the IP address.
The Role of DNS Servers
A Domain Name System server (DNS server) is a special device that helps translate URLs into IP addresses, similar to how a contacts app translates names into phone numbers.
The basic idea is:

items: You type a URL into your browser, like comptia.com , and press Enter.
Your device sends a request to a nearby DNS server, asking, “What is the IP address for comptia.com ?”
The DNS server looks in its catalog of stored records to find the match.
If it finds an entry, it sends the IP address back to your device.

blocks.text: After that, your device can contact the correct server directly using the IP address. This all happens very quickly, usually in a fraction of a second, so you only notice that the website appears in your browser.
Why IP Addresses and URLs Matter
IP addresses and URLs might seem like background details, but they affect how you use the Internet every day:

items: Ease of use – URLs let you use simple names instead of long strings of numbers.
Accuracy – IP addresses make sure data goes to and comes from the correct device.
Speed – DNS servers and stored records help your device find sites quickly.

blocks.text: Understanding the basic relationship between IP addresses, URLs, and DNS helps explain what is happening when you type a web address and a site appears almost instantly on your screen.
It turns a “mysterious” process into something you can picture and reason about, even as a first-time learner.

What tools and features do most web browsers share in common?
How can you navigate websites effectively and find what you need on a page?
What options are available to personalize or customize how a browser looks and behaves?
How can add-ons, extensions, and privacy features change the way you browse?
What browser settings can you use to have the best experiences online and to keep your
private information safe?
What steps can you take to keep your browser working well and solve basic browsing
problems?

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 3.3 Explain the purpose and proper use of software.
3.4 Given a scenario, configure and use web browser features.

blocks.text: Using a web browser is one of the main ways to interact with the internet. Any time you search for information, open a website, stream a video, or log in to an online account, you are using browser tools and features, even if you don’t think about them. Knowing how browsers work helps you stay more organized, efficient, and safe online.

Most browsers share common parts, such as the address bar, tabs, and menus. They also offer options to personalize how pages look, save your favorite sites, and control privacy and security settings. With a bit of practice, you can adjust a browser to fit your needs and troubleshoot common problems when something doesn’t work as expected.
Web Browsers

A web browser is a program or application that allows you to view and use websites. It works by asking for resources, meaning the contents of a web page or site, from a web server and displaying them on your computer screen. Web browsers can deliver websites from local servers (for example, within a school or company's own network), or from anywhere on the Internet. Tim Berners-Lee is credited with creating the first web browser and the protocol needed to transfer a webpage from one computer to another. Since their creation, web browsers have evolved to become one of the most important tools.

There are many different browsers available. At the time of writing, Google's Chrome browser is the most popular browser worldwide, with Safari, Firefox, Opera, and Microsoft Edge among the top spots. These well-known products are similar in how quickly they load webpages and how easy they are to use. Their differences are where they get users' attention. Some have stronger privacy protections, some use fewer computer resources to run, and others have note-taking and productivity tools built in to the browser application. Each of these popular browsers has a large community of users who can answer questions, in addition to the developers who build and support them.
Type "do a barrel roll" into the Google search box in the middle of the Chrome browser. This is one of Chrome's many hidden features.
Compatible Browsers

In the past, different web browsers didn't always follow the standards for how websites should look and work. These rules are made using formats like HyperText Markup Language (HTML) and cascading style sheets (CSS) . Microsoft's Internet Explorer browser, once the most commonly used browser, was famous for not following these rules. A lot of websites and online tools were made to work just with Internet Explorer, which meant they might not work right on other browsers.

Today these problems are not very common at all. The popular web browsers follow industry standards much more closely. There can still be problems with website compatibility, however, especially on older websites. These websites may have important information, but just aren't updated very often. If you encounter a compatibility problem, you may need to use an older browser.
Mobile Browsers

More and more people, no matter how old they are, are using their phones and mobile devices to go online. It's easier and more comfortable to browse on a phone, and it makes sharing content on social media much faster. Mobile browsers are designed specifically to work with smaller touch screens. They have a simpler user interface that's easy to use with just your fingers. Additionally, websites often load more quickly on mobile browsers, so you don't have to wait as long.

As mobile browsing has gotten more common, web developers have kept up by making their sites easier to use. Single-column page layouts make it easier for users to scroll through, and simplifying the content makes it easier to find important information. Responsive designs adjust both text and images to fit the screen, because the mobile browser tells the web server to deliver the mobile-friendly version of the site.
Shared Browser Traits
Modern browsers, both desktop and mobile, share a lot of similar features. One of the most user-friendly is the ability to search within the address bar at the top of the browser window.

If you type a valid uniform resource locator (URL) , or web address, into the address bar and press Enter, it takes you to that web page. If you type text that isn't a URL, the browser will search the web using its default search engine.
Modern web browsers have other similar features, including:

items: Navigation buttons: Move backward and forward through webpages you have recently viewed. If you hold down either button a window of recent history will appear.
Refresh button: Forces the browser to reload the current website. The F5 key will also do the same for most browsers.
Home button: Returns a browser to the default starting webpage.
Address bar: Displays the name of the website or universal resource locator (URL) of the current web page.
Browser tabs: Allow several websites to be opened in one browser window.
Bookmarks: Store websites so you can easily visit the same site again later.

blocks.text: Web Browsing Software
Every device with an operating system (OS) comes bundled, or pre-installed, with a browser from that OS's parent company. If you have a Windows computer, you'll get Microsoft Edge.

Apple devices like Macs, iPhones, and iPads come with Safari. Linux computers usually come pre-installed with Mozilla Firefox. But the most popular browser by far is Google Chrome. Only Android phones and tablets come with Chrome already installed. This is because Google owns Android. It's interesting that so many people go out of their way to download Chrome on other devices. It shows just how much people like it, or perhaps how much they've gotten used to it. You can have several browsers if you want. In fact, it's probably a good idea since some websites work better on different browsers.

Chrome is the most popular browser, though modern browsers generally have all the same features. Whatever browser you choose, it's almost certainly going to be the most-used piece of software on your computer. You can install any browser for free, and it will stay on your system until you decide to remove it.
Smartphone Browsers

Smartphones come with a browser too, but people don't use them as much as they do on a computer because many other apps compete for their attention. The major browsers you find on a PC, like Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, are also available for Android and iOS. Safari is the one exception, only available on Apple devices. If you sign in to an account linked to a browser, it will sync your settings and bookmarks. With a smaller screen on mobile devices, you have to scroll more to see a web page, which can be tiring. Also, the touch interface, which is the main way to interact, can be less precise, making some webpages harder to navigate.
Website Navigation

There are millions of websites, each with its own design and content. However, there are some patterns and features that are more common than not. This table will go over some navigation features on the TestOut website that are similar to many sites you'll see as you use the web.
Image 1: Website Example
Table 6: Website Navigation Features
Features/Terms Description
1. Link to Home Page Many corporate websites have their company logo near the top left of each page of their website. Generally, the logo is also a hyperlink to the website's home page.

2. Navigation Bar Most corporate websites have a group of links that take you to different pages of the website. This is usually called the navigation bar. A few options you'll commonly see in navigation bars are:

items: About: This link gives you a general overview of the company's purpose and sometimes profiles of top company leadership.
Catalog: Especially common for retail sites, this option takes you to the list of items available to purchase.
News: This link takes you to a page where you can see recent changes and other happenings at the company.
Contact: This lets you know your options for contacting the company.

blocks.text: Contact information often includes a phone number, email addresses, and physical addresses.

items: Support: Many software sites have a page dedicated to providing individualized help to customers with problems.

blocks.text: Features/Terms Description

3. Sign Up/Login The first time you use a new website, you'll often need to create an account with them to access certain features. This usually involves clicking a Sign Up button and then filling in a form with your personal information. If you already have an account, you can click Login to enter your username and password to gain access to your account.

4. Chat with a Representative Companies frequently include an option to open a chat window, where you'll be connected with a customer service representative. This is a great way to get help immediately when you need it, rather than having to wait for support to get back to you.
Personalize the Browser

Internet and website traffic may have started with small groups focused on special interests, but it's now a huge part of the world economy. Most browsers are free to use, and ensuring you enjoy using their product is how they make money from advertisements and other revenue streams.

You have a choice in which browser you use, and you can choose how to make it work best for you. Your device operating system will provide a default browser, which means it will automatically select that browser for you. For example, a Windows computer may come pre-loaded with Microsoft Edge. An Apple product will default to Safari. If you prefer something else though, you can download a different browser to your device and set that as your default, or regular browser. After that, any time you open a website link your device will open it with the browser you prefer.
Browser Profiles

Browser profiles are one way to personalize this tool. Your browser profile can store a lot of information about you, including your name, your photo, passwords to different websites, payment methods such as credit cards, and your address. Storing all these items is optional.
You don't have to save this information in your browser profile. Many people do, however, because it saves a lot of time when buying something online.

Browser profiles also save you time by keeping your preferences, or settings, the same no matter which device you use. If you have a saved profile on Firefox, for example, you can use a different computer but sign in to Firefox's browser and still see your profile information.
When you synchronize, or sync, your account, your browser will collect your browsing history, preferences, settings, and bookmarks across the many devices that you've used.

Left: Used with permission from Microsoft. Right: The software demonstrated is Chrome by Google, Inc. CompTIA does not have any affiliation with any of these companies, and the products and services advertised herein are not endorsed by any of them.

Browser bookmarks are a time-saving feature for quickly returning to favorite pages. Each browser handles bookmarks a bit differently, and the way they do it can change as the browsers update or evolve.
When switching browsers, you don't have to recreate all your bookmarks. Most popular browsers have a feature that lets you import your bookmarks at the push of a button.
Search Engines
Your browser lets you choose a default search engine in its settings. Google is by far the most commonly used, but there are many others, such as Bing, Yahoo, and DuckDuckGo.

In 2014, Yahoo paid $375 million to Firefox to be the default search engine for the browser. Why would they spend so much money for this? Because there is a lot of money to be made when you're one of the most commonly used search engines.

Google was founded by two college students, Sergey Brin and Larry Page, who were studying computer science. They wanted to make a search engine that was better than the ones available at the time. There were many search engines already in the market at that time, but they all had pretty similar functionality. What Sergey and Larry created ended up being much more effective than the others. The main idea of Google's search method is that if a lot of other websites link to a website, it means that the website is popular. Being popular means a website will show up higher in the search results that Google returns when you use it to search.
Customize the Browser Appearance
In a browser, you can change a variety of settings to make it look and feel the way you want.
Most browsers let you pick different colors, patterns, designs, and pictures to make it look the way you want. Some browsers even let you upload your own pictures to use as a background.

So for example, if you love Star Wars, you can make your browser look like it's part of the Star Wars universe with backdrops for every new tab you open. Most of these features are free, but a few might cost a little bit of money.
Accessibility Features

In Chrome, you can choose between light or dark mode. Dark mode can be easier on your eyes, especially in dim light, while light mode might make things easier to read. If you're using a laptop outside on a bright day, dark mode with light text can make the screen easier to see.

If you have trouble seeing, browsers can help you out. There's a setting called high contrast that makes text on web pages easier to see by changing the background colors. High contrast simplifies the visual elements, such as images, and focuses on text.

You can also zoom in or out on web pages. Each browser and operating system has shortcut keys available for this. Other browser settings let you change the font style, which can help some users read the text more easily.

The Chrome browser has a feature that can read web pages out loud to you. You can pick some text you want to hear or have the whole page read back to you. This is helpful for people who have a hard time seeing the words on the screen, or if you just want to listen to the information instead of reading it.

Users with low vision or visual impairments may want to use a different browser entirely. While screen readers can be helpful, including the Chrome read-aloud feature, most of them will read every single thing on the screen. A free browser called WebbIE allows low-vision users to focus on the main content of a webpage, ignoring graphics and links that could cause them frustration.
Understand Browser Add-ons

You can tailor your browser's functionality by adding extensions or add-ons. Different browsers may use different names, but the goal is the same: new features for your browser. These are often developed by third-party companies not associated with the browser.

Each browser has an extension store where you can search for any kind of extension. There are extensions that tell you the weather, help you write better, and even check prices for things you want to buy.
Pop-up Blockers
One of the most popular types of extensions is a popup blocker. These help reduce the number of ads on webpages. They also stop annoying ads and commercials on video sites like YouTube.
There are many popup blockers to choose from, and new ones come out often. Most are quick and free to download from the online store for each browser.
Extensions and Privacy

Most extensions you can get for free, and the ones that cost money usually don't cost very much. People who use the extensions can leave ratings, just as they would for other products, so you can see if the extension is worth your time and effort.

Unfortunately, hackers have found out that extensions can be an easy way to sneak into what you're doing online. When you have them turned on, or enabled, they might pop up out of nowhere and try to get you to click on a link. This could take you to a spoofed website, one that pretends to be something else, to obtain your personal information.
Removing Extensions

Extensions are easy to manage. Inside the extensions window you can enable, disable, or completely remove an extension. When removing one, you can typically provide feedback to alert the developers or the browser maker if there's a problem.
Use Browser Privacy Features

The Internet and the Web are public places, for the most part. Anyone can visit, anyone can set up a shop, and anyone with the right tools can obtain sensitive data. However, there are many ways to keep yourself safe online. To make sure you're safe while you browse the Internet, you just need to spend a little time setting up your safety nets.
Autofill

Browsers can remember your usernames, passwords, addresses, phone numbers, and even credit card details for different websites. Browsers will remember your credit card number and expiration date, but to reduce the risk of theft, they won't store the 3 or 4-digit security code on the back of your card.

It's important to understand that keeping your username and password saved is usually fine for sites like ones with tips for your favorite video games. However, for websites that have your banking information or other private data, it's better not to let the browser fill in those details automatically. Depending on what makes you feel safe, you can let the browser remember your username, but it's a good idea to type in your password yourself each time, or to use a password manager.
Incognito and Private Mode

If you don't want your browser to track your activity, you can use a special mode. In Chrome, it's called "Incognito Mode." In Safari, Firefox, and Edge, it's called "Private Mode." You can find this option in the browser's main menu. While you use it, the browser won't keep track of the sites you visit or the searches you make.
The software demonstrated is Chrome by Google, Inc. CompTIA does not have any affiliation with any of these companies, and the products and services advertised herein are not endorsed by any of them.
Another aspect of private browsing is that the browser doesn't store cookies or temporary files.

Cookies are like little notes a website leaves on your computer to remember you by. In private mode, it only allows cookies that are directly related to the website you're visiting, and it gets rid of them once you close the page. Most browsers will let you choose to block third-party cookies, which come from other sites.

Private mode doesn't hide everything. Websites can still see your IP address. For true anonymity, you need a virtual private network (VPN) or a proxy. These services route your traffic through a secure tunnel, hiding your location from the websites you visit.
Maintain the Browser

Keeping your Internet browser running smoothly is important for a fast and safe online experience. Here are some ways to maintain your browser: 1. Adjust privacy and security settings: Get to know your browser’s privacy and security settings.
Adjust them to your comfort level to protect your data and browsing habits.
2. Regularly review permissions: Check the permissions you’ve granted to websites (like location, camera, microphone) and turn off or revoke any that you don't need anymore.
3. Back up your data: Regularly back up your bookmarks and other important data in case you need to reinstall your browser or switch to a new device.
4. Update regularly: Always keep your browser updated to the latest version.
Updates often include security patches, new features, and performance improvements.
5. Clear browsing data: Periodically clear your browser's cache, cookies, and history.
This can help speed up your browser and protect your privacy.
The software demonstrated is Chrome by Google, Inc. CompTIA does not have any affiliation with any of these companies, and the products and services advertised herein are not endorsed by any of them.
Browser Cache

Whenever you go to a website, your computer needs to download all the website's assets (meaning, its text, images, code, and more) from the Internet. If your Internet is slow, this can take a bit of time. To speed things up, your browser keeps saves some of these assets, especially images, on your computer's hard drive.

This stored data is called the browser cache. Getting assets from the cache is much faster than getting them from the Internet over and over. This means websites you've visited before load more quickly. This practice of caching websites began when the Internet and webpages were new, and most people only used dial-up services. Internet speeds were much slower. If a website could be saved to load faster the next time you visit, that's a big plus for the website owner. It made browsing that particular site a lot easier.
Browser caches are really useful, but every once in a while they can cause problems. If a file in the cache gets damaged, or corrupted, it can cause some websites or apps to break down.

This happens because your computer keeps using the corrupted file from the cache instead of getting a new, working one from the Internet. That's why clearing your cache is one of the first things to do if your browser is behaving strangely.

If you use your browser to keep track of your passwords for your favorite sites, be careful when you clean out your cache. Most browsers give you the option to keep your saved passwords safe when you're clearing everything else. After you clear your cache, you might not see a big change in how fast your browser works. But you will see the most updated version of websites and some pages might load a bit quicker. Plus, you might fix some problems with websites not working right. Clearing your cache also makes things more secure, because the cache can hold onto private and personal information.
Browser Compatibility

Sometimes, websites don't load correctly. You might refresh the page a few times, but it still doesn't look right. This could be because the browser you're using isn't compatible with the website. The easiest fix is to try opening the website in a different browser. It's a good idea to have more than one browser on your computer for this reason. But why does this happen? It's because some websites were made for older browsers, not the new ones we use today.

When the World Wide Web became mainstream in the 1990s, companies of all sizes hurried to create website content. Just like today, the people who made those websites designed them to work best with the most popular browser. For a long time, the most popular browser was Microsoft's Internet Explorer.

Browsers have changed a lot over the years, and Internet Explorer isn't even supported anymore. But some companies haven't updated their websites to be compatible with modern browsers. There are many reasons for this. Maybe the website still works fine, and the company doesn't want to spend time and money to change it. It could also be that the company doesn't know how to update it. Another reason might be that very few people use the website, or they use it so rarely that it doesn't bother anyone.

This compatibility issue is why, in Windows 10, Internet Explorer is still available as an app. In Windows 11, you can switch the modern browser Edge to "IE mode," where it works like Internet Explorer used to.

items: 3.3 Explain the purpose and proper use of software.

6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.

blocks.text: Searching is perhaps the most common activity to do on the internet. Knowing how a search engine creates and presents results and practicing using advanced search tools will result in better internet searching and faster, better results.
Search Engines
Search engines are used on a daily basis to find websites, information, and local businesses.
Search results are populated based on our searches, search habits, location, and many other factors.
Using Search Engines
Features/Terms Description
1. Search Bar Users will use this textbox to enter their search requests.
2. Search By Voice Search requests can be dictated and entered into the search bar using this button.
3. Search Button Users will use this button to search when they have completed entering their search request.
4. I'm Feeling Lucky This button will take you directly to the first search result when you type in a request.
5. Search Settings The settings button can be used to alter search filters, change search settings, and view search history.
Search Terms
Term Definition Explanation
Crawling Process of using bots to scour the internet for new content and web pages.

Each search engine builds algorithms that will scour the internet for web pages. If a web page links to another web page, it will follow, or crawl, through the links until it finds the end or circles back to the main page.
Term Definition Explanation
Indexing A database of information on all websites that have been crawled by a search engine.
As search engines crawl the internet, they will create a database of each web page and save keywords from the web page that users may search for.
Ranking Ordering how relevant web pages are to a specific search.

When a user runs a search, the search engine will review all the web pages it has indexed and match their keywords to the search. It will then organize the matching webpages by those that have the most matches to the original search. These results are then served up to the user.
Different Search Engines
Below are some popular search engines.
Logo Search Engine Description
Google Chrome The most used search engine in the world. Its name is synonymous with searching the internet.
Bing Microsoft's search engine.
It focuses on giving more streamlined and accurate results for image and video searching.
Yahoo One of the original search engine competitors. It is still a powerful tool and is used greatly in overseas countries.
Logo Search Engine Description
Duck Duck Go A search engine that focuses on user privacy. Duck Duck Go does not collect or store any user personal information.
Searching Online

The World Wide Web contains billions of pages of content that have been indexed by online search engines. However, without basic skills in finding and evaluating content, you might still have a difficult time locating the information you're looking for. The table below summarizes general tips for finding and evaluating online information.
Table 7 : Online Search Tips
Tip Description
Use the Browser Address Bar In addition to entering URLs such as http://www.CompTIA.org to visit websites, it's possible to enter search terms directly into the address bar.

You can enter the URL for a preferred search engine such as google.com or bing.com, and then begin entering search terms. However, a faster method is to simply enter one or more search terms separated by spaces into the address bar and they'll be forwarded to the default search engine.

Sift Through Search Results Search engines use complex algorithms that rank websites according to their popularity, responsiveness, and overall relevance. These rankings influence which sites are displayed near the top of your search results.

Most search engines also highlight links to related content sponsored by advertisers. As you sift through search results, if you're looking for products or services related to your search terms, you might want to consider clicking on an advertised link. Otherwise you'll want to ignore them and scan the list for more reliable, objective information. It's often a good idea to click through a few pages of results, since the most relevant pages might not be at the top of the list.

Narrow Your Search At the top of the list of search results, most search engines include a few options for narrowing your search to specific result categories. For example, you can click News and see news articles related to your search terms. Or you can click Images or Videos to view media results. Another option for narrowing your search is to return to the Search box and add or clarify search terms. You can also put some or all of the terms in quotations, which tells the search engine to display results containing that exact phrase instead of results that include each of the individual words.
Tip Description

Use Advanced Search Options All of the popular search engines have some kind of advanced search option. Advanced searches provide several ways to refine and narrow your search, including fields for exact words and fields for words you do not want to be found in the returned results. You can also narrow the search by language, region, domain, and file type.

One important thing to note about advanced searches is that the search filters are cumulative. This means you can apply as many of the filters as you want and they'll all be applied at the same time. If your search ends up being too narrow, you can go back and remove some of the filters or try alternative phrases.

Verify Facts Since information on the internet is not regulated by a fact-checking body, it's important to verify claims by looking at multiple sources. Don't trust one or two sources of unverified pieces of information.
Investigate Author Biases If you have any reason to doubt the reliability of an author's claim, find out more about his or her affiliations and investigate possible biases.

What is the author's purpose? Is it simply to inform as objectively as possible, or is it to persuade you or sell you something? Does the author seem to be overly emotional or making outlandish claims?
Use Scholarly Sources for
Academic Research

If you're working on academic or professional research, limit your searching to scholarly authors who have credentials in their field. Online academic databases such as Google Scholar are configured to limit search results to scholarly sources.
Citations and References
Giving credit to the work and ideas of others is incredibly important, in both formal writing and informal settings like on social media.
Formal Citations

In formal academic writing, specific citation styles are required. Citations appear both in the text and in a compiled list known as a bibliography, reference list, or works cited list. Below are popular citation styles with examples for a book, a scholarly article from an online journal, and a news article.
Style Description and Examples

APA APA is the most popular and widely used citation style in the academic world but is not often used by students before college studies. This is because APA was developed by the American Psychological Association as a citation style for scientific publications and is used in many fields, especially in the social sciences.

Note that APA citations emphasize the year of publication in citations and de-emphasize personal details about the authors, like the first name. This reflects the need in scientific circles for current research and a focus on the content and not the individual researchers.
Style Description and Examples

MLA MLA is the most familiar citation style for teenage students, as it is used frequently in the humanities (like English literature) and is taught widely in American middle schools and high schools.

Note that MLA citations emphasize the author and de-emphasize the date by not including it in citations in the text and not including it in the works cited entry until the very end. This reflects the importance of the author or artist in creative and literary works, as well as the timeless nature of art and literature.
Style Description and Examples
Chicago notes and bibliography The Chicago style has two variants, but only the notes and bibliography version is discussed here since the other style is similar to APA.

The Chicago style uses footnote markers in the text and either a footnote at the bottom of the page or a bibliography at the end of a chapter or a paper. It is popular in historical scholarship and a few other fields. It is not as common as APA or MLA.
Note that Chicago citations are the least intrusive to the reading experience, without parenthetical citations at all.
Informal Citations

Even when not writing formal or academic papers, giving credit to original creators is still important. Never post someone else's work without naming the creator and, where possible, providing a link to their content directly.
Type Example

Good Example Note how in this post, the author included a link to the original creator's page and included information about how the image was taken. Because this particular image is in the public domain, no special permission was required.
Type Example
Bad example Note how in this post, there is no mention of who the original photographer was, and there isn't any indication that the photo was used with permission.
If this author had taken the photo, there would be no issue at all. But, in this case, the author of the post was not the photographer.
Giving someone credit is not the same as obtaining permission to post someone else's work, so always get permission from the original creator before posting or reusing someone else's work.
Special Considerations for Social Media

Many social media platforms make it easy to give original creators credit. Many platforms allow users to repost, which is automatically linked back to the original poster. Other platforms have integrated media tools, whether for music, memes, or more. Music selections will typically play with the song title and artist automatically embedded, and the app has negotiated permissions on behalf of its users. Other platforms use complex algorithms to detect music or video from other posters and send advertising revenue to the original artist automatically. Most memes are used under the fair use provisions, meaning they often don't require attribution or permission to use as long as you're not selling them. Regardless of the platform you use, you should always try to give credit when using ideas, images, music, or art from others. Plagiarism Plagiarism is the act of using someone else's content and pretending that you are the original creator.
Plagiarism has serious consequences and should always be avoided. Here are examples of different types of plagiarism:

items: Direct plagiarism - Word-for-word copying of someone else's work without using quotations or giving credit (attribution)
Self-plagiarism - A person submitting work with past work of their own mixed in
Mosaic plagiarism - When a person borrows phrases without using quotations
Accidental plagiarism - When a person forgets to cite sources, misquotes their source, or unintentionally paraphrases a source. Accidental plagiarism can be just as serious as intentional plagiarism.
