blocks.text: Social media refers to a group of apps and websites that allow users to individually share content, connect with one another, and interact with ideas and people. Social media is one of the largest uses of the internet today and is a part of modern digital life for most active internet users. But using social media responsibly doesn't always come as naturally as tapping the like button. It can take work and discipline, but being responsible leads to better communities and better experiences for you.
Social Media

Social media platforms can serve different purposes beyond general social interaction. Some are aimed at professional networking or public messaging, while others are used to reach large audiences quickly.
Bluesky

Bluesky allows users to post short messages, videos, and pictures, which can be viewed by other users. It is commonly used by celebrities, politicians, and other high-profile figures as a means of reaching out to large numbers of followers at once.
LinkedIn
LinkedIn is the world's foremost professional networking service. People create LinkedIn accounts to be connected with other professionals, which can be invaluable when looking for a job.
Risks of Social Media
Social media has some obvious benefits in terms of its ability to connect and bring people together. However, it also comes with some risks. Consider the following precautions:

items: The sense of anonymity provided by the internet can lead some people to post obnoxious or harmful comments that they would never consider making in person. Avoid being a "troll."
Because extreme and contentious opinions tend to get the most engagement, social media algorithms will promote them notwithstanding the damage they do to our society.
Be wary of strangers who might be misrepresenting themselves and their motives for the purpose of scamming or misleading other people.
Because it's extremely difficult to erase online information, be careful what you post.

blocks.text: Creating a professional online presence is particularly important when you're interviewing for a job. Hiring managers will often investigate the postings of prospective employees.
Protect and carefully monitor your digital identity, which includes your patterns of online interaction and anything you post about yourself on social media.

items: If you have children, closely monitor their social media use. Children are often more trusting of strangers and more likely to share personal information that would make them vulnerable to predators.

blocks.text: Social Networking
The world is interconnected like never before, thanks to social media. You will explore how these networks are formed.
Social Media Networks

There are many types of social media networks. Each network serves a purpose for the type of connections or media shared and distributed. Below are five common types of social media networks and their primary purposes.
Type Purpose
Social These networks' primary focus are building relationships, conversations, customer service, and social awareness. Common examples of this network type are:

items: Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn

blocks.text: Media sharing These networks are centered on sharing photos, video, live audio and video, and other media.
Common examples of this network type are:

items: YouTube
TikTok
Instagram

blocks.text: Discussion forums Community-based networks with users seeking information or discussions on a variety of topics.
Examples of this network are:

items: Reddit
Hive
Quora

blocks.text: Type Purpose

Book marking and content creation Networks used to find, collect, discuss, and share ideas, content, and media. These networks allow you to group posts to individual lists or "boards" for easy sorting. Examples include:

items: Pinterest
Imgur
Flipboard

blocks.text: Customer review Used to find, share, and critique products, businesses, and services. Reviews are created by users and used to evaluate the business. Examples include:

items: Yelp
Google Reviews
Trip Advisor

blocks.text: Content Formats
The content format of each platform will depend on the network type. Many social media networks share multiple content formats. Some of the most popular content formats include:

items: Articles
Email newsletters
Blog posts
Images
Videos
Podcasts
Infographics
Live streams

blocks.text: Social Media Platforms

A social media platform is a service or website used to publish activities, comments, photos, and other media with groups and the public. There are social media platforms for every type of media and user. Each platform utilizes its own terminology for creating and sharing media.
Below is a list of popular social media platforms and their network type.
Logo Website Network Type
Facebook Social media network. Used to find friends, build and join groups, and share ideas, images and videos.
Logo Website Network Type
YouTube Media sharing network. Used to create and share video content with the public.
LinkedIn Social media network. Used for building professional networks, verifying skills, and job searches.
Pinterest Book marking and content creation network. Marketed as a visual discovery engine. Used to find and group ideas for home, style, inspiration and more.
Yelp Customer review network. Yelp is an online directory for finding local businesses and reviewing their services.
User Reviews
The internet is a free and open environment - anyone can upload articles, images, and videos.
This can be an issue for customer reviews on social media platforms. It is important to be able to filter out bias and fake reviews.
Determining False Reviews
It is possible you will encounter fake and biased reviews when looking at reviews for local businesses and restaurants. Here are some general tips on how to avoid falling for fake reviews.

items: Look at the Dates

When looking at reviews, be sure to look at the dates of the review. If a product or business has two or three bad reviews spread across months and suddenly ten good reviews in the past week, this is a sign of trying to skew the ratings.
The opposite is true, too. If a series of bad reviews appear in a short amount of time, the competition may be trying to steal their customers.
Look at the Details
If a simple product "changed my life" or a review seems overly detailed about everything but the product or service, this is a sign of fake reviews.
Check the Reviewer
Many sites utilize other logins such as Facebook or Google. Try to verify that the person writing the review is not a relative of the owner.

Also check other reviews by the reviewer. If this person has written two hundred reviews in the last month, they may not be honest. Verify that the reviewer is reviewing products they have actually used.
Check if the Reviewer is Verified
Many websites will label reviewers as "verified purchase" or "check in" for users reviewing businesses. These reviews have verified users leaving the reviews.

blocks.text: False Review Example
Here is a simple example of what some of these false reviews could look like. Look at this image and make note of the similar dates, details, and potentially unverified reviewers.
Explore Public Platforms
The following are a few popular Customer Review platforms:
Logo Platform Details
Google Reviews Google Reviews is integrated into
Google Search and Google Maps.

It allows users to leave reviews for all types of businesses. You must have a Google account in order to leave a review, but anyone can view reviews. Google allows check-ins and pictures to be uploaded with their reviews.

Yelp Yelp is an online directory for local businesses. This includes restaurants, barbers/hairdressers, gas stations, etc. Regular reviewers can be promoted to Yelp Elite status, meaning they are verified reviews and are allowed other features. Yelp allows check- ins and pictures to be uploaded with their reviews.

Amazon Reviews Amazon offers a large variety of products. Items can be reviewed based on accurate product description, packaging, and shipping speed. Amazon allows verified purchase reviewers, pictures, and videos to be uploaded with their reviews.

Ebay User Reviews Ebay allows users to sell their own items. Users are reviewed based off their honesty, accurate product description, packaging, and shipping speed. Ebay only allows text reviews of their users.
Content Sharing
A large portion of our time is spent on social media. Most of us are consumers, but content creators work hard to update their content, build audiences, and promote their brand.
Content Ownership

Although you may not think of yourself as a content creator, if you have produced any type of content online, you are a content creator. A content creator is anyone who has participated in uploading a post, video, audio, or picture to a social media platform. As a creator, you need to understand the concept of content ownership.
Content ownership describes who is responsible and accountable for the created content.

Although they create the content that is being distributed, content creators will not always have full legal rights to their media. Content creators are responsible for the media they upload, any messages within the uploaded media, and distributing the media. However, when creators produce content for a company, they typically sign a contract that gives the company full rights to any media they create.
Content creators need to read and understand the terms of any agreement with employers or platform providers.

These creators need to read the terms of service when creating accounts on the different social media platforms. When we create online accounts and get screens for licensing and terms of service, it is tempting to select next, agree, and check any boxes without reading. As a creator, this is very important information. The terms of service will explain the social media platform's role in hosting and displaying your content. Platforms generally hold the right to remove posts, suspend accounts, and shut down the platform at will. Many reserve the right to use any content uploaded to their platform in any way the company desires.

The social media platform manages the system that will display your content. It is important to note that while creators own their content, most platforms hold the right to remove posts, suspend accounts, and shut down the platform at will. Examples of former platforms that have shut down their services include Vine and Google+.
Privacy Implications

As a content creator, you will undoubtedly spend large amounts of time online researching, creating, and editing your content. Those who make a career out of content creation must be especially careful not to divulge any personal information in their content. There have been instances where creators have been hacked, physically tracked down and harassed, and forced to deal with other problems.

Creators should avoid sharing the personal information of others as well. Privacy rights are highly protected in online environments. Always ask permission before sharing any content regarding someone else's personal information.
Content Distribution

Content distribution is how the creator's content is shared or "distributed" to their intended audiences. There are three methods of content distribution. These methods range from free to paid. Each method adds more distribution of the creator's content.
Method Description

Owned Distribution This is a hard-earned distribution. Think of it as trying to spread information by word of mouth. This type of distribution includes a creator's website, blog, and any other form of distribution that requires physical involvement from the creator.
Earned Distribution This type of distribution is when content is shared by viewers or subscribers with others. This includes reposts, reviews, mentions, and other forms of sharing or liking content.
Paid Distribution This would include paying for advertisements or featured status on social media, search engines, articles, or even paying other content creators or influencers for promotion.

Most paid distribution utilizes algorithms to help distribute content to users. When you like or share a post, the app makes note of the type of content you have shown interest in. The algorithm in the app will then search through its library of paid ads and accounts to find the paid content that fits closest to your interests.
User Communities & Forums
Forum type social media is useful in helping users ask questions, provide feedback, give advice, and to discuss all types of information.
Content

The content of forum-type social media is mostly text. Although you can add pictures, videos, and links, their main purpose is to start discussions or ask questions. Since everyone is allowed to post and comment, moderators help manage the forum and remove any rude or rule-breaking posts and comments. Moderators are often elected by the members of the forum group.
Archiving
Information in forums is usually locked or archived after a certain duration of time. Once archived, posts can be viewed but can no longer be commented on.
Platforms

There are many forum-type social media platforms. Some are general platforms where any question or discussion can be posted. Others are specialty-driven and geared toward specific issues or populations.
Logo Website Network Type
Reddit One of the largest forum websites in the world, Reddit has a community for almost everything.
If a community does not exist, you can create one. Communities are broken into groups called subreddits. Each subreddit is moderated by a select number of group members.
Quora Quora focuses on questions and answers. Where other forums are built around discussions, Quora looks to help its users find answers to their questions. All content is generated by users.
Users vote on the answers provided by the group to determine the best answer to the question.

Stack Overflow Stack Overflow is a question and answer website that focuses on programming issues. Users can pose questions to problems they encounter while developing code, learning to code, or just running everyday programs.
Logo Website Network Type

Discord Discord is a voice, video, and text chat app that's used by tens of millions of people to talk and hang out with their communities and friends. People use Discord daily to talk about many things, ranging from art projects and family trips to homework and mental health support.

Tripadvisor The Tripadvisor Forum is an aspect of the Tripadvisor website that has proven to be a valuable resource for people to gain insight into distinct aspects of travel as well as different destinations.
Online Streaming

There are two main ways to watch videos from the internet: downloading, which creates a copy of the complete video file on your local computer, and streaming, which transmits the data to your computer in a continuous flow, allowing you to watch the video as it downloads. The table below describes the most common options for viewing online videos.
Table 8: Ways to Watch Online Videos
Method Description

Downloading When you download a file, you create a copy of a file from a web or network server and save it to your local computer. After the file has been downloaded, you can open it at any time, even if you don't have a network connection. You can also make changes to the file and create additional copies. Downloading uses the TCP protocol, meaning your computer and the server communicate back and forth to make sure the download is an exact copy of the original. While this ensures the quality of the downloaded file, it makes the process much slower.

Live Stream Live streams transmit data in real time as it's created. Some examples are online video calls, traffic cams, and gaming streams. Live streams are kind of like listening to the radio. They send data directly to your device, where it's played and then immediately discarded. Live streams can't be paused or stored, and you can't go back to a previous part of the stream.

On-Demand Stream The videos in this course are an example of on-demand streaming. With on-demand streaming, you can watch a video or listen to an audio file at any time if you have an internet connection. Data is sent from a server to your device, which starts temporarily storing the data. This is called buffering. When there's enough data in the buffer, playback begins. With on-demand streaming, you can pause and skip to different parts of the file. However, the files are temporary and don't remain on your computer, so you can't modify them or make copies.

blocks.title: What you should be able to answer
items: What types of personal data do companies collect when you use the internet?
How is your personal information used by websites and online services?
What steps can you take to protect your privacy online?
Why is it important to understand data collection practices?

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 6.1 Explain fundamental security concepts and frameworks.

blocks.text: There is always a push and pull when it comes to data collection. When you use the Internet, you do the best you can to keep your information private. Companies also do the best they can to improve their bottom line. In order to better understand this relationship, you need to know how data is collected, how it's used and, most importantly, what makes up your data.
Personal Data

Technology brings many wonderful tools that enhance our lives. Our ability to store data in the cloud is one of the many features that make life convenient. Being able to share bits of our lives, thoughts, feelings, and experiences online with friends and family is another example of technology making our lives better. However, this can be risky as well. You never know how others will take what you share, and certain details about you in the wrong hands can backfire on you. Take a closer look at what matters when it comes to protecting your personal data online and the digital footprint you leave behind when using the Internet.
Digital Footprint

Everything you do online can be tracked. Even something as simple as browsing a website or using a search engine is considered data that can be collected and used. Many times, the information gathered is sold to third parties who use it for analysis, marketing, or both. But it can also be gathered and used by those with bad intentions toward you. It's always best to be careful.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, cookies are small text files that allow websites to save information about you and how you're using their platform. They do it so that the next time you visit the same website, it can automatically show you your preferences or display saved information like your username, password, or more.

At the same time, the website owners can also access this information about you and use it for other purposes like analyzing what content you spent the most time on, what new products they could develop that would interest you based on how you used their services and so on. They could also use information saved, such as your email address, to send you advertisements. On the other hand, if a hacker were to discover this kind of information about you, they could use it in numerous ways to scam you, pretend to be you, sell your information to others, and more.
Being aware of the type of digital footprint you leave behind, such as the types of websites you visit and the information you provide in what you type, watch, or click on, is important.
The Importance of Your Data

When you go into a store, the workers there don't know a lot about you. They can see your clothes or if you're with friends and make some guesses, but they can't tell what you might want to buy. Sometimes, when you're paying, the cashier might ask if you want to join their discount club. If you say no thanks, that store can't really find out any more about you.

But when you shop online or even just visit a website, you end up sharing a lot more about yourself. The websites and apps can collect data that tells them where you are, what other websites you've been to lately, what kinds of things you've bought, and even your email address. To the people who run these websites and apps, this information is incredibly important.
Image by mizinra © 123rf.com.
A Data-based Picture of You

Your personal information is special because it's unique to you. Personal information is one way to describe anything that can show who you are. Social security numbers, insurance numbers, and passport numbers are some of the most well-known examples of personally identifiable information (PII) . There's also information that might not seem important by itself, like your first name, how old you are, and the city you live in. But when you put these pieces together, people with bad intentions, or threat actors, can figure out who you are.
People have had this kind of information for a long time, even before the Internet was around.
Now, because of Internet connections and the way we use the online world, it's a lot easier for threat actors to find this information. It’s more important than ever to keep it all safe.
Safely Managing Data
This personal information can be good for businesses that want to know more about their customers. Companies can use what they learn about you to sell you things you might like.

When you agree to a company's rules (for example, when you sign up for something online), in a sense you're giving them permission to use your information, or some of your PII. But you also expect them to keep your data safe and not share it without your consent. Not every company or organization meets this expectation, unfortunately.

If someone misuses your personal data, it could cause you a lot of trouble. This is called identity fraud. It's when someone pretends to be you and might try to take your money or mess up your credit score. Your credit score is important because it helps you get things like home loans or credit cards. If your credit score goes down because someone did something they shouldn't, you could have a hard time with your financial future.
Types of Personal Data

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: Imagine living in a cabin in the woods without Internet. You could still use a computer or tablet, and you wouldn't have to worry about keeping your personal information safe. But for everyone else, there are effective ways to keep our private information safe while still staying connected.
The first step in protecting your personal information is to understand exactly what it is.
Direct PII

Personally identifiable information (PII) includes data that could reveal a person's identity. This information can be linked directly to you. It's data that you want to protect, because someone could use it to impersonate you. Some examples of direct PII include:

items: Full name (first name, middle name or names, and last name)
Home address
Phone number
Social Security or National Insurance number
Email address
Bank account number
Passport number
Driver's license number
Login credentials (a username and password combination)
Vehicle identification numbers (VINs)
Browser history
Social media posts
IP addresses

blocks.text: A lot of this information is unique to just one person. For example, your passport and driver's license are issued only to you and no one else. Other pieces of PII might not be specific to just one person, such as a home address you might share, but it's still private. For safety reasons you wouldn't want to just give that information out to anyone.
Indirect PII

Some types of personal information are tied to you in less obvious ways, but they're still important to keep private. These bits of information are more general, or indirect. Each piece could be true for lots of people, but when you combine them with more specific details, they can create a complete picture of who you are. That complete picture could lead to identity fraud. These are a few examples of indirect PII:

items: Your postal code or ZIP code
Gender
Height, weight, eye color
Race
Last name (if it's a common one where you live)
Job position and employer

blocks.text: It's important to be cautious about sharing too much of your personal information with people you don't know. This data can lead threat actors directly to you, and cause you a lot of trouble.

Some people might think they don't have much money to steal, or they're not important or famous, but that doesn't mean they're not targets for identity fraud. Everyone has direct and indirect data, and PII has become a new type of asset in the digital world.
How Companies Use Your Data

In places where businesses aim to make as much money as possible, they try to sell more things. In the digital age these companies can gather information about what you like, based on where you shop and what you buy online. They use this data to show you ads for products similar to ones you've bought before, or targeted advertising.

Businesses use targeted advertising to make your shopping experience, or even your scrolling experience all about what you like and need. They can also make their products and services better with this information. Those same companies can also turn your data into a product and sell that information to other businesses. Buying and selling data can help companies improve their bottom line. How it impacts the rest of us is up for debate.
Collecting Data

Think about the things you've bought lately. How did you first learn about them? Maybe a friend told you, or perhaps you saw an ad while scrolling through social media. The algorithms behind all the tech used today watch what is looked at online, what you click on, and what you buy.
From this, they figure out what you might like. Then, they show you new things based on that.
This is what makes online marketing so powerful. It's incredibly precise in the products and content it serves up to you, and all this makes the company more and more money.

Collecting data helps discover new ideas and opportunities never known about before. Think about music apps. They look at the songs and playlists you like and then suggest new music you might enjoy. This same idea is used for other things, like different products and services.
Data Analysis

After collecting your data, companies then take a closer look at it. They're looking for a pattern that you might fit into so they can offer you something you're likely to purchase. If your personal data, such as your location, age, and interests, line up with what they're selling, then they have succeeded. This is called data analytics.

Consider someone named Kai as an example. If Kai has been on social media talking about visiting an animal shelter and has also been shopping for dog toys recently, the company looking at this data might connect the dots. They could start showing Kai ads for dog beds or more posts about dogs on social media. If they also know where Kai lives or how old Kai is, they can get even more specific. Kai might start seeing ads for dog groomers nearby, or events held at the local dog park.
All of this happens very quickly and at a very large scale with the help of algorithms and computer processing. Human analysis isn't necessary anymore when tracking huge amounts of data.
Big Data

Big data is a term that started when computers began collecting huge amounts of data. As the amount of information kept growing, organizations found ways to analyze it to make decisions based on insights and trends. They use this information for current and future products, marketing, and pricing.
Masking Data

Even though there are laws and rules about privacy that offer some protection, not everyone likes the idea of their personal details or shopping habits being shared everywhere. There are many independent search engines whose goal is to keep your information private.
DuckDuckGo, BraveSearch, and Swisscows are just a few of these types of search engines.

They offer consumers a browsing experience that's different because it doesn't keep track of what you search for online. This means your searches stay private. Some of these organizations allow users to rank results, include child- and family-friendly default settings, and offer stronger encryption and better levels of privacy. In addition, they're very open and transparent about how they keep your information safe and make sure you know what's happening with your data.
Monetizing Data

Companies collect a lot of information all the time, and looking closely at this data can help them make more money. For instance, if you go to your favorite coffee shop every Saturday at 9:00am, and lots of other people do something similar, the shop starts to see patterns in what their customers do. They can use this information to make your shopping experience even better. One big reason they collect all this data is for targeted marketing or advertising, which means they show you ads for things they think you'll like.
Data becomes an asset for a company. They can sort through this data to create and make money from new products or services. Even though you can't touch data, it's incredibly valuable.
Data Brokers

There are businesses called data brokers whose whole job is to collect, sort, organize, and then sell a lot of information, all neatly put together for the people who buy it. Your information might be included in what they sell. When they handle personal data, they are required to follow laws and regulations about keeping information private.

When companies sell data, they often put together information from people who like similar things. Going back to Kai and their new dog. If a company knows what Kai has been searching for online and has Kai's email, they might put Kai's data together with others who like dogs. A local dog groomer would be happy to pay for this data because it could help them find new customers. This type of targeted data helps the dog groomer reach out to the right people— those who live nearby and love dogs. So, if the dog groomer sends ads to these dog lovers, they're more likely to get more business than if they just put an ad in the newspaper.

You also need to know that this data has to be legally appropriate to use, or licensed. Licensing is important because ownership, whether that's the individual or the company, depends on the rules written into a licensing agreement. This means that sometimes companies must get permission to share or use the data. You can usually find these details in the fine print of a Terms of Services agreement.
Data as Income

You can actually make money from your own data. A good way to do this is by filling out surveys, where you share your thoughts and information with companies. When you complete a lot of surveys, you get points that you can use to purchase products or services. Also, some mobile apps will give you discounts or prizes if you agree to share your fitness or health information with them.
Privacy in Social Media

Since it started in the late 1990s, social media has become a big part of everyday life for many people. Whether they're catching up with family and friends, helping out a cause they believe in, or growing their business, over 5 billion people around the world (at the time of writing) are using social media right now. That huge audience generates a huge amount of personal data.

That personal information can be useful for advertisers, who want to sell you things, and for threat actors who want to take things from you. It's important to know as much as you can about how to protect your privacy on social media platforms.
Who Owns Data on Social Media?

Understanding who owns your data isn't easy. The social media platform you're on decides the rules for how your personal data can be used. These sites let you control your privacy settings, like who can see your profile and what you post, who can tag you, and the kinds of ads you see. But it's important to know that usually, these social media sites own your data. They often have the permission to use your personal info in ways they want, which might include selling it to advertisers and other businesses. This permission is part of the agreement you make when you use their sites.

Think about the pictures, videos, and posts you share with your friends and family. Once you put them on the platform, the site owns them. By using the site, you're letting the site owners use your content to show you ads and to track your activity. These sites also keep track of simple things like where you are, when you log in, and how long you stay on. All this data belongs to the site owners.
Safely Using Social Media

Keeping your personal information secure is an important part of protecting your personal safety, professional reputation, and it can help your mental well-being as well. Here are some ways you can take control of your personal data:

items: Adjust privacy settings: Most social media platforms offer customizable privacy settings that allow you to control who can see your posts, profile information, and photos. Set your profiles to private, limit posts visibility to friends or followers you trust, and control how people can search for you.

Be mindful of what you share: Avoid sharing sensitive personal information such as your home address, phone number, date of birth, and financial details. Think twice before posting content that could be used against you or could reveal too much about your personal life.

Review and clean up your friends list: Regularly review your friends or followers list and remove people you no longer wish to share your information with. This helps make sure that only people you trust have access to your posts and personal information.

Be cautious of quizzes and games: Many social media quizzes and games require access to your profile information and can collect personal data. Be careful about participating in these activities, and always check what permissions they are asking for.

Check and understand the platform's privacy policy: Review the social media platform's privacy policy to understand how your data is collected, used, and shared. This can help you make informed decisions about what information to share and how to adjust your privacy settings.
Regularly review your activity: Many social media platforms offer tools to review your activity, such as posts you're tagged in, apps connected to your account, and login history.

blocks.text: Use these tools to monitor and manage your online presence.
By taking these steps, you can improve your privacy on social media and protect yourself from potential risks.
Privacy in Communications

The ways you communicate and share information, in both personal and business life, have expanded dramatically. Texting, messaging, emailing, and file sharing are some of the most common ways, or channels, of transmitting data. It's important to understand the different privacy expectations for these channels, so you can effectively manage and protect your personal information.
Texting (SMS) Safety

The most immediate way to get in touch with someone, aside from a phone call, is to message them. Texting uses the short message service (SMS) protocol over a cell phone network, and doesn't actually use the Internet at all. Texting is incredibly convenient, but it does not have very good security. The fact that SMS texts are sent in plain text, with no encryption, is just one reason.

Because SMS texts operate on cellular or phone connections, there is not the same level of built-in security as there is in Internet communications. Text messages aren't usually a target for hackers, but they can be viewed and saved by law enforcement. Some carriers store SMS texts for just a few days, but others store them for much longer. This long-term storage can make your private information vulnerable to court orders that release your data, or to large-scale hackers that target the phone company.
Instant Messaging Safety

Instant messaging apps communicate only over the Internet and can be installed on any device that can connect to a network. Some examples of instant messaging are Facebook Messenger, WhatsApp, Telegram, and Snapchat.

Instant messaging can be safer than SMS texting in some cases. Apps that provide end-to-end encryption are the most secure. End-to-end encryption is a method of secure communication that prevents third parties from reading your data while it's transferred from one system or device to another. WhatsApp and Signal are two examples of apps that provide this level of data safety.

Just as with any service, it's important to understand who owns your messages. Facebook and its parent company Meta have come under fire for the way it has shared or sold its users' plain- text messages to other companies. Meta has said that this is part of how they do business, while privacy advocates disagree.
Email Safety

When you send an email using popular services like Gmail or Outlook, they usually don't encrypt your email. Securing email in this way would be much too expensive for both you and for the email service. This is because email came about when the Internet was much newer, and much smaller. It really wasn't designed to be all that private.

On most email services like Gmail and Outlook, you can choose to make your emails secret by turning on a special setting called encryption. Each service has its own way of doing this, and usually, you can only do it for one email at a time. But even with this option email still has some security concerns. Emails are stored in plain text, meaning they're stored in a way that anyone can read them. This is the case in your inbox and on the email server too. Hackers, authorities, and the email service itself can read your emails if they work at it hard enough.
File Sharing Safety

A popular way to send files to a website and get files from it is using the File Transfer Protocol (FTP) . FTP has been used for a really long time, almost as long as people have been sharing files with each other over the Internet. Back when the Internet was just starting, people weren't too worried about who might be peeking at what they were sending.

FTP is easy to use, but it sends files and login information (like your username and password) in plaintext, a way that anyone could read if they tried. This means someone could easily grab your file while it's being sent. Another issue with FTP is that some networks let people in to their storage servers anonymously, without knowing who they are. This allows threat actors to read or download files without anyone knowing. FTP also doesn't automatically encrypt the files for safety. The standard now is to use secure versions of this protocol.
Safely Using Internet Communications
It's important to be careful and not trust every email you get, especially if it's from someone you don't know asking for your personal info or telling you to click on a link or download something.

Always look closely at the email address to make sure it's truly from who it says it's from. If you're not sure, it's a good idea to reach out to the company or person the email claims to be from, but use their official contact info to do so. You can also use tools that sort your emails and security programs that can spot and stop these tricky emails, known as phishing attempts, from getting to you. Protect yourself and avoid these kinds of behaviors:

items: Responding to phishing emails: Don't respond to phishing emails that appear to be from real sources (such as your bank, a government agency, or a familiar service provider) but are actually attempts by threat actors to steal your personal information. These emails often ask you to confirm personal details, click on a link, or open an attachment. Some of these emails pretend that there's some emergency, or that you owe a lot of money. Always double-check.

Answering unsolicited requests for information: Don't provide sensitive information in response to unexpected emails or messages that request personal details, account numbers, passwords, or other PII. Legitimate organizations typically do not ask for sensitive information via email.

Not verifying email sender's identity: Always verify the identity of an email sender before sharing personal or sensitive information. Cybercriminals can spoof, or copy, email addresses to make them appear as if they are coming from a trusted source.
Clicking on suspicious links or attachments: Clicking on links or downloading attachments from unknown or suspicious emails can lead to malware being installed on your device.

blocks.text: This malware can then be used to capture keystrokes, access files, and steal personal information stored on your device.
Digital Privacy
When the internet is involved, privacy is never a simple issue. The following table summarizes the privacy you can and can't expect when you use the internet.
Table 9: Privacy Expectations
Term Description

Social Media & Email Social media, email, instant messaging, and file sharing services have controls that let users decide what information is available to which people. However, any information you share will likely be made available to third parties, including advertising firms, government institutions, and others interested in analyzing big data.

Marketing Metadata By agreeing to a company's Terms of Use, you allow them to extract metadata from your activity. Metadata, or “information about information,” can include where and when you use the service, what sites you access, keywords from your posts and messages, and what device you're using.
Companies analyze this data for marketing and advertising, and can sell it to other companies.
Term Description

Secure Transactions Entering personal information or conducting financial transactions online is convenient and efficient. However, consumers need to adopt safeguards to protect themselves against identity theft and fraud.

Safeguards include sharing your mobile device only with people you trust, never using public Wi-Fi to conduct ecommerce and personal transactions, using strong account passwords, verifying that all online transactions are conducted using data encryption (HTTPS), and only conducting ecommerce transactions with businesses you trust.

Internet Usage Monitoring Most companies require employees to agree to an Acceptable Use Policy (A UP) that governs computer and internet use at work. Policies vary, but nearly all prohibit accessing adult content or engaging in illegal activities. Any communications made through a company's network, including private email, may be stored and monitored. Exercise judgment and caution when using company computers for personal use, even when allowed by the AUP.
Privacy Regulations

Data privacy rules are made to keep people's private information safe, make sure the financial system is secure, keep the Internet and online businesses reliable, and to protect national assets from cybercrime. Whether these rules apply to a company depends on what kind of business it is, what kind of information it deals with, and where it does its business.

There are 194 countries in the world and the degree of privacy laws varies significantly from one country to another. More than 65% of countries in the world have enacted legislation to help protect the privacy of their citizens. Of those who do not have laws in place, many are drafting legislation to keep track of how companies will handle data collected from their citizens.

Personal Data and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Privacy, as it relates to your personal information, means that your details should be kept safe and treated fairly. Fairness and the right to privacy, as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) describes it, means that no one can take or use European Union residents' personal data without letting the owner know clearly and getting their approval. The owner would have to give this consent freely, knowing exactly what their information will be used for, and it should be explained in easy words, not complicated legal talk. The GDPR also lets the people it governs change their mind anytime, check what personal information companies have, fix it if it's wrong, or even ask them to delete it. Failure to comply with GDPR rules can result in incredibly large fines.
Personal Data in the United States

The United States doesn't have as extensive or as strict a set of laws as the European Union does. Unfortunately, because of the lack of blanket regulations in the United States, companies in many states can collect and sell personal data as they see fit, without your knowledge.

California has the CCPA (Calif or nia Consumer Privacy Act), which is designed to provide the individual with more control and security over personal information. The CCPA is a law that helps people living in California know what personal information companies collect about them, why they collect it, and who they share it with. It lets people in California see their personal information, ask for it to be deleted, or say no to having it sold. This law affects any company, no matter where it's located, if it sells things or services to people in California, makes more than $25 million a year, deals with the personal information of 50,000 or more people, households, or devices, or gets half or more of its money from selling personal information.

The United States also has the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIP A A) . This law focuses on the health insurance industry and was enacted in 1996, around the time the Internet was becoming mainstream. HIPAA was designed to make sure that doctors and health insurance companies keep your medical records safe and private. HIPAA says these groups must protect your information and can't share it with anyone without your consent.

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 6.3 Explain password best practices.
6.4 Identify common use cases for encryption.

blocks.text: Locks protect physical assets like a car or a home. To protect digital assets such as bank accounts and insurance numbers, you rely on password protection. In this lesson you will understand the importance of both passwords and encryption. These two concepts work together to form the foundation of cybersecurity.
Computers, phones, websites, apps, network devices all have login credentials. These credentials are a unique combination of a username (or possibly an email address) and a password.
A good password is one which you’ve made it difficult for hackers to crack. Strong passwords include all the following elements:

items: Uppercase letters, or capital letters.
Lowercase letters, or small letters.
Numbers.
Symbols, such as #@+_$%^ .
Length.

blocks.text: Changing Passwords

When you first set up some computer equipment, you will typically find a default username and password already in the system. Routers, modems, IoT devices and more all have default usernames and passwords. More often than not, the default is "admin" and "password," and that's the same for every single model of that device. It's good security practice when setting up the device to change these credentials. If it's the default, anyone can easily discover what they are with a quick Internet search.

There are a few devices that come out of the box with no password at all. Manufacturers let the user decide if they think a password is needed. As a general rule, if a device connects to a network or if it handles sensitive information, you need to turn on the password feature.
Beyond Passwords

Many accounts offer another layer of protection with the addition of two-factor authentication (2F A) . In addition to the credentials, you will use your smartphone as the second part to the login process, with either a specific app on the phone or a text message sent to the phone number on file. The app will ask to confirm that you are logging into a website or account. There is typically a time limit for you to provide this confirmation, which might mean that you'll have to make a second or third attempt to confirm your status. These steps make hacking into accounts significantly more difficult.
Password Best Practices
Industry best practices and guidelines for password security include these things to avoid:

items: Avoid sharing passwords: Don't give your password out to anyone for any reason.
Avoid reusing passwords: If you use the same password in more than one place, such as for both your bank app and your streaming service account, your password is more vulnerable to attack.
Avoid incrementing passwords: This practice uses a base password and adds a number every time you need to change your password. For example, “password1” followed by

blocks.text: “password2.”

items: Avoid using birthdates, pets' names, and other easily guessed details: Especially if you share this type of information on social media, you should stay away from using it as part of your password.
Avoid using only dictionary words: If your password has a regular or common sequence of only letters, like "balloon" or "marigold" or "photograph" then they are much easier to break.
Avoid using common patterns and sequences: Don't use repetitive strings, such as “1234” or

blocks.text: “xoxo” or "abc123.” Ultimately, the best and most secure password is long, uses several types of characters, and (most importantly!) is one you can memorize.
Password Management

Think of all the websites you visit that require you to create an account with a password to access them. Now, think of all the apps you use for school, work and daily life. How many of those also need you to create an account with a username and password? Most people have dozens, maybe hundreds, of accounts online. If you're following good security practices and using different credentials for every single one, you will likely need a system to manage all your passwords.
Some of the most common ways to manage multiple passwords and usernames include:

items: Password managers
Physical documentation
Digital records

blocks.text: Password Managers

A password manager is a digital organizer for multiple passwords. They can be free, such as Google Chrome's Password Manager, or they can be paid services such as Keeper and Dashlane. You can install these organizers as a browser extension or as an app. Every time you log into one of your accounts the service will record your username and password combination.
The password manager encrypts the password for that site, or generates one that's complex.

These generated passwords might be readable, meaning you can recognize each character, but they won't be a words or phrases you recognize. This makes it harder to crack. One example is: X%3a*!4q_e23#Fl4t9 After that you will only need to remember the master password associated with the password manager service. Also, If you are using a password manager, best practices would be to change your personal passwords to one randomly generated by the manager, to increase the security for your accounts.

Password managers can be safer and more secure than trying to keep track of passwords on your own. For example, most people are in the habit of using the same password for multiple accounts. If threat actors uncover that password on one website, all the other accounts are at risk too. By securing all passwords under one password manager you can increase your digital privacy. Of course, if these password manager services get hacked, your accounts could be exposed too.
Physical Documentation

Another choice is to write down passwords in a physical notebook and keep them in a safe place, such as a locked cabinet or a home safe. This extra layer of security can prevent losing your password collection to a home robbery. Overall, though, this physical type of password manager can provide peace of mind for those who are not comfortable leaving their passwords on the Internet.
Digital Records
Keeping track of passwords in a document on your phone or computer is another option. It's convenient, but not always the most secure. If you do choose this method it's important to take precautions.
In the movies a hacker might type away at a computer, trying to guess passwords and gain access to systems and files. In real life, actual hackers write scripts that automate the process.
These scripts look for keywords, including the word ‘password.’ Don't name your file "My Passwords," and be sure to set some kind of password control settings on the document itself.
Should I Change My Password?
Is it time to change your password? This depends on several factors:

items: Is your password very short?
Does your password include only letters, and doesn't include any numbers or symbols?
How much of your sensitive information does the website or app have?
Are you using the same password on more than one site or app?
Have you heard about any data breaches at the organizations for which you have a password?

blocks.text: If you've read through this lesson and have a feeling that you might not have the best passwords, take a few minutes now to change them.
Account Types

Think about what your password is guarding. For example, if your questionable password is protecting your favorite files on a 3D printing website, you may not need to change your password. The saved files, while important to you, are not sensitive information. That company might sell your email address and make money from that, but in this example you have not given them any financial details. However, if you did use this same questionable password on other sites, ones where you do share sensitive data, you should update your passwords.
Data Breaches
Did a website where you have an account get hacked? How can you find out if this happened?

You might hear about it on TV or online, or the company itself might tell you. But there are times when people don't find out until months later. If you hear about a hack it's important to change your password right away. Also, check if you used the same password on other websites or apps. Sometimes, a company will make everyone with an account change their password. If you notice anything suspicious happening with your account, such as messages you didn't send, that's another sign you should change your password.

It's very common to hear about a large company getting hacked and a lot of private information getting stolen. One of the first big breaches happened at Target Stores in 2013, when hackers took over 40 million credit and debit card numbers. Since then, there have been thousands more data breaches, and it's likely there will be even more in the future.

Will your personal info get stolen? We hope not, but it's hard to say for sure where hackers will strike next. The best thing you can do is keep an eye on your credit score and stay updated with the news. Often, if a company's data gets breached, they'll offer a free year of credit monitoring to help those affected.
Encryption Basics
Encryption transforms clearly understood writing into ciphertext, which is unreadable.

Encryption protects the data and only lets authorized people, people with the key, to read the message. The key to decoding the material is an encryption algorithm, or the specific steps to uncover the hidden meaning.
The Caesar cipher is one of the best known early uses of encryption. The Roman emperor Julius Caesar scrambled written messages to prevent enemies from learning his military plans.
It was a simple system in which letters were transposed to make a message look like nonsense.

Caesar's generals, the people who were intended to get the message, had the key and could accurately rearrange the letters. If the message was intercepted, though, enemies would not be able to figure out his plans.

This encryption method works by shifting each letter in the alphabet a certain number of spaces to the right or left. In the example below, the cipher is shifting to the right by three letters. A becomes D, B becomes E, C becomes F, and so forth. To decrypt the message, the reader must know how many spaces to shift the letters.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, to encrypt the plaintext word COMPTIA using the Caesar cipher with a shift of 3 letters to the right, COMPTIA would become FRPSWLD.
Try making your own Caesar cipher.
Modern Encryption

Today's encryption is so complex that not even the biggest and fastest supercomputers can figure them out. Ironically, computers are the ones that make these unbreakable codes. Without them, it would take people days just to make one secret message.
The modern process of encrypting data involves taking the raw data, in an easily readable form, and changing it into a form that prevents unauthorized people from reading or using it.

Computers use complex mathematical algorithms to create the encryption keys. Encryption keys are commonly 128 bits, or characters long. This is another way of saying 128-bit encryption, the most common type of encryption today. It is 2 to the 128th power, written as 2128. If you were to write out a string of 128 characters, it would look like this: 1100101010011100101001010110010101011001010101100101010110010101011001010110010101 1001 0101011001010101100101010110010101011001010101100101011001010110010101011001010101 1001 How much time do you think it would take to crack encryption this long?
Encrypting Data

Any information could be encrypted, but not all information needs to be encrypted. Government and industry rules can mean that bank account information is protected, but the business address is not. Grandma’s secret recipes probably don’t need to be in cipher, but the top secret recipe for Coca-Cola will be.

Sometimes a group or company will play it safe and encrypt any information that comes to their computers. Because information can travel quickly from one place in the world to another with just a few clicks, it is important to keep sensitive data hidden from hackers and other online attacks. However, the cost of encrypting every single piece of data all the time can be very high. Knowing when to encrypt information can save a company lots of money.

By understanding what state their data is in, if data is at rest or in transit, organizations can figure out the best ways to keep it safe. They can decide what kind of protection each type of data needs, find any weak spots, and decide where to spend money to keep data secure. This way of looking at data also helps make sure that organizations follow rules and best practices for keeping data safe.
Encrypting Data at Rest
Data at rest is when data is sitting still, saved somewhere such as on a computer or in the cloud.
In this state, data is held in some form of persistent storage.

Think of it as information that's not going anywhere, like last year's taxes stored in a database, archived pictures, or committee meeting notes from 5 years ago. When data is just sitting there, it is possible to encrypt it. You can do this for the whole device, just the databases, or even just certain files or folders. You can also set up special permissions, such as a list of who's allowed to look at or change the data. Another method of encrypting data at rest is the lock screen of your mobile device.

When you encrypt data at rest, you offer another layer of protection beyond the internal systems in place. However, encrypting data at rest can be more complicated than with data in transit, because the encryption keys must be kept secure for a longer period of time.

Another part of storing data is keeping encrypted information for only a short time. When you log into a website, it will keep a session token or session ID. This special code shows who you are while you're logged in. But when you log out, the token disappears. The next time you visit the site, a new token is generated and held in this non-persistent storage.
Encrypting Data in Transit

Data in transit, or data in motion, is when data is moving from one place to another over the Internet or a network. This can happen when you're sending an email, visiting websites, logging into your computer remotely, or when files are being moved between online storage spaces.
To keep this data safe while it's moving, there are special security protocols that protect that traveling data.
One type of protocol is the HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) . This is a very common way to encrypt information transferred over the Internet, from a browser to a website.
Many online shopping sites and mobile apps use HTTPS, making your credit card information unreadable when you make a purchase.

A virtual private network (VPN) is another way of encrypting information as it flows from point to point across networks. Using a VPN prevents threat actors from reading your data. The VPN protocol creates a safe tunnel, kind of like a secret passage, to keep everything you do online private. This means that even when your Internet activity goes through equipment belonging to Internet service providers, nobody can peek at what you're doing.
