What scam tactics do attackers use to trick people online?
Why are you a target for cyberattacks, even if you think you have nothing worth stealing?
How can misinformation and fake news be a security risk?

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.

blocks.text: There's nothing to be gained and much to be lost by not securing your data. No matter if you're using cloud storage to save your school work, or if you're working in an office at a workstation, you need to be aware of possible threats. You might be confident in your tech skills, but there are lots of threats to look out for, with new ones popping up every day. This lesson will discuss more about these threats and some of the most common variations to watch for.
You are the Target
You might think that hackers and cybercriminals only go after big companies or wealthy people.
But the truth is, everyday people are the most common targets. If you have an email address, a social media account, or a phone number, someone out there would love to take advantage of you.

Why? Because regular people are often easier targets than large organizations. Big companies spend millions of dollars on cybersecurity teams and software. Most individuals don't have those kinds of defenses. Cybercriminals know this, and they count on it.
What Are They After?
Attackers want different things depending on the situation, but some of the most common goals include:

items: Money: They may try to steal your credit card numbers, bank login credentials, or trick you into sending them money directly.
Personal information: Details like your full name, address, date of birth, and Social Security number can be used to commit identity fraud.
Access to your accounts: Once someone has your login credentials, they can lock you out of your own accounts, send messages as you, or use your accounts to attack other people.
Access to other people: If an attacker gets into your email or social media, they can use your identity to trick your friends, family, and coworkers.

blocks.text: Why You Specifically?

It's not always personal. Many attacks are sent out to thousands or even millions of people at the same time. The attacker doesn't know you or care about you specifically. They just need a small number of people to fall for the trick, and the attack pays off.
Think of it like a fisherman casting a wide net. The fisherman doesn't pick which fish to catch.
They throw the net and see what they get. In the same way, attackers cast a wide net of fake emails, text messages, and websites, hoping that some people will take the bait.

Other times, attacks are more targeted. An attacker might look through someone's social media profiles to learn details about their life. They can use that information to craft a more convincing message. The more information that's publicly available about you, the easier it is for someone to build a believable story to trick you.
The Good News

You don't need to be a tech expert to stay safe. Most attacks rely on tricking people, not on breaking through complex security systems. That means the biggest thing you can do to protect yourself is simply to know what to look for.
Common Scam Tactics

Before diving into specific types of attacks, it helps to understand the playbook that scammers use. Even though scams can look very different on the surface, most of them rely on the same basic tricks to get people to act without thinking.
Creating Urgency

One of the most common tactics is making you feel like you need to act right now. You might see a message that says your account will be locked, your package can't be delivered, or you owe money that's overdue. The goal is to make you panic and react before you have a chance to stop and think about whether the message is real.
Legitimate companies rarely demand that you take immediate action through a text or email.

If you do receive an urgent-sounding message, take a moment to slow down. Go directly to the company's website by typing the address into your browser, or call their official customer service number. Don't click the link in the message.
Pretending to Be Someone You Trust

Scammers often pretend to be from a company, organization, or person you already know. They might pose as your bank, a delivery service, a government agency, or even a coworker. The message might include official-looking logos, colors, and language to make it seem real.

This is called spoofing, and it works because we naturally trust familiar names and brands. The best defense is to never assume that a message is real just because it looks official. Always verify through a separate channel before sharing any information.
Offering Something Too Good to Be True

Free gift cards, surprise prizes, job offers with huge salaries, and investment opportunities that guarantee big returns are all common bait. If something sounds too good to be true, it almost certainly is. Scammers use these offers to get you excited enough to share personal information or click a dangerous link.
Using Fear and Threats

On the other end of the emotional spectrum, some scams try to scare you. A message might threaten legal action, claim you've been caught doing something wrong, or warn that your computer has been infected with a virus. The goal is to make you anxious enough to follow the attacker's instructions.

Remember that real law enforcement, banks, and government agencies will not contact you through a random text or email demanding money or personal details. If you're unsure, reach out to the organization directly using contact information you find on your own, not from the suspicious message.
Protecting Yourself
Knowing these tactics is your strongest defense. Here are a few habits that can help keep you safe:

items: Slow down: Don't let urgency push you into a quick decision.
Verify independently: Contact the company or person through their official website or phone number, not through a link in the message.
Be skeptical of unexpected messages: If you weren't expecting a message about a prize, a problem, or a payment, treat it with caution.
Talk to someone: If you're unsure about a message, ask a friend, family member, or coworker for a second opinion before you respond.

blocks.text: Phishing and Smishing

Phishing and smishing attacks happen when someone tries to trick users into giving away their private information through a communication that looks like it's from a real place, like a bank or an online store. The message usually contains a link to a counterfeit site or to a valid site that the attacker has been able to compromise. The goal is to prompt the user to input confidential data, such as online bank account numbers and passwords, which the threat actor then steals.
Phishing Attacks

Hackers don’t always know if the victim has a particular account. So they send an email blast to tens of thousands of users, with the hope that if they pick a large business with more customers, then they'll be more successful. With this phishing method, they have a better chance of connecting with a user who does have an account with that business, and who will fall for this attack.

Be careful about your state of mind when you read emails. If someone tries to trick you with an email when you're not paying much attention or feeling tired, you might not notice that it's a fake. Remember one of the golden rules of email: no matter how legitimate it appears, always open your browser and go directly to the website yourself to log in. If your user ID or name field is set to auto complete, make sure it does actually auto complete. If it does not, this is another hint of a potentially counterfeit site.
Always think before you respond to requests like this and consider the possibilities. Do you even have an account with the company that is allegedly reaching out to you?
Spear Phishing Variation

Spear phishing, another technique thieves use is to send emails directed at their target rather than an email blast. The goal is still the same: get users to take action that leads to compromises. The difference is the ability to target the individual with details unique to them, in theory convincing enough to leave no doubt the email must be legitimate.
Another angle on email scams is making them appear to have come from a friend or coworker.

Hackers can forge email headers to make it seem like the email came from someone you know, when that might not be the case. The best way to know for sure is to reply to the email, asking if they actually did intend to send it to you. Often, the address is not correct, and the email will not make it to the recipient. Also, be aware that viewing an email can’t give you a virus, but opening up attachments and clicking on links can infect your system. Overall, have a bit of healthy skepticism when an email lands in your inbox and trust your instincts.

One of the worst things that could happen is someone getting into your main, or primary, email account. This is because many people use one main email account to reset passwords for other things. So if someone tricks you into sharing your email password, that's not the only thing that's in danger. Once they have control of that, they can use it to get into your other accounts by changing the passwords.
These attacks are more difficult now, though still not impossible, thanks to the advent of 2-factor authentication.
Smishing Attacks
You have probably seen or heard about victims of smishing. With this type of attack, the victim receives a text, or SMS, message claiming to be from a reputable company or service provider.

The message typically warns users about unauthorized activity. Because many companies legitimately use text messages as personalized alerts, these attacks are very effective. Like the ever-increasing sophistication of phishing attacks, smishing schemes come in many elaborate forms. Some common types of smishing attacks include:

items: Account Verification Scams: The victim receives an email or text message claiming to be from a reputable company, like a financial institution or shipping carrier. The message typically warns users about unauthorized activity or asks them to verify account details, and to do so immediately. When users click on the provided link, though, they’re directed to a fake login page where threat actors can steal their credentials.
Prize or Lottery Scams: An attacker tells victims they’ve won a prize, lottery, or sweepstakes.

blocks.text: But to claim their prize, they have to provide personal details, pay a small fee, or click on a link. The goal is to steal either sensitive information or money.

items: Tech Support Scams: Users receive a message warning them about a problem with their device or account with instructions to contact a tech support number. Calling this number can lead to charges, or the “technician” may request remote access to the device, potentially leading to data theft. A very common touch in this scam is to show the user incidental

blocks.text: Windows logs that list errors. These logs and errors are legitimate, common, and not a threat to the user's system, but they can scare the user into giving the thief hundreds of dollars to "fix" the problem.

items: Bank Fraud Alerts: Messages appear to come from the victim’s bank, warning about unauthorized transactions or suspicious activities. The user is prompted to click on a link to verify their transactions or call a number, which are both controlled by the attacker.

Tax Scams: Around tax season, many people receive messages claiming to be from tax agencies. These messages often promise tax refunds or threaten penalties for supposedly unpaid taxes. If someone is overly eager about a refund or intimidated by the penalties, they may hand over their personal or financial details.
Service Cancellation: The attacker tells the victim that a subscription or service they have

blocks.text: (like a utility or software subscription) is about to be canceled due to a payment issue.
They’re urged to click on a link to “resolve” things, which leads them to a phishing page.
Social Engineering Overview
These stories are all examples of threat actors using social engineering, rather than complex cyberattacks, to take advantage of people.

In 2020, scammers created a Google Drive document containing links to a phishing site. Then they tagged people in a comment, saying they wanted to work together on a project. The targets received a legitimate Google notification about the comment, which included the harmful link. Feeling flattered at being asked to collaborate, the victims clicked the link, visited the phishing site, and inadvertently provided their login credentials and other sensitive information. This simple trick took advantage of Google's notification system to get people to share important and private data.

When the internet was taking off, tech companies lagged behind in keeping their customers safe. When Sarah Palin was announced as the United States vice presidential candidate in 2008, she went from being an unknown to the center of attention. After all the news coverage on her life story, her email account was hacked by a college student. The hacker discovered answers to common security questions simply by reading those detailed stories.

Scammers created fake social media accounts impersonating celebrities, using them to promote fake cryptocurrency giveaways or investment opportunities. These counterfeit profiles can look legitimate and use persuasive language to make it all seem believable. In 2021, these fake celebrity account scams resulted in over $2 million in cryptocurrency losses for unsuspecting users. Scammers rely on the fact that people trust well-known public figures.

Social engineering takes many forms, but always with the same goal: to get you to reveal personal or sensitive information about yourself or your organization. Think of it like someone trying to get you to tell them a secret about someone else that you promised you wouldn't tell.

It's "social" because this kind of security threat happens between people, and relies on the ways we expect people to behave in social interactions. It's "engineering" because the threat actors manipulate those social interactions to get what they want.
Types of Social Engineering
There are many ways threat actors can use social engineering to accomplish their goals. New ways evolve all the time, and it's outside the scope of this course to cover every one of them.
The best way to deal with social engineering is to recognize potential threats and respond well in these situations. Some of the more common ones are listed here.

"My biggest social engineering observation from the real world is that "standard" or front-line employees don't think they are important enough to be targeted. I saw this when I was a network administrator for a national sports organization. The receptionist there did not filter guests at all! She just sent them wandering through the building looking for the person they were to meet. When the IT Department tried to enforce a rule about guests signing in and their host being called to escort them, she resisted. We discussed how she could be socially engineered by someone wearing a furnace repair company shirt. She blew the whole thing off that no one would ever do that. But in reality, that is how that kind of attack happens all the time." -- Damon G, network administrator Using Social Media You probably share stories, photos, and thoughts on social media to connect with friends and family. Someone can learn a lot just by looking over those posts, even ones you didn't necessarily upload yourself. Your social media presence may have some personal details, but not all the ones someone needs to answer common security questions. To complete the puzzle, a hacker might come up with new ways to get the missing pieces of information.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, be careful when you get friend requests from people you don’t know. A hacker could build a social media profile from scratch, just to make it seem like they're someone you'd want to be friends with. If you do fall for their story, they could end up learning enough to take over your accounts and pretend to be you, maybe writing or buying things you never wanted.

You should know what kind of information is private and when, if ever, it's okay to share it with others. One example is your mother's maiden name—an innocent fact, but not something to share with anyone but your close friends. Details like your mother's maiden name, the street you grew up on, and the name of your childhood pets are examples of indirect personally identifiable information (PII) .
Lunchtime Attacks

Always remember to lock your computer and phone when you're not using them. This helps prevent lunchtime attacks, where an attacker gets access to an account through an open desktop. This could allow someone pretend to be you by sending emails in your name, or compromising other accounts you happen to be logged into.

You can set your computer's display properties to use a password-protected screen saver to lock the desktop after a certain amount of downtime. In this case, shorter is better. The minimum amount of time is one minute. But sometimes a minute is all the time a threat actor needs.

Walking away from a PC for lunch or a break leaves plenty of time for threat actors to sit in front of your workstation and explore your files. In Windows, a quick tap on the Windows logo and ‘L’ key at the same time will lock the system and display the login screen, requiring anyone to enter the password before they can use it. You can also do this with the mouse by selecting the option from the start menu.
Shoulder Surfing

Shoulder surfing is when someone tries to sneak a peek at your passwords or PINs by looking over your shoulder while you're typing them on a computer. This usually happens in public places. Be extra cautious when entering a password or PIN while someone else is around. To help reduce this risk, there are privacy screens which you can drape over the top of a monitor or laptop screen to prevent people from seeing it, unless they're directly in front of the display.
This helps prevent what's called shoulder surfing.
Tailgating

Tailgating happens when criminals gain entry into a building or area by following others who have the authority to get in. You may walk into public buildings and not think twice about being courteous to strangers and holding the door open. One way to stop this is with a vestibule, which is a set of two doors that only allows one person in at a time. One of the doors requires proper credentials. With one door open, the other can’t be opened. The credentials could be an ID card, biometrics, or typing in a PIN.
Fake News and Evaluating Misinformation

The phrase "see it to believe it" once meant that in order to believe something, you had to see it with your own eyes. But with advancements in video production and photo editing, it has become hard to identify something as real or fake. And with the internet being a repository for anyone to publish whatever they want, regardless of whether it's true or false, you must learn how to check the credibility of what you see or read on the internet.
Identify the Source: Knowing who publishes information, news, or images can help us determine whether it is legitimate. Here are some tips for finding the source:

items: Look for the name of the organization publishing the information on the webpage to see if it's familiar.
Double-check the URL in the address bar to see if it looks authentic.

If a website looks poorly designed and amateurish, this information may also be written by someone who is not experienced. But also be aware that very slick, well-designed webpages can also contain bad information.
Check for previous work from the author.
Check the website's links. Reputable websites will link to each other. If you click on a link and it doesn't work, this could be a red flag.

Blog and social media posts are not reliable sources of information. Always use good judgment and be wary of content published by strangers that you can't verify. Local exceptions to this rule are common, directly from an institution or about local happenings.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, your local power company may post that there is an outage in your area, or someone in your neighborhood may post a photo of a stray dog looking for the owner.
Check for Trustworthiness: Not all sources are created equal. Here are some tips to determine whether a source is trustworthy:

items: Is the information on a website associated with a trusted institution that has been around for many years, with a proven track record of reliable information? Look for established institutions. Sites run by government agencies, nonprofit organizations, foundations, colleges, and universities are generally more trustworthy than information from anonymous individuals.
Don't confuse reliability with page rank. Don't think that because it is at the top of the search results, the information can be trusted.
Check the date of a website; you should always be looking for the most up-to-date information possible. Look for the "last updated" date on the page.
Search the name of the website or author to check their credentials.
Is the information on a site supported by evidence? Has the information been reviewed? Is there another source that can verify the information? Is the information free of emotion?
Are there spelling and grammar errors?

blocks.text: Identify Possible Bias: Even trustworthy sources can publish factual content that is only one side of a story or issue. Here are some tips to identify bias and evaluate how that might affect how the news was presented:

items: Ask yourself, does the information sound like opinion, hearsay, or even propaganda?
Does the author's point of view appear objective and impartial?
Be wary of content promoted by companies or businesses. They are often trying to sell something, and sponsored opinions will lean in their favor.
Ask if there are political, cultural, or other personal biases in the tone, conclusions being drawn, or the details included.

blocks.text: Being aware of bias can help you think critically about the information you encounter, even if you share some of the same viewpoints as the authors. If a bias is identified, asking how the information reinforces that bias can help you better evaluate the completeness, fairness, and overall quality of the information.

items: 6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.

blocks.text: Every time you open a web browser, you are stepping into an environment full of both useful resources and potential risks. Websites track your activity, online stores ask for payment details, and pop-ups try to grab your attention. Knowing how to manage your browser settings and recognize safe practices can make a big difference in protecting your personal information.
In this lesson, you will learn how browser cache, history, and cookies work, how to shop online safely, and what security settings help keep your browsing experience private and secure.
Safe Internet Browsing
When you use a computer and web browser to access pages and other resources over the Internet, you must be aware of the ways you can keep any information you transmit secure.

By securing your information, you can also prevent any malicious software (malware) from infecting your computer. Safe web browsing practices are essential for protecting your personal information and ensuring the security of your online activities.
Certificates

When you go to a website, there's a lot happening that you don't see. Your browser and the website's server are like two people meeting and shaking hands. This "digital handshake" checks that both sides are who they say they are. This is where a security certificate comes into play. Security certificates are digital documents that verify the identity of a website and allow an encrypted connection. It's like an ID card for websites, showing that they're legitimate.

Most websites have these certificates. They purchase a certificate from a trusted company called a Certificate Authority (C A) . These authorities investigate the website to make sure the website is who it really says it is, and then issues the site a certificate. When your browser sees this certificate, it checks a few things:

items: Is it from a trusted CA? In fact, a certificate that has been self-signed by a website owner is not very safe, because they have not been verified by a third-party CA.

Is it still valid and not expired? If the certificate has expired, that means it's been some time since the CA verified the website. Any changes to the website after the expiration date may threaten your safety.

blocks.text: This all helps keep your information safe when you're online.
You can view a website's certificate by clicking on the lock icon in the address bar. Check the issuer, the date it was issued and the date it expires, and that it's issued to the correct website.
Make sure it's not a different version or a misspelled version of the website's name.
The software demonstrated is Chrome by Google, Inc. CompTIA does not have any affiliation with any of these companies, and the products and services advertised herein are not endorsed by any of them.
HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS)

Shopping online is one of the most popular activities on the web. A big reason why it's grown so much is because technology has made it safer to pay for things online. When you're ready to buy and need to put in your payment details, the website makes sure there's a secure link between your browser and the store's website. This keeps your personal and payment details safe.

The protocol, or set of rules, that does this is called HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) . It's like the regular HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP) used for website communication, but made secure with additional protocols. Even if a hacker tries to peek at the data being sent, the secure connection scrambles your payment data. This way, threat actors can't intercept your details while they're being sent over the Internet.

Today, it's not just shopping websites that keep your information safe. Almost every legitimate website uses this protocol to make sure they are who they say they are and to encrypt the data you send them. What you see on your end is a little padlock to the left of the website's address at the top of your browser. This padlock means your connection is secure. The Chrome browser holds more information, so there's more than just a padlock to look for. Click on two horizontal lines to the left of the web address to see more about the site's security.
Browser Cache and History

Every time you visit a website, your browser quietly saves information about that visit. Two of the most important things it stores are your browsing history and your browser cache. These features make your browsing experience faster and more convenient, but they also come with privacy and security considerations.
Browsing History

Your browsing history is a list of every website you've visited. Browsers keep this list so you can easily go back to a page you've been to before. If you remember visiting a website last week but can't recall the exact address, your history can help you find it again.

However, browsing history also means that anyone who uses your device could see what websites you've visited. On a shared or public computer, this could expose personal information. For this reason, it's a good habit to clear your browsing history when you're done using a computer that other people also use.
Browser Cache

The browser cache is a storage area on your device where the browser saves pieces of websites you've visited, such as images, logos, and layout files. When you return to a website, the browser loads these saved pieces from your device instead of downloading them from the Internet all over again. This makes pages load much faster the second time around.

Over time, the cache can grow large or the files stored in it can become outdated. When that happens, you might notice that a website doesn't look right or doesn't work the way it should. Clearing the cache forces the browser to download fresh copies of everything, which often fixes these kinds of problems. Clearing the cache is one of the first things to try when troubleshooting browser issues.
Private Browsing

If you don't want your browser to save your history or cache at all, you can use private browsing mode. Different browsers call this feature by different names. Chrome calls it Incognito, Firefox calls it Private Window, and Edge calls it InPrivate. No matter what it's called, the idea is the same: once you close the private window, the browser deletes the history, cookies, and cached files from that session.
Private browsing is useful when you're on a public or shared computer, when you're shopping for a surprise gift, or anytime you want your browsing session to leave no trace on the device.

Keep in mind, though, that private browsing does not make you invisible on the Internet. Your Internet service provider, your school or employer, and the websites you visit can still see your activity.
Clearing Your Browsing Data
Most browsers let you clear your browsing data from the settings or history menu. You can usually choose what to delete, including:

items: Browsing history: The list of websites you've visited.
Cached images and files: The saved pieces of websites stored on your device.
Cookies: Small files websites use to remember your preferences and track your activity.

blocks.text: You can also choose a time range, such as the last hour, the last 24 hours, or all time. If you're troubleshooting a problem or cleaning up for privacy, selecting "All time" is usually the safest choice.
Cookies

When you go online, most websites put something called cookies on your device. Cookies are small text files, stored on your device, that allow websites to track what you do online. Cookies allow the website to remember what pages you visited, what you searched for, or hold on to the items you put in your shopping cart but didn't buy. They can also make websites work better.
The primary reason website owners do this is to show you more ads and learn more about what people like you are interested in.
One Browser Only

It’s important to understand that cookies are specific to each browser. Imagine you're using Chrome to shop online and you put some items in your shopping cart. If later you switch to using Safari and notice your shopping cart for that site is empty, it's because Chrome and Safari don't share cookies. They each remember things separately. Also, cookies can keep an eye on what you do on different websites. This helps companies show you ads that are more about what you like.

Here is an example of one company's cookie policy: This website uses cookies and other tracking technologies to enhance user experience, display targeted ads, and to analyze performance, user activity, and traffic on our website. We also may share personal information about your activity on our website with our advertising, analytics, and business partners.

This policy says a lot in just two sentences. It describes how cookies support the website, and it tells you how the website owner will use your personal information. If you agree to the policy, your choices and settings for that website are saved in a cookie, and you won't be prompted again. If you don't agree to the policy, the website will ask you over and over, every time you visit.
Cookie Consent

When you visit a website, you often get to choose the types of cookies you want to allow. You can say yes to all cookies or just the ones that are needed to make the website look and run better. Websites will let you read about how they use cookies, but not many people actually do that. It's nice that websites tell you about their cookie rules, but they really hope you'll consent to allow all their cookies on your device. This way, they can keep an eye on what you do online and learn more about you.

You may have heard that "Clearing your cookies will clean up your computer and make it run better" at some point. While clearing out these small text files can help web pages load faster or fix a website display issue, they will not affect the overall performance of your computer.
Ecommerce Safety
Ecommerce refers to buying and selling products or services electronically on the internet.

Online shopping is incredibly convenient, but it also creates opportunities for criminals to steal your money and personal information. By following a few simple habits, you can shop online with much more confidence.
Be Careful What You Share

When shopping online, websites will ask you for personal details like your name, address, and payment information. Only share this information when it's required by a business you recognize and trust. Many online stores offer to save your credit card number for future purchases. While this is convenient, it also means your financial data is sitting on that company's servers. If the company ever suffers a data breach, your information could be exposed. When possible, avoid saving payment details in your online accounts.
If you use a mobile device for shopping, think of it the same way you would think of your wallet.
Don't hand your phone to someone you wouldn't hand your credit card to. Your phone may have payment apps, saved passwords, and autofill information that could give someone access to your accounts.
Avoid Public WiFi for Purchases

Public WiFi networks, like those at coffee shops, airports, or hotels, are not secure. When you connect to public WiFi, other people on the same network may be able to see the data you send and receive. This makes it risky to enter passwords, credit card numbers, or any other sensitive information while connected to these networks.

If you need to make a purchase while you're away from home, use your phone's cellular data connection instead of public WiFi. Cellular connections are much harder for attackers to intercept. If you must use public WiFi, a virtual private network (VPN) can encrypt your connection and add a layer of protection.
Use Credit Cards Over Debit Cards

When shopping online, use a credit card instead of a debit card whenever possible. Credit cards offer stronger fraud protection than debit cards. If someone makes an unauthorized purchase on your credit card, you can dispute the charge and you typically won't be responsible for the amount. With a debit card, the money is taken directly from your bank account, and getting it back can be much more difficult and take much longer.

Some banks and credit card companies also offer virtual card numbers. These are temporary card numbers linked to your real account that you can use for online purchases. If the virtual number is stolen, the thief can't use it again because it expires after one use or a short period of time.
Shop with Legitimate Businesses

Not every online store is what it appears to be. Scammers create fake websites that look like real retailers, complete with product photos, customer reviews, and professional-looking designs. These fake storefronts exist to collect your payment information or to take your money without ever shipping a product.
Before you buy from a website you've never used before, take a few steps to check if it's legitimate:

items: Examine the URL closely. Look for slight misspellings or extra characters in the web address, such as "amaz0n.com" instead of "amazon.com."
Search for the website's name along with the word "reviews" or "scam" to see what other people have experienced.
Check if the business has a social media presence with real customer interactions over time.
Be cautious of websites that only accept unusual payment methods, like wire transfers or cryptocurrency.

blocks.text: When using peer-to-peer payment services such as Venmo or Zelle, limit your transactions to people you know and trust. These services are designed for sending money to friends and family, not for purchasing items from strangers. Most peer-to-peer payments can't be reversed once they're sent.

Watch for Deals That Are Too Good to Be True If a deal seems unbelievably good, it probably is. Scammers frequently advertise products at prices far below what you'd find anywhere else. The goal is to get you so excited about the deal that you overlook warning signs and hand over your payment information. A popular item at 90% off from a website you've never heard of should raise a red flag.
Security with Online Browsing

In today’s computer-driven environment, most people download files from the internet every day without giving them a second thought. However, downloading the wrong file can lead to disaster. Criminals often make malicious programs and try to pass them off as legitimate files.
If you download one of these, the criminals can take over your computer, steal your money, or access your private information.
Here are some good safety measures to take when downloading files.
Be Wary of "Free" Downloads

One trick hackers like to use is to offer something for free that you'd normally have to pay for, like a movie, album, or video game. What the user doesn't know is that the movie or music file also contains malware that will infect your system when you download it. To protect yourself, be skeptical of anyone or any site that makes promises that seem too good to be true.
Only Download from Reputable Sources

If you want to download something from a website you've never heard of, do an internet search for the site first. If you have a hard time finding the site on a search engine, it's probably not legitimate. Never download email attachments from people you don't know or trust. Many viruses spread through email. Even attachments from people you know can be risky. Make sure the person intended to send you the file if you weren't expecting it.
Use Antivirus Software

Most modern computers and devices come with antivirus software already installed. For example, Windows systems come with Windows Defender. To make the best use of this software, make sure it's turned on, up to date, and set to run weekly scans of your computer.

blocks.text: Technology is a powerful tool, but spending too much time online can take a toll on your mental health. Social media, notifications, and endless scrolling are designed to keep you engaged, and it can be hard to step away. Understanding how technology affects your emotions, sleep, and relationships is the first step toward using it in a healthier way.

In this lesson, you will explore how addictive design keeps you hooked, what technology overuse looks like, how cyberbullying affects people, and practical strategies for setting boundaries and developing healthy coping skills. You'll learn about how apps and platforms are designed to keep you hooked, how to spot the signs of tech overuse, and how to set healthy boundaries. You'll also explore cyberbullying, coping skills that don't involve a screen, and how to talk about your feelings when technology starts to feel overwhelming. The goal isn't to stop using technology. It's to take back control so you can enjoy it without it taking a toll on your wellbeing.
Tech Affects Your Mental Health

Technology is a huge part of everyday life. You use it to stay in touch with friends, get schoolwork done, watch videos, play games, and much more. Most of the time, technology makes life easier and more fun. But like most things, too much of it, or the wrong kind of experience with it, can start to affect how you feel.

Your mental health is the way you think, feel, and handle what happens around you. It includes your mood, your stress levels, how well you sleep, and how you feel about yourself. Technology can affect all of these things, both positively and negatively.
The Good Side

Technology isn't all bad for your mental health. It gives you access to helpful resources like meditation apps, workout videos, and online communities where people support each other. It lets you stay connected with friends and family, even when they're far away. And when you use it intentionally, it can be a great tool for learning new skills, exploring creative hobbies, and solving problems.
The Not-So-Good Side

Problems tend to show up when technology starts taking over your time or affecting how you feel about yourself. Spending hours scrolling through social media can lead to comparing yourself to others, which can make you feel like you're not good enough. Getting constantly interrupted by notifications can make it hard to focus or relax. And staying up late looking at a screen can mess with your sleep, which has a direct impact on your mood and energy the next day.
Over time, these small effects can add up. That's why it's worth learning how technology might be affecting you so you can make smarter choices about how you use it.
Manage Screen Time

Managing your time effectively and staying in control of your emotional well-being when using technology is essential because it directly shapes how you think, feel, and function throughout the day. With constant notifications, endless content, and the pressure to stay connected, it's easy for technology to consume more time and energy than you intend. When you set boundaries around your screen use, you protect your focus, reduce stress, and create space for healthier habits.
You are the Product - Addictive by Design

Most of the apps and websites you use every day are free. You don't pay for social media, video platforms, or search engines. So how do these companies make money? The answer is advertising. The more time you spend on an app, the more ads you see, and the more money the company earns. That means keeping you glued to your screen is their business model. In other words, you are the product.

To keep you coming back, many platforms use design techniques that are specifically built to be addictive. Understanding how these tricks work is the first step toward taking back control of your time and attention.
Notifications

Every buzz, ding, and banner on your phone is designed to pull you back into an app. Even when you're trying to focus on something else, a notification about a new like, comment, or message creates a little spike of curiosity that's hard to ignore. Over time, these constant interruptions train your brain to check your phone automatically, even when there's nothing new to see.
Infinite Scroll

In the past, websites had pages. You would reach the bottom, and that was a natural stopping point. Many modern apps have removed that stopping point entirely. Social media feeds, video platforms, and news apps use infinite scroll, which means new content loads automatically as you swipe. There's never a clear endpoint, so it's easy to keep going far longer than you intended.
Likes, Streaks, and Rewards

When someone likes your post or you hit a new streak on an app, your brain releases a small burst of dopamine, the same chemical that makes you feel good when you eat your favorite food or win a game. Apps take advantage of this by giving you unpredictable rewards. You never know exactly when the next like or comment will come, so you keep checking. This is the same psychological pattern used in slot machines, and it's incredibly effective at keeping people engaged.
Algorithmic Feeds

The content you see on most platforms isn't random. An algorithm studies what you've watched, clicked on, and lingered over, then serves you more of the same. The goal is to show you content you're most likely to engage with, which keeps you on the platform longer.
The problem is that this can create a narrow view of the world and expose you to increasingly extreme or emotionally charged content, because that's what tends to get the most clicks.
Autoplay

Video platforms and streaming services often start playing the next video or episode automatically before you can decide whether to stop. This removes the moment of choice where you would normally close the app or turn off the screen. It's a small thing, but it adds up to a lot of extra screen time.
Why This Matters

None of this means you should stop using apps entirely. But it does mean that when you feel like you can't put your phone down, it's not just a willpower problem. These apps were built by teams of designers and engineers whose job is to make them as hard to put down as possible.
Knowing that puts you in a better position to recognize when an app is pulling you in and to make a conscious choice about whether you want to keep going.
Need for Balance - Pros and Cons
Technology isn't good or bad on its own. It all depends on how you use it and how much. The trick is finding a healthy balance where you get the benefits without letting it take over your life.
The Pros
There's no question that technology makes a lot of things better. Here are just a few of the ways it helps:

items: Staying connected: You can keep in touch with friends, family, and communities no matter where they are. A quick video call or message can make a big difference when you're feeling lonely.

Learning and growing: Online classes, tutorials, and how-to videos let you learn just about anything on your own time. Whether it's a school subject or a new hobby, the resources are right at your fingertips.
Getting things done: From organizing your schedule to paying bills, technology saves you time on everyday tasks so you can spend that time on things you enjoy.
Entertainment and creativity: Music, games, art, video editing, and so many other creative outlets are available through your devices. Technology opens up new ways to express yourself and have fun.
Accessing help: If you need health advice, mental health resources, or just want to look up an answer to a question, it's usually just a few taps away.

blocks.text: The Cons
On the flip side, technology can cause real problems when it starts to take up too much of your time and energy:

items: Social comparison: Scrolling through curated posts and highlight reels can make you feel like everyone else's life is better than yours. What you're seeing is rarely the full picture.
Sleep disruption: Using screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep. The blue light from screens and the stimulation from content both interfere with your body's ability to wind down.
Reduced face-to-face time: The more time you spend on devices, the less time you might spend talking to people in person. Real, in-person connection is important for your emotional health.
Distraction and lost time: It's easy to pick up your phone for a quick check and suddenly realize an hour has gone by. Those small interruptions add up throughout the day.
Stress and overload: A constant stream of notifications, messages, and news can leave you feeling overwhelmed and anxious.

blocks.text: Finding the Balance
The goal isn't to eliminate technology from your life. That's not realistic, and it's not necessary.
The goal is to be thoughtful about how you use it. Ask yourself questions like:

items: Am I using this app because I want to, or just out of habit?
Is this making me feel good, or is it making me feel worse?
Have I spent time today doing things away from a screen?

blocks.text: When you start paying attention to how technology affects your mood, energy, and time, you can make small adjustments that lead to a much healthier relationship with your devices.
Tech Overuse / Mental Health Links

It's one thing to know that too much screen time isn't great for you. It's another thing to recognize when it's actually happening. Tech overuse doesn't always look dramatic. Most of the time, it builds up gradually until it starts affecting how you feel without you even realizing it.
Signs of Tech Overuse

There's no exact number of hours that defines "too much" screen time because it depends on what you're doing and how it's affecting you. But here are some common signs that technology might be taking up more space in your life than it should:

items: You reach for your phone first thing in the morning and it's the last thing you look at before bed.
You feel anxious or restless when you can't check your phone.
You've lost track of time online more than once this week.
You're staying up later than you should because of your screen.
Activities you used to enjoy, like hanging out with friends, playing sports, or reading, feel less interesting than being on your device.
You feel worse after using social media, not better.

blocks.text: If a few of these sound familiar, that doesn't mean something is wrong with you. It just means it might be time to make some changes.
How Overuse Affects Your Sleep

One of the most well-documented effects of too much screen time is poor sleep. Screens give off blue light, which signals your brain to stay awake. When you're scrolling or watching videos right before bed, your body has a harder time producing the hormones it needs to fall asleep.

On top of that, the content itself, whether it's an intense game, a heated comment section, or a suspenseful show, keeps your mind active when it should be winding down. Poor sleep leads to trouble concentrating, irritability, and lower energy the next day, which can create a cycle where you reach for your phone even more to pass the time.
How Overuse Affects Your Mood

Constant exposure to social media, news, and online drama takes a toll on your emotions. You might start comparing your life to what others post, feel pressure to keep up with trends, or get pulled into arguments that leave you feeling drained. Even passively scrolling, without posting or commenting, has been shown to lower people's mood over time. When technology becomes the main source of your social interaction, it can also make you feel more isolated, even though you're technically "connected" to hundreds of people.
How Overuse Affects Your Focus

Your brain adapts to the constant stimulation of notifications, short videos, and rapid content switching. Over time, it gets harder to concentrate on longer tasks like reading, studying, or having an in-depth conversation. You might notice that you feel bored more quickly or that you need more stimulation to stay interested in something. This isn't a permanent change. Your focus can improve once you start giving your brain regular breaks from the nonstop flow of content.
How Overuse Affects Your Body
Mental health and physical health are closely connected. Spending too much time sitting with a device can lead to headaches, eye strain, neck and back pain, and a lack of physical activity.
When your body doesn't feel good, your mind usually doesn't either. Taking regular breaks to move, stretch, and look away from the screen helps both your body and your brain reset.
Technology Addiction, Anxiety and Depression

You have learned about the signs and effects of tech overuse. But what happens when overuse goes even further? For some people, the pull of technology becomes so strong that it starts to feel less like a choice and more like a need. When that happens, it may cross the line into something more serious.
When Overuse Becomes Addiction

Technology addiction is when you feel unable to stop using a device, app, or platform even though it's causing problems in your life. It's not just about spending a lot of time on your phone. It's about feeling like you have to, even when you know it's hurting you.
Some signs that tech use might have crossed from a habit into something more serious include:

items: You've tried to cut back but can't seem to do it.
You feel irritable or upset when you can't use your device.
You're neglecting responsibilities like schoolwork, chores, or your job because of screen time.
Your relationships with friends or family are suffering because of how much time you spend on your device.
You use technology to escape negative emotions like boredom, loneliness, or stress, but feel worse afterward.

blocks.text: The Connection to Anxiety

Anxiety is a feeling of worry, nervousness, or unease, often about something with an uncertain outcome. Everyone feels anxious sometimes, but for some people, technology can make anxiety significantly worse.
The constant flow of notifications creates a feeling that you always need to respond right away.

Social media adds pressure to keep up appearances, get enough likes, or stay on top of what everyone else is doing. Fear of missing out, often called FOMO, can make you feel anxious every time you put your phone down. And the 24/7 news cycle can leave you feeling like the world is more dangerous or chaotic than it actually is.
Over time, these small stresses can build into a constant background hum of worry that makes it hard to relax, even when you're away from your screen.
The Connection to Depression

Depression is more than just feeling sad. It's a persistent state of low mood, lack of motivation, and disinterest in things you used to enjoy. Technology doesn't directly cause depression, but it can contribute to it in several ways.

Spending hours comparing yourself to others on social media can wear down your self-esteem over time. Replacing real-world social interaction with online communication can increase feelings of loneliness. And if tech use is interfering with your sleep, physical activity, or daily routine, the disruption to those basic needs can make depressive feelings worse.
It can also become a cycle. You feel down, so you scroll to distract yourself. The scrolling doesn't actually help, so you feel even worse, which makes you scroll more.
You're Not Alone

If any of this sounds familiar, it's important to know that you're not the only person dealing with it. These are common experiences, especially for people who grew up with smartphones and social media as a normal part of life. Recognizing the pattern is the first and most important step. In the upcoming topics, you'll learn practical strategies for setting boundaries, building healthier habits, and knowing when to ask for help.
Cyberbullying

Cyberbullying occurs when someone intentionally and repeatedly uses technology to hurt, harass, mistreat, or make fun of another person. It's important to look more closely at how to recognize the signs of cyberbullying and understand effective ways to respond if it happens to you or to people around you. Learning how to identify and handle cyberbullying not only protects your own well-being but also helps create a safer and more respectful online environment for everyone.
Types of Cyberbullying
Cyberbullying can be done in different ways. The table below describes a few of the most common tactics bullies use on their victims.
Type Description
Comments, posts, written messages Any kind of written content, such as text messages, chats, posts, comments, and so on, could be considered cyberbullying if they include any or all of the following:

items: Hurtful, mean, embarrassing rumors about the victim
Threats against the victim
Calling the victim hateful names
Using profane or aggressive language towards the victim
Making hateful or hurtful remarks regarding the victim's ethnicity, race, religion, or any other personal characteristics or appearance.

blocks.text: Pictures, videos Bullies can also resort to sharing embarrassing pictures or videos of the victim. This content could have been taken sneakily, acquired without permission, or even faked with the use of Photoshop and other photo editing tools. No matter how it happens, the pictures and videos are always shared online without the victim knowing or consenting to it before it's in the public eye.

Fake accounts Bullies often choose to make fake accounts to do their bullying so that it's hard to trace them and so there's a better chance they can go unpunished for what they do. They may even make a fake account pretending to be their victim.

Hateful, anti pages Some bullies even go as far as creating a page, website, server, chat room, or channel dedicated completely to destroy the victim's reputation. As they gather bigger crowds, the situation can quickly escalate out of control.
Type Description

Doxing, doxxing Doxing, sometimes written as doxxing, has an interesting history. It started in the nineties when hackers would successfully uncover the secret identities of other rival hackers and expose them online. They referred to this as docs or dox.

Eventually, this trend grew and started being referred to as doxing/doxxing. Nowadays, anyone who digs the internet to find personal or private information on another person and then shares their findings online for all to see is doxing. Information can be obtained in many ways, but a few of the most used resources include the following:

items: Social media
Tracking usernames
Searching domain names
Phishing
Government records
Tracking IP addresses
Reverse cellphone lookup
Packet sniffing

blocks.text: Doxing can be punishable by law, but it depends on the kind of information they shared and how they obtained it. If they share your email and phone number that they found on your social media, that's not as severe as sharing your address, social security number, or bank account info they got through phishing you. Some of the most common information revealed through doxing includes:

items: Criminal history.
Private conversations (written or audio).
Personal pictures.
Embarrassing personal details.
Home address.
Workplace or school details.
Social security numbers.
School records.
Phone numbers.
Bank account or credit card information.

blocks.text: Doxing is often done by bullies but can sometimes be motivated by revenge. The victim could decide to get back at the bully by exposing them anonymously. Such cases are just as punishable as when done by a bully. The motives don't make it less illegal.
Identify and Deal with Cyberbullying
Cyberbullying can be tricky to identify, but the good news is that once you do, you can take steps to prove it and stop it. The table below describes these steps in more detail.
Step Description
Identify Some bullying is more subtle than others.

Sometimes bullies try to convince you it's nothing by saying things like "it was just a joke," "don't take it seriously," or "just kidding." But the truth is, if you're feeling hurt, burdened, or depressed by their teasing, it could be considered bullying.
Even if they claim it's innocent if you're constantly being targeted, it's bullying. At the end of the day, if you're not happy with it, it's bullying, no matter what intentions they claim to have.

Communicate your boundary Once you've identified yourself as a victim of bullying, try your best to communicate your dislike of their behavior by asking them to stop with the jokes and teasing. Even if they come back with answers like "lighten up," "don't take it so seriously," "it was just a joke," or any other excuses, be polite but firm in drawing your boundary by responding with something like "I know it's just a joke, but I don't like it. Please stop." Gather evidence If you've asked them to stop a few times, but the bullying keeps happening, it's time to gather evidence if you haven't already started doing so. Screenshot posts, chats, and profiles. Save pictures, videos, and audio. Build a record of anything you can use to show what's happening and how long it's been going on.

In the meantime, try ignoring your bullies. If politely asking them to stop didn't work, instead of calling them out or arguing with them, just ignore it as best you can. Talking back and engaging with them might escalate their behavior. Silence might lead them to stop if they're after a reaction from you.
Report If it's still happening after trying your best to resolve the situation, it's time to seek outside help. You can do this in a few ways:

items: Block them on all apps they interact with you.
Report to the app managing team who monitor this kind of situation and address it appropriately.
Talk to an adult you trust and feel comfortable sharing something this sensitive. It could be a family member, a teacher, a coach, a counselor, a neighbor, etc.
Contact a mental health helpline. They have professionals who can guide you on further steps to take.

blocks.text: Take a break Bullying can really take a toll on your health. If it becomes too much, consider taking a break from social media or other apps where the bullying happened. Stop all notifications and don't log in until you've recharged and feel ready to join the online world again. It's perfectly fine and even healthy to need a break once in a while.
Setting Healthy Boundaries

You've seen how technology can affect your mood, sleep, focus, and relationships. The good news is that you don't have to just accept it. Setting boundaries with technology is one of the most effective things you can do to protect your mental health. A boundary is simply a rule you create for yourself about when, where, and how you use your devices.
Create Tech-Free Zones

One of the simplest boundaries you can set is deciding that certain places are off-limits for devices. For example, keeping your phone out of the bedroom helps you sleep better. Not bringing it to the dinner table encourages real conversation with the people around you. You don't have to ban devices from every room, just pick one or two places where you'd benefit from being fully present without a screen.
Set Time Limits
Most phones have built-in tools that track how much time you spend on each app. You can set daily time limits so that the app reminds you or even locks when you've hit your limit.

These tools aren't perfect, since you can always override them, but they give you a moment to pause and ask yourself if you really want to keep going or if you'd rather spend your time on something else.
Control Your Notifications

Not every notification deserves your immediate attention. Go into your phone's settings and turn off notifications for apps that don't need to interrupt you. Keep the ones that genuinely matter, like calls or messages from close family, and silence the rest. This one change alone can make a huge difference in how often you reach for your phone throughout the day.
Build a Routine

Instead of letting your phone decide when you engage with it, build technology into your day on your terms. For example, you might decide to check social media once after lunch and once in the evening, but not first thing in the morning or right before bed. Having a plan removes the "just one more check" cycle that eats up so much time.
Set Social Boundaries

Boundaries aren't just about screen time. They're also about how you interact with people online. It's okay to unfollow or mute accounts that make you feel bad. It's okay to not respond to every message right away. And it's okay to say no to group chats, online arguments, or trends that don't interest you. Your time and your emotional energy are yours to protect.
Start Small

You don't have to overhaul your entire routine overnight. Pick one boundary that feels manageable and try it for a week. Maybe it's no phone in bed, or maybe it's turning off social media notifications. Once that becomes a habit, add another one. Small, consistent changes tend to stick better than big dramatic ones.
No-tech Coping Skills

When you're feeling stressed, anxious, or just drained from too much screen time, one of the best things you can do is step away from your device and try something that doesn't involve technology at all. These are called coping skills, and they're simple activities that help you calm down, reset, and feel better.
Everyone is different, so not every strategy will work for every person. The important thing is to try a few and figure out what feels right for you.
Move Your Body

Physical activity is one of the fastest ways to change how you feel. It doesn't have to mean going to a gym or running a mile. A short walk around the block, some stretching, doing jumping jacks, or even just dancing to your favorite song can make a noticeable difference. Exercise releases chemicals in your brain that boost your mood and reduce stress. Even five or ten minutes can help.
Practice Deep Breathing
When you're feeling overwhelmed or anxious, your breathing tends to get fast and shallow.

Slowing it down on purpose sends a signal to your brain that it's safe to relax. Try breathing in slowly through your nose for four counts, holding for four counts, and breathing out slowly through your mouth for four counts. Repeat this a few times and notice how your body starts to calm down.
Write It Down

Putting your thoughts on paper can help you process what you're feeling. You don't have to write anything fancy or organized. Just grab a notebook or a scrap of paper and write whatever comes to mind. Sometimes getting thoughts out of your head and onto paper makes them feel less overwhelming. You can also try writing down three things you're grateful for. This simple practice can shift your focus from what's going wrong to what's going right.
Spend Time with People

Face-to-face interaction is something that screens can't fully replace. Talking to a friend, family member, or anyone you feel comfortable with can remind you that you're not alone. It doesn't have to be a deep conversation about your problems. Sometimes just laughing, sharing a meal, or being around people who care about you is enough to lift your spirits.
Do Something Creative

Drawing, painting, playing a musical instrument, building something, cooking, or any hands-on activity can be a great way to unwind. Creative activities give your mind something to focus on besides your worries, and the sense of accomplishment you get from making something can be a real mood booster.
Spend Time Outdoors

Nature has a calming effect that's hard to get from a screen. Sitting outside, taking a walk in the park, or even just standing in the sunlight for a few minutes can help reduce stress and improve your mood. You don't have to go on a wilderness hike. Just getting some fresh air and a change of scenery is often enough.
Rest Without a Screen

Taking a break doesn't always mean watching something or scrolling. Sometimes the best kind of rest is truly doing nothing, or doing something quiet like reading a physical book, listening to music with your eyes closed, or just sitting somewhere comfortable and letting your mind wander. Giving your brain a break from constant input helps it recharge.
Talk About Your Feelings and Get Help
One of the most important skills isn't really a tech skill at all. It's the ability to recognize how you're feeling and ask for help when you need it.
Why Talking Matters

It's normal to think you should handle things on your own, especially when the problem feels embarrassing or hard to explain. But keeping difficult feelings bottled up usually makes them worse, not better. Talking to someone you trust doesn't mean you're weak or broken. It means you're doing something smart to take care of yourself.
When you say something out loud, it often becomes easier to understand. A feeling that seemed overwhelming in your head can start to feel more manageable once you've put it into words.
And the person you're talking to might be able to offer a perspective you haven't considered.
Who to Talk To
You get to choose who you feel comfortable opening up to. Here are a few options to consider:

items: A friend: Sometimes just venting to someone your age who gets what you're going through is enough to make you feel better.
A family member: A parent, sibling, grandparent, or other relative you feel safe with can be a great source of support and advice.
A teacher, coach, or school counselor: These are people who are trained to help and who genuinely care about your wellbeing. They can also point you toward additional resources.
A mentor or community leader: If you're part of a club, religious community, or other group, there may be trusted adults there who would be happy to listen.

blocks.text: How to Start the Conversation
Starting a conversation about your feelings can feel awkward, and that's completely normal.
You don't need a script. Even something simple can open the door:

items: "I've been feeling really stressed lately and I'm not sure why."
"Something has been bothering me and I could use someone to talk to."
"I don't know if this is a big deal, but I wanted to tell someone."

blocks.text: You don't have to have all the answers or even know exactly what's wrong. The point is to start the conversation. The person you're talking to can help you figure it out from there.
When to Seek Professional Help
Sometimes what you're going through needs more than a friendly ear. If you're experiencing any of the following, it's important to reach out to a professional like a counselor, therapist, or doctor:

items: You feel sad, anxious, or hopeless most of the time and it's not getting better.
You've lost interest in things you used to enjoy.
You're having trouble sleeping, eating, or concentrating for weeks at a time.
You feel like you can't cope on your own anymore.
You have thoughts of hurting yourself or feel like things would be better if you weren't around.

blocks.text: These feelings are serious, and there are people trained specifically to help. Asking for professional help is one of the bravest and most important things you can do for yourself.
Resources
If you or someone you know needs immediate support, these resources are available around the clock:

items: 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 for free, confidential support 24/7.
Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741741 to connect with a trained crisis counselor.
SAMHSA National Helpline: Call 1-800-662-4357 for free mental health and substance use referrals.

blocks.text: You don't have to be in a crisis to use these resources. They're there for anyone who needs someone to talk to.

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 3.5 Identify common uses of artificial intelligence (AI).

blocks.text: Artificial intelligence is changing how people interact with technology. AI chatbots and assistants can answer questions, generate content, write code, and even create images, all from a simple text conversation. But to get the most out of these tools, you need to understand what AI is, how it works, and how to communicate with it effectively.

In this lesson, you will explore what AI is and how it has evolved, discover the different types of generative AI tools available today, and learn the key elements of writing effective prompts, including goals, personas, context, and constraints.

Artificial intelligence (AI) isn't a new idea. People have been discussing it and trying to get it going for decades. But in the last few years, it's really started to take off. Better computer hardware has helped a lot.

At its core, AI is made up of specialized computers with lots of video cards. Unlike traditional computers that rely mainly on their central processing units (CPUs) , AI computers rely on their video cards to do most of the work. These AI computers learn from the world around them, which for them means other computers and the vast amounts of information they hold.

They use machine learning and algorithms to gain knowledge and improve performance. They take in a lot of data and make decisions based on what they've "learned" without needing to be constantly reprogrammed.

Computer programs do tasks they're programmed to do, but with AI, the programs can learn and change. As humans, we take our natural intelligence for granted. But could a computer become aware and have consciousness in the same way we do? This idea is common in science fiction, but remember, fiction means it's not real, at least not at the moment. It will be a long time before computers can feel emotions like humans do, if ever.
AI Enhancements

AI has already improved a number of different industries, like healthcare, social media, and chatbots. In healthcare, AI can look over medical scans to find things that might be potential health problems. This is the industry that people pay attention to most because it concerns human life. Creating medicines that are specific to each person will become more common.

On social media, AI can help by checking content and making suggestions based on what users like and who they're connected to. Companies use chatbots to answer common questions when someone tries to contact the help desk. This allows the company to save money on employees having to personally answer the phone. Chatbots can also be used at big conference events to answer questions that attendees send in through text messages.

AI holds the promise of revolutionizing many industries such as medicine, where AI can improve diagnostic accuracy and find new ways to use existing drug treatments. In addition, the personalization of products and services tailored to each individual will see significant growth.

Alan Turing proposed the idea of a computer becoming smart enough to fool a human when he wrote his ground-breaking paper on the subject in 1950, "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." He posed the question, "Can machines think?" Additional AI Concepts You've learned about several key areas where artificial intelligence is already making an impact — from robotics and natural language processing to expert systems and big data analytics.
Beyond those topics, there are a couple more AI concepts worth understanding.
Table 10: Additional AI Concepts
Concept Description

Generative AI Generative AI is a type of computer program that can create new things like stories, pictures, recipes, or essays. One example of this is ChatGPT, which is a program that can have a conversation with you just like a real person. Generative AI is in its infancy, but it has already had a major impact on businesses, schools, and individuals.

Gaming Scientific research in artificial intelligence has been applied to video games since the mid-twentieth century. In the early years, AI development was focused on how to beat human players. More recently, AI has been applied to enhance players' gaming experiences. AI elements in gaming include complex machine learning systems and more believable visuals that capture natural human emotion.
Using Generative AI

There's a type of artificial intelligence (AI) that most everyone can get the hang of quickly called generative AI. You can access it these days through a web browser or as an app on your computer or smartphone. Generative AI makes original and creative content and generates code. These two skills are often not found together in humans because people who are good writers aren't always great at programming, and vice versa. We used to think of these as left-brain (logical) and right-brain (creative) skills, but that's actually been proven to be a myth.
Still, people do tend to be better at one type of thinking than the other.
Written Language

If you need to write a report, market a product, or create a professional cover letter for your resume, generative AI can be very helpful. It's amazing how quickly it can come up with an original and interesting story. While great authors can do this too, AI can churn out pages much faster than any human can.

AI is helpful in language translation. It can quickly and accurately translate from one language to another. Gaming has also improved with AI, as it can create detailed and immersive game worlds much faster than a team of developers can.
Software Development

One of the strengths of AI is its ability to help with programming code. As programmers type, AI assistants can suggest code, making the creation process faster. AI can also generate small pieces of code and sometimes even whole programs. Additionally, AI can help find and fix errors in the code.
Image Development

Generative AI has become popular in art and design as well. You can tell a computer what kind of art you want, and it will create almost anything you can imagine. You can get original, photo-like images or paintings in different styles and themes just by giving instructions to the AI. Music has also been touched by AI, as it can help write and create music. However, using AI rather than humans to create art can hurt artists. As of now, it's still hard to program true creativity.
AI Tools and Models

Have you ever wished for a tool that could write stories for you, create original artwork in seconds, or help you brainstorm better ideas at work? In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has grown by leaps and bounds, making tasks that once seemed impossible or too technical suddenly accessible to everyone, even if you don't have a tech background. You will explore what AI tools and models actually are, what you can do with them, and where you can find them.
What Are AI Tools and Models?

When you use ChatGPT, Copilot, or Gemini, you are actually interacting with two different types of technology: one is the chat tool that you see and interact with and the other is a generative AI model that powers the chat experience behind the scenes. AI companies are constantly working to improve both the chat tools you use and the models that help those tools become more and more helpful.
In many cases, one tool will actually give you access to multiple models behind the scenes.

Most tools have simplified this completely by automatically determining the best model for the task based on your prompt. For example, if your prompt asks for a text summary, a tool like ChatGPT will route it to a text-processing model (like GPT -5). If you ask for a picture, it seamlessly routes the request to an image-generation model (like GPT Image). However, some still let you manually select different levels of 'thinking,' such as choosing a 'Standard' model for quick, everyday tasks or an 'Advanced' reasoning model for complex problem-solving.

Everyday Uses (And Some Surprising Ide as!)
The real magic of AI tools is in how they help you every day. Here are a few examples: At Work:

items: Drafting emails or summarizing long documents
Generating reports or slides with just a prompt
Visualizing ideas for marketing or product design
Improving your code or learning new programming languages

items: Researching and organizing notes
