blocks.text: The Settings App is where you configure nearly every aspect of Windows. From adjusting display resolution and scaling to personalizing the desktop background, lock screen, and taskbar, the Settings App gives you centralized control over how your computer looks and performs. It also includes options for managing devices, apps, power consumption, accessibility, and privacy.

Windows also uses user accounts to control who can access the system and what they are allowed to do. Understanding the difference between standard and administrator accounts, how to create and manage accounts, and how to set strong passwords are essential skills for keeping a system secure.
Windows Settings
The Settings App is the central place in Windows to customize how the computer looks and functions. Within the Settings App are several options you can use to configure the system.
Image 1: Settings App
Table 18: Settings App Options
Option Description

System In System, you will find various tools to configure settings for display, sound, notifications, power, and more. In addition, it provides options for Windows activation, recovery, system specifications, and configure other system preferences.
Bluetooth & devices In Bluetooth & devices, you manage peripheral devices such as printers, the mouse, and the keyboard.

Network & internet In Network & internet, you manage your network settings when connecting the system to a network. For example, some of the items are changing network adapter options, configuring VPN settings, defining a proxy, and more.

Personalization The Personalization option lets you change the way Windows displays different elements. For example, you can customize the current theme by selecting which desktop background, window color, and screen saver you want to use. Other options allow you to configure fonts, the taskbar, and what happens when you lock the screen.

Apps The Apps option lets you explore the new and refreshed apps for Windows 11, ranging from Video to the Microsoft Store. You can configure startup and default apps, plus find many app tools to stay creative and productive.
Accounts In Accounts, you can update your info, create and manage user and e- mail accounts, configure sign-in options, or set up parental controls.
Time & language In Time & Language, you set the date, time, region, and language used by the system.
Gaming In Gaming, you configure controller, keyboard, or locations preferences for gaming on the system. Use it to optimize your PC for play.

Accessibility In this section, you configure accessibility settings for the system. For example, you can set the font size, configure visual effects for cursors, change mouse and touchpad settings, and enable the magnifier.

Privacy & security Privacy & security gives you control over how your camera, microphone, and personal data are used by different apps. You can assign various permissions for Windows or app functionality. There is also a link to the Windows Security app to configure firewall and antivirus settings.
Windows Update Windows Update lets you configure how and when updates from Microsoft are downloaded and installed on the system.
Windows User Account

Windows user accounts control who can access the system. Anyone who wants to use the computer must authenticate by providing credentials such as a username and password, a fingerprint, or a smart card. After logging in, the rights assigned to a user account determine what level of access they have to files, applications, and system settings.
You manage user accounts in Windows by opening the Settings app and navigating to Accounts > Family & other users.
Image 1: Manage User Accounts in the Settings App
Table 19: Windows User Account Management Tasks
Task Description
Create a New User Account You can create multiple user accounts on the same Windows computer from Accounts > Family & other users in the Settings app. There are two main paths:

items: Microsoft account: Enter the user's existing email address. They will receive login information and can sign in with their Microsoft credentials.
Local account: Select Add a user without a Microsoft account, then provide a username, password, and security questions for account recovery.

blocks.text: Family members can also be added with roles such as Organizer (can modify family and security settings) or Member (can edit settings based on their age).
Task Description

Change the Account Type By default, new user accounts are created as standard users with limited access to the system. Standard users can run applications and make a limited number of configuration changes, as long as those changes do not affect other users or the security of the system.

An administrator account has complete access and can make any changes. For security reasons, most accounts should remain standard users. Only a very limited number of trusted users should have an administrator account.
To change an account type, navigate to Accounts > Family & other users, select the user, and choose Change account type.
Create or Assign a Secure
Password
When creating a password for yourself or other users, use a strong one that is not easy to guess. A strong password: 1. Is at least seven characters long.
2. Uses lowercase and uppercase letters, numbers, and symbols.
3. Does not contain any words that can be found in the dictionary.
4. Does not contain any personally identifying information, such as:

items: Names of family members
Names of pets
Names of employers
Birth dates
Government identification numbers
Favorite sports teams

blocks.text: Delete a User Account If a user account is no longer needed, you can remove it from Accounts > Family & other users. Select the account, then choose Remove. Be aware that selecting Delete account and data will permanently remove all of the user's files.

blocks.text: Once you are comfortable navigating Windows and managing files, it is time to learn how to keep the system running smoothly. Windows relies on background services and processes to function properly, and tools like Task Manager and Task Scheduler give you visibility and control over what is happening behind the scenes.

This lesson also covers device drivers and system updates. Device drivers are the software that allows your operating system to communicate with hardware like printers, keyboards, and video cards. Windows Update automatically downloads security patches and bug fixes, but understanding how to manage updates and install drivers yourself is essential for maintaining a reliable system.
Task Management

All Microsoft Windows systems include a Task Manager, which is a program that allows you to monitor how your computer is performing at any given moment. It displays information about the software, processes, and services running on your computer. With Task Manager, you can find out things like how much computing power each task is using or which users are logged onto the computer.
Using Task Manager
You won't find Task Manager listed in the Start menu, but there are several ways to access it.

You can press Control + Alt + Delete at the same time and choose Task Manager from the menu that appears. You can also type task manager in the Windows search bar, or right-click any empty area of the taskbar and select "Task Manager" from the pop-up menu.
Task Manager is especially useful for handling programs that aren't responding. You can quickly end programs or processes to stop them from running.

Each process uses its own memory and system resources. Sometimes a program freezes or too many programs are running, which can slow down your computer. By closing certain programs in Task Manager, you can free up memory so other programs and the operating system run better.

Task Manager shows important details like which programs are using the most central processing unit (CPU) , memory, disk, and network resources. High resource usage from any single program can slow down your computer.

The "Processes" tab lists all running programs and background tasks. You can highlight a program and click "End Task" to stop it immediately. By sorting by memory or CPU usage, you can quickly identify which programs are consuming the most resources and end them to free up performance.
Network Performance
The "Performance" tab shows real-time graphs and statistics for CPU, memory, disk, network, and GPU usage. This is useful for diagnosing slowdowns and identifying hardware bottlenecks.
System Services

A service is a program on Windows that runs in the background without you needing to interact with it at all. These services help with different tasks on your computer, like signing in, browsing the Internet, or searching for files. Both Windows and other programs, like antivirus or backup software, can install services. Programs like Adobe Acrobat take advantage of services to optimize performance.

If you want to see which services are running, type "services" in the Windows start menu. From the Windows tool that pops up, you start or stop services and change their settings, like forcing them to start automatically when you turn on your computer.

Knowing which services are running at any given time is important because they support important functions like printing, Windows updates, and Bluetooth, among others. When your computer boots up, many of these start automatically without your direction. But you have ultimate control over what they do on Windows, and you can pause, resume, or restart them when you want.
Task Scheduler

As you're working with services and tasks, you might need to set up when certain ones should run. Task Scheduler is a Windows tool that automatically starts an application or runs a script based on events.

Task Scheduler sets tasks to run at specific times. A task can be a simple application or a batch file (a file with commands). They can be set to run once at a future date or on a regular basis, maybe daily or weekly. You can access Task Scheduler through its own console or in the Computer Management console. The Computer Management Console is a tool that helps you manage various parts of Windows in one place.

Tasks that are often scheduled to run regularly include backups, malware scans, and system updates. Triggers are the conditions that start these tasks, like a specific day, time, login, or other system events. You can set up Task Scheduler to run a program, send an email, or show a message when the trigger occurs. It's a powerful tool that's often underutilized.
If you have the free version of an anti-spyware or anti-malware program, one of the limits is not being able to schedule scans. You can set up Task Scheduler to run a weekly scan on the program.
Now you've got the free version and a perk of the paid version!
Plug-and-Play Installation

When you connect a device to a Windows PC, it often uses Microsoft's Plug-and-Play (PnP) technology. This means Windows detects the new device and tries to install a driver for it. The system checks the hardware ID and searches its database of drivers to find the right one. The goal is to make it easy for users, especially those who may not have much technical knowledge, to set up the hardware right away without any problems. The driver helps the device work smoothly.
To check the status of your devices, open the Windows Device Manager. The alphabetical list will show you which devices didn't install with Plug-and-Play and need attention.

Devices connected via USB are hot-swappable, meaning you can add or remove them while the system is running. If a device isn't hot-swappable, you need to restart the system when adding it or shut it down before removing it. Another benefit of Plug-and-Play is that Windows manages resources like Input/Output addresses, interrupt request numbers, and memory access to help prevent conflicts.
Driver Installation

Windows includes an inventory of generic drivers that will sometimes provide full functionality for a piece of hardware, and other times will provide only basic functionality for devices. For example, with a standard keyboard or mouse, the basic functionality is normally all that is needed. However, your unique situation may require full functionality, either because of a work or school policy, or because you want to optimize a piece of equipment like a gaming mouse.

In addition to the repository of default drivers, Windows will also try to locate a driver through Windows Update. If no driver is available for the hardware, you will need to obtain one from the device manufacturer.

It's important to know the exact make and model of the hardware, and the correct version of Windows. For example, Windows 10 and Windows 11 have different drivers. Also, before Windows 11, older versions of Windows came in 32-bit and 64-bit versions. It's important to install a driver that matches your computer's 32-bit or 64-bit version, or it won't work.

In addition to the manufacturer's website, there are many other websites that offer free driver downloads. Be careful with these sites because some might include corrupt software or malware with their download. To help avoid problems from bad drivers, Microsoft has a rule that all drivers must be digitally signed to prove they are safe. This process goes through Microsoft Windows, and once the driver is checked and verified, it can be installed on your computer.
Drivers and Devices

For hardware to work properly, it needs software called a driver that tells the operating system how to use it. On Windows, if the exact right driver isn't installed, the hardware isn't going to work. Over the years, Windows has gotten better at finding the right drivers for the installed hardware on its own. But there may still be times that you'll need to find the correct driver and install it manually yourself.

To view device drivers, open Device Manager in Windows. From there, you will see an alphabetical list of every piece of hardware connected to the computer. If there is a problem with any of the drivers, Windows will let you know with a symbol to the left of the device name.
There are a few symbols: a yellow exclamation point, a red cross or blue question mark, or a black downward arrow.

Each icon is a variant on the idea that the driver may be missing or corrupt. You can update, disable, uninstall, or check for hardware updates to these drivers. You will need to use these options when a device is acting up or not acting correctly.

Windows usually downloads and installs the latest drivers for your device through Windows Update. But some devices don't update automatically. In those cases, you might need to update the driver yourself. When you choose to update the driver, a new window will pop up with two choices: "Search automatically for drivers" or "Browse my computer for drivers." The automatic search is useful when drivers can be downloaded through Windows Update.

Companies that make hardware like video cards, sound cards, and Bluetooth devices offer driver packages on their websites for users to download and install. Updating drivers can fix problems with a device and sometimes make it work better.

Updating device drivers is often listed as a way to fix problems with hardware. However, the success rate of these tweaks is not as high as it would appear. It doesn't hurt to see if an update will fix a problem, but don't get your hopes up.
Windows Update
Windows includes a feature called Windows Update to keep your operating system up to date.

The default setting for Windows Update is to automatically identify, download, and install operating system updates for you. It is possible to manually force Windows to check for updates by selecting the Check for updates button. These updates can occur in two different methods:

items: Some updates will be installed in the background while the system is running.

Other updates require the system to be shut down and restarted for them to be applied. By default, updates will be automatically installed during a restart when you are not using the system. Windows will display a prompt and allow you to reschedule the restart.

blocks.text: Image 1: Configuring Windows Update in the Settings App
To access Windows Update select the Windows Start icon and then Settings. From the Settings App, select Windows Update.
Pause updates

While it is not recommended to turn off updates, there are times when you need, or want, to prevent updates. The Pause updates option allows you to stop updates for one to three weeks. However, there is a maximum of 35 days. Once the time expires or you select to resume updates, Windows will download and install the latest required updates. Pause will often be disabled until the updates are installed.
A few examples of when you would pause updates include:

items: It is common for professionals who are traveling on business, giving presentations, and using limited network connections to disable updates.
If there is an error that occurs during an update, you may need to pause updates to continue working until the issue can be resolved.
When using slow or secure network connections, allowing Windows to constantly check for and download updates can affect performance and could be restricted.

blocks.text: Update history
Reviewing a list of installed updates can help you identify whether you are protected by critical security updates. Selecting Update history will list of all installed updates.
Advanced options
Advanced options allow you to take control of when the updates are downloaded and installed instead of relying on the default settings. Some key settings are:

items: Recieve update for other Microsoft products: enable this function to have updates for

blocks.text: Microsoft Office or other Microsoft applications included in the list of available patches.

items: Get me up to date: this option instructs Windows to restart, even if it is during regular hours, if an update requires it.
Download updates over metered connections: enabling this option will instruct Windows to check and install updates on metered connections. This could cost you more depending on the connection plan.
Notify me when a restart is required to finish updating: determines if you receive a notification when the system needs to restart due to an update.
Active hours: by default, Windows will not restart during the hours of 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM.

blocks.text: Select this option if you need to adjust the time range.

items: Optional updates: enable this option to include notifications of updated drivers or features.

blocks.text: Windows Update does not provide maintenance for non-Microsoft applications installed on the system. To update these applications, you must go the vendor's website and manually check for updates, or refer to the documentation to enable automatic updates.
Software Patching and Updates

Software is always changing, and operating systems (OS) are constantly being improved and expanded. Productivity software gets both minor and major updates in the background. Many of these updates are meant to make programs work better and to improve security, and are usually free of charge. They can also add new features and make the software work better with new hardware. As IT professionals, it's important to always keep operating systems and software up to date with software patches.
Patch Management

Patch management is an important maintenance task to make sure computers run reliably and securely. It involves several steps, like checking for software updates and testing them before deploying them to all the company's computers. IT professionals test the patches to make sure the update doesn't cause problems with the existing system. If it works well, the update is then put on all computers on the network and checked again. Finally, the IT team documents or writes down the changes they made.
Microsoft Patches

Microsoft products follow a support lifecycle policy. Windows versions get about 10 years of mainstream support. During this time, they receive all kinds of updates, including new features, security fixes, and bug fixes. After this period, the OS enters the extended support phase, where Microsoft still provides free security updates to keep systems safe, but any non-security updates are not available without an additional paid support agreement. Once an OS reaches the end of its life, Microsoft will no longer support it at all. The OS will still work, but Microsoft won't fix bugs or provide patches for security issues.

In 2003, Microsoft established a regular cadence of updates on the second Tuesday of the month. While there were updates at other times, the second Tuesday of every month was known as "patch Tuesday" to allow administrators a dedicated day to push out updates to their systems. In 2015, they stopped this practice to help reduce the chances of cyber attacks. One common attack is a zero-day attack. This type of attack takes advantage of a vulnerability, in either software or hardware, that the vendor didn't know about before. They are called zero-day because the exposed system has been known for zero days by the vendor. This means that the vendor hasn’t had the opportunity to provide a patch to fix the problem.
Updating Non-Microsoft Software

Software from companies other than Microsoft also gets updated from time to time, but not as often. When these updates are available, you might see a prompt asking if you want to update when you open the software. Technicians can also manually check the publishers' websites for any new versions of the software.

blocks.title: What you should be able to answer
items: What is a command-line interface, and why do IT professionals use it?
What are the basic commands for navigating directories and managing files in the Windows
Command Prompt?
How does the Linux terminal differ from the Windows Command Prompt?
What are the basic commands for navigating directories and managing files in Linux?

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 3.1 Identify components of an OS.
3.2 Explain the purpose of operating systems.

blocks.text: While graphical interfaces make everyday tasks easy, command-line interfaces (CLIs) give you direct, powerful control over your operating system. IT professionals, developers, and system administrators use the command line to navigate file systems, manage files, troubleshoot problems, and automate repetitive tasks more efficiently than clicking through menus.

In this lesson, you will learn the basics of both the Windows Command Prompt and the Linux terminal. You will practice common commands for navigating directories, creating and deleting files and folders, and viewing directory contents. By the end of this lesson, you will be comfortable working in a text-based environment on either platform.
Windows Command Line

A Graphical User Interface (GUI), pronounced gooey, is the most common way we control a computer. Being able to use a mouse or your finger to click or double-click icons to start programs or open folders is what has made the computer more accessible to everyone.

Another way to send commands to a computer is by using a Command Line Interface (CLI). A CLI works by typing commands, then hitting Enter to execute the command. The CLI program for Windows is called Command Prompt, and it can be opened like any other program from the Start menu or the Search Bar. If a person can learn these commands and how to use them, the power of the command line is much greater than a GUI interface like File Explorer.
Here is the list of useful Windows CLI commands for managing, moving, creating, and deleting files. There are many more commands available, but this is a good place to start.
Windows Command Line Commands

Command Description dir Short for directory, the dir command displays a list of files and folders in the current directory. It's like double-clicking a folder to open it up to see what's inside. Your prompt looks like this: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s> This prompt is telling you that you are in Frank's Documents folder. To look inside the Documents folder, you type the dir command. Here is an example: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s> dir After you type dir, and press the Enter key, the files and folders inside the Documents folder are displayed on the screen. Folders are just names, and files in the directory have the filename and the file extension: Homework Memes Lyrics.docx Allowance.xlsx C:\ Users \F rank\Document s> cd The change directory command, or cd, is how you move from one folder to another or from one hard drive to another in the Command Line.
To move into the folder, you type cd a space and the name of the folder, and then press Enter.
To continue the example above, to move into the

Homework folder, you type: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s> cd Homework The prompt will show that you're in the new folder, changing it to: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> This folder has a subfolder called English. To move into that folder, it would look like this (both the command and the new prompt): C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> cd English C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k\English> To move backward, you use the cd.. command. To move back up to the Homework folder, you type and run this command: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k\English> cd..

C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> md mkdir The md or mkdir command stands for make directory. This command will create a new folder in the current location. To use it, you type md or mkdir a space the name for the new folder, and then press Enter.
You want to make a folder called Math inside

Frank's Documents folder. It would look like this: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> mkdir Math You could use the dir command to see the contents of the current folder, including the new folder: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> dir English Math Essay1.docx C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k>

Command Description copy The copy command copies files from one location to another. To use it, you type copy a space, and the name of the file you want to copy, including the file extension. You then add another space and type the name of the directory you want it copied into, and then press Enter.
For example, you could copy the Essay1.docx file in

Frank's Homework folder to the English folder. You type and run: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> copy Essay1.docx English You have made a copy of the file in the English folder. Note that as long as the destination folder is a direct subdirectory of the current folder, only the name of the folder is required. Copying the file to other locations can get more complicated. del The del command stands for delete. The del command is used to remove a file from the computer. To use it, you type del a space the name of the file you want to delete, and then press Enter.
For example, you could delete the original

Essay1.docx that you copied into another folder. You type and run: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> del Essay1.docx The file is deleted from the computer. Be very careful when using this command! rd The rd command stands for remove directory and is similar to the del command, but instead of deleting a single file, it deletes an entire folder and its contents. To use it, you type rd a space, the name of the folder you want to delete, and then press Enter.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, you could delete the Math folder from inside Frank's Homework directory: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> rd Math The folder is deleted from the computer. Be very careful when using this command!

You can use the dir command to see the contents of the folder: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> dir English C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> cls The cls command stands for clear screen. It clears the previous commands from the Command Prompt interface, making it easier to focus on what you're working on. To use it, just type cls and press Enter: C:\ Users \F rank\Document s \Home w or k> cls Linux Command Line There are many versions of the Linux Operating System, and most have custom graphical user interfaces. But one thing they all have in common is a powerful command line interface. To be able to run command-line commands in Linux, you must open a Terminal. To open a Terminal, find the search tool in the Linux GUI and type terminal, then press Enter. Once the terminal window opens, you are ready to start typing commands. Here is a list of Linux Command Line Interface commands you will use in the labs.
Linux CLI Commands
Command Description pwd At first, you may think pwd is short for password, but not in Linux. The pwd command stands for Present Working Directory. The command displays the current directory.

A user named Frank is working in his Home directory, and he types pwd and presses Enter at the command prompt; /home/Frank will display on the screen. ls The ls command is similar to the Windows dir command. It displays a list of files and directories inside a directory (folder). It's like double-clicking a folder in the graphical user interface.
In Linux, the Terminal color codes files and folders to make it easy to know what something is. Here is a common color scheme:

items: Directories are blue
Text files are white

Executable files are green touch The touch command is used to create an empty file without any content. You can use this command when you don't have data to store in the file when you create it. cd The Change Directory cd command is the same as the Windows cd command. It is the command that allows a person to move from one directory to another.

blocks.text: Like in Windows, the cd.. command allows a person to move backward through the file system. mkdir The Make Directory mkdir command is also the same as the Windows mkdir command. Use the mkdir command to make a directory (folder). cp This is the Linux copy cp command. It works the same as the Windows copy command. Use it to copy files and directories from one place to another.

An important thing to remember about the cp command is that it leaves a copy of the source file or folder; you have two copies. mv The Move mv command moves a file from one place to another. The difference between the mv command and the cp command is that the mv command removes the source file or folder and places it in the destination. You are left with one copy. rmdir The Remove Directory rmdir command deletes a directory (folder). It is similar to the Windows rd command. rm The Remove rm command can be used to delete a folder or file. It is similar to the Windows del command. clear This command clears the screen.
Command Description whoami This command displays the current user name.

items: What types of local storage do computers use, and how do SSDs, HDDs, optical drives, and
flash drives compare?
What are Storage Area Networks (SANs), Network Attached Storage (NAS), and file servers,
and how do organizations use them?
What data should you prioritize when creating backups, and why are personal files the most
important?
What is a system backup, and how do incremental backups help keep a system recoverable?
How does cloud storage provide backup solutions, and what are its limitations?
How can you restore deleted files, and why is it important to regularly test your backups?

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 2.3 Compare and contrast storage types.
5.1 Explain the value of data and information.
5.4 Explain basic data backup concepts.

blocks.text: Nearly everyone who has worked with a computer has a story about losing their data, usually at the worst possible time. Hardware failures, software problems, cyber attacks, and accidental deletions can all cause data loss. To avoid costly and uncertain recovery efforts, it's important to understand both how data is stored and how to protect it through backups.

In this lesson, you will explore the different types of local and network storage, learn which data to prioritize when creating backups, compare system and cloud backup strategies, and discover how to restore deleted files and test your backups.
Computer Storage

Computers need long-term storage to keep information when they are turned off (called persistent storage). Without it, they would lose data every time they shut down. The most common types of computer storage are also called local storage.
Connections and Transfers
Before we talk about different types of storage drives, we need to describe how data moves between the central processing unit (CPU) and memory.

Serial Advanced Technology Attachment (SA T A) is the interface and communications standard for transferring data from the motherboard to a storage drive and back again. The drive could be a mechanical hard drive, a 2.5-inch SSD, or an optical drive. The SATA standard includes a specific connection type, along with a cable and identical connectors on a motherboard and drive.
SATA is the connector used in servers, desktops, and laptop computers. SATA supports disk hot-swapping, which means you can change the drive while the computer is powered on.
This feature is often used in servers, which can't afford downtime. Motherboards usually have multiple SATA ports, letting you connect a variety of SATA-based devices.
Solid State Drives (SSD)

Desktops and laptops use a special type of flash storage called solid state drives (SSD) . SSDs are much faster and last longer than hard drives, but they are more expensive per unit of storage. Many people don’t need a lot of storage and often use cloud storage, or renting space on someone else's computer, to add more storage capacity.

SSDs connect to the motherboard using either an M.2 or SATA interface. M.2 is the hardware specification, or size and shape, of the SSD. Most people prefer M.2 because it provides a faster connection than SATA.

The motherboard and the SSD use both a connector, either M.2 or SATA, and a protocol or set of rules to transfer data. That protocol is called non-volatile memory express (NVMe) , created specifically for transferring data to and from SSDs. When you combine an M.2 connection with NVMe, you get incredibly fast data transfers.

If you add more SSDs to your computer, you can take advantage of the PCIe expansion slots and their interface. The PCIe interface is better and faster than the older SATA interface, which was mainly used for traditional hard drives or optical drives. PCIe is a computer interface used to connect high-speed parts, like video cards and other expansion cards, to the motherboard. It makes data transfer speeds to the motherboard much faster. PCIe is most commonly used with M.2 SSDs.
Hard Disk Drives (HDD)

For decades, people used hard disk drives (HDD) as the most common type of long-term storage. Hard disks store data on magnetic disks inside a protective case. Because technicians usually install hard disk drives inside computers, moving them between systems is difficult. If you need a portable hard drive, you can use an external drive that connects to the computer with a USB cable.
Hard disks can store large amounts of data, but their moving parts can fail over time or if they get shaken too much. Hard disks are relatively cheap and can hold a lot of information.

Hard disks come in two sizes: 3.5 inches and 2.5 inches. The 3.5-inch size is common in desktops, and the 2.5-inch size is common in laptops. This measurement represents the approximate diameter of the disk inside the drive. The drives spin at a set speed, with 3.5-inch HDDs spinning at 7200 revolutions per minute (RPM) and 2.5-inch HDDs spinning at 5400 RPM.
The capacity of an HDD keeps increasing, with some of the biggest drives holding over 20TB.
To give you an idea of how much that is, songs in MP3 format are about 1 MB per minute. With 20TB, you could hold 5,000,000 songs! As technology improves, these numbers will likely get even bigger.
Optical Drives

Desktop computers and some laptops used to include an optical drive. Optical drives store information using light instead of magnetism. They read microscopic light and dark spots on the bottom surface of disks to represent binary 1s and 0s. You can install three types of optical drives in a computer or connect them externally using a USB connection. Those three types of optical drives are CD-ROM, DVD, and Blu-ray.

Optical drives are backwards-compatible with older optical disks. This means that newer technologies can read older types of storage. For example, a DVD drive can also read CD-ROM disks. Similarly, a Blu-ray drive can read both DVD and CD-ROM disks. However, an optical drive specifically designed for CD-ROMs will not be able to read the newer Blu-ray disks.

Optical disks can store a lot of data. Blu-rays can hold 25GB, DVDs can hold 4.7GB (some can double this capacity), and CDs can hold 700MB. The downside of optical media is that they are slow to read and write. Optical discs are also susceptible to physical damage; if the bottom of a disc gets scratched, the computer may not be able to read it. Optical discs come in both read-only and read-write formats. Writing information to a read-write disc (called burning) can be slow.
Flash Drives

Flash storage uses special non-volatile memory chips to store data. This means you can remove power from a flash storage device and its contents will stay intact. The most common flash drives connect to a computer via USB ports, either USB Type A or USB Type C.

Once you connect a flash storage device and the operating system recognizes it, you can store data on it and read data from it, just like with an internal drive. Flash memory devices have the following advantages:

items: Portability: You can easily move a flash storage device from one system to another. (In

blocks.text: Windows, make sure to eject the device before unplugging it from the USB port or card reader.)

items: Capacity: They provide a lot of storage capacity in a small physical package.
Flexibility: Flash storage works well in many devices, including digital cameras, smartphones, digital camcorders, and tablets.

blocks.text: External Hard Drives
You can connect external hard drives to computers to add more storage space. For desktops and laptops, you usually use a USB Type A or USB Type C connector.
External drives come with a case that protects the drive and provides access to the connection ports. The capacity of an external drive can range from 500 GB to over 10 TB.
Network and Shared Storage

Organizations generate and collect large amounts of data that must be stored, managed, and backed up. Depending on their needs and regulatory requirements, some organizations must retain data for extended periods. Several network-based storage solutions help businesses manage this data efficiently.
Storage Area Networks (SAN)

Typically, businesses and organizations keep the servers and network equipment in the same office as the employees. But if they have a lot of data, or multiple business locations, they may need many servers. To make things easier, they could set up one centralized location away from the office to manage and back up all this information.

The IT department can set up Storage Area Networks (SAN) so everyone who needs the data can access it quickly through high-speed Internet connections. In these cases, users won't even know the data is stored somewhere else.
SANs are fast-moving networks that let server computers share large amounts of data with each other. They also have special equipment so people can tap into their apps and programs.

SANs are great for putting all the storage from different computers into one place. It's common for them to connect in with fiber cables so that the data inside will travel extremely fast. SANs communicate on a block level, which is a more direct and speedy way, breaking up data into chunks so it can be found quickly.
Network Attached Storage (NAS)

A network attached storage (NAS) is a smaller scale version of a SAN. These boxes connect to a local area network (LAN) using a wired Ethernet connection. Once connected, users on the same network can see and access shared files and folders. A NAS usually has multiple hard drives set up in a configuration called a redundant array of independent disks (RAID) . This setup helps prevent data loss if one of the drives fails. For extra protection, a backup solution stores the same data somewhere else, preferably off-site.
File Servers

Powerful computers or servers were first used as file servers, putting all necessary information in one place. Once set up, IT decides who gets access to what data. File sharing was a powerful feature even before the rise of the Internet. The data could also be easily backed up. Imagine backing up a single computer; it's not too hard. But backing up each individual workstation would be much more difficult. A server is a powerful computer expected to be up, or working, almost all the time, often referred to as 24/7 or 99.9% of the time. This feature is essential for keeping workers productive.
What Data Should I Back Up?

Most people understand the importance of saving copies of their data files somewhere in case of an emergency. This is called "backing them up." To do this, you make a copy and put it in a different location. If there is a major event, such as a cyber attack or a hard disk failure, you have a way to get all your valuable information back, or at least a good portion of it. The problem is that making duplicate copies can take a lot of time and effort, so many people don't do it regularly. That's unfortunate because it's much easier to save electronic data than paper files.
File Backups

Users can often confuse backing up a file with having a copy of the file. They might move, but not copy important files to an external USB flash drive, often because they don't fully understand the importance of backups. Simply moving the file would delete the file from their computer and move it to the USB drive. Later, when the external USB drive fails, the user loses the data completely because it was saved only on the USB drive. The second location could easily have been the original computer where the data was created.

Backing up files is all about saving what users create. These are the most important parts of computer backups. For example, an employee might spend hours working on a report or creating an animation; these are the things you want to back up. The rest of the computer (like its operating system and apps) can be reinstalled, but once files are lost, they are gone for good.
Backup the Essentials

The good thing is that you don't need to back up operating system files one by one because they aren't critical. If the OS crashes, reinstalling it is relatively simple. The same goes for programs; reinstalling them is usually easy, too. This is even more true now that software is available online instead of on physical media like DVDs. You can usually log in to your online account and download the program again.

However, you may want to keep the customizations you made to a certain program. It is smart to back these up separately if possible. Then you can merge the changes with the replaced program after you restore it.
Think about how important your personal files are. What would happen if you lost one? How would you get it back? Your personal data files are difficult or even impossible to recreate.

Losing a school project would be frustrating because you'd have to type it all over again. Even worse would be losing family vacation photos from years ago; you can't go back and take those pictures again.
System Backups

In addition to backing up your data files, it's also important to back up your whole computer system. Setting up a computer takes time. You need to install the operating system, all the updates, the hardware drivers, the necessary programs, and any settings to make the system run well. Because this takes so much effort, saving everything with a system backup makes it much easier to recover your computer if something goes wrong.

Regularly backing up your entire computer is more complicated than just copying some folders or files to an external hard drive. System backups usually involve creating a fully bootable disk image. This means taking a full snapshot of your system at a given time. If you manage to do that successfully, you'd follow up with incremental backups. Most of the operating system, applications, and other files don't change much on a day-to-day basis. Incremental backups only save the files that have been added or changed since the last backup occurred. If your system crashes because of a failed hard drive or virus, you can restore it by using the last full backup and then all the incremental backups made since then.

Another benefit to making a full system backup is that it preserves all your important data and application settings. If you back up all the key data folders, such as Documents, Pictures, Desktop, and other user folders, your system will likely be fine. However, occasionally a user saves their personal data in a less common location. Employees at companies with IT departments need to take care not to save their important data in a less common location, such as creating a folder called "My Stuff" on the root C: drive without the technician knowing.
Otherwise, the data might not get backed up.

Something to think about as a technician is how much time a fix will take and, just as importantly, how much of your personal time will it take? If a system recovery is an hour, but you only need to spend five minutes to get it started and then can let it complete on its own, that free time can be spent on other tasks.
Cloud Backups

The rise of cloud storage, or using space on another computer through the Internet, has changed the way many businesses back up their data. In some cases, cloud storage can fill the need for a company to have an offsite backup location. It offers a convenient, flexible, and scalable option compared to traditional backup methods. However, one downside is that cloud backups need a lot of network bandwidth and a reliable Internet connection. This means that backing up and restoring data from the cloud can take much longer than using local storage devices.
Cloud storage solutions are increasingly common for both homes and businesses alike.
Companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft give users some free cloud storage space when they use their products. There are also business-oriented options like Dropbox and Amazon.

You can use these services with a web browser or an app on your smartphone or tablet. On Windows 10, there's a built-in cloud storage service called OneDrive, which you can access through File Explorer.
Backup Services in Business

Backup services like Carbonite are very popular, especially for businesses where data continuity is crucial for daily operations. Carbonite installs a program on the user's computer and automatically backs up any files or folders it's told to. Businesses see investing in cloud storage as similar to buying insurance; they want to prevent anything that could halt their operations and cost them money. The storage cost is usually considered part of their other business expenses. Storing the data off-site is the most beneficial aspect of this investment. If something is lost or deleted at the main location, there's now a way to get it back.

Very large businesses don't always make a full copy of an individual user's computer. Instead, all users' data is stored in the cloud. If a laptop is then lost or stolen, for example, the owner can get a new one with the company's basic setup. With Microsoft System Center Configuration Manager, setting up a new laptop or desktop is incredibly fast, taking about 30 minutes from start to finish. A user just signs in to the new computer, logs in to OneDrive, and their files are restored.
Microsoft also saves all user settings, such as browser bookmarks, email signatures, and desktop backgrounds, in the cloud so the user can easily move from one computer to another.

Users can be living far away, get a new laptop shipped to them, and then just sign in to set everything up with a fresh install of Windows. This makes things easy for the IT staff, the executives, and the employees.
Restoring Data

Operating systems give you a second chance with deleted files by adding an extra step before they're completely removed. In Windows, the Recycle Bin, and in macOS, the Trash, move files out of your main folders but keep them just in case you want them back.

There is a key difference between Microsoft and Apple when it comes to deleting applications, however. On Apple computers, you can drag unwanted applications to the Trash, and you can still get them back if you change your mind. On Windows, when you delete an application from within Settings, it's gone for good and doesn't go to the Recycle Bin.

You can also skip the Recycle Bin/Trash and permanently delete files and folders by holding down certain keys. On Windows, press Shift + Delete. On macOS, press Option + Command keys (next to the spacebar) while hitting delete. You can also drag the item to the Trash in the lower right corner of the screen. Both operating systems have different icons to show a full bin with at least one item inside, and they change to an empty bin when there's nothing in there.
Backup Testing
You'll want to test your backups from time to time to make sure they're working properly.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: Imagine thinking that you'd been backing up all your files for months, only to find out that a really important personal file was never saved! Here are some things to look at when testing your backups:
items: Error Detection: Problems with the backup media (the physical parts of the backup device) or with their configurations can cause backup failures. Depending on the error, the whole backup might be canceled, or some data might not go through. Backup software usually has ways to check if the backup worked and will report errors in a log file. This makes the backup process take longer, but generally that time doesn't interfere with work because most backups are done during off-hours, like in the middle of the night. In the end, it's well worth the trouble.
Configuration: When you create a new backup job (and periodically after that), it's a good idea to make sure that all the data is there as planned and being backed up as expected.

Test Restore: It's also a good idea to test if you can successfully restore your backups. Do this in all cases. When you get new backup software, when you test old backup media, when you check a new backup job, or if you just do random spot checks to save time. When you do a test restore, you should save the data to a different folder so you don't accidentally overwrite what's already there.

What is Software?

system (OS) reads and follows these instructions. It's important to know that application
software is made for a specific operating system. Most of the time, it's made for Microsoft

But there's also a lot of software made for Apple's macOS and Linux systems, too.

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 3.3 Explain the purpose and proper use of software.

blocks.text: Software is what makes computers, phones, and other devices useful. From writing a document to streaming a movie, every task you perform on a device relies on some type of application.
Understanding the different categories of software and what they are designed to do is an important part of being comfortable with technology.

In this lesson, you will explore the major types of software people use every day, including productivity suites, communication and collaboration tools, diagramming and graphics applications, entertainment and gaming software, and educational platforms. You will also learn how cloud-based software works, why learning one program helps you pick up others, and how remote assistance tools allow technicians to support users from anywhere.

Software is a set of instructions that tells a computer what to do. The computer's operating system (OS) reads and follows these instructions. It's important to know that application software is made for a specific operating system. Most of the time, it's made for Microsoft Windows, because that's the most popular OS in the world. If a software developer wants to make a lot of money, then Windows is the safest bet, because over 1 billion devices are using it!
But there's also a lot of software made for Apple's macOS and Linux systems, too.
Smartphone Applications

Smartphone applications, or apps, started coming out in the 2000s and have become a $200 billion business. Just like software for computers, mobile apps include productivity tools, social media, and games. But they're designed to work better on mobile devices, which have smaller touchscreens.

Some things are suited perfectly for mobile phones, like instant messaging apps. Before everyone had phones in their pockets, something similar existed for computers, but it was a little bit more clunky. If you got a new message, you couldn't just pull your phone out and respond; you had to go to your desktop computer to use the app.
Screenshot reprinted with permission from Apple Inc.

The same is true of entertainment. Streaming video and audio from our phones lets you watch movies and TV shows, or listen to our favorite songs, wherever you are. Social media apps are also very popular on mobile devices. You can share stories and pictures with your friends and family, or comment on a classmate's status. Mobile games are fun, simple ways to pass the time, and navigation apps help us to not get lost.

Additionally, you don't even have to go into the bank to know how much you have in your account or to pay your bills. It's all available on your bank's finance app. Many large companies will have their own apps as well, making it easier for customers to use their services.
What is Productivity Software?
Productivity software helps people create documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and more.
These tools save time by replacing manual processes with digital workflows.
Commercial Software

Microsoft Office is a widely used productivity suite that includes Word for documents, Excel for spreadsheets, PowerPoint for presentations, and Outlook for email. Microsoft also offers online versions of these tools. Apple provides its own free suite for Mac users, including Pages, Numbers, and Keynote.
Free Software

Google offers a free suite with word processing and spreadsheet tools that support real-time collaboration on shared documents. Open-source alternatives like OpenOffice and LibreOffice provide similar functionality to Microsoft Office and run on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
SaaS and Web-Based Software

Many of the productivity tools discussed earlier are available as both installed software and web-based applications. Instead of installing a program on your hard drive, you can access it through a web browser. This model is called Software as a Service, or SaaS.
How SaaS Works

With SaaS, the application runs on a cloud server rather than on your local device. You access it through a browser like Chrome, Edge, or Firefox. Because the processing happens in the cloud, SaaS apps can run on almost any device with an internet connection, regardless of its operating system. This makes it easy to switch between a desktop computer, a laptop, and a phone without losing your work.
Benefits and Drawbacks

SaaS applications are convenient because they do not take up storage space on your device and are always kept up to date by the provider. They also make it easy to collaborate with others in real time. However, they require an internet connection to work, and many charge a monthly or yearly subscription fee. If you stop paying, you may lose access to the software and the files stored within it.
Common Examples
Google Workspace (including Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides) and Microsoft 365 (online versions of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint) are two of the most widely used SaaS platforms.
Other examples include project management tools, email services, and even design applications. As internet speeds continue to improve, more software is moving to the web- based model.
Software for Every Job
You may have noticed a theme. Different types of work need different software. Even with these differences there is a lot of common ground across software types.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, many types of employees need Internet access to do their jobs. Email is a given because it's an easy way to share ideas and objectives with others in the company. Online collaboration has become a normal part of a job, and is, or will become, common across industries.

Hospitals have special software for medical staff. This software is crucial because it stores patient records. Auto mechanics use software to keep track of repairs and expenses. They also look up diagrams for replacing parts on different cars. The banking industry has specialized software to help calculate current interest rates. Event planners have their own types of applications. There is literally software available for every type of job.

But remember, if it all seems daunting to learn about so many different programs, learning one is like learning many. You'll almost certainly be able to transfer your knowledge to another program or another industry. No time is wasted; what's important is to get started and to try to have fun while doing it.

As a technician, you'll use your knowledge to help a company with its software needs. In large companies, different departments might use programs that other departments don't. Having a basic grasp of the software that exists will help you keep the office running smoothly for management and allow you to excel at your job much faster.
Diagramming and Graphics Software
Diagramming software is made for a specific purpose, so you may not encounter it as often.

It's used to make visual representations of projects, in other words, diagrams. For example, flowcharts can illustrate a project's steps so a team can understand the process better. Some of this software is used in IT departments to create network diagrams for large networking projects. Diagrams are great for helping everyone understand the structure of a project or task and stay on the same page.
Digital Whiteboards

Online whiteboards are perfect for brainstorming together as a team. Miro is an example of an online workspace where everyone can add to team whiteboards. It doesn't have to be just text; it can be pictures, videos, and links to other websites. Miro's goal is to make remote work as productive and collaborative as face-to-face work. It also works great during times of remote learning in schools because teachers and students can work on the whiteboards as if they were in the classroom.

Lucidchart is a popular web-based app that makes it easy to create charts, whether they are simple or complex. Since everyone can see the charts, it's easier to get a better idea of the scope of the project. Both Miro and Lucidchart have mobile apps for Android and iOS devices.
While it's nice to be able to view charts on your phone, the small screens can make it hard to see complex diagrams clearly.
Digital Imaging Software

Imaging software helps you capture, edit, and process digital pictures. Common tasks include cropping, resizing, rotating, adjusting brightness and contrast, and adding text or design elements. You can preview changes and compare the original with the edited version before saving.
Video Software

Digital video editing software ranges from professional tools like Adobe Premiere and Final Cut Pro to free options like iMovie and Microsoft Clipchamp. Most computers come bundled with basic video editing software that can handle common home projects. Smartphone apps and built-in social media editors also provide quick mobile editing options.
Digital Image Facts

One of the most amazing developments in computer technology is the ability to create and display high-quality images. Before computers, photographers shot pictures onto film, which had to be developed in a laboratory before the pictures could be printed on paper. Now, anyone with a smartphone can take a photograph and instantly share it with someone on the other side of the planet.
Image 1: RGB Colors
RGB Display
Computer monitors are made up of tiny red, green, and blue lights called an RGB display.

Each set of three lights is called a pixel. By combining these primary colors of light at varying brightness levels, each pixel can display any color on the visible spectrum. Combining two colors produces the secondary colors: red and green make yellow, red and blue make magenta, and green and blue make cyan.
Raster vs. Vector Images

There are two main types of digital images. Raster (or bitmap) images store the color of each individual pixel, making them ideal for detailed photographs. However, raster files use a lot of storage space and become pixelated when scaled up. Vector graphics store points and curves instead of individual pixels, making them scalable without losing quality. Vectors are commonly used for logos and fonts, but they require specialized software to create and usually lack the fine detail of raster images.

Digital Sound & Video

In the early days of recording, sound and video had to be recorded and stored using analog methods, which means they had to physically represent the images and sound waves they wanted to record. If you’ve ever seen a movie played from a film reel or listened to a vinyl record, you’ve experienced analog recording. Today, however, most sound and video are recorded digitally, which means they are encoded as ones and zeros.
Digital Sound

Sound is caused by vibrating objects that create pressure waves in the air. Digital recordings capture this continuous wave by dividing it into discrete segments, each assigned a value called a sample height. Bit depth determines how much memory stores each sample (e.g., 8-bit vs.
16-bit), while sampling rate measures how many samples are taken per second. Most modern recordings use 44.1 kHz and 16-bit depth for high-quality audio.
Digital Video

Videos consist of a sequence of still images (frames) shown in rapid succession. Frame rate measures how many frames are displayed per second, with most digital video running at about 30 fps. Resolution measures the pixel dimensions of each frame; higher resolution means a clearer image. Color depth determines how many colors each pixel can display. Eight-bit color supports 256 colors per pixel, while 24-bit color supports millions.
Communication Software

Beyond productivity and creative tools, some of the most commonly used software is designed for communication. Whether you are sending a quick message to a friend or coordinating a project with coworkers, communication software keeps people connected.
Email

Email remains one of the most widely used forms of digital communication. Providers like Microsoft Outlook, Google Gmail, Apple iCloud, and Yahoo Mail let users send and receive messages, attach files, and integrate with calendar applications. Email is essential in both personal and professional settings for sharing information and keeping records of conversations.
Messaging Applications

Instant messaging apps allow users to send quick text-based messages from a phone or computer. Common examples include SMS text messaging, Apple iMessage, WhatsApp, and Slack. These tools support both one-on-one and group conversations, making them a fast alternative to email for everyday communication.
Video Conferencing

Video conferencing tools like Zoom, Microsoft Teams, and Google Meet allow people to hold face-to-face meetings over the internet. These tools are especially important for remote workers and students who need to participate in meetings or classes from different locations.
Most video conferencing apps also support screen sharing, chat, and recording.
Collaboration Software

Collaboration just means to work together. Collaboration software is software that helps everyone work together effectively when it comes to technology. The goal is to make it easy for groups of people to focus on a common goal or task. This is especially important today, when it's more common that coworkers or classmates aren't in the same location.
Communication Apps

There are many software tools available for improving teamwork, such as Slack, Microsoft Teams, Google Workspace, and more. The essential features of these apps are the Instant Messaging and video conferencing, which makes working remotely much easier.

These apps are crucial for filling in that face-to-face communication gap. A Zoom call can take the place of a meeting in the conference room, and a team Slack channel can substitute for the water cooler talk that lets coworkers get to know each other. Remote work saves companies money by reducing the need for office space and personnel, so even though it's a little more complicated, it's in their interest to find ways to replace the interpersonal communication that used to happen at the office and keep everyone feeling involved.

"To Zoom" has become a verb in its own right, meaning to have a video conference call. The biggest problem with a Zoom call is dealing with the different time zones of people working in different parts of the United States or the world. For example, if some people are on the East Coast and others are on the West Coast, there's a three-hour time difference between them.

When the East Coasters are leaving for lunch, the West Coasters are just starting their day. It gets even harder when some people are in North America, and others are in Europe, Asia, or Africa. Think of the 12- to 14-hour time difference between the United States and China. It could be noon in one place and midnight in the other. But then again, you can work in your pajamas no matter what time of day it is!
File Sharing

An early part of working together online was file sharing. You could upload a file to a cloud storage service, and then email a link to someone so they could access it. Services like Dropbox, OneDrive (which used to be called SkyDrive), and iCloud have been offering this for over a decade. They let you store a limited amount of files for free, but if you need more space, you can pay a small monthly fee.

The benefit to this is that it's so easy to share large files this way. Email services usually limit attachments to about 25 MB. Also, sharing files in the cloud is better than emailing them back and forth. You can work on a file while automatically saving it to the cloud. And the person you shared it with can make changes without waiting for you to send it back. This way, you know that you're always working on the most up-to-date version, which isn't always the case with email.

Cloud service providers also keep older versions of files in storage, so you can go back to an earlier version if you need to. For example, you mess something up enough that it's better to just start over from an earlier point. Since there are backups, you don't have to worry about losing something forever. There's probably going to be some version of a file that you can retrieve if something happens to your local computer, like an accidental deletion, ransomware, or a system crash.
Collaboration Tool

One of the main reasons computers are so commonly used in businesses is how easy they make it for groups of people to work together on a project. The table below describes some common digital collaboration tools.
Table 23: Collaboration Tools
Term Description
Discussion Boards Online forums where users hold topic-based discussions in threads.
Threads start with an original post, and responses appear below in order.
Screen Sharing Allows users to transmit their screen to others in real time. This is especially useful for technical support and remote troubleshooting.
Webinars Online presentations where one user projects their screen to remote viewers. Commonly used to present to large audiences simultaneously.
Resource Management Software that helps teams divide projects into smaller tasks, assign them to individuals with due dates and instructions, and track overall progress.
Collaborative Editing Lets multiple users work on the same document, presentation, or spreadsheet simultaneously. Many tools are web-based and run through a browser.
Calendaring Online calendars that help teams coordinate schedules by showing when each member is busy or available for meetings.
Gaming and Media Software
Software is not only used for work and communication. Entertainment software is a major category of applications that people use every day for streaming media, sharing content, and playing games.
Video and Audio Streaming

Video streaming services let users watch movies, television shows, and user-created content on demand. Audio streaming services provide access to music, podcasts, and audiobooks. The content available varies by platform, and most services offer both free and paid subscription options. Because streaming delivers media over the internet, it does not require downloading large files to your device.
Gaming Software

Gaming is one of the largest segments of the software industry. Games are available on computers, smartphones, tablets, and dedicated gaming consoles. Online gaming services connect players across the globe, and most are tied to a specific hardware platform or PC storefront. Mobile games range from simple puzzle apps to complex multiplayer experiences, making gaming accessible to a wide audience.
Social Media

Social media platforms allow users to share photos, videos, and updates with friends, family, and the public. Many social media apps also include built-in tools for editing images and videos before posting. These platforms are available on both mobile devices and desktop computers, and they often combine entertainment with communication features.
Educational Software

In addition to entertainment, software plays a major role in education. From online courses to interactive study tools, educational software helps people learn new skills at their own pace and from virtually any location.
Learning Management Systems
A learning management system (LMS) is a platform that delivers and tracks educational content.

Schools and businesses use LMS platforms like Canvas, Blackboard, and Google Classroom to distribute assignments, host discussions, and record grades. These systems make it possible for instructors and students to interact, whether they are in the same room or on opposite sides of the world.
Online Learning Platforms

Online learning platforms offer courses on a wide range of subjects, from programming and graphic design to business and science. Many platforms provide video lessons, quizzes, and hands-on labs that let learners practice what they have studied. Some courses are free, while others charge a fee or offer certificates upon completion.
Study and Reference Tools

There are also many apps designed to help with studying and research. Flashcard apps, note-taking tools, and citation managers help students organize information and prepare for exams. Reference tools like digital encyclopedias and translation apps provide quick access to information on almost any topic. Together, these tools make it easier to stay organized and make the most of study time.

Why is it important to remove unused software from your system?
