blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.

blocks.text: Whether you are managing a personal device or working in IT, knowing how to find, install, and remove software safely is essential. Software is available from many sources, including app stores, publisher websites, and third-party download sites, but not all of them are trustworthy.
Downloading from the wrong place can expose your system to viruses, malware, and other security threats.

In this lesson, you will learn how to identify safe sources for software, understand how app stores review and distribute apps, and explore different types of software licensing. You will also walk through the steps for installing software on both Apple and Windows systems, and learn when and how to remove software you no longer need.

For the first few decades that personal computers were available, software was sold only at physical shops. Retail stores had a few programs on floppy or compact disc (CDs) you could buy, while stores that specialized in computers and tech had a bigger selection. As the Internet became more popular, people began to download their favorite programs more often than they bought packaged software. Software companies actually liked this change because it saved them money. They didn't have to manufacture CDs, put them in fancy boxes, and ship them out to stores anymore.
Know Your Sources
Walking into stores and going through shelves full of software back in those days could be fun.
You never knew what you were going to find. Shopping online for software now can be fun, too.

However, when you work in IT or manage your own system, it's important to make sure that the software you download is coming from a trustworthy source. The last thing you want is to be the one who accidentally brought a virus onto the company network, or who let the home network get hacked.

When shopping online, you can be sure your software is safe and malware-free by getting that software directly from the source. Make sure you're on the software producer's website, and you know your purchase will be safe. Sometimes, threat actors create fake websites that look similar to the real ones, often by using a misspelled version of the correct site's name. Luckily, these fake sites usually don't copy the real site's content. Instead, they use other tricks to make money off of you, such as getting you to download harmful programs onto your computer.
There are so many programs available for download these days that it can get overwhelming.

Like most people, you'll probably search the web for answers. This is another place where problems can arise, so make sure to go over a website carefully before proceeding with its suggestions. Just visiting a website won't harm your computer, but clicking on a pop-up window or downloading a file can. Trust your instincts and just exit the site if something feels off. If you're unsure, pop open a new tab in your browser and look for reviews about the site or product. If the top results show a lot of issues or complaints, look for something else.
Remember, there are so many companies competing to make the best software out there that there will almost always be another option.
Trusted Sources for Software

Programs on tablets and phones are called apps. You might have some that came pre-installed, and you might have downloaded others from the mobile app store. These online stores offer all kinds of content, like games, productivity tools, photo-editing software, and more. The apps will be organized in categories, with each one having its own icon, like a book cover. You can also read reviews about them from other customers in the app store or by searching online.
What Is an App Store?

An app store is a platform where users can search for and download a variety of apps for different devices. In most app stores, the majority of apps are free, but there are some that you have to purchase. One exciting thing about these stores is that they're constantly being updated with new content to explore. When you open an app store, you'll see a home page with suggestions, new releases, and popular downloads.
Major companies like Apple and Google have their own app stores for their smartphones and tablets. The apps available in these stores are chosen by the company that runs the store.

This means that before an app is released, it goes through a review process to make sure it works well with the company's devices, is of good quality, and doesn't have any harmful or inappropriate content.
Because of this review process, app stores are one of the safest ways to install software.

The Microsoft Store, Google Play Store, and Apple App Store all work to ensure that only trusted apps are available for download or purchase, reducing the risk of accidentally installing malicious software.
App Distribution

Downloading an app is easy. First, you need to create an account that links your device to the specific app store. Once you find the app you want, you'll be able to click a 'Get' button or something similar. Then the app will be installed on the device. Usually, if you've purchased an app, it's yours to keep. This means that you can delete it from your device and re-download it later without paying again. This is nice for when you get a new phone because you can log back into your account, and your apps will automatically download to the new one.
Another feature of app stores is that they provide updates when developers release them.
These updates are meant to fix bugs or address complaints users have made. Sometimes, developers also add new content and features to keep people interested in their product.
Updating is done through the app store, which usually has a section for this purpose. These updates are almost always included in the original purchase price.
Common App Stores
Apple's App Store is the main place to get content for products like the iPad, iPhone, and Mac computers. It connects with a user's Apple ID to share content across all their Apple devices.

There are actually two app stores in the Apple world: one for mobile devices running iOS and one for computers running macOS. These stores also offer digital media like music, videos, eBooks, and podcasts.

Amazon not only sells physical products but also offers a variety of apps for its own devices and tablets. These include the Kindle line of products and smart devices like Alexa smart speakers. Some Amazon apps can be used on different platforms, including the Kindle Reader.

Google Play is the main place to get content for Android and Google devices. In 2012, it combined several separate digital stores, including Books, Games, Movies & TV, and Music, into one big store that offered all these apps together. It comes pre-installed on Android phones and tablets and has a huge selection of programs that are easy to find and add.

The Microsoft Store (formerly called the Windows Store) offers apps for computers and devices running Windows or using Microsoft technology. This includes Windows tablets and all versions of Microsoft's gaming platform, Xbox. When Windows 10 came out, Microsoft combined several different digital stores into one. This new store includes the Windows Marketplace, Windows Phone Store, Xbox Music, Xbox Video, and Xbox Store. You can download media directly onto an Xbox system just like you can with other Microsoft products.
Software Licensing

You might not think too much about whether the software you install on your computer or phone is properly licensed. As an individual, you may feel like a small fish in a big ocean of consumers. But when you work in an IT department with hundreds of computers, following software licensing rules is an important business concern. Software publishers don’t appreciate, and can prosecute, people who use their products without paying for them. A license is a type of receipt that permits you to run the product you paid for. Installing unlicensed software breaks copyright laws. You can be fined for this behavior. Beyond that, it's simply wrong.

When you first install a software program, you have to read and agree to the rules for using it, which is called the End User License Agreement (EULA) . These rules can be different for different programs, but usually, they say that you can only install that particular software program on one machine. That's why you need to be extra careful if you're in charge of an office environment where all the machines need to have the same piece of software installed.

The good news is that software makers don't expect large companies to buy individual copies for each person. Instead, they offer companies a blanket or site license, which lets them install the software on as many computers as they need for one price. This makes things easier for the IT department because they don't have to keep track of licenses for every single computer.
Subscription Model

A big change in software ownership over the years has been the shift to monthly subscription plans. Developers came to realize that they could end up making more money this way. Before this model became popular, many consumers would buy the software and not upgrade to a new version (and pay for that new version) for a long time. With a subscription plan, you pay every month and always get the latest version and updates. You can also expect better security and performance, and direct access to the software's tech support team.
Product Keys and Serial Numbers

A common way to link purchased software to its owner is by using a key or serial number specific to that product or license. These keys or numbers are long strings of unique letters and numbers given out after purchase to prove ownership. Usually, you must enter this key or serial number when you install the software, which also registers it with the developer. In the past, you would find these keys somewhere in the box or on the label of the CD case. Nowadays, most licenses are emailed out. The main purpose of these keys is to help prevent piracy.
Open Source vs. Proprietary
Since the early days of computers, there's been a small industry of independent programmers creating free-to-use software programs. This is known as freeware or open-source software.

Open source means that the code used can be viewed and even modified by anyone. So if you know how to program, you can change the source code to make the software look or work differently. You can even add on your own features. In addition to that, if you change something, you can redistribute your modified version to others. There are some open-source licensing rules you'd need to follow, but they're much less restrictive than rules created by big companies.

In fact, open-source software is usually a collaborative effort. Programmers from around the world all add their own touches to the code until there's a final product. One of the most common examples of open-source software is the Linux operating system.

On the other hand, there is proprietary software, which is made by companies that sell it for profit. Some of the well-known companies that make proprietary computer and gaming software are Microsoft, Adobe, Sony, and Oracle. To use their products, you need to buy a license and agree to their terms and conditions.
Piracy

Software piracy occurs when someone makes or shares copies of a software program without permission. It is illegal to use these unauthorized copies, known as pirated copies. Pirated software is dangerous because it can have viruses hidden inside, or the program might have been changed in ways that make it less stable and more likely to crash. This creates a big security risk and is a major concern for IT departments. If you use pirated software, you will not get security updates or support for the product. There are also serious legal risks, like the possibility of lawsuits and significant financial penalties.
Installing Software
Most software installs in the same basic way. Not every app will have all these same steps, but this is the most common method.
1. First, you'll open the program and agree to the license agreement.
2. Next, you're asked where on the system you want it installed.
3. Then, you click to start the installation.
4. Finally, the software installs in a few seconds.

Sometimes you may need to restart your computer to finalize it. After the software is installed, there are often settings you can change. It's a good idea to adjust these early on to get the best use out of the application.
While these steps give you the general outline, there are some differences between the major manufacturers.
Apple Software
Apple computers have three common ways to install software.

items: The App Store: The App Store is Apple's official place for iOS and macOS apps, where you can browse through millions of choices. The nice thing is that Apple checks these apps for security and compatibility.

Installation packages: A lot of Apple software for macOS comes as installation packages with a .pkg file extension. You can download these packages from the developer's website or from websites that aggregate or collect software.

Disk image files: Software might be distributed as a disk image file (.dmg). You can download these files from the developer's website as well. When you open a .dmg file, it mounts a disk image onto your computer. You can then drag and drop the software into your

blocks.text: Applications folder to install it.
Windows Software

There's a wider variety of websites that offer software for Microsoft Windows, compared to what's available for Apple. It's common practice to visit a publisher's site to get software. Some websites collect all kinds of software in one place. Be sure to review these websites to ensure they are reputable.

Installing software on Windows has been pretty much the same process for a while now. Most files come as an .exe, which is an executable file. After you download it, you double-click on the file to start the installation. On Windows 11, the software is usually saved in one of two folders: Program Files or Program Files (x86). You'll see a series of prompts, like the license terms and choosing the installation location. Sometimes, you might need to restart your computer after the installation is done.

You can also install apps directly from the Microsoft Store, which comes preinstalled with Windows. The Microsoft Store verifies apps for security and compatibility, making it one of the safest ways to add software to your system.
The x86 in program files is in reference to 32-bit software, which goes back to the x86 architecture on Intel processors from decades ago.
Downloading Software Safely

Before installing an app downloaded from the internet, make sure the website or publisher is a trusted source. Download the installation file and scan it for viruses and other malware before running it. Most anti-malware programs, like Windows Defender, will scan downloaded files automatically. When you're confident the file is safe, run it and follow the on-screen instructions.

In some cases, you may still encounter software distributed on a CD or DVD. To install from a disc, insert it into the drive and follow the on-screen prompts. If the installation doesn't begin automatically, you may need to adjust your computer's AutoPlay settings. After a disc-based installation, check the vendor's website for any available updates.
Removing Software

Sometimes you install software on your device, and for whatever reason, it just sits there unused and forgotten. In IT, it's a good practice to remove any unused software. This can help you avoid potential threats that could end up harming your network. Old programs can be a security risk because they might no longer receive updates. Also, keeping unused software can cause issues with license compliance, so in most cases it's better to just remove it.
Another reason to remove unused software is to free up storage space on your hard drive.
Getting rid of these programs can improve your system's performance. Many programs run in the background and use up resources, which can slow your computer down.
Different manufacturers have their own ways of removing unwanted software.

items: Apple: On Apple's macOS, you just drag and drop. Find the app you don't need anymore in your Applications folder, click and grab the icon, and then drag it to the trash can in the bottom right of your screen. If you change your mind and haven't emptied the trash yet, you can go back into the trash can and then drag it back to your Applications folder. It will work just like before.

Windows: With Windows, removing an app requires a few more steps. First, open Settings and go to Apps. Find the app you want to remove and click the three dots on the right. Then choose the option to Uninstall. (Cer t ain programs can't be uninstalled; they only have the option to "Modify").

blocks.text: If an app is being stubborn and won't uninstall the normal way, which does happen occasionally, you can use special software to help. One of the best tools for this is Revo Uninstaller.
Some computers come out of the box with extra software and trial versions (unkindly referred to as "bloatware"). Once you know you don't need these programs, you should remove them, too.
If a software program stops working, the best solution is often to uninstall it and then reinstall it.
Some programs have a "Repair" option, which can be faster and preserve your custom settings.
You might also see a "Change" option, which lets you add or remove parts of the program to your liking.

blocks.text: Digital document creation is one of the most common uses for a computer. Whether you are writing an academic paper, drafting a letter, or designing a poster, word processing software gives you the tools to create, format, and edit text documents with ease.

In this lesson, you will learn what a word processor is and explore popular word processing applications, including Microsoft Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice Writer, and Apple Pages. You will discover how these programs differ in cost, features, and collaboration capabilities, and learn about mobile word processing options for working on the go.
Word Processing Software

Word processors like Microsoft Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice Writer, and Apple Pages are available as desktop applications and browser-based tools. The following image shows a typical word processor interface in Microsoft Word.
Everyday Uses for Word Processors
Word processors are not just for writing essays. Here are some ways you might use one in everyday life:

items: Resumes and cover letters — Format a professional-looking resume with headings, bullet points, and consistent styling.
Letters and memos — Draft formal or informal correspondence for work, school, or personal use.
Reports and research papers — Organize long documents with headers, page numbers, footnotes, and a table of contents.
Flyers and posters — Combine text, images, and shapes to create simple marketing materials.
Notes and outlines — Jot down meeting notes or build an outline before starting a bigger project.

blocks.text: Common Word Processing File Formats
Word processing files come in different formats depending on the software that created them.
Knowing the common formats helps you open, share, and convert files between programs.

items: .docx — The default format for Microsoft Word. Supports rich formatting, images, tables, and tracked changes.
.odt — The open-source format used by LibreOffice Writer. Most word processors can open it.
.pages — Apple Pages' format. Other programs may not open it directly, so you may need to export to .docx or PDF before sharing.
.pdf — A read-only format that preserves the exact look of your document. Useful for sharing a finished file when the reader does not need to edit it.
.txt — A plain-text format with no formatting at all. Useful when you only need the words and nothing else.

blocks.text: Word Processors vs. Other Tools
A word processor is not always the right tool. Understanding how it compares to other options helps you choose the best one for the task.

items: Word processor vs. spreadsheet — A spreadsheet is designed for numerical data, formulas, and calculations. Use a word processor when your document is mostly text with some tables or images.

Word processor vs. presentation software — Presentation software creates visual slides for speaking to a group. Use a word processor when the reader will consume the content on their own and needs full paragraphs of detail.
Word processor vs. text editor — A plain text editor like Notepad saves only raw text with no formatting. Use a word processor when you need fonts, colors, images, headers, or page layout.

blocks.text: Mobile Word Processing Software

Mobile devices also have options for word processing, including all the ones we've discussed and others made just for smartphones. These can be really handy for quick document creation and editing, especially if time is of the essence and you're not at a computer. Like Google Docs, mobile options rely on online storage, but they also let you access your documents offline.
Some of these mobile apps are free, while others might have a one-time cost or a monthly subscription fee.

blocks.text: Managing and getting useful information from data can be tricky, but spreadsheets make it easy to organize and use data.
Spreadsheet Software
Spreadsheet software helps you organize, calculate, and visualize data. The following image shows an example of a spreadsheet in Microsoft Excel.
Everyday Uses for Spreadsheets
Spreadsheets aren't just for accountants or data analysts. Here are some ways you might use a spreadsheet in everyday life:

items: Personal budgets — Track income, expenses, and savings goals each month.
Grade tracking — Record assignment scores and calculate your current average.
Event planning — Manage guest lists, RSVPs, seating charts, and costs.
Inventory — Keep track of items you own, sell, or need to reorder.
Scheduling — Build shift schedules, project timelines, or workout plans.

blocks.text: Any time you need to organize information into rows and columns, or perform calculations on a set of numbers, a spreadsheet is a good tool to reach for.
Common Spreadsheet File Formats
Spreadsheet files come in different formats depending on the software that created them.
Knowing the common formats helps you open, share, and convert files between programs.

items: .xlsx — The default format for Microsoft Excel. Supports formulas, charts, formatting, and multiple worksheets.
.csv — Comma-separated values. A plain-text format that stores data without formatting.

blocks.text: Nearly every spreadsheet program can open CSV files, making it one of the most portable formats.

items: .ods — The open-source format used by LibreOffice Calc. It can be opened by most spreadsheet programs.
.numbers — Apple Numbers' format. Other programs may not open it directly, so you may need to export to .xlsx or .csv before sharing.

blocks.text: Spreadsheets vs. Other Tools
A spreadsheet is not always the right tool. Understanding how it compares to other options helps you choose the best one for the task.

items: Spreadsheet vs. word processing table — Word processing tables are great for small, static tables in a document. Use a spreadsheet when you need to calculate values, sort data, or work with more than a handful of rows.

Spreadsheet vs. database — Databases are designed for very large data sets and for connecting related tables together. A spreadsheet works well for smaller data sets that one person or a small team manages.

blocks.text: Mobile Spreadsheet Software

You can also use spreadsheets on mobile devices through apps. Smartphones have downloadable spreadsheet apps, but they're not as commonly used because the screens are so small and you have to try to work with the touchpad. But, at the end of the day, these apps offer the same features as their desktop counterparts. And you can easily check a spreadsheet anytime and make quick edits to the numbers on the mobile version.

blocks.text: Whether you are pitching an idea at work, presenting a school project, or sharing photos at a family gathering, presentation software helps you organize your message into visual slides that keep an audience engaged. Tools like Microsoft PowerPoint, Google Slides, Apple Keynote, and LibreOffice Impress each offer different features, price points, and collaboration options, so choosing the right one matters.

In this lesson, you will learn what presentation software is and how it turns ideas into slides. You will explore popular licensed and free applications, discover common presentation file formats, compare presentations to other tools like documents and videos, and learn about online and mobile options for creating slideshows on the go.
Presentation Software

Presentation software lets you create slides that combine text, images, charts, and animations into a visual aid you can show to an audience. The following image shows a presentation being edited in Microsoft PowerPoint.
Everyday Uses for Presentations
Presentation software is not just for the workplace. Here are some common situations where a slideshow can help:

items: School projects: Present research findings, book reports, or science fair results to a class.
Business pitches: Propose a product idea, share quarterly results, or walk a client through a plan.
Training and tutorials: Teach a process step by step with visuals and diagrams.
Community events: Share photos and highlights at a club meeting, church service, or volunteer orientation.
Personal projects: Create a photo slideshow for a birthday party or a travel recap for friends and family.

blocks.text: Common Presentation File Formats
Presentation files come in different formats depending on the software that created them.
Knowing the common formats helps you open, share, and convert files between programs.

items: .pptx: The default format for Microsoft PowerPoint. Supports animations, transitions, speaker notes, and embedded media.
.odp: The open-source format used by LibreOffice Impress. Most presentation programs can open it.
.key: Apple Keynote's format. Other programs may not open it directly, so you may need to export to .pptx or PDF before sharing.
.pdf: A read-only format that preserves the look of your slides. Useful for sharing a finished presentation when the viewer does not need to edit it.

blocks.text: Presentations vs. Other Tools
A slideshow is not always the right choice. Understanding how it compares to other options helps you pick the best one for the task.

items: Presentation vs. document: A word processing document works well when your audience needs to read detailed information on their own. Use a presentation when you are speaking to a group and want visual support.

Presentation vs. video: A recorded video can reach viewers who are not in the same room or time zone. Use a live presentation when you want to interact with the audience, answer questions, and adjust your delivery in real time.

Presentation vs. infographic: An infographic packs a lot of information into a single image that people can scan. Use a presentation when you need to walk the audience through information step by step over multiple slides.

blocks.text: Other Online Presentation Tools

There are other popular online tools for creating presentations. Prezi lets you build non-linear, zoomable presentations instead of traditional slide-by-slide formats. Canva provides drag-and- drop templates that make it easy to design polished slides without much experience. Both are free to start with and offer paid plans for extra features.
Mobile Presentation Software

Not surprisingly, there are mobile versions of all these products, plus other presentation apps made just for smartphones. Some apps are designed specifically for presentations in places like schools. Some of these are free, some have a one-time cost, and many require a monthly subscription fee.

blocks.text: Communication software is at the center of how people connect in both personal and professional settings. From sending a quick text message to joining a video conference with colleagues across the globe, the tools you use to communicate have a direct impact on how effectively you share information, collaborate on projects, and build relationships.

In this lesson, you will explore the most common types of communication software, including phone and text messaging apps, email clients, instant messaging and collaboration platforms, calendaring tools, and videoconferencing applications. You will learn how each type of tool works, when to use one over another, and how to apply good communication habits in a professional environment.
Digital Communication

The video above provides an overview of common digital communication methods, including email, instant messaging, forums, texting, and video calls. Beyond those topics, here are additional details worth understanding about email addresses, messaging interoperability, and social media.
Table 2 4: Additional Digital Communication Details
Method Description
Email Each email must be sent from and to one or more unique email addresses.

Email addresses are composed of two elements, separated by the @ symbol: The local-part and the domain. The local-part is the name of the individual mailbox. The domain name says where the email address is hosted - often the name of a website. An example email address would be local-part@domain.com.

Instant Messaging Unlike email, instant messaging applications require all users to have accounts with the same service provider. This means a Hangouts account cannot instant message with a Hotmail account.

Social Media Social media is a technology that helps people share their lives with others over the internet. Generally, each user on a social media platform creates a unique profile with information about themselves. This information can include photographs, biographical information, work and education history, likes and dislikes, political ideology, religion, and much more. Then, using the social media site, they connect their profiles to the profiles of other people. Connected profiles can share content, such as text posts, pictures, and videos.
Text and Phone Apps
Your smartphone comes with built-in apps for making phone calls and sending text messages.
These are the most basic communication tools on any mobile device, and understanding how they work will help you stay connected in both personal and professional settings.
Phone Apps

Every smartphone includes a phone app that handles voice calls over a cellular network. When you make a call, your voice is converted into a signal and transmitted through your carrier's network to the person you are calling. Most phone apps also include features like a contacts list, call history, voicemail, and the ability to set up conference calls with multiple people.

In addition to traditional cellular calls, many smartphones support Voice over Internet Protocol (V oIP) calling. VoIP apps like Google Voice, Skype, and WhatsApp use your internet connection instead of a cellular signal to place calls. This can be especially useful when you are connected to Wi-Fi but have weak cell reception, or when you need to make international calls without high carrier fees.
Text Messaging Apps

Text messaging, or Short Message Service (SMS) allows you to send short written messages through your phone carrier's network. You can also send photos, videos, and audio clips using Multimedia Messaging Service (MMS). These services are tied to your phone number, so anyone with a cell phone can receive your messages regardless of the device or operating system they use.

Many smartphones now also support Rich Communication Services (RCS), which is an updated standard that adds features similar to internet-based messaging apps. With RCS, you can see typing indicators, read receipts, and send higher-quality images, all through your phone's default messaging app.
Choosing Between Phone and Text
Phone calls and text messages each have strengths depending on the situation. A phone call is better when you need to discuss something quickly or when the tone of your voice matters.

Text messaging works well for short updates, sharing links or images, or when the other person may not be available to talk right away. In a work environment, understanding when to call versus when to text is an important part of professional communication.
Messaging Apps

Messaging apps go beyond traditional texting by using your internet connection to send messages, images, videos, and files. These apps have become some of the most widely used communication tools in the world, both for personal conversations and workplace collaboration.
Personal Messaging Apps

Apps like WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, iMessage, and Telegram allow you to send messages to individuals or groups over the internet. Unlike SMS, these apps typically require both you and the recipient to have the same app installed. In return, you get features that standard texting does not offer, such as read receipts, typing indicators, voice messages, video clips, and end-to-end encryption for privacy.

Many personal messaging apps also support group chats, where multiple people can participate in a single conversation. Group chats are useful for coordinating plans, sharing updates with family members, or staying in touch with a circle of friends.
Business and Collaboration Messaging

In the workplace, messaging has moved beyond simple chat. Collaboration platforms like Microsoft Teams, Slack, and Google Chat organize conversations into channels or groups based on projects, departments, or topics. This structure helps teams stay organized and find relevant discussions without scrolling through unrelated messages.

These platforms also integrate with other productivity tools. For example, you can share files, start video calls, assign tasks, and connect third-party apps directly within the messaging interface. This makes them a central hub for day-to-day work communication, reducing the need to switch between multiple applications.
Messaging Etiquette
Because messaging feels casual, it can be easy to forget that your messages leave a record.

In a professional setting, you should keep your messages clear and respectful. Avoid sending too many short, fragmented messages in a row, as this can be distracting to the recipient. If a conversation becomes complex or requires detailed discussion, it may be better to switch to a phone call, video call, or email.
Email

Email is one of the oldest and most reliable forms of digital communication. Whether you are sending a quick note to a friend or submitting a formal report at work, email gives you a way to deliver written messages, attach files, and keep a record of your conversations.
How Email Works

When you send an email, your message travels from your email provider's server to the recipient's email server using standard internet protocols. The recipient can then read your message whenever they check their inbox. This makes email an asynchronous form of communication, meaning both people do not need to be online at the same time.
Every email address follows the same format: a username, the @ symbol, and a domain name.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, in the address jsmith@example.com, "jsmith" is the username and "example.com" is the domain where the mailbox is hosted.
Webmail vs. Desktop Email Clients

There are two main ways to access your email. Webmail services like Gmail, Outlook.com, and Yahoo Mail run entirely in your web browser. You do not need to install anything, and you can check your email from any device with an internet connection. Webmail is a popular choice for personal use because it is free and easy to set up.

Desktop email clients like Microsoft Outlook, Mozilla Thunderbird, and Apple Mail are applications installed on your computer. These programs download your messages and store them locally, which means you can read and organize emails even when you are offline.
Desktop clients are commonly used in business environments because they offer advanced features such as calendar integration, contact management, and support for multiple email accounts in one place.
Key Email Features
Most email services share a common set of features that help you manage your communications:

items: Attachments: You can send files such as documents, images, and spreadsheets along with your message.
CC and BCC: Carbon copy (CC) sends a copy of the email to additional recipients. Blind carbon copy (BCC) does the same but hides those recipients from other people in the message.
Folders and labels: You can organize messages into folders or apply labels to keep your inbox manageable.
Search: Built-in search tools help you find specific messages by keyword, sender, date, or attachment type.
Spam filtering: Email providers automatically detect and separate unwanted or suspicious messages from your inbox.

blocks.text: Calendaring

A digital calendar is more than just a place to mark dates. Calendaring software helps you schedule events, set reminders, coordinate with other people, and manage your time across personal and professional commitments. Most digital calendars sync across your devices, so your schedule is always available whether you are at your desk or on your phone.
Common Calendaring Tools

Several calendaring applications are widely used today. Google Calendar is a free, web-based tool that integrates tightly with Gmail and other Google services. Microsoft Outlook includes a full calendar alongside its email and contacts features, making it a popular choice in business environments. Apple Calendar comes built into macOS and iOS devices and syncs through iCloud. Each of these tools offers similar core features, so the best choice often depends on which ecosystem of apps and services you already use.
Key Calendaring Features
Digital calendars include features that make scheduling easier and more reliable:

items: Events and appointments: You can create entries with a title, date, time, location, and description. Some calendars let you add video call links directly to the event.
Reminders and notifications: You can set alerts to notify you before an event starts, helping you stay on track throughout the day.
Recurring events: If you have a meeting or task that repeats on a regular schedule, you can set it to recur daily, weekly, monthly, or at a custom interval.
Shared calendars: You can share your calendar with coworkers, family members, or classmates so everyone can see each other's availability and avoid scheduling conflicts.
Invitations: When you schedule a meeting, you can send invitations to other people. They can accept, decline, or suggest a different time, all from within their own calendar app.

blocks.text: Calendars in the Workplace

In a professional setting, calendaring software plays a central role in coordination. Teams use shared calendars to schedule meetings, track deadlines, and reserve conference rooms. Many organizations rely on calendar integration with email and messaging platforms, so meeting invitations and updates flow automatically between tools. Developing good calendaring habits, such as keeping your availability up to date and responding promptly to meeting invitations, helps your team work together more efficiently.
Videoconferencing Apps

Videoconferencing apps allow you to have face-to-face conversations with other people over the internet. Whether you are attending a remote class, joining a work meeting, or catching up with family in another city, these tools bring the experience of an in-person conversation to your screen.
How Videoconferencing Works

Videoconferencing uses your device's camera, microphone, and internet connection to transmit live audio and video to other participants. Most apps use Voice over Internet Protocol (V oIP) to handle the audio portion of the call, which means the sound travels over the internet rather than through a traditional phone line. As long as you have a stable internet connection, you can join a video call from a computer, tablet, or smartphone.
Popular Videoconferencing Apps
Several videoconferencing platforms are widely used today:

items: Zoom: Known for its ease of use and reliability, Zoom is popular for business meetings, online classes, and personal calls. It supports features like breakout rooms, screen sharing, and virtual backgrounds.
Microsoft Teams: Integrated with Microsoft 365, Teams combines video calls with messaging, file sharing, and collaboration tools. It is widely used in corporate and educational environments.
Google Meet: A browser-based option that works with Google Workspace. It requires no software installation and is accessible to anyone with a Google account.
FaceTime: Built into Apple devices, FaceTime offers a simple way to make video calls between iPhones, iPads, and Macs.
Skype: One of the earliest video calling apps, Skype supports video calls, voice calls, and messaging across multiple platforms.

blocks.text: Common Videoconferencing Features
Most videoconferencing apps share a set of core features that improve the meeting experience:

items: Screen sharing: You can share your screen so other participants can see a document, presentation, or application you are working with.
Chat: A text chat panel runs alongside the video call, allowing you to share links, ask questions, or comment without interrupting the speaker.
Recording: Many apps let the host record the meeting so people who missed it can watch later.
Mute and camera controls: You can turn your microphone or camera on and off during a call, which is useful for reducing background noise or maintaining privacy when you are not speaking.

blocks.text: Tips for a Good Video Call
To get the most out of a video call, make sure you have a reliable internet connection and a quiet environment. Position your camera at eye level so you appear natural on screen.

Use headphones or earbuds to reduce echo and background noise. If you are joining a professional meeting, mute your microphone when you are not speaking and be mindful of your surroundings, since other participants can see what is behind you.

blocks.text: Email remains one of the most important tools for professional and personal communication.
Whether you are applying for a job, coordinating with coworkers, or keeping in touch with family, knowing how to compose, send, and manage email messages is an essential skill.
An email client like Microsoft Outlook gives you powerful features for organizing your inbox, formatting messages, and staying on top of your schedule.

In this lesson, you will learn how to create and send email messages using Outlook, including how to address recipients with To, CC, and BCC fields and how to attach files. You will also learn how to reply to and forward messages, recognize and handle spam, and follow the rules of netiquette to communicate professionally online.
Email Software

The most commonly used email software is Microsoft Outlook. It was released in the 1990s and is part of the Microsoft Office suite, which also includes Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and other Microsoft productivity tools. Outlook makes it easy to manage and organize your emails.

You can create folders to keep similar emails together, making them easy to find later. You can also send emails right away or schedule them to be sent later. Outlook has features like filters that move junk email to its own folder, helping to keep your inbox clear of spam. Just remember to check the junk folder occasionally in case a real email ends up there.

Outlook has grown over the years to become a powerful productivity information manager, almost like a personal assistant. It stores your contacts so you have a list of people you know or have met, along with their phone numbers, full names, home addresses, and more. It has a calendar feature where you can set appointments, manage meetings, and send meeting requests. You can also share your calendar with others so they can see when you're free and schedule appointments with you without having to bother you on your own time. You can also jot down notes and make to-do lists. And you can sync all this across different devices.
Many people choose to use their web browser over the app version of the email service (called an email client). The browser version is what's known as Software as a Service (SaaS) .
Everyone's emails are stored on the hosting company's servers, and when you log in to your account, you see a copy of your emails. Gmail is another example of this.
Outlook

Microsoft Outlook is a fully featured email client. This means it does much more than let you send and receive email. Outlook includes features for tracking messages, setting up automatic replies, importing and exporting data, creating and managing calendars, keeping track of notes and tasks, and creating contacts and contact groups. Rules of Netiquette

Netiquette refers to the rules of etiquette that should be observed while using computer networks, such as the internet. Using a computer to interact with other users tends to impart a sense of anonymity, which can cause you to behave in ways that are impolite or even offensive.

To keep this from happening, all network users should adhere to a set of guidelines called netiquette. The overarching rule of netiquette is this: Don't do or say anything to another person online that you would not do or say if you were looking at them face to face.
Several more specific guidelines will help you achieve this goal.
Table 26: Guidelines of Netiquette
Guideline Description
Show Consideration for Other
Users' Time

Before making an online post or sending an email, make sure it is worth the time of those who will read it. A common violation of this rule occurs when someone forwards a mass email message of questionable origin to everyone in their address book. Before doing this, consider the following:

items: Verify the authenticity of the information you're sending.
Ask yourself whether the recipients actually need (or even want) to read it.

blocks.text: Use Appropriate Spelling and
Grammar
The anonymity of the internet frequently makes users careless about following spelling and grammar rules. This can make a message difficult to read and can even make it impossible to decipher.
Avoid using all capital letters. On the internet, this is considered shouting.

Write Clearly and Concisely A lot of internet users are careless about how they communicate ideas in messages and posts. To respect other users' time and to make sure your ideas are communicated correctly, be sure your posts and email messages are:

items: Clear. Read through your message and make sure your point is clearly stated. Remember, the reader may not have the same background that you have. Will they understand what you are trying to say?
Concise. Be brief and to the point. Nobody likes to wade through a ten-page email or post trying to find important information.

Readable. Use understandable terms when you write. Many internet users prefer to use shorthand terms in their posts and messages, such as u r ("you are") and idk ("I don't know"). While using shorthand can reduce the amount of time needed to compose a message, it makes it much more difficult to read. It can also obscure the meaning and intent of your message, resulting in misunderstandings.

blocks.text: Guideline Description
Avoid Being a Troll A troll is someone who deliberately tries to create conflict among users.

Expressing your opinion is encouraged on the internet; however, trolls are not usually interested in engaging in a healthy dialogue. Instead, they seek to cause contention and disrupt the conversation. Trolling tactics that are commonly used include:

items: Posting provocative, offensive, and even hateful messages to incite a response from other users.
Posting off-topic messages in an attempt to start an argument.
Posting obscene or menacing messages to harass another user.

blocks.text: If you encounter a troll, the best response is to just ignore them.

Obey the Law Be familiar with the laws in your jurisdiction surrounding computer use and cybersecurity, and abide by them. For example, all fifty states in the United States have laws to stop cyberbullying. In the United Kingdom, the Communications Act of 2003 criminalizes the act of being an overly aggressive internet troll who targets a specific individual.

blocks.text: Hertz, Bytes, and Metric Prefixes

How fast is your internet connection? What size hard drive do you need? How much memory does your computer currently have? How much cloud storage do you need? These are common questions when working with computers and networks. The answers will include terms that you need to be familiar with.
Hertz

Hertz is a measurement of how many times a repeating process happens per second. If you clap your hands one time a second, you are clapping at 1 Hertz. If you clap your hands 10 times every second, you are clapping at 10 Hertz.

The term Hertz is used to describe the speed at which a device runs. The internal parts of a computer, laptop, tablet, or phone need to work together to process and move data. To do this, all devices use a master clock to keep devices synchronized.
The signal the master clock produces is called a square wave. A square wave has sharp edges.

It rises, then moves to the right, then drops and moves to the right. The amount of time it moves to the right is the same after a rise or a fall. When the square wave rises is the start. After the fall, the wave moves to the right, which is the end of the wave.

The process of moving up and over, then down and over, is called a single cycle. Here is an example of multiple cycles together. If all four cycles happen in one second, then this clock signal would be running at 4 Hertz (4Hz).
Metric Prefixes
Most modern computers run at extremely high clock speeds, some in the Gigahertz (GHz).

The most recognized device that uses Hertz in its specifications is a computer's Central Processing Unit (CPU). If your computer has a 3.4 GHz processor, it is capable of processing 3,400,000,000 operations per second.

Metric Prefixes Modern computers and networks process data at super high speeds, and modern storage devices are able to store extremely large amounts of data. Because the numbers being used are so large, we use metric prefixes to help us.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, a computer has a hard drive capable of holding 500 billion bytes of data. You would have to label it as a 500,000,000,000-byte hard drive. It's much easier to express it with a metric prefix. Using a metric prefix, we could rewrite the size as a 500-gigabyte hard drive.
Here are examples of common metric prefixes used with computer speeds and sizes.
Prefix Definition

Kilo (K) Kilo represents thousands, or 103. A single capital K is used to represent Kilo in an expression. Here are some examples of its use: 5 Kb = 5000 bits 100 Kb = 100,000 bits 25 KB = 25,000 Bytes How would you express this amount in Kilos?

27,000 Hertz Answer: 27 KHz Mega (M) Mega represents millions, or 106. A single capital M is used to represent Mega in an expression. Here are some examples of its use: 10 Mb = 10,000,000 bits 500 MB = 500,000,000 Bytes 2 Mb = 2,000,000 bits How would you express this amount in Megs?

47,000,000 Hertz Answer: 47 MHz Giga (G) Giga represents billions, or 109. A single capital G is used to represent Giga in an expression. Here are some examples of its use: 25 Gb = 25,000,000,000 bits 450 GB = 450,000,000,000 Bytes 2 Gb = 2,000,000,000 bits How would you express this amount in Gigs?
575,000,000,000 Hertz Answer: 575 GHz
Prefix Definition

Tera (T) Tera represents trillions, or 1012. A single capital T is used to represent Tera in an expression. Here are some examples of its use: 14 Tb = 14,000,000,000,000 bits 755 TB = 755,000,000,000,000 Bytes 2 Tb = 2,000,000,000,000 bits How would you express this amount using Tera?
407,000,000,000,000 Hertz Answer: 407 THz Kilo, Mega, Giga, and Tera help express large numbers. Take a look at some metric prefixes used to express small amounts.
Prefix Definition

Milli (m) Milli represents one-thousandth, or 10-3 , and looks like this: 0.001 A lower-case m is used to represent milli in an expression. Here are some examples of its use: 15 ms = 0.015 seconds = 15 one-thousandths of a second.
110 ms = 0.110 seconds 9 ms = 0.009 How would you express this amount in millis?

0.019 seconds Answer: 19 ms Micro (µ) Micro represents one-millionth, or 10-6 , and looks like this: 0.000,001 The Greek letter mu (µ, rhymes with you) is used to represent micro in an expression. Here are some examples of its use: 27 µs = 0.000,027 seconds 8 µs = 0.000,008 seconds How would you express this amount in micros?

0.000,259 seconds Answer: 259 µs Nano (n) Nano represents one-billionth, or 10-9 , and looks like this: 0.000,000,001 A lower-case n is used to represent nano in an expression. Here are some examples of its use: 54 ns = 0.000,000,054 seconds 7 ns = 0.000,000,007 seconds How would you express this amount in nanos?

0.000,000,075 seconds Answer: 75 ns Pico (p) Pico (pronounced peeko) represents one-trillionth, or 10-12 , and looks like this: 0.000,000,000,001 A lower-case p is used to represent pico in an expression. Here are some examples of its use: 34 ps = 0.000,000,000,034 seconds 2 ps = 0.000,000,000,002 seconds How would you express this amount in picos?

0.000,000,000,535 seconds Answer: 535 ps Storage Units Most people don't think much about what's stored on their devices when they're not in use, but all our devices need to have storage capacity to work properly. Storage in a computer is called "persistent" because it holds data even when the power is turned off. This data can include the operating system like Windows or iOS, as well as all the apps and user files added to the system.

Each piece of data has a file size, which is the number of bytes it takes up. Computer storage for files has grown to be measured in gigabytes (GB) or terabytes (TB). These units can also be used for memory and storage drives. A gigabyte (GB) is about one billion bytes. A terabyte (TB) is one thousand times bigger than a gigabyte!

How and for how long data is stored differs between memory and storage drives. Memory is "non-persistent" or "volatile" storage, which means it only holds data while the computer is powered on. A solid-state drive (SSD), on the other hand, keeps the data permanently.

The smallest addressable unit in memory is a byte. Once you gather 1024 bytes, it is called a kilobyte (KB). This number isn't the usual 1000 you're used to, because computers count in binary, not decimal. For example, two to the 8th power is 256, and two to the 10th power is 1024. These are common numbers in computing because they are "round" in binary.

As you keep multiplying up to 1024 kilobytes, you get to the next storage unit: megabytes (MB). After megabytes come gigabytes (GB), then terabytes (TB), followed by petabytes (PB), exabytes (EB), zettabytes (ZB), and yottabytes (YB).

Most files today are measured in megabytes (MB). Music and photos are good examples. Larger files, such as videos, are usually measured in gigabytes (GB). Only small text files are measured in kilobytes (KB) these days.

Adding commas to numbers greater than 999 is not common in IT communications. This is because different regions separate the thousands digit in different ways. For example, European standards use the period to separate thousands and a comma for decimal points, while in North America this is reversed. Additionally, the comma in programming is used to separate items when coding. To avoid confusion around the world, it was simply decided to leave off any punctuation.
Throughput Units

Throughput measures how much of something passes through something else in a certain amount of time. The term isn't limited to just computing. It can also mean things like the number of pages you can read per hour, the number of patients a doctor sees in a day, or the number of customers visiting a store in a week. All these examples are different ways of describing throughput. It measures how fast things move or get done.

With computers, this means how much data moves through the system in one second. With networking, it's similar but slightly different; it’s about how much data moves from one place to another in one second. You can also think of it as the amount of data passing through the network at any given moment.

It's important to know that throughput is not the highest or lowest amount. Throughput is the total amount over a certain block of time. Think of it like a bus: if the network were a bus, throughput would be like counting all the passengers the bus carried in one day.
In fact, one of the main jobs when managing a network is to monitor throughput so you can make changes if necessary. A slow network can make everyone unhappy and less productive.
Moving Bits

When you talk about how much a storage drive or memory can hold, you use bytes to measure that capacity. But when you talk about how fast data moves, you use bits, which are much smaller than bytes. In fact, one byte is equal to eight bits. Network transfers break it down to the smallest units possible, bits per second. But when you check your Internet speed, the results are shown as Mbps, which means megabits per second. If you want to send a video to a friend over the Internet, the speed is measured in megabits (Mb) or gigabits (Gb) per second.
Bandwidth

When talking about sending data over the Internet, the term bandwidth is used. Bandwidth is the highest amount of data that a network can handle at once. For example, if a network has a bandwidth of 50 megabits per second (Mbps), it can't send data faster than that number.

Going back to the bus analogy, think of it like this: bandwidth is the maximum number of passengers the bus can carry at one time. Bandwidth describes the bus's seating capacity, and throughput describes how many people the bus actually transports in a certain amount of time, carrying passengers over many trips throughout the day.
Throughput Units

To restate the throughput measurements, when data is moved between parts within a computer or between different computers on a network, this is measured in bits per second (bps). Just like with storage, using bits per second can make for very long numbers, so larger units are used to make it easier to understand. Here are some of those units:

items: Kilobits per second (Kbps): One thousand (1, 000) bits per second. Slow network links are measured in Kbps.
Megabits per second (Mbps): One million (1, 000 , 000) bits per second. Wireless networks and residential Internet links typically have this rate of throughput.
Gigabits per second (Gbps): One billion (1, 000 , 000 , 000) bits per second. The latest PC bus standards and networks can support this higher level of throughput.
Terabits per second (Tbps): One trillion (1, 000 , 000 , 000 , 000) bits per second. This sort of capacity is found in major telecommunications links between data centers, cities, and countries.

blocks.text: Throughput Obstacles

Multiple factors can affect a network's throughput. Some things that can slow it down are latency, errors that cause data to be sent again (retransmissions), and the communication rules (protocols). Some protocols have built-in features like congestion avoidance and flow control, which can impact throughput. If a data packet gets lost, it might need to be resent. If this happens a lot, it can cause more congestion and slow down the network.
Your Internet Service Provider (ISP) gives you a certain amount of bandwidth. You might have a plan for 50 Mbps or 100 Mbps, which means that those are your expected download speeds.
However, the actual speeds you get might be different from what is advertised. Inside your home network, speeds between devices can be faster because they don't depend on the Internet bandwidth.

It's common for ISPs to underpromise and overdeliver. You may be paying for a 100 Mbps package, but doing a speed test will probably yield slightly faster speeds. This is an easy way for ISPs to make customers feel good by giving them a little something extra, at no cost to the ISP.

Another obstacle can be the amount of traffic passing through the network. If there's a lot of traffic on the network at once, congestion occurs, making everything slower. The more traffic there is, the harder it is for data to move quickly, just like cars on the freeway.

The cables you use also affect your network speed. The network can only be as fast as its slowest part. For example, if you have fast cables and network cards but a slow network switch, the switch is going to slow everything down. This is called the weak link.

"I worked with a client whose network was inexplicably slow. We could not figure out what the problem was. The ISP was functioning just fine, the routers and switches were new and double-checked, older laptops were replaced. Finally, we looked at the network cable inside the building. Whoever built the building decided to save money by installing CAT 3 cable, when the standard was at least CAT 5e at the time.

A smaller CAT number means less capacity, so business at that client was incredibly slow." -- R. Turner, network administrator Processing Speed Processing speed describes how fast the computer itself works during a given operation or task. A computer's speed is measured by its internal clock and its processors, also known as the central processing unit (CPU). This speed is measured in Hertz (Hz) , where 1 Hz means one cycle per second. A cycle would just be how many times a process reoccurs.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, if you clap your hands once every second, you're clapping at 1 Hertz. If you clap 10 times every second, you're clapping at 10 Hertz. Hertz (Hz) are used to describe how fast a device runs.
Clock Speed

On a computer, laptop, tablet, or phone, the internal parts move data around using a synchronized clock. All these devices use a master clock to stay synchronized, or to stay working together smoothly.

The signal from the master clock is called a square wave. These square waves work for computers because they represent binary digits: the 1s and 0s. The wave goes up and over, then down and over in one cycle. If you see four cycles happening in one second, the clock signal is running at 4 Hertz (4 Hz).

Over the years, processors, just like other major computer parts, have gotten better. At first, processors were measured in Megahertz (MHz), which means 1 million cycles per second. This speed was common for the first 20 years of personal computers. But as technology improved and we got to over 1000 MHz, we started measuring them in Gigahertz (GHz), which means 1 billion cycles per second.

Today's processors usually run at between 2 and 4 GHz. The largest producers of Windows- based CPUs, AMD and Intel, have processors that tend to run within this range. And the fastest CPUs can reach up to 6 GHz. If your computer has a 3.4 GHz processor, it can handle 3.4 billion operations per second. Think about that for a moment: over 3 billion operations in just one second! Can you think of any other machine that works that fast?
It's hard to get CPU speeds faster than they are now, as this amount of activity creates a lot of heat.
Heat is an enemy of computers, especially laptops.
Even though servers are powerful types of computers, they don't have specialized processors.
Servers use the same kind of processors as the ones in your home computer. They actually get their enhanced performance from having multiple CPUs work together.

2.5 Compare and contrast common types of input/output device interfaces.

blocks.text: While the internal components are what make a computer work, it is the external devices, also called peripherals, that you see and interact with every day. Peripherals include keyboards, mice, monitors, webcams, speakers, and other input/output devices. Understanding how to connect, configure, and troubleshoot these devices is essential for anyone who works with computers.

In this lesson, you will explore the different types of peripheral devices and how they connect to a computer. You will learn about input devices like keyboards and mice, output devices like monitors and projectors, and how to identify common ports and connectors including USB, HDMI, DisplayPort, and audio jacks.
Keyboard and Mouse

The majority of users interact with computers using a keyboard and mouse. Sometimes, you may also use a touchscreen along with these devices. If your computer has a touchscreen, you can simply touch the screen just like you would click the mouse. Additionally, in Windows, you can bring up an onscreen keyboard, which serves as a handy alternative to the physical keyboard.
Using the Keyboard and Mouse
A touchpad sits below the keyboard on every laptop, and you use it to move the pointer.

However, many people find the touchpad uncomfortable and prefer using an external wireless mouse. Lenovo first made laptops with a small mouse in the middle of the keyboard, called a trackpoint. Other laptop makers followed with similar setups, often in their business-class systems. With some practice and finger movements, you can make the mouse pointer move quickly around the screen.

Some keyboards have returned to an old technology that was almost abandoned because of cost. These keyboards use mechanical switches for each key. When you press them, they make a distinctive sound and provide tactile feedback. They are popular with programmers, gamers, and tech enthusiasts.

Designers have created keyboards and mice to be more comfortable to use. Spending many hours in front of a computer can cause injuries to your hands, arms, and shoulders from repetitive movements. Ergonomic designs position the keyboard in a way that is easier on your upper body.
Some keyboards include a built-in mouse, usually on the right side of the keys. These work great for multimedia setups in a family room, especially when using the television.

Surprisingly, modern US and US-Int er national keyboards have the same layout for letters and numbers that typewriters have used since 1874. This layout is known as the QWERTY design, named after the first six letters on the top left of the keyboard, next to the tab key. This layout has become widely known, but it is not the only keyboard layout available. For example, French language speakers can use a layout called AZERTY, which positions the letters for faster typing in French.

Inventors August and William Dvorak created another layout called the Dvorak layout. This layout aims to let you type faster and be more ergonomic. Both Microsoft and Apple allow you to switch your keyboard to the Dvorak layout, but unless you physically move your key caps, you will have to memorize the letter positions.
Connection Types

Wireless technology helps get rid of many cords around our computers. You can connect a keyboard, a mouse, or both wirelessly using the same USB adapter. The input devices send a radio frequency (RF) signal to the adapter plugged into the computer. Bluetooth mice and keyboards also work with laptops and sometimes desktops, just like their RF counterparts. The operating system usually loads the drivers needed for full functionality without any issues.
However, a programmable keyboard might need a special driver to be fully operational.
While wireless connections help keep things neat, wired connections are still very popular.

Wired connections give power to the device, so you don't need to charge it separately. For example, you don't need batteries for a wired mouse like you do for a wireless one. USB connections are the most common type of wired connectors. Today, most new and high-quality devices use USB Type C connectors. Even though USB Type A is older, it's still a very common connector for input devices, and in the electrical infrastructure throughout the world. Many homes, airports, hotels, and other public places have USB Type A ports in their electrical outlets for charging.
Video and Audio Devices
Beyond monitors, there are many other audio and video peripherals worth understanding.
Cameras and Microphones

Laptops have had built-in webcams since the early 2000s, but they really became part of daily use in 2020, when Zoom calls became as common as brushing your teeth. Webcams not only let people see each other, but also usually have a microphone, making them a great substitute for what comes standard on a laptop. They can be used for video calls, and major operating systems have speech recognition software that uses the microphone. This software is very good at listening to your voice and typing the words into the computer.

Tablets and smartphones also have cameras and microphones. Early phones had to have a microphone to receive voice input, and cameras were added soon after. Camera quality kept improving, and another camera was added to the front of tablets and phones. Taking selfies would be very hard without the front camera on your phone. FaceTime and Google Meet let you make video calls with friends, family, and co-workers. These features work because of the cameras built into every mobile device.

Microphone quality can vary a lot. Some microphones sound tinny and hollow, while others give rich, full audio close to a professional recording studio. All-in-one computers have built-in webcams, and some headphones also include a microphone, so you can hear and talk at the same time. People often use these headphones for online multiplayer gaming or when they want to keep the sound from bothering others.
Network Connectivity

A smart TV adds the ability to connect to the Internet, giving users a portal to streaming content. With this access, they can watch TV with free and paid services, listen to music, and browse the Internet (even if browsing with your remote control is a bit cumbersome). Many smart TVs can be joined with smart speakers, making it easy to jump into a user's favorite shows. There are many creative uses for smart televisions. One example of this is a fitness class that can be streamed right to the TV, bringing the gym to the family room.

One of the conveniences of a smartphone, tablet, or laptop is the ability to wirelessly connect to a larger display. Once connected, the device can transmit audio and video. "Casting>" is a popular way to do this. It lets your mobile device send a signal to a projector or TV. The most popular casting options are Google Cast (used with devices like Chromecast), Apple AirPlay and Miracast.
Projectors
Projectors work with computers to pass along what’s being displayed on the computer screen.

Most often, they will be paired with a laptop, allowing the presenter to show the small screen to more people on the projector. The presenter can also choose to mirror the displays of the screens, showing the same content on both, or span them in a way which allows one view on the projector and a different display on the laptop. This can be useful for a presenter, for example, if they are showing slides. This gives them the ability to look ahead at the next slide in their presentation while showing the current slide to the audience.
Speakers and Headphones

Speakers and headphones let you hear sound from things like online TV, movies, live events, or music. The operating system (OS) on your computer also has sounds to make your experience better and to give alerts. For example, when you start your PC, it plays a startup sound. When you plug in a USB flash drive, Windows makes a sound to let you know it recognized the device.

Early computers had a basic internal speaker that made simple beeps to let you know if you clicked wrong or if a program was working. Now, both speakers and headphones have gotten much better at providing great sound. Speakers can now offer options like 5.1 surround sound and stereo output with rich bass and treble.

High-end audio uses a format called Sony/Philips Digital Interface Format (SPDIF). Many high- end motherboards have this digital audio interface built into the back. To use it, you also need speakers designed for SPDIF. This setup can provide excellent sound quality.
Connecting Audio and Video Peripherals

The 3.5mm audio jacks on the back of computers are color-coded to indicate whether they are for input or output. There is a pink jack designated as the standard for input. This is the place to plug in a microphone. If you are using a set of speakers or headphones, they would plug into the green jack, which is for output. There may be additional 3.5mm ports, but these two are the most common. Some speakers will also add another 3.5mm jack on one of the speakers to plug in headphones.

To support their mobile devices, Apple made the Lightning plug and socket, a proprietary or special set of connectors. This plug charges the battery, moves data, and sends audio signals to headphones and speakers. In 2021, the European Union decided that all makers of small electronics, like smartphones, must use the USB-C connector. Because of this, the Lightning connector is now being switched to USB-C.
Apple also created the Thunderbolt connector, a high-speed data transfer cable and connector.
Thunderbolt connectors use the USB-C standard, with high data transfer speeds, the ability to charge laptops, and connect multiple monitors.

Some speakers connect through the 3.5mm audio port and add a USB Type-A connection to boost the audio power. This works because USB provides a little bit of power. It's a handy way to make your speakers louder without needing another power plug.
