blocks.text: Printers and scanners are essential devices used in homes, schools, and offices. They come in different types, connect to computers in various ways, and require proper setup in the operating system before they can be used. Beyond printing, protecting your equipment from power outages and electrical surges is equally important for keeping your data safe.

In this lesson, you will explore the differences between laser, inkjet, and 3D printers, learn how scanners and OCR technology work, discover how to install and manage printers in Windows using the print queue, understand how an uninterruptible power supply protects your equipment, and learn how to check whether your computer meets the system requirements for new software.
Windows Printing Facts
The following provides step-by-step details for each of these tasks, as well as how to manage the print queue.
In order for your computer to send documents to a printer, several components are required.
Image 1: Windows Printing
Table 28: Windows Printing Components
Component Description
1. Computer The computer that will assist with routing print jobs to the printer.
2. Application The application creates print jobs and sends them to the printer.
3. Printer Driver The printer driver is software running on the system that contains instructions to tell the computer how to communicate with the printer.
4. Connecting Medium The printer can be connected to the computer in a number of ways, including a USB cable, a network cable, or a wireless connection.
5. Printer The printer creates the documents sent from the application.
When you print a document, the following process occurs: 1. The application you are using sends the print job to the printer.
2. Windows stores the print job in a temporary file on the system's hard disk drive.
This is called the print queue.
3. The printer driver will reformat the print job so the printer can understand and process it.
4. Windows waits for the printer to become available.
The printer must be:

items: Turned on.
Not jammed.
Finished printing all other print jobs.

blocks.text: 5. Windows moves the print job from the print queue to the printer.
6. The printer prints the document.
Several commonly used Windows printing management tasks are described in the following table:
Table 29: Windows Print Management Tasks
Task Description
Connect to a Printer To connect a printer to a computer, do the following: 1. If necessary, load the latest printer drivers on the computer so that it can communicate with the printer.
You must use the correct driver for the make and model of the printer.

Windows 11 includes a large number of preinstalled print drivers. If Windows doesn't have a driver for your printer, you must visit the website of your printer manufacturer, download the correct printer driver, and then install it.
2. Plug the printer into a power outlet.
3. Set up the printer connection by type:

items: USB connection: plug one end into the printer and other into the computer.
Bluetooth connection: follow the printer instructions to pair the device with your computer.
Wireless connection: follow the printer instructions to connect it to the same wireless network as the computer.

Network or Shared Printer connection: Windows should find printers that are available, but if they don't it helps to get the printer path from the network administrator or the person who shared their local printer.

blocks.text: 4. Power on the printer if it is not already on.

5. On the computer, open the Settings App and select Bluetooth & devices > Printers & scanners . Verify that the new printer has been added. Windows should automatically detect the printer, especially for USB and Bluetooth connections, and make it available for use.
6. If the printer is not listed, do the following:

items: In the Printers and scanners dialog, select Add Device .
Windows will attempt to detect the printer again.
Select The printer that I want isn't listed .
Options will be available for each type of connection, where you can enter shared printer names, browse to locate them, or use an

blocks.text: IP address for a network connection.
The path to a shared printer is usually \
\computer_name\printer_name.

items: Add the device and verify it is now listed under Printers & scanners.

blocks.text: Specify the Default Printer If you have more than one printer configured on your system, you can specify which one is the default printer. The default printer is the one that print jobs will be automatically sent to unless you manually specify a different printer.
To set the default printer, do the following: 1. Open the Settings App and navigate to Bluetooth & devices > Printers & scanners.
2. Turn off the option Let Windows manage my default printer.
3. Select the printer you want to set as the default.
4. Select Set as default.
Task Description
Manage Print Jobs in the Print
Queue
You may have to manage print jobs as they are queued up waiting for the printer. To do this, complete the following: 1. In the notification area of the taskbar, select the printer icon.
You can also choose the printer in the Printers & scanners dialog and select the Open print queue option.
Each print job in the queue is shown on a separate line. The jobs are shown in the order they will be printed.
2. You can do the following with the jobs in the queue:

items: To temporarily pause all printing without removing any of the print jobs, select Printer > Pause Printing.
To cancel printing all documents, select Printer > Cancel All

blocks.text: Documents.

items: To pause printing on a single print job, select the job and then select Document > Pause. When you're ready to print again, you can select Document > Resume.
To cancel printing a single print job, select the job and then select

blocks.text: Document > Cancel.

items: To restart a single print job, select the job and then select

blocks.text: Document > Restart.
Share a Printer You can share a locally-connected printer on the network. This allows other users to send print jobs to the printer through your computer.
Your computer must remain powered on for network users to be able to send print jobs to the shared printer.
To share a printer, do the following: 1. File and printer sharing must be enabled in Windows. To enable it, do the following:

items: Open the Settings app and select Network & internet in the left pane.
Select Advanced network settings in the right pane.
Select the private or public network where you want to enable sharing.
Turn on the file and printer sharing option and save the changes.

blocks.text: 2. Open the Settings App and navigate to Bluetooth & devices > Printers & scanners.
3. Choose the printer you want to share and then select Printer properties.
4. Select the Sharing tab.
5. Select the Share this printer check box.
6. In the Share name field, type a name for the printer. This is the printer name in the shared printer path.
7. Click OK.
Printers and Scanners

Even though many organizations use digital storage, paper is still important. Printers are a key part of today's technology and are used in many different areas. Public services, healthcare, and schools still use printed forms and records. Businesses also need to print things like receipts, price tags, menus, and flyers, even if they use a lot of digital systems.
Printer Basics

There are two main types of printers: laser and inkjet. Businesses, government offices, and schools usually use laser printers, while individual consumers more commonly use inkjet printers for convenience and cost savings. Laser printers can be combined with copiers in a larger-scale build, ideal for many institutions, though many models can fit on a desktop. Inkjet printers are more commonly found in the desktop size.

The laser printer uses toner cartridges filled with toner, a powder-based print medium. They are called laser printers because they have a laser inside them, which develops the image onto a drum, and as the drum spins, it attracts the toner, which transfers and then fuses it to the paper. Inkjet printers use cartridges filled with ink, which are ejected onto the paper in very small droplets.

You will find laser printers in black and white and color varieties, while inkjet printers always print in color. Both types of printers use the same three colors: yellow, magenta, and cyan (blue). The printer can blend these three colors to create any color of the rainbow.

You can set up a printer to work best for you. To save paper, you can print on both sides if your printer has that feature, and you can set this option as the default in the operating system. To save color ink or toner, you can print everything in black and white, and temporarily change the setting to color for specific print jobs.

A fun addition to the printer family is 3D printers. They create objects in three dimensions using resin, a liquid that hardens into solid shapes, or filament, a type of plastic string that melts and forms layers. However, the size of their build area limits them. In consumer-level 3D printers, this area is a square or rectangle with dimensions of around 8 inches by 7 inches by 7 inches.
Scanning Technology

Some printers include software that can scan an image and "read" the characters, turning them into a document that you can edit, search, and save like a regular document. This software is called Optical Character Recognition (OCR). More powerful all-in-one printers have a useful feature called an Automatic Document Feeder (ADF), which allows you to place a stack of documents in the top feeder and have them scanned or copied automatically.

When it became popular to connect scanners to computers, manufacturers quickly combined them with printers to create all-in-one devices that can print, scan, and copy. Even today, some of these printers can also send faxes. While you might think of scanners as part of all-in-one printers, some companies make dedicated scanners that can quickly scan documents. These dedicated scanners are common in offices with lots of paper because they make it easy to turn paper documents into electronic files.
Connecting Printers and Scanners

Printers connect to a computer or network using either USB, an Ethernet cable, or a wireless connection. Almost all modern printers have USB and wireless (also called Wi-Fi) connections, and most also have an Ethernet port. You can use USB and one of the network options at the same time.

However, a printer can't use both wired and wireless connections at the same time because it needs an IP address to be part of a local area network (LAN). Most printers can only have one IP address, so when one network connection is used, the other is turned off.
Image courtesy of CompTIA.
Uninterruptible Power Supplies

Businesses and organizations do a lot to protect their data and equipment, like creating off-site storage and buying strong security systems. These steps are usually too expensive for most people. So, how can the average person protect their data? One good option is to use a battery backup system.

A battery backup stores energy to use if the main power in a building or home goes out. This battery backup is called an uninterruptible power supply (UPS). You place it between the wall outlet and the devices that need emergency power. In addition to keeping power on during a blackout, the UPS has filters that stop damage to sensitive electronics from electrical spikes and surges. It also has multiple outlets, so you can plug in several things at once, like a computer, monitor, network equipment, and other accessories.

All network and server setups are expected to have a battery backup. You can measure a battery backup's capabilities in two ways: VA and run time. VA, which stands for volt-amperes, indicates the maximum electrical load the UPS can handle. Run time tells you how many minutes the UPS can supply power before it runs out.
Image by magraphics© 123rf.com.
Using the UPS

Unplugging a computer to turn it off isn't a good idea. It's better to use the operating system to shut it down. Battery backups often come with software and a USB connection that monitors the power. If there’s a power outage, the battery backup will tell the computer to shut down properly. This stops sudden shutdowns that can harm the operating system. When the OS is damaged, the computer might act strangely or not start up correctly.

When the UPS notices that power isn't coming in, it beeps at regular intervals. This alerts people nearby about the power problem. You can replace the internal batteries in a UPS, so you don't have to buy a whole new unit. This saves money and helps the environment.

blocks.text: The motherboard is the central circuit board that connects and powers all the components of a computer. In this lesson, you will explore the different types of motherboards, their specifications, and the role they play in both desktop and mobile devices. You will also learn about the various buses, expansion slots, and proprietary designs found in laptops, tablets, and smartphones.

Additionally, this lesson covers the essential firmware that controls the motherboard, including BIOS and UEFI. You will discover how firmware starts the computer, manages hardware checks, and how modern UEFI provides advanced features and security. By the end of this lesson, you will understand the key steps and considerations for installing and configuring a motherboard in a variety of devices.
The Motherboard
The motherboard is a large circuit board that acts like the computer's spine. It links all the parts together and sends electrical signals between them.

As you saw in the video, motherboards come in different sizes and form factors, including standardized designs like ATX and micro-ATX, as well as proprietary designs made for specific systems. This topic takes a closer look at the specifications, buses, and expansion slots found on desktop motherboards, as well as the proprietary motherboards used in laptops, tablets, and smartphones.
Motherboard Specs

A motherboard is made to work with specific types of central processing unit (CPU) and memory, and will have sockets designed to hold those specific types of components. The most widely used brands of CPU are Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Intel.

AMD CPUs and Intel CPUs are very different and can't be swapped with each other. Each type of motherboard will have sockets for certain AMD or Intel CPUs. The socket that holds the CPU uses a zero insertion force (ZIF) mechanism to push the processor into the motherboard and keep it in place securely. This helps prevent the motherboard from bending, which could cause permanent damage.

There are fewer options when it comes to memory and how it works on motherboards. Memory types have been pretty standard over the years, with the Double Data Rate (DDR) family being the most common in recent decades. DDR memory changes every 4–6 years, and each generation has different slot connectors. The latest one is DDR5. The most important thing to remember is that as long as you match up the parts that are designed to work together correctly, your computer will run well.
Computer Buses and Expansion Slots

The motherboard is what connects peripheral devices, such as they keyboard, mouse, printer, and speakers, to the computer's CPU. The motherboard has all the connectors and circuits needed for these devices to link up with the CPU. If you look closely at a motherboard, you'll see the many connectors and ports where different computer parts can be attached. If you look even closer, you'll notice small groups of parallel wires on the surface. These wires form buses, which are groups of wires that connect different devices together.

A bus is a communication system that lets data move between different parts internally. The word "bus" comes from the Latin word "omnibus," which means "for all." If you take a close look at a motherboard, you'll notice that it has many small wires running across it. These tiny wires, or circuits, make up the bus, which is printed on the circuit board (PCB). The computer bus is responsible for transferring power, data, and clock timing.
One of the great things about a motherboard is its expansion slots, which let you add more features to your computer. Over the years, the design of these expansion buses has changed.

Because the bus design depends on the motherboard and CPU, it's good to know the types of bus systems that have been used and are still in use. Older systems had a peripheral component interconnect (PCI) bus. But today's systems have what are called PCI express (PCIe) slots.

The PCIe slots on the Motherboard come in different sizes, x1, x2, x4, x8, and x16, with x1 and x16 being the most common. The speed of PCIe slots has also increased over time, from 1.0 to 5.0, with each new version being twice as fast as the one before. But to take advantage of a slot's speed, a motherboard will need to support it.

When you're looking to buy a motherboard, try to get one with four memory slots. This way, adding more memory later won't be as expensive. For example, your new computer might come with 2 sticks of 8GB memory, for a total of 16GB. There's a chance you'll want more memory in a couple of years. If the system you buy has four memory slots, you'll have two empty slots to add more memory to. But if you only have two slots, you'll have to remove the old memory to add more, which can be costly.
Laptop, Tablet, and Smartphone Motherboards
Not all motherboards follow the ATX standard. Laptops, tablets, and smartphones use proprietary motherboard designs that are unique to each model.
Type Description
Laptop Motherboards
Laptop motherboards fall into the proprietary form factor type.

items: The motherboard and the case are designed specifically for each model.
If the motherboard needs to be replaced it must be replaced with a specific model.
Laptop motherboards are not designed to be modular. The CPU and other components are soldered onto the motherboard and cannot be easily replaced.

blocks.text: Tablet Motherboards Like laptop motherboards, tablet motherboards are a proprietary form factor.

items: All parts, including CPU, memory, and storage, are soldered onto the motherboard and can be difficult to replace.
Normally, if a tablet malfunctions the entire device is disposed of and replaced.

blocks.text: Smartphone Motherboards
Like tablet motherboards, smartphone motherboards are a proprietary form factor.

items: All parts are soldered onto the motherboard and can be difficult to be replaced.
Normally, like a tablet, if a smartphone malfunctions the entire device is disposed of and replaced.

blocks.text: The Firmware and BIOS

When a computer is powered on, the basic input/output system (BIOS) or Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) is what starts up and checks the hardware components on the motherboard. This is the beginning of the boot process. It happens before the operating system loads and is made possible by a low-level set of instructions called firmware—that's what the BIOS and UEFI both are. The UEFI is responsible for the power-on self-test (POS T) and is the first software to run when a computing device starts up.

The term BIOS has been used for so long (many decades, in fact) that it's hard for techs to switch and call it UEFI. If you hear someone mention a motherboard's BIOS, they probably mean UEFI, unless it's a very old system.

The BIOS provides industry-standard code that starts up the essential parts of the computer by performing checks on critical hardware components such as RAM, CPU, and peripherals. You won't see this very often, though. Most motherboards nowadays use the newer UEFI firmware.
UEFI has a modern look, supports bigger storage drives, lets you use a mouse, and has better security when booting. And computers with UEFI can start up in the old BIOS mode if needed.

You can upgrade the UEFI by "flashing" the code on its read-only memory (ROM) chip. This is best done from time to time to help the motherboard work better. You can download the new firmware from the PC manufacturer, such as HP or Lenovo. Or if you have a custom-built system, you can get the firmware from the motherboard manufacturer instead—ASUSTeK and GIGABYTE are popular ones. The UEFI is non-volatile, which means it keeps its settings even when the computer is turned off.
The term "flashing" dates back to early BIOS chips, which were literally flashed to update the coding. This was done with a beam of light that erased the chip and allowed it to be reprogrammed.

a closer look at the different CPU manufacturers and connection types, optimization features

safely.

process 64 bits, while older ones processed 32 bits. A 64-bit CPU handles 64 bits of data at

blocks.text: A computer is made up of many internal components that work together to process information, store data, and display output. Understanding what these parts do, how they connect, and how to troubleshoot them will help you make informed decisions when upgrading, purchasing, or repairing a computer.

In this lesson, you will explore the central processing unit (CPU) and how it connects to the motherboard, how memory (RAM) temporarily stores data for fast access, and how storage drives keep your files safe when the power is off. You will also learn about graphics processing units (GPUs), sound cards, and power supplies, and discover basic troubleshooting steps for diagnosing common hardware problems.
The Central Processing Unit (CPU)

As you learned in the video, the central processing unit (CPU) is the computer's brain, processing billions of instructions per second at speeds measured in GHz. This topic takes a closer look at the different CPU manufacturers and connection types, optimization features like multi-core processing and cache memory, and the cooling systems that keep CPUs running safely.

CPUs are also categorized by the number of bits they can process at one time. Modern CPUs process 64 bits, while older ones processed 32 bits. A 64-bit CPU handles 64 bits of data at once, making it faster than a 32-bit CPU.
CPU Manufacturers
Intel and AMD are the main companies that make processors for consumers and servers, and they've led the market since the late 1970s.

Different CPUs connect to the motherboard in different ways. All Intel CPUs use a land grid array (L G A) design, which means they have hundreds of little pads on the underside. Most AMD CPUs use a pin grid array (PG A) design, which means they have hundreds (sometimes thousands) of pins.
These pins or pads fit into the motherboard socket, which has the same layout. So, if an AMD CPU has pins, the motherboard will have an equal number of matching pads.

In the last decade, at time of writing, Apple started making its own CPUs for its systems. Apple doesn't call them just CPUs because its chips have the memory built in. This includes not just the cache memory but also the main memory, which Apple calls unified memory, used by the computer. With the memory and CPU 'under the same umbrella,' computing time is faster.
Another improvement in Apple silicon is its efficient processing, which doesn't use a lot of power, leading to longer battery life on its laptops.
Another important type of processor is the ARM processor. These processors use a simpler set of instructions for computing and are very common in smartphones and other mobile devices.
Optimizing CPUs

As computers got faster, manufacturers wanted to make CPUs even quicker. They did this by adding more "brains" or cores onto a single chip. Today, CPUs have multiple cores to boost computing power. CPUs can have 4, 8, 16, or even more cores.
CPUs can also almost double their computing power without adding another core. Intel calls this hyperthreading, and AMD calls it simultaneous multi-threading.

CPUs have a small amount of cache memory. Cache is a special type of memory that stores data the CPU uses frequently, making it faster for the CPU to access this data. Adding cache memory helps the CPU work even faster.

Even though CPUs don't have moving parts, they get very hot. This is because they process billions of instructions every second. To keep them cool, they are built with both active and passive cooling. Manufacturers will use a heatsink, thermal paste, and a fan to remove the hot air, depending on the size of the computing device.
The Memory
As you saw in the video, random-access memory (RAM) is the computer's short-term memory.

It temporarily stores the programs and data the CPU is actively using. RAM is volatile, meaning everything in it is lost when the computer is turned off. This topic explores the differences between volatile and non-volatile memory, memory features like DDR generations and dual- channel architecture, and how to determine the right amount of memory for your needs.

You might wonder, why not use the storage drive that already holds everything? The problem is that storage drives, like mechanical drives and solid-state drives, are too slow to keep up with a CPU. If storage replaced memory and interacted with the CPU instead, the computer would move very slowly.
Volatile vs Non-Volatile Memory
Random access memory (RAM) and read-only memory (ROM), used in the firmware and BIOS system, might look similar at first glance. Despite both being pieces of memory, they do serve different purposes.
Random access memory (RAM) has these features:

items: Volatile: Stores data temporarily, while the computer is powered on, and does not save data while the computer is turned off.
Fast: Data can move in and out of RAM very quickly, making it easy for the computer to process many instructions at once.
Removable: Memory modules or sticks clip into slots on the motherboard, and can be replaced as needed.

blocks.text: Read-only memory (ROM) has these features:

items: Non-volatile: Stores data permanently, even without power.
Slow: Data retrieval from ROM is a comparatively lengthy process, and ROM does not contribute to processing speed.
Permanent: Manufacturers permanently attach ROM chips to boards within devices.
Programmable: Some types of ROM have code or instructions that can be rewritten when needed, such as when firmware updates are released.

blocks.text: Memory Features
Many of today's desktops, laptops, and smartphones have between 6GB and 16GB of memory.

If you want a more powerful system, you can add more RAM, maybe 32GB or more, and servers can have even more memory. These aren't strict rules, though. Servers might have more or less RAM, and you can add as much memory as your motherboard can handle.

When you look at a memory stick, you'll see gold contacts on both sides. This is called a dual inline memory module (DIMM). DIMMs were introduced in the 1990s and are still the standard format for memory today.

Memory has other characteristics in addition to its capacity. Memory speed doubled around 2000, or the turn of the 21st Century. This faster speed was termed Double Data Rate (DDR) and speed jumped up to 200 MHz (megahertz, or one million hertz), twice as fast as previous memory rates. As the industry continued to improve, memory moved on to DDR2 a few years later, doubling in speed again. Every following generation of DDR has doubled the speed of the previous generation and has followed the basic naming structure. From DDR3 to DDR4 to DDR5 in today's computers, at the time of writing.

Another characteristic of memory is that it’s interchangeable across different brands and models of computers. For example, if you have a new HP computer and want to put some of that memory into a new Dell, you can easily do that. This works because both use DDR5 memory, so it will work in either system. However, one tech company doesn’t always follow the same rules: Apple. Unfortunately, on their laptops and all-in-one systems, they solder the memory onto the motherboard, making it impossible to change.

When a computer crashes a lot, a bad memory stick could be the reason. Windows includes a built-in tool to test the memory. You can find it by typing ‘Windows Memory Diagnostic’ in the Start search box. This program takes some time to run, depending on how much memory your computer has. To check all the memory, the tool reboots your computer and starts checking the RAM before loading Windows again.
How Much Memory?

One of the most important things to understand about computers is that memory handles what is actively loaded when your computer is turned on. People often ask, "How much memory should I have?" The answer depends on how many programs you run and how many tabs you have open during a computing session.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, if you only work with one program at a time and close it before opening another, you don’t need a lot of memory; 8GB would be fine. However, if you multitask with multiple programs and lots of tabs in your browser, you’ll want more memory. Consider getting 16GB to help your system run smoothly while you switch between websites and programs.

The future of memory technology looks bright. Manufacturers keep increasing memory capacity, and this trend will likely continue. The growth in memory capacity has been amazing, with computers now having over 50 times the storage they did just 25 years ago.
Manufacturers also focus on using less power, especially for laptops, to extend battery life.
Additionally, memory speeds are getting faster, which helps make computers run more quickly overall.
The Graphics Processing Unit (GPU)

As you learned in the video, a graphics processing unit (GPU) handles all of a computer's visual output. Most Intel CPUs include integrated graphics that share system RAM with the CPU, which is enough for basic tasks. Most AMD CPUs need a separate graphics card. This topic covers dedicated graphics cards for high-performance needs, as well as resolution, frame rates, and the specialized memory that makes modern GPUs so powerful.
Enhanced Graphics

Computers that are used for gaming, video editing, and 3D modeling and animation need a dedicated GPU for more powerful graphics processing. In order to provide this additional power, you can install a dedicated graphics card. The best dedicated graphics cards, also called video cards, are expensive because they include the graphics chip, along with their own specialized RAM and cooling.

Video cards offer multiple outputs, like HDMI and display ports, so you can connect more than one monitor. Also, remember that graphics cards use a PCIe x16 interface to install into the motherboard of a desktop computer.

There is a graphics card for every budget. Integrated graphics are the cheapest, while high-end graphics cards can cost a lot of money, sometimes over $1,000. Many companies make video cards and GPUs, but Nvidia is the biggest and most popular one in the market.
Image by nikkytok © 123rf.com.
Resolution and Frame Rate
A video card makes incredibly realistic images by using higher resolution, faster frame rates, and special video memory.

Video resolution is represented by two numbers. These numbers tell you how many pixels make up the image, both across (horizontally) and up and down (vertically) on a screen. For example, a common resolution is 1920 x 1080, also called 1080p. Higher resolution means more pixels, which gives you more realistic images with better details. Moving up to 4K displays means a resolution of 3840 x 2160, which is twice as good as 1080p.

Frame rates are measured in Hertz (Hz), which describes how often a display updates. A higher frame rate makes graphics and animations look smoother, especially when the action gets faster. Frame rates range from 30–60 frames per second (fps) and can go up to 120 fps on some high-end graphics cards. Also, ray tracing is a technique that makes the lighting in a scene look real by accurately showing reflections and shadows, just like in real life.

Video cards and their GPUs have their own processing and memory systems. This is similar to, but slightly different from, the CPU's processing capabilities. The GPU has cores, or individual processors, that are designed to speed up graphics processing. These cores work together to handle multiple tasks at the same time. Because they compute at a very high rate, they also have fans to keep the unit cool.

The video card also has memory that is different from traditional memory. The GPU video memory is specialized for fast rendering, made to meet the specific needs of a GPU. A modern video card might have 16GB of Graphics Double Data Rate (GDDR6) memory. The ability to handle a lot of smaller tasks very quickly is one of the strengths of a GPU that makes it ideal for artificial intelligence (AI), as well as video and graphics development.

blocks.text: Networks are everywhere. Every time you check your email, stream a video, pay with a credit card, or connect your phone to a Bluetooth speaker, you are relying on a network to move information between devices. Understanding how networks work is essential for anyone who uses modern technology, whether at home, at school, or in the workplace.

In this lesson, you will explore what a network is, how computers communicate using the client/ server model and protocols, and the key components needed for a network connection. You will compare wired and wireless connections, learn how Ethernet cables are built and tested, and discover the protocols that make web browsing, email, file transfer, and troubleshooting possible.

Whether you realize it or not, you are always surrounded by networks that constantly share information. The ideas about time and place are changing. The world feels like a global village where distance doesn't stop you from connecting for business, school, or social reasons. If you live in an area with a strong digital infrastructure, it's hard to imagine life without all the network systems that are so important to your daily life.
You might think of things like secure browsing and email as obvious examples of networking, but there are other ways networks impact the way you live.
Networks in Daily Life

Every time you use a debit or credit card, the store's register is connected to other computers through a network. Your card details are automatically sent to your bank or credit card company to check and update your balance. This also happens when you shop online, such as when you purchase a movie ticket or order food through a delivery app.

The world of entertainment is also more and more dependent on networks. When you connect your mobile device to your Bluetooth earbuds, a wireless speaker, or connect to your car, you have a direct connection from one device to another. A short-range connection like this is also known as a personal area network (P AN). Streaming services have changed how we watch television, movies, and more. Digital cameras can connect directly to local networks, making it easier for more people to create and share content.

In addition to their impact on leisure time, networks bring safety into people’s lives. Networked communication systems are important for controlling transportation. They help manage things like traffic lights, pedestrian crossings, air traffic control, and train signals.

Networks are a bigger part of your life than you might have thought. They are involved in almost every part of modern life. When you understand them better, you can make your personal devices work better for you. If you really like learning about how networks work, there are many job opportunities in many different fields that focus specifically on network operations.
What Does a Network Do?
A network is a group of computer systems connected together so they can share information.
The Internet is the largest possible example of this. In a network, all the computers can ask for and send information, but usually most computers ask for information, and only a few send it out.

Think of a computer network like a school. Most of the computers on a typical network are like students who take instructions and receive information. A few computers are like teachers who give out the information. It's most likely that you're using one of the many devices that receive information, such as when you click on the next page in this course, or when you check your email. The computers that give you this data are part of a smaller group that shares out data with you and with people all over the world.
For computers to share information over a network, several key components must be in place.
Each computer must have network media, a network interface, and network protocols.

items: Network media: The pathways that connect computers together. Media, when we're talking about networking, describes the different ways we store or transfer information. Computers move information across wired connections using coaxial cables, Ethernet cables, or fiber optic wire. Information can also move wirelessly, through radio signals in Wi-Fi. Computers must have either a wired or a wireless connection to be part of a network.

Network interface: An interface is the point at which two different systems interact with each other. A network interface is where your computer makes a connection to the bigger network. Each computer needs to have a network interface, which is a special spot for it to plug into the network (with cables) or to connect wirelessly. This is typically done using a piece of hardware called a network interface card (NIC). NICs are often included in the original computer build, but can be added later if your computer doesn't come with one. If you upgrade your system with a NIC after you buy it, this is called an expansion card, and it's easily installed on your computer's motherboard.

Network protocols: A shared set of protocols, or rules, serves as a common language among computers. These rules are set up at the operating system (OS) level. All the computers on the network must use the same protocols so that they can understand each other as they share data back and forth.

blocks.text: Using Networking Components

A wired system, one that uses cables to connect to the network, will most often use Ethernet cabling as its network media. Those cables use specialized sockets and plugs to make this connection. The IT industry calls these RJ-45 or registered jack type 45. The RJ-45 standard makes it easy for industry professionals and for computer manufacturers to create network connections. The RJ-45 plug or clip attaches to the ends of the cable. One end plugs into your computer, and the other end plugs into the socket on the wall plate. On the other side of the wall plate is another network cable. If you're at home, this belongs to the internet service provider (ISP). If you're at work or at school, this network cable belongs to the organization, and it runs to other networking devices before connecting to the Internet.

Wireless networks use radio signals instead of cables to communicate. Connecting to a Wi- Fi network is a bit more complex. A computer needs a wireless network interface. Different computers have different ways of connecting to Wi-Fi. Many desktop computers already have Wi-Fi built in, but others need something called a wireless network adapter. The easiest way to add Wi-Fi to these computers is by plugging a small device called a USB wireless adapter into a USB slot. Laptops usually have Wi-Fi built in, so you don't have to add anything. But you might have to turn the Wi-Fi on.

Once you have a wireless network adapter set up, or you have your laptop's Wi-Fi turned on, you can then connect to a Wi-Fi network. On a Windows computer, click on the Network icon that's usually at the bottom-right of your screen. A menu will pop up showing all the Wi-Fi networks it can find nearby. Pick the one you want to join and click "Connect." Then, if it asks for it, type in the Wi-Fi password and click "Next." Some public Wi-Fi networks in places like cafés or libraries won't need a password.
Connecting to a Network

For computers that use Windows, Microsoft has set up a few ways to check if your computer is hooked up to a network or the Internet. One way is by looking at a special icon that appears in the bottom-right corner of the screen, in the area called the system tray. If your computer is connected with a cable, you'll see an icon that looks like a computer. If you're using Wi-Fi, you'll see an icon with curved lines that look like waves. The number of waves shows how strong your signal is. If you can't connect to the internet, the icon changes to a picture of a globe with a "no" symbol over it.
Going further into Windows Settings gives you more details about your computer's connections.

The network settings tell you if you're connected with a cable or wirelessly, and they also show you other options you have, like to use VPNs, share your internet with other devices as a mobile hotspot, or use proxies.
Wired Network Connectors
This topic looks more closely at the twisted pair copper cables used inside homes and offices, specifically how Ethernet cables are built, and you can make your own.
Image by Thuansak Srilao © 123rf.com.

Inside an Ethernet cable, there are eight wires grouped into four twisted pairs. Each pair is assigned a color: orange, green, blue, or brown. One wire's insulator (the plastic covering) is mostly white, striped with the color, and the second wire has an insulator with a solid color.
When you're ready to connect the wires, you need to untwist them and line them up in a certain order in the connectors. This order can follow either the T568A or the T568B standard.
The order of the colors is important because devices can't communicate properly without the correct alignment.

In T568A, the green pairs are wired to pins 1 and 2, and the orange pairs are wired to pins 3 and 6. In T568B, these pairs swap places, so orange is terminated to pins 1 and 2 and green to 3 and 6. It's important to avoid using a mixture of the two standards. T568B is probably the more widely deployed of the two.
Making Cables

You can make Ethernet cables yourself with some tools and a little bit of know-how. Raw cables are sold in large hardware and home improvement stores, as well as online, in lengths of 100 to 1,000 feet. You can then cut these lengths to the exact size you need. After cutting, you'd either attach RJ-45 clips to the ends or connect the cable to a wall jack.

Learning to make cables yourself is useful if you want to get a job in IT eventually. Sometimes, you'll need a cable with a specific length, but you won't have one that's the right size. Also, when you need to run cables to devices, especially through ceilings and walls, it's easier to move them around without the RJ-45 clips getting in the way.
Here are some of the basic tools needed to make your own Ethernet cables:

items: Crimper: A crimper is a tool that helps connect an RJ-45 cable to its clip. To do this, you first make sure that the eight wires inside the cable are in the right order according to the

blocks.text: T568 standard you're using. Then, you put them into the clip, and next, into the crimper. You squeeze the crimper to secure everything together. After you've done this on both ends of the cable, you should use a cable tester to check if all the wires are set up correctly.

items: Punch Down: A punch-down tool is used to push each of the eight wires into a patch panel or a wall jack. When you press the cable into the right spot with this tool, it makes a satisfying click sound. Before you start punching, it's very important to check that the tool is facing the right way so everything is done correctly.
Cable Tester: A cable tester checks if a new cable, or one already connected to a patch panel or wall jack, is working. It quickly tells you the status of each of the 8 wires. The tester

blocks.text: uses lights or an LED screen to show you the statuses so that you know if the cable was made in the right way. More complex testers can even tell you how long a cable is.

items: Toner Probe: A toner probe is a useful tool for figuring out where a network cable starts or ends. It comes in two pieces. One piece plugs into the network, usually at a wall socket, and emits a sound or a tone (that's why it's called a toner). The other piece is the probe, which you move over the various network cables to listen for that sound. This helps you determine which cable goes with which port. It's a big time-saver, especially when the network cables aren't clearly marked.

blocks.text: Wireless Network Connectors

An access point (AP) allows wireless or mobile devices to connect to the network. The AP can connect to the network using a cabled connection, and can provide wireless connections to other devices such as smartphones, tablets, and laptops. At first, only large companies and government organizations had APs, but now anyone can have them at home, with new improvements in technology. When you have several APs working together, it's called a mesh network, which works great for covering large areas with Wi-Fi.
Most of the time, enterprise APs are connected to the main network with an Ethernet cable.

But the ones you might have at home usually just pass the Wi-Fi signal from one AP to another without cables. You could buy packages of two, three, or more APs to put around your house if you wanted. Then all your devices would have a stronger Wi-Fi connection. The more coverage you need, the more APs you could add.
Common Networking Protocols
Beyond those core protocols, there are additional protocols and tools worth understanding for email, file transfer, network management, and troubleshooting.
Email Protocols

You just pressed send on an email message. How will it get to the recipient? What protocols are used to send and receive email? Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) is the protocol used to send messages from one person to another. There are two common protocols you should know about for retrieving messages:

items: Post Office Protocol (POP) version 3: POP3 is an older protocol that is being replaced by

blocks.text: IMAP. It allows for email messages to be retrieved on a single computer. It is important to know that POP3 removes the message from the email server and stores it on the device used to access email. These messages will not be accessible by other computers.

items: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) 4 : This protocol is preferred to get your email messages. It keeps the message on the server but allows you to modify it as if it were stored locally. As a result, multiple devices (computer, phone, etc.) can be used to access the email messages.

blocks.text: File Transfer Protocols
File transfer protocols provide the ability to send and receive files over the internet.

items: File Transfer Protocol (FTP): This is the standard protocol used to transfer files between a client and a server.
SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP): This is the secure version of FTP that uses another protocol called SSH or Secure Shell Protocol to protect the information being transferred.

blocks.text: Network Services
There are many protocols in this category but we selected one common protocol that you should know about.

items: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP): DHCP helps network administrators assign IP addresses to the devices on their networks. Instead of going to each device and manually configuring the IP address, DHCP will assign an address when the device connects to the network.

blocks.text: Common Troubleshooting Utilities
Utilities are small programs that are built into the operating system. There are two commonly used methods to solve network problems.

items: The ping utility sends a message from one computer to a target computer over a network and then listens for a response. This utility allows you to perform a quick test to determine if there is connectivity between the computers. If it doesn’t get a response, there’s something wrong with the connection. If it does, then you know there is a physical connection and the

blocks.text: IP address configuration is correct, and you need to look somewhere else.

items: The tracert utility follows the path of a packet of information across the network to its destination. It displays each router, called a hop, through which the information passes on its way. It usually lists the hop number, the time it took, and the IP address and name if available. It is used to see if one of the links takes a long time, indicating a problem. If it stops and displays timeout messages, then you know something is blocking that path. That is where you need to start looking.

blocks.text: Networks come in many shapes and sizes, from a small home setup connecting a few devices to a massive corporate system spanning entire countries. Understanding the different types of networks and how they are organized helps you make better decisions about how to connect, share resources, and stay productive.

In this lesson, you will explore the different types and sizes of networks, including PANs, LANs, and WANs. You will learn how network topologies describe the physical and logical layout of connected devices, compare the client-server and peer-to-peer networking models, and discover how wireless technologies like Bluetooth and mobile hotspots let you connect on the go.
Network Server

In the client-server model, servers are dedicated computers that provide services to all the clients on the network. Examples of network services include email, file sharing, online gaming, voice over IP, and printing. By consolidating all network services to a server, clients can all have equal, unrestricted access to the services. The table below describes a few basic kinds of servers. Keep in mind that each of these services can be consolidated on the same physical hardware.
Table 30: Server Types
Term Description

Mail Server Mail servers provide email service to a network. In many ways, they're like virtual post offices. They store incoming mail and send outgoing messages, either to users on the same network or on other networks around the world.

Web Server Every site you've visited on the World Wide Web, including this one, has been hosted on a web server. Web servers store web pages as hypertext documents. Whenever they get a request for one of their pages, they transmit the appropriate file to the requester using HTTP.

Database Server Database servers store databases, which are huge repositories of organized data. Clients on the network can send queries to the database server, which returns specific information about the data. Clients can also use queries to add, remove, or change data as appropriate.

Gaming Server Gaming servers keep track of events in multiplayer video games. Most online games have players simultaneously sending inputs via their mouse and keyboard (or controller). The game server receives all these inputs and re-transmits them to the other players, making the game play out in real time for everyone involved.
Networking Models
There are two important models that describe how computers interact on a network: client- server and peer-to-peer.

The client-server relationship is a basic concept in networking. It's one way of looking at how one computer (a server) and another computer (the client) on the same network talk. The client requests information and resources, and the server fulfills those client requests. The servers are powerful, dependable computers that are expected to be available all the time, every day, without taking a break.

In addition to the client-server model, where one computer requests and others respond, computers can have a peer-to-peer relationship model. It's a meeting of two equals. Both computers can request resources, and both can provide resources to fulfil those requests.

Peer-to-peer architecture allows smaller groups to share information just as easily as groups with more computing power. Peer-to-peer architecture makes it easier to share files, stream video, and resist security threats.
Local Network Types
A local area network (LAN) is a group of connected computers that are physically close, usually in the same building. These computers are linked up using a centralized device called a switch.

Think about a school's computer lab, where all the computers are connected. Everyone could save their work on the same computer, or to the same server, or print out documents on the same printer. Everyone uses the same Wi-Fi from the same router to get to the internet. Your home probably has a LAN, too, with your family's phones, tablets, and computers sharing the internet through a router.
LANs can be small, like the Wi-Fi network at your house, or they can be much bigger, like in a large company. That's called an enterprise network. Setting up a LAN has lots of benefits.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, every computer or device on this type of network can share resources with each other. The most important thing they can share is an Internet connection. They can also share files, printers, and anything else on the network itself.
Local Area Network Examples

An intranet is a private LAN, a bit like a miniature Internet that's just for people in the same company or organization. It works a lot like the Internet, but it's not part of the global Internet that everyone in the world uses. Only people who with permission can get access. Intranets are great for sharing files and collaborating together at work. You can share all sorts of things like documents, spreadsheets, or slideshows. And these files are stored safely, can be backed up, and can be shared over and over again without the worry of being stolen by someone from the outside.

You might hear the term small office, home office (SOHO). This is a network made for a small business that you can set up in any office space or at home. The most important part of this setup is the router. A SOHO router can do more than the regular routers people have at home.
Thanks to technology getting better over the last few years, working from home has become a lot easier and more common. A SOHO is a great option for this scenario.
Key Features of Local Area Networks

There are some primary elements that make up a LAN. First, there are one or more people called network administrators who oversee the LAN. These admins try to make sure that everything on the LAN is safe, and they decide who can use what. If you were an admin, you could control other computers on the network right from your own computer! This remote access can help save a lot of time, especially when there may be hundreds of computers connected to the network.
A LAN network is typically very fast, because all the devices are close to each other. It uses network devices called switches and routers to connect all these close-together pieces.
Switches help move data around, and the router manages the connection to the wider internet.

To keep everything secure, a LAN will also have firewall put in place. These might be built in to the router or be a separate device that stops hackers from getting in. Security is important because a LAN also connects to the Internet.

One of the best things about a LAN is that everyone can share one internet connection, which means you only have to pay for one internet service provider (ISP). And things like printers can be shared, so you don't need as many extra devices cluttering up space. The sharing resources part is a huge benefit of learning how to set up a LAN.
Wide Area Network Types

Large organizations link many local area network (LANs) together to make a wide area network (W AN) that can cover huge areas, like whole countries or even the whole world. For example, if you have an enterprise that has a headquarters and branch offices spread across different cities, each branch will have its own LAN, and all these company LANs will be connected into the larger WAN. A router is usually used to make the connection between a LAN and a WAN, but sometimes dedicated telecommunication lines are used as well.

A private network is how businesses keep their data safe from the outside Internet. Only computers authorized by the company can use their network. This is essential for those companies that want to keep their internal information secret.

WANs are managed from one central location so that the IT team can look after the whole network from one place. This is possible because the same rules apply everywhere, no matter the location. This makes the job a lot easier.

WANs provide many advantages, such as allowing all users in a company to use the same applications, firewall, and resources. This is beneficial because otherwise each device would have to be installed on individual machines, costing more time and money. The biggest advantage of the WAN is seamless communication and sharing of information across the organization.

Many WANs are used with a virtual private network (VPN). A VPN allows users in remote locations to use the Internet to connect to a WAN and access all the network resources as though they were in their company's main office. The VPN keeps the network private through data encryption.
Wide Area Network Examples
A metropolitan area network (MAN) links smaller LANs into one larger, centralized network.

Think of it like this: if each LAN is a small neighborhood, then a MAN is a big city that connects all those neighborhoods together. A MAN is bigger than a neighborhood but not as huge as a whole country (that's what a WAN is like). You'll probably find MANs used mostly by colleges, big cities, or even by towns that are close to each other.

There are also wide area networks based in the cloud. One example would be Amazon Web Services (A WS). It uses the power of cloud networks to stay turned on almost all the time and has the flexibility to shrink or grow depending on what a specific company needs.
The Internet is really just a giant WAN that connects lots of smaller networks from all around the world. The difference is that where many WANs are privately owned, the Internet is for everyone.
