blocks.text: Every time you browse the web, stream a video, or send an email, your data passes through a series of networking devices that guide it to the right destination. Understanding what these devices do and how they work together is essential for anyone who uses or manages a network, whether at home or in a business environment.

In this lesson, you will explore the roles of modems, router, switches, and firewalls, and learn how network interface card connect your devices to the network. You will also examine network addresses, ports, and protocols, and compare the different types of Internet connections available today, including cable, DSL, fiber, cellular, satellite, and fixed wireless.
Networking Devices
This topic covers additional details about modems, router types and configuration, switch features like PoE and VLANs, and how firewalls protect your network.
Modem

A modem is a device that takes the signals from your internet service provider (ISP) and translates them into a form your devices can understand. It "modulates" and "demodulates" the signals, which is how it got its name.
A modem maintains your connection to the ISP. It sits between two networks, your own home local area network (LAN) and your ISP's network, and allows data to move between the two.
Usually, your ISP will provide the modem for you, though you can purchase and use your own.

On the consumer side (that's your side), the plugs are made to be universal, so just about any device with a network connection can join up. In most cases, the modem will probably come with a router as well, which lets you connect your devices either with cables or wirelessly.
Router

A router moves data between networks using IP addresses. Inside most home routers, there is also a built-in switch that handles local traffic. Routers have Ethernet ports on the back where you can plug in devices such as your desktop computer. They also send out Wi-Fi signals so that your phones, tablets, laptops, and smart home devices, the ones on the Internet of Things (Io T), can connect to the internet wirelessly.
Routers are available in two different types:

items: Consumer routers: These are ideal for small offices or homes, because their signal strength is not very strong, and is best suited to smaller areas. Consumer routers offer both wired and wireless connection options.

Commercial routers: This type of router has both a stronger signal and higher capacity, making it perfect for large companies that rely on constant traffic management. Commercial routers offer only wired connections.

blocks.text: Routers have an area called the interface that you can access either on a web browser or with a command line interface (CLI). On the interface, you can set things up the way you want, such as giving your Wi-Fi network a name or setting a password. Maintain your router by updating its firmware whenever a new version becomes available.
Switch
Switches can be small, with just 4 connection ports, or very large, with up to 96. Each port has an RJ-45 connection for your Ethernet cable.

Some switches can send electricity through the cables along with the data. This is called Power over Ethernet (P oE). It's handy for devices like Wi-Fi routers, security cameras, and office phones that require power to work. Some switches also have ports for fiber cables, which let data travel over longer distances.
There are two types of switches:

items: Unmanaged switches: This type of switch allows you to simply plug in an Ethernet cable, and it will work. An unmanaged switch does not allow for any type of configuration or changes to its performance.

Managed switches: This type of switch lets the user control how it operates or configure its settings. One example of this feature is the ability to set up a Virtual LAN (VLAN) on a managed switch. This allows you to make a small, separate network within a larger one. It's like having a private room in a big house, where only certain devices are allowed in.

blocks.text: Firewall
In practice, every network that connects to the Internet needs a firewall. Your home router has one built in, and businesses use dedicated firewall appliances with more advanced features.
Firewalls are like filters. They let good data in and keep bad data out. How can data be bad?
One example of bad data is when someone might try to send packets of data programmed to steal your personal information or a company's top-secret files.

Firewalls can help by splitting the network into separate areas that keep critical systems sealed off from the internet. Additionally, they can manage virtual private networks (VPNs), which let data tunnel safely through the internet, encrypted.
Network Ports
When your computer is part of a network, it's moving a lot of information very quickly. The network needs to have rules, or protocols, to help guide the traffic so it gets to the right place.

Just like the post office accurately delivers your mail by reading your street address and postal code on the envelope, network traffic is easier to manage with network identifiers such as IP addresses and ports.

Network ports are unique numbers that the operating system assigns to different types of network traffic. They work like parts of a mailing address, sending deliveries to specific places. Port numbers help to direct the information on a network, depending on what kind of information it is. For example, when you send an email to your co-worker, the bundle of data includes the port number 587. It's like a special ticket that sends the data to a corresponding port on your co-worker's computer.

Some port numbers are reserved for the most common services, like email or for transferring files. Other services get a port number only when they're in use. Once that service is done using the port, the number goes back to being unassigned. Some types of ports are turned off.
Just as warehouse doors can be opened or shut, closed ports mean you cannot enter.
Port Forwarding
Port forwarding is like telling a letter carrier to send your mail to a new address if you're not at home. You would still want to receive your information, even if you were at a different location.
That's essentially what you're telling the router or firewall it has to do with the packets of information when you use port forwarding.

A common port for this is port 3389, used for the remote desktop protocol (RDP) on a graphical user interface (GUI). This basically lets you connect to any other Windows computer anywhere in the world!
To make this happen, you have to set things up correctly on both computers and the internet router, which is a bit like making sure both doors are unlocked and open so you can walk through.
Port Number Name Definition

21 File Transfer Protocol (FTP) Standard protocol used for moving files between computers 22 Secure Shell (SSH) Provides for secure communication between devices 23 Telnet Provides for unsecure communication between devices 25 Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) Used for sending email. However, it has been deprecated in the last decade 53 Domain Name System (DNS) Provides a translation between friendly domain names and IP addresses 80 Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Provides communication standards for clients and servers on the World Wide Web 110 Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3) Used by email programs for incoming email 143 Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) Used most commonly for receiving email 443 Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) Establishes encrypted communication between clients and servers on the World Wide Web 587 Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) Used for outgoing email Port Scanning Network administrators use port scanning tools to check which ports are open on a computer or server. A port scan sends requests to a range of port numbers and reports back which ones responded. This helps administrators understand what services are running on a device and identify potential security risks.

An open port means a service is actively listening for connections on that port number. For example, if a port scan shows that ports 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS) are open, you know the device is running a web server. If unexpected ports are open, it could indicate a security vulnerability that needs to be addressed.
Port scans typically report ports in one of three states:

items: Open: A service is actively listening and accepting connections on this port.
Closed: The port is accessible but no service is listening on it.
Filtered: A firewall or other security device is blocking access to the port, so its status cannot be determined.

blocks.text: Port scanning is an important part of network security. By regularly scanning the devices on a network, administrators can find and close unnecessary open ports before an attacker exploits them. Common port scanning tools include Zenmap, which provides a visual interface for scanning a target IP address and displaying the results in an easy-to-read format.
Network Addresses

Think of a small network, like one in a small office. It's small enough to have only a couple of desktop computers, a printer, and a server. Each one of these devices has its own set of addresses which allow it to communicate with all the others.

Network addresses are essential components in computer networking, enabling devices to communicate with each other. There are two primary types of network addresses: physical addresses and logical addresses. Understanding these differences is crucial for network design, troubleshooting, and ensuring efficient communication within and between networks.
Physical Addresses

Every device, whether it's a computer, a Wi-Fi adapter, or something else, comes with a special code called a media access control (MA C) address, also called a physical address. This code is unique to each device, hardcoded into the device's network interface card (NIC), and it cannot be changed. Here's an example of a MAC address: 70-D9-5B-36-C2-EE You can see there are six parts, each with two numbers or letters. These two characters are hexadecimal numbers, separated by dashes ( - ) or colons ( : ). The hexadecimal numbers represent a 48-bit binary number. This number is used by switches in a local area network (LAN) to direct packets of data to their proper destination. Each MAC address is unique to each device, hardcoded into the device's NIC, and it cannot be changed.
Physical addresses have these characteristics:

items: Duration: Physical addresses are permanent and hardcoded into the NIC.
Use case: Physical addresses are used for local network communication.
Notation: Physical addresses are represented in hexadecimal format.
Assignment: Physical addresses are assigned by the NIC manufacturer.

blocks.text: Logical Addresses

To make sure that every device on a network can be found, each needs its own unique Internet Protocol address (IP address). Logical addresses are like special codes that software gives out, but these codes can be changed, either by a network administrator or by an automated system called the dynamic host configuration protocol (DHCP).

One of the most common forms of logical addressing is the IPv4 addresses. Think of it like a phone number, but for computers and other devices. Just like you write your phone number in a specific way (first the country code or area code, then exchange prefix, and so on), the IP address has a special pattern too. It looks like four sets of numbers written with dots in between them, for example: 192.168.1.1 This way of writing is called dotted decimal notation. Each part of the address is known as an octet, or group of 8 bits.

In IP addressing, we call a group of 8 bits an "octet," but not a byte. Why is that? It's because the word "byte" is so closely related to the concept of storage. Using "octet" is a way to be clearer when talking about IP addresses.

The IT community will express, or write, an IPv4 address in only one of two ways. We can write it in dotted decimal notation, where each octet is a number between 0 and 255: 131.107.2.200 We can also express an IPv4 address in binary. In this case, each octet is an 8-digit binary number, as in this example: 10000011.01101011.00000010.11001000 For the majority of people, the dotted decimal notation is easiest to read. This is by far the most common way to write IPv4 network addresses.
Here are some key things to remember about IPv4 addresses:

items: They are made of 32 bits.
The address is split into four octets (which means four groups of 8 bits).
Each octet is separated by a period, or dot.

blocks.text: IPv6 Addresses

The IPv4 system had been working fine until recently. The problem is that as more devices (such as phones, tablets, and computers) connect to the internet, we're starting to run out of IPv4 addresses! Servers, routers, and other Internet-connected devices are moving away from IPv4 addresses to IPv6, because it offers more combinations of unique numbers.

These are a bit different. They're made up of eight sets of four hexadecimal numbers. And that small detail makes a huge difference. While IPv4 could give us over 4 billion different addresses, using IPv6 can give us a huge number of them. Imagine a 1 with 36 zeros after it—340 undecillion addresses, that's how many!

Here's an example of what an IPv6 address looks like: 59C2:339A:0000:4BE5:C12D:6842:1F3E:09E2 It's a pretty long number, 128 bits long, to be exact. This means that by using IPv6 addresses, the global community won't run out of internet addresses anytime soon.
Logical addresses have these characteristics:

items: Duration: Logical addresses can be either static or dynamic, and can change over time.
Use case: Logical addresses are used for communication across different networks.
Notation: Logical addresses are represented in either decimal (IPv4) or hexadecimal (IPv6) format.
Assignment: Logical addresses are assigned by network administrators or dynamically by

blocks.text: DHCP servers.
The Network Interface Card (NIC)
Most motherboards today include a built-in NIC, while some high-end motherboards and server boards feature two or more network ports. NICs come in wired (RJ-45 ) and wireless varieties.
The topic cover NIC speeds, form factors, and driver considerations in more detail.
NIC Characteristics
The most important feature of a NIC, whether wired or wireless, is its speed. Early wired NICs ran at 10 Mbps. Nowadays, 10 Gbps is becoming common for local area networks (LANs).
Most offices today use 1 Gbps speed, providing fast connections to servers and the Internet.
Remember, these speeds are only as fast as the slowest part of the network.

A network interface card that connects to a motherboard slot is called a PCIe x1 card. If it's a wireless card, it will have antennas sticking out the back to make the signal stronger. It's more common to use USB Wi-Fi or wired adapters instead.

With a USB adapter, you can easily plug it into a desktop or laptop. It might seem strange to use a Wi-Fi adapter on a laptop, since laptops already have built-in Wi-Fi. However, if the built-in Wi-Fi stops working, you can quickly fix it by plugging in a USB adapter. These adapters come with either a USB type A or USB type C connector.
A NIC also has something called a MAC address. This is a unique code made up of six pairs of hexadecimal numbers, unique to every device, that allows the device to connect to a network.

Windows usually does a good job of automatically loading drivers for most wired NICs, so they work right away. However, wireless adapters can be a bit trickier and often need a driver to work correctly.

You might wonder, "How can I download a driver from a website if I don't have Internet access?" This is when having access to a second computer is helpful. You can use the second computer to download the driver to a flash drive, and then use the flash drive to move it to the computer with the waiting NIC.
Cable Internet
Coaxial cable is a copper-based cable run from an internet service provider (ISP) into a neighborhood, then to a home or business. This is called cable Internet.
This list summarizes the basic elements of cable Internet:

items: Equipment required: Coaxial cable, modem, router
Speed: 10 Mbps up to 2 Gbps, depending on location
Latency: 10 ms up to 50 ms

blocks.text: Cable TV started a long time ago, even before the Internet was around. At first, it was for people living in rural areas who couldn't get TV signals because they were too far from big cities and TV stations. Cable TV offered more channels than the regular TV you could get through an antenna, and people really liked it. So, the cable companies thought it would be a good idea to also bring cable to people living in big cities and the suburbs. They didn't know back then that the cables they were putting down could one day be used for the Internet.

The physical coaxial cables are made up of four different components. At the center is the inner conductor, typically made of a solid wire coated in copper or silver. Transmissions on a network travel along this inner wire in the form of electrical signals. To protect the transmissions, the wire is surrounded by an insulator, and around the insulator is a metallic shield. To complete the cable, the entire assembly is coated with a plastic jacket. The most common coaxial connector is the F-type connector, which has a swiveling head that screws onto its port.
Image by destinacigdem © 123rf.com.
Image created by Colin and reproduced under the Creative Commons Attribution ShareAlike 3.0 license.

Today, cable is the most popular way to connect to the Internet. Cable is fast, doesn't have much delay, is usually on without interruptions, and is reasonably priced. In some places, cable Internet can go as fast as 2 Gbps, which is more than what most homes or small businesses need. But for those who want super-fast Internet, it's a great choice. The latency, or how long it takes for data to go back and forth, is usually between 10 ms and 50 ms. This is good enough for browsing the Internet and for people who like to play online games.

Cable Internet is different from other Internet services because the connection to a house or business is shared with other people nearby. That shared connection was noticeable in some areas years ago, when everyone in the neighborhood got on the Internet at the same time. But now, cable Internet has gotten a lot better at sending a lot of data through the cables, so even if everyone is online at the same time, most people won't see their Internet slow down much at all.
Digital Subscriber Line (DSL) Internet

Digital Subscriber Line (DSL), one of the original broadband offerings, is a common way for small offices or homes to get Internet service. Just like cable Internet, DSL uses infrastructure that was put in place before the Internet became common. Telephone lines can carry Internet signals the same way they carry your voice, as long as the telephone wire is of good quality.
The Internet data travels over the telephone line using high frequencies, which are outside the range that voice calls use.
This list summarizes the basic elements of DSL Internet:

items: Equipment required: Telephone line, modem, router
Speed: 5 Mbps up to 30 Mbps (rarely up to 100 Mbps), depending on location and wire quality
Latency: 20 ms up to 50 ms

blocks.text: Most telephone wires are made of copper, which is a highly conductive metal that is very efficient at carrying electrical signals. Copper is not only good at conducting electricity, but it's also flexible and strong, making it perfect for phone wires.

Telephone or DSL wires are usually set up in a twisted pair cable. This means that the copper wires are twisted around each other in pairs. The reason they're twisted is to keep away unwanted signals from outside and to stop the wires from interfering with each other's signals.

Each copper wire is covered with an insulating plastic material to keep it from touching other wires and to protect it from environmental damage like water and rust. There's also an outer layer, or jacket, made of plastic materials that wraps around the coated wires. This jacket helps protect the wires from getting damaged by things like sunlight, water, and changes in temperature. This makes sure the phone wires work well, no matter the weather.

Most residential DSL services are asymmetric (ADSL), meaning that downloading is faster than uploading. Businesses and freelance professionals who work with videos and sound prefer to use a different kind of DSL, called symmetric (SDSL) connections. This is because both downloading and uploading speeds are the same in SDSL, which is great for sending and receiving large files. Usually, DSL Internet can go as fast as 30 Mbps, but there are some that can reach up to 100 Mbps.
DSL's ping or latency times are similar to other ISP options, with average rates between 20 ms and 50 ms.

Your DSL Internet speed depends a lot on the quality of the telephone wiring and how far you are from the local phone company's exchange or hub. The farther away you are, the weaker the Internet signal gets. When the signal gets weaker, the Internet slows down. This is called attenuation, and it's one of DSL's main drawbacks. The maximum range of DSL wiring is typically about 3 miles (5 km). In addition, the DSL or telephone wires in some areas may also be of relatively poor quality and be more likely to experience signal interference. To help solve this problem, some telephone ports are fitted with a microfilter to prevent the data signals from interfering with other traffic on the same line.
Fiber Internet
Some of the larger digital subscriber line (DSL) companies realized many years ago the limited Internet capability of copper wires, and found a solution in fiber Internet.
This list summarizes the basic elements of Fiber Internet:

items: Equipment required: Fiber optic cable, router
Speed: 100 Mbps up to 25 Gbps
Latency: 10 ms to 25 ms

blocks.text: Fiber optic cables work by using light to carry information, sometimes as fast as 70% of the speed of light. They have a central core made of clear plastic or glass that the light travels through. Around this core there is a special layer of reflective cladding that acts like a mirror.

When some of the light strays out of the core, this mirror-like layer bounces it back into the middle so it keeps going along the cable. Then, there are one or two layers that wrap around this cladding to keep the central core safe from getting broken or damaged. Finally, all of this is covered with a plastic outer layer.

Fiber cables terminate, or end, in a few different types of connectors. The subscriber connector (SC) and the local connector (L C) are the most common. The SC is a push/pull design, allowing for simple insertion and removal. The LC is a small-form-factor connector with a tabbed push/ pull design. LC is similar to SC, but the smaller size allows more cables to be attached in a smaller space. LC is a widely adopted form factor for higher Internet speeds.
Image by YANAWUT SUNTORNKIJ © 123rf.com.

Small form-factor pluggable (SFP) transceivers are important in many networks based on fiber optic cable. They help switches and other key parts of the network talk to each other. SFPs are popular because they are small, can connect in different ways (using copper or fiber optic cables), and can be hot-swapped, or changed out without turning off the system.

While it is more expensive, the SFP is less likely to experience electromagnetic interference and can save on power costs. This type of port is best suited to large-scale deployments, such as businesses with large networks.
Image by Zdenek Maly © 123rf.com.
Infrastructure

Fiber Internet is different because it doesn't need a modem. Instead, it uses something called a fiber-optic network terminal. This changes the Internet signal into a form that your devices, like phones and computers, can understand. Unfortunately, fiber was not built out along with the other technologies, cable and DSL, decades ago. And therefore, fiber is still not widely available.

Fiber Internet is a newer way to get Internet to homes and was not set up a long time ago, like cable and DSL Internet. To get fiber Internet directly into homes and businesses, Internet service providers (ISPs) have to spend a lot of money, so it's not available everywhere. A common solution that's used in cities and some rural areas is called Fiber to the Curb (FTT C).
This means the ISP puts in a fiber network that ends at a big box or cabinet on a street close by.
Then, the last step from the cabinet to each house uses ordinary telephone wires with a special kind of DSL called Very High Bit Rate DSL (VDSL) to make the connection.
Speed
Fiber optic cable is a connection type that allows for very high-speed symmetric connections.

This means that if you have 500 Mbps download speed, you will have the same 500 Mbps upload speed. Fiber has been able to hit speeds of 25 Gbps. It is the fastest of all connection types we discuss in this course.
Latency is also very low with fiber, normally coming in at a rate that works well for surfing and gaming. An average ping rate may be from 10 ms to 25 ms.

Fiber Internet is also very reliable, with uptime or availability as good or better than any other service. Another advantage of fiber is its ability to travel over a great distance. All of this leads to faster load times and higher quality streams.
Wireless Internet
The newest player in broadband service is wireless Internet, offered by cell phone companies.
Using the same cell coverage that works with your phones, cellular carriers are beginning to offer the option of home or small business Internet.
This list summarizes the basic elements of wireless Internet:

items: Equipment required: Modem, router
Speed: 40 Mbps up to 300 Mbps
Latency: 1 ms up to 30 ms

blocks.text: Cellular technology delivers an Internet signal to your home without cables. Your Internet service provider (ISP) sends digital information using cellular radio waves, which travel from one cell tower to another. Devices that use this kind of Internet, like your phone or modem, receive these radio waves to connect to both the Internet and the telephone network.

One good thing about wireless Internet is that you can put your modem anywhere in your house. With other types of Internet, you have to connect it to the wall plate where your cable comes into your building. But with a wireless modem, you just need to plug it into an electric socket. Just remember, if the signal isn't strong, you might have to move the modem closer to a window.

The 6th generation of wireless Internet, called 6G and 6E, is the newest kind of network technology. It's much faster and more responsive than the older versions. With 5G, you can download things at speeds between 40 to 300 Mbps and upload between 10 to 50 Mbps. This speed is good enough for most things you do online. The latency, or ping rate, is also pretty quick, usually around 30 milliseconds. 6G and 6E are even faster, though they're not yet (at the time of writing) as widespread as earlier generations like 5G. More and more places are getting 6G, so its coverage is growing.

Another advantage of wireless is that it gives people more options to choose from when they're deciding on Internet service providers (ISPs). For a long time before 4G, 5G, and 6G/6E wireless Internet became popular, not much had changed with ISP choices. Because there are so many companies offering 5G and 6G/6E Internet coverage, and because their cell coverage is expanding, consumers have more options than ever when choosing an ISP.
Other Wireless Connections

Unlike cable Internet, mobile or cellular Internet, and fiber, the Internet types covered here are less well known. These methods of connecting to the Internet can be useful in certain situations where traditional Internet doesn't work well, or isn't available.
Satellite Internet
Satellite Internet is often the only option in rural areas where other types of Internet can't reach.

Usually, satellite Internet is not as fast as other types of connections, but people are willing to accept these drawbacks because it's the only choice they have. Internet service providers (ISPs) don't want to lay cables for hundreds of miles to reach far-off places.
Satellite Internet is not available only to remote locations! If you're almost anywhere in the world, you may still have the option to get to the Internet through a satellite.

Three companies offer satellite Internet: HughesNet, Viasat, and Starlink. HughesNet and Viasat have been around for a long time, giving people satellite Internet for many years. Starlink is newer and started offering satellite Internet in 2020. All of these companies use satellites that orbit the Earth. They make sure there's always at least one satellite close enough to the antenna you set up at your place, so you can get the Internet signal.
Just like with other kinds of Internet, you'll need a modem and a router to connect your devices.

While a satellite doesn't rely on cables or other physical connections, you will need to have a satellite dish to receive the data. Most people attach the dish either to the roof or to the side of their building. The satellite company can help with positioning the dish in the right direction to get the best possible signal.

The speed of satellite Internet is on the low side of average. The download speed can be anywhere from 12 Mbps to 250 Mbps, and upload speeds are almost always 3 Mbps. The latency, or ping rate, is a bit of an issue because it's usually over 100 ms. This happens because the Internet signal has to travel a long way: from your dish to a satellite in space, then back down to Earth to connect to the Internet server, then back to the satellite, and finally back down to Earth again to reach your dish. This means things like online gaming are not likely to work well on satellite Internet because of the slow response times.

Two final drawbacks to satellite are data caps and weather. Data caps mean that there might be limits on how much data you can use, depending on your plan. If you go over this limit, your Internet could slow down quite a lot. Bad weather can also impact your Internet signal. Heavy thunderstorms, snow, and dust storms can interrupt your satellite service.
This list summarizes the basic elements of satellite Internet:

items: Equipment required: Satellite dish, modem, router
Speed: 3 Mbps up to 250 Mbps
Latency: 100 ms and over

blocks.text: Fixed Wireless Internet

In places where it's hard to get fast Internet, like fiber or cable, there's another way to connect using an antenna. This method is called fixed wireless. It uses a special outdoor antenna that can handle all kinds of weather, from big storms to heavy snow. It's not as common as other Internet types, but it's a good choice for people who don't have many options. The Internet signal is sent from towers using radio frequency waves through the air straight to where you live or work.

For fixed wireless to work correctly, the place where you're setting up the antenna needs to be within 10 miles of the tower. Also, there can't be anything blocking the line of sight between the tower and the antenna, like buildings or trees. The signal can come from towers on top of buildings or even water towers. You would install the antenna on the outside of a building, and then a cable runs from the antenna to a modem inside your home to a router.
Speeds of fixed wireless can vary, but are generally 15 to 30 Mbps for download speeds.

However, in the right environment, speeds can be as fast as 100 Mbps. Upload speeds will be much slower, as low as 1 Mbps or less. Latency or ping rate is within the range of other services, on average, from 20 to 60 ms. The cost for fixed wireless tends to be higher than other forms of broadband.
This list summarizes the basic elements of fixed wireless Internet:

items: Equipment required: Antenna, modem, router
Speed: 1 Mbps up to 30 Mbps
Latency: 20 ms up to 60 ms

blocks.text: Wireless Antenna Types

The type of antenna used in a wireless connection determines how far and in what direction the signal travels. Choosing the right antenna is important for getting the best performance out of a wireless network. There are two main categories of wireless antennas:

items: Omnidirectional antennas send and receive signals in all directions equally, creating a 360- degree coverage pattern. These are ideal for general-purpose wireless access points where devices may connect from any direction, such as in a home or office. The trade-off is that the signal is spread out, so it doesn't travel as far in any single direction.

Directional antennas focus the signal in one specific direction, creating a narrow beam that travels much farther than an omnidirectional signal. These are also called high-gain antennas because they concentrate the signal strength into a focused path. Directional antennas are the best choice when you need to create a point-to-point wireless link between two specific locations, such as connecting two buildings across a parking lot or campus.

blocks.text: Because the signal is focused, it also avoids broadcasting to areas where coverage isn't needed, which improves both performance and security.

When deciding which antenna to use, consider what the wireless connection needs to accomplish. If devices will connect from many locations around the antenna, choose omnidirectional. If the goal is to connect two fixed points over a longer distance, choose directional.

blocks.text: To connect to the Internet, you need an Internet Service Provider (ISP). ISPs are the companies that maintain the infrastructure, from cables and satellites to cell towers, that deliver Internet access to homes and businesses. With so many providers and plan options available, understanding how ISPs work helps you choose the right service for your needs and budget.

In this lesson, you will explore what ISPs offer, how tiered service plans work, and the equipment your ISP provides to get you online. You will also learn how to measure Internet performance using bandwidth, latency, and throughput, and understand what those numbers mean for your everyday experience.

To get on the Internet, you need to subscribe to an Internet Service Provider (ISP). Even though all ISPs provide you with access to the Internet, there are different ways they can make this happen. They might be the company that gives you cable TV, your phone company, or your cell phone service. Some companies only give you Internet, while others might offer Internet along with cable TV or cell phone service. All of these companies maintain their own infrastructure, meaning the Internet delivery equipment, and offer technical support to their subscribers.

Many ISPs will also offer email addresses and website hosting. Email addresses, typically offered free of charge, will use the ISP's domain name. For example, "YourName@ProviderName.com." Keep in mind that when you leave the ISP, you might not be able to keep this address. Some providers will host a website and register a domain name for you. This service is typically available for an additional fee.

The majority of providers offer tiered service plans. This means that they have 2 or more different Internet speeds available, with different price points for each level. For example, a basic service may give you an average speed and cost $50 per month, while the next tier up offers a speed that is three times faster and costs $100 per month. The needs of your home or business depend on the number of devices you have that need to connect to the Internet, and how much bandwidth the devices will be using.

Each ISP has limitations based on its infrastructure and your location. Every ISP in your area will have its good points and drawbacks. It's important to know what makes them different so you can choose the best one for what you need.
Understand ISP Equipment and Performance

When you're selecting an Internet Service Provider (ISP), you need to think about a few important things. Consider how much it costs, what other customers say about it, and look at independent performance reports that show how well it works. Depending on where you live, you might have many ISPs to choose from, or you might be more limited. It's also key to know what kind of equipment you need and how fast you want your Internet to be.

It is also worth noting that any data you transfer over an Internet connection is processed by, and may be stored on, the ISP's computers. When you use an ISP, you are trusting them not to snoop on your unencrypted Internet traffic.
Equipment

Your Internet service provider uses their infrastructure to transmit the Internet signal to your home or organization. This means that each ISP deploys its own cable, establishes its own satellites, or sets up its own cell towers. For example, in older neighborhoods where houses and roads were built before everyone started using the Internet, an ISP might have to dig up the ground to put in cables. In places where people are building businesses and homes for the first time, ISPs usually install their cables when the other basic services like water and electricity are being set up. This infrastructure brings the Internet up to the building. After that, different equipment takes over inside the building to make sure you can connect to the Internet.

Most companies use a modem, a device that modulates and demodulates, or changes, the Internet data. It changes the Internet signal into a form that your devices, like phones and computers, can use. After the modem changes the signal, it sends the signal to your router, a device that has ports for wired connections and also sends out a wireless signal. The router then forwards the signal information to your devices. This way, all your devices, from computers to tablets, can use the Internet.
Speed
The most common way to compare Internet service providers is to look at how fast they are.
ISPs measure their performance in upload and download speed, or bandwidth, and in latency.

Latency, also known as ping rate, is how long it takes for a signal to get from your computer to the Internet server. This time is measured in milliseconds, which are thousandths of a second (one millisecond is just 0.001 of a second). Most people who use the Internet are comfortable if the time is 50 milliseconds or shorter. If the time is between 10 and 20 milliseconds, that's considered very good. If you like gaming online, you probably pay a lot of attention to how fast your Internet service provider's (ISP) latency speeds are. If these speeds start to get too slow, your game doesn't react as quickly as it should, which can make it tough to do well.

When you see an Internet plan, it usually shows two bandwidth numbers: one for download speed and one for upload speed. Both speeds are measured in millions of bits per second (Megabit s per second, or Mbps) or in billions of bits per second (Gigabit s per second, or Gbps).

Most of the time, your ISP gives you a lot more speed for downloading, something like 80% to 90% of your total Internet speed. This means only 10% to 20% is left for uploading data to the Internet. This kind of connection is called an asymmetric connection because the download speed is much faster than the upload speed. As Internet speeds get even faster, this difference gets bigger, sometimes going up to 95% of the total for downloading and only 5% for uploading. ISPs do this on purpose because most people use the Internet more for downloading, like watching videos or browsing websites, than they do for uploading. One example of someone who does need more upload speed might be a YouTube creator, who would be uploading large files of content on a regular basis.

The speeds of Internet service discussed here range from as slow as 10 Mbps to as fast as 1 Gbps, or 1 billion bits transferred every second. Some Internet service speeds are even higher with multi-Gigabit speeds offered in some areas. Another term you will hear to describe Internet connections is broadband, which means a high speed connection that's always available. The term "high speed" can be a little bit vague, so in the United States the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has defined it as at least 100 Mbps of download capacity, and 20 Mbps of upload capacity.
If you're curious to check your Internet performance, go to www.fast.com to see your speed.

2.8 Identify basic networking concepts.
2.9 Explain the basic capabilities of a small wireless network.

blocks.text: A wireless local area network (WLAN) lets you share an Internet connection with every device in your home or small office without running cables through walls and ceilings. Once a router is set up, phones, tablets, laptops, and printers can all connect and share files, print jobs, and Internet access. Understanding how wireless networks work, what equipment you need, and how to connect your devices will help you build a reliable home network.

In this lesson, you will explore how small wireless networks operate, compare Wi-Fi standards and frequency bands such as 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz, and learn the steps for connecting a device to a Wi-Fi network. You will also examine how newer standards like Wi-Fi 6E improve speed and reduce interference.
Understanding Small Wireless Networks

A small wireless local area network (WLAN) is a good way to spread an internet connection around. Think of the Wi-Fi router as the center of a circle, emitting Wi-Fi waves in every direction. Anything like your phone or computer inside of that circle can pick up those waves and connect to the Internet.
The best part of small wireless networks is how simple it is to share an Internet connection.

Once you link your computers, tablets, or printers to the network, they can start sharing files and print jobs immediately. Plus, if you're not at home or you're away from the office, you can still utilize your network from just about anywhere with remote access.
Learning the requirements of a Wi-Fi network can help you set up the best one for your needs.

If everyone using your network wants different things, from super-fast Internet to document sharing, you will need to set up a network that allows all these things to happen. Selecting the right equipment means everyone can get what they need.

"One of my small office clients called me out to figure out why one of their printers was unreliable. They had checked all the mechanical stuff (there was ink in it, there was paper, there were no paper jams), so I was there to check on the networking side. Sometimes the printer worked, sometimes it didn't, and there was no pattern or reason to it. By looking at the whole network I found the solution. The wireless signal strength at the printer's location was very weak. It was too far away from the router, and the printer was just barely getting a connection. Sometimes the connection would just drop off altogether. I recommended that the client either connect the printer to the router by using a cable, or add a wireless access point between the router and the printer." -- Rob P., network technician Securing Your Wireless Network When you set up a wireless network, one of the most important steps is making sure it's secure.

Without security, anyone nearby could connect to your network and use your Internet, or worse, access your personal files. That's why every home router lets you set a password and choose a security mode.
The security mode tells the router how to protect the data traveling through your network. Think of it like choosing the type of lock for your front door. Here are the main options you'll see:

items: WP A2-PSK (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 - Pre-Shared Key): This is the most common security mode for home and small office networks. It requires every device to enter the same password (the pre-shared key) to join the network. WPA2 is considered secure for everyday use and is supported by nearly all modern devices.
WP A3: This is the newest security standard. It provides stronger protection than WPA2, but not all devices support it yet. If your router and all your devices support WPA3, it's the best choice.

blocks.text: Along with the security mode, the router uses an encryption algorithm to scramble the data so that outsiders can't read it. The most common algorithm is AES (Adv anced Encryption Standard). AES is fast and very secure. When setting up your router, you should always make sure it's using AES encryption. Older options like TKIP are slower and less secure, so avoid them if possible.

To secure a wireless network, you'll typically log into your router's settings through a web browser, navigate to the wireless security page, select WP A2-PSK as the security mode, confirm that AES is the encryption algorithm, and then set a strong password. A strong password is long, includes a mix of letters, numbers, and special characters, and is hard for others to guess.
Testing Network Connectivity with Ping

Once your network is set up and devices are connected, how do you know everything is actually working? One of the simplest ways to test if two devices can communicate is by using a command called ping.

Ping is a small program built into every computer. It sends a quick message to another device on the network and waits for a reply. If the other device responds, you know the connection between them is working. If it doesn't respond, something might be wrong, like the device is turned off, disconnected from the network, or there's a problem with the cables or Wi-Fi.
To use ping on a Windows computer:
1. Right-click the desktop and select Open in Terminal (or search for PowerShell in the Start menu).
2. Type ping followed by a space and the name or IP address of the device you want to test.
For example: ping Home-PC2
3. Press Enter.
The results will show one of two outcomes:

items: Reply from [address]: This means the other device received your message and responded.

blocks.text: The connection is working.

items: Request timed out or Destination host unreachable: This means the other device didn't respond. It could be powered off, not connected to the network, or there may be a problem along the way.

blocks.text: Ping is a quick and easy way to check whether your network is healthy. If a device isn't responding, you can start troubleshooting by checking if it's powered on, connected to Wi-Fi, or plugged into the network with a cable.
Wireless Band Options
The 802.11n Wi-Fi standard (also called 4G Wi-Fi) was the first to use two wireless frequency bands for improved data rates. Those were the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz frequency bands.

Then came the 802.11ac (5G Wi-Fi) standard, which was even faster, reaching speeds of up to 1.3 Gigabits per second (Gbps). However, it only worked on the 5 GHz band. The older 2.4 GHz band is still in use on older (also called legacy) wireless standards like 802.11b/g/n. Today we have 802.11ax (6G and 6E), which is widely supported by modern devices.

Most routers support the different types of Wi-Fi that are available: the most commonly used standards of 802.11n (4G), 802.11ac (5G), and 802.11ax (6G and 6GE). This is good because it means you can use both old and new devices together on your router.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For instance, you might have a new router that uses 802.11ax, but your computer and tablet only support the 802.11n or 802.11ac wireless standards. That shouldn't be a problem. It's also important to know that the speeds you see listed for routers are the fastest possible maximums.
It's what they could possibly get to in theory, but in real life, it's probably not going to be quite that fast.
Bands and Wireless Function

The 2.4 GHz frequency band is like a busy street that other devices such as cordless phones, microwaves, and Bluetooth also use. This can cause traffic jams, making things not work as smoothly. That's why 5 GHz is a better choice. Think of 5 GHz as a less crowded street with more lanes (or channels) so that everyone can get where they need to go without bumping into each other. In other words, there is less interference. Your router keeps things running smoothly on this frequency band.

But there is a catch: when it comes to how far the signal can go, 2.4 GHz can travel longer distances than 5 GHz. Again, 5 GHz offers a faster connection. So if you want speed and don't mind being a bit closer to your router, 5 GHz is the way to go.

At the time of writing, the newest Wi-Fi standard is 6E, which operates in the 6 GHz band, a step up from 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. This higher frequency has many benefits, including more bandwidth than 2.4 and 5GHz. This provides additional channels and results in less congestion. Because it’s less crowded, there is also less interference. In addition, 6 GHz has shorter wavelengths which reduces latency. Of all the benefits, the most significant is the faster speeds, with theoretical possibilities of multi-gigabit transmission. In order to achieve these speeds, both the router and connected device will need to have the newest Wi-Fi 6E equipment.

2.9 Explain the basic capabilities of a small wireless network.

blocks.text: Network connectivity issues are some of the most common problems you will face when working with technology. Whether it is a weak wireless signal, a disconnected cable, or a misconfigured device, knowing how to identify and resolve these issues is an essential skill.
Understanding wireless network standards, speed factors like latency and attenuation, and the OSI model gives you the foundation to pinpoint where problems occur.

In this lesson, you will learn about wireless network standards and the factors that affect network speed. You will also explore the OSI model and its role in troubleshooting, then walk through the CompTIA Troubleshooting Methodology, a structured six-step process for identifying, resolving, and documenting network problems.
Wireless Network Standards

The properties of radio waves are the same as other waves you might know about, such as ocean waves. These properties include amplitude (the height of peaks and the depth of troughs), frequency (the number of peaks per unit of time), and phase (the angle of a wave at a point in time). Modulation, which is what a modem does to the Internet signal, changes one or more of those properties to encode data into a signal.

There are many different types of communication that use radio waves. Broadcast television, AM and FM radio, military communications, garage door openers, satellites, Near Field Communication (NFC), and mobile phones all use radio waves to transmit information.

Near Field Communication (NFC) is a type of wireless technology that works over short distances. You can use it with smartphones and smartwatches to talk to or share files, or even pay for things, with other nearby devices. It only works when the devices are very close, less than 2 inches apart.
Wi-Fi standards use modulation to keep other radio waves and electronic signals from interfering with Wi-Fi signals.
Standardizing Wireless Communications

The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) established technical standards for wireless communications and has been revising them as technology improves. These 802.11 standards, better known as Wi-Fi, define specific ways that a modem encodes data into a radio signal.
The numbers "802.11" are part of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) index, and aren't related to wireless performance.

For someone working on wireless networks, it's important to know the variations in types of Wi-Fi. These differences between generations affect network performance, what features the network can support, and what devices are compatible with the wireless signal. When a professional sets up Wi-Fi to cover an entire office, they have to think about how strong the signal is and whether it will work in different office locations.
Wireless Network Speed

How fast does a website load on your computer? In most cases, you expect websites to load pretty much instantly, almost as soon as you click or tap. When you measure how fast a website loads, it's like calculating how fast a car is going on the road. Just like a car has a speedometer that displays its speed, the internet speed tells you how much data is being pushed from one place to another, usually starting from the point of the central server.
Latency

When you click on a link or type in a website address, you usually have to wait a bit for the website to show up in your browser, right? That waiting time is called latency or lag. This is the delay that occurs during the sequence of steps when packets of data travel over the Internet.
The shorter the wait, the better your internet connection is (at least, as it relates to latency). We measure how long the wait is in milliseconds (ms), or one-thousandth of a second.
The IT industry measures latency by running a test called ping, named after the command that starts it off. You may hear the term "ping rate" to describe latency.

Excellent latency times are short, in single digits, and good ones are under 50 ms. With rates over 150 ms, you'll start to notice delays. Even if your internet is fast at downloading, you might still have a slow ping rate, which can make things feel sluggish.

Gaming is the area most concerned with low latency. With online games, small delays can really affect your performance and cause you to fall behind your opponents (and probably annoy your teammates, too). It's definitely not good if there's a lag between you pressing a button and when that action actually occurs in the game, if for nothing else than the fact that you won't get to respond quickly to whatever happens next. So, getting your ping rate or latency lower can really make your online gaming experience better, if that's something you're into.
But know that there's not always something you can do. Latency can get worse if the network is juggling a lot of data, or if there are lots of people using the internet at the same time.
Attenuation and Interference

As you move away from a wireless router, the signal strength of your device diminishes, and your internet connection slows down. This is attenuation, or the loss of signal strength. You can see the number of bars of signal strength drop as you move farther from the source of your signal. You might also see a compromised signal if you are behind or beneath certain types of walls or ceilings, depending on the type of building material. Even trees and other vegetation can block or reduce the power of your Wi-Fi signal.

Interference is unwanted signals or noise that collide with and degrade the Wi-Fi signal. These signals or external sources can clash with the intended transmission, causing your wireless data to become distorted and hard for your device to decode. Other types of radio wave transmissions typically don't interfere with Wi-Fi, because different signals are designed to operate in different bands. However, microwaves, baby monitors, and your neighbor's wireless network can disrupt your wireless signal. The effects are the same as you would experience with attenuation: a decrease in the Wi-Fi signal strength and network speed.
Standardize the Troubleshooting Process

Problems in your computer system can happen for many reasons that you can't control, and some that don't seem very clear. Devices might stop working, old cable connectors can come loose, and software may get corrupted. Whether you're working on your own computer or a network, you will make everyone on the network happy by fixing problems and keeping systems working smoothly. To do this well, you need to know the basic tools and steps for troubleshooting a network. Fixing problems is an important part of tech knowledge and abilities.
Some problems can be very complex, and therefore it's important to follow the steps outlined.

The first step is to use a troubleshooting process that gives you a clear and complete set of steps, called a standard operating procedure (SOP), to fix IT problems. This procedure includes finding out what the problem is, thinking of a possible solution, trying out the solution, and making sure the problem is fixed. The CompTIA Troubleshooting Methodology is one example.
Identify the Problem
The first step in fixing a problem is to figure out what the problem is, and how widespread it is.

To identify the problem, you should talk to the user, watch the problem happen, understand the symptoms, and check if anything has changed in the system recently. This step is crucial as it sets the foundation for diagnosing and resolving the issue effectively.

If one user can't print, but their back-up printer down the hall is working, that doesn't have the same urgency as a user who can't get on the Internet. Staying productive is an important part of overall tech goals.
Interview Users

Ask users what they were doing when the problem started and if they noticed anything strange before it happened. For example, they might tell you that before they left the office yesterday, they tried to shut down their computer, but Windows said it was going to install a feature update. This big update might have affected a program, and now it won't load correctly. Try to get as much information as you can. Putting in some detective work can really help here.
Duplicate the Problem

If you can, it's best to see the problem yourself to get more accurate information. Try to repeat what the user did to see if you get the same result. Seeing exactly what the user experienced helps you understand the problem better, especially if the user doesn't fully understand the process or does things differently. If you can replicate the problem, then you can move on to figuring out how to fix it.
Identify Symptoms One at a Time

After you replicate the problem and confirm that it's still there, you need to write down all the important symptoms and error messages. Symptoms could be things like a program not loading or a common action not working. Error messages, which often show up in pop-up windows, are meant to help fix the problem. The average user might not understand these messages, and you might not either at first, but writing down what you see will help you find the solution.
You figure out a problem in your system by looking at the symptoms. By knowing what usually causes these symptoms, you can test each possible cause until you find the right one.
Sometimes, symptoms come from more than one cause. This kind of problem is less common but much harder to solve.
Understand Recent Changes and Review Documentation

Many help desks have a knowledge base, which is a place where they keep information about common problems or issues specific to their environment. These knowledge bases are collections of what support technicians have learned over time. You can search them by issue, symptom, or error message. Troubleshooters usually check the knowledge base early in the process so they don't waste time trying to solve problems that are already known.
It's also important to know what has happened recently to the system you're working on.

The knowledge base might be the best place to check if anything has changed recently, like new software versions, different settings, or recent updates to the operating system. On the individual computer, you can check the history of Windows updates in the Settings app under "Update History." You can also look for recently-installed apps on the computer, which might be causing the problem.
Establish a Theory of Probable Cause

If you get clear and accurate answers to your questions in the first step, you'll know how serious the problem is. You'll find out how many users or systems are affected and where to start looking for the problem. By figuring out where the problem started, you'll have a good starting point. Check previous help tickets, especially if they are for the same computer, server, or part of the network.
Question the Obvious

Don't ignore an easy solution to a problem. What seems like common sense to you as a tech might not be obvious to someone else. For example, if a desktop computer isn't on the Internet and the Windows symbol at the bottom of the screen shows a globe with a tiny X, it means the network connection is broken. You know that the night before, your coworkers moved to new cubicles and took their computers with them. Don't be afraid to check behind their system to make sure an Ethernet cable is plugged in.

There's a funny but sometimes true saying about fixing system problems: "Have you tried rebooting the system?" Even though it sounds simple, restarting the system can sometimes fix problems and is easy to do with little downside.
Consider Multiple Approaches

Don't just focus on one way to fix a problem. Internet issues can be caused by problems in the operating system (OS), or by a physical problem with one of the network components, or by a problem with your Internet Service Provider (ISP). For example, a good way to check Internet issues is to try a different operating system. This can help you see if the problem is with the installed OS. With a bootable Linux flash drive, you can plug it in, turn on the computer, boot from the flash drive, and have a fully functional operating system for testing. Once the OS is loaded, test the Internet. If it works, then the problem is with the OS. If it doesn't, the problem is somewhere else, and you can move on to the next option.
Start At One End of the System

Work step by step, either forwards or backwards, from one point to the next. If a system doesn't have Internet, start by testing the RJ-45 port on the back of the computer. Then check the Ethernet cable, then the cable's connection to the wall jack, and finally the port on the switch at the other end of the cable.
Test the Theory
By questioning the obvious and using a step-by-step approach, you should gather enough information to come up with an initial idea or theory about what might be causing the problem.

Remember, you might be wrong. Without jumping to conclusions, use your troubleshooting skills and tools to test your idea. This idea will be the basis for your testing and confirmation in the next step.
Theory Confirmed

If your idea is confirmed, figure out the next steps to fix the problem. This means making a plan of action. Some fixes will be simple, while others might be more complicated. For example, if Windows keeps crashing and you find out it's because of a failing hard drive, the obvious step is to replace the drive. After replacing the drive, load the operating system and test the system again to make sure it boots to the desktop without any issues.
Theory Not Confirmed

If your theory is not confirmed, come up with a new idea or ask for more help. Take a breath and step back to look at the situation again. You might need to gather more information. Did you miss something when you were trying to identify the problem?

It's important to remember that asking for help is a key part of troubleshooting. If you can't find a solution or figure out what's causing the problem, you need to ask for help. This help can come from checking the documentation again, looking it up on the Internet, or asking your coworkers or manager. You should try to solve the problem on your own first, but if you can't, it's important to get more help so you don't get stuck.

Solving a problem often means breaking it down into smaller parts. For example, if you can't connect to a network, figure out if the problem is with the hardware or the software. This helps you get on the right track and not waste time going in the wrong direction.
Establish a Plan and Implement the Fix

The fourth step in the troubleshooting process is to make a plan to fix the problem and then put it into action. This means creating a detailed plan based on what you found out about the problem. The plan should list the steps needed to fix the issue, whether it's an easy fix or a more complicated one. Once you have the plan, you will follow it to fix the problem and then test to make sure the issue is solved.
Make Sure You Understand the Process

Think through the process in your head or write it down. Make sure you have the tools and equipment you need, and the proper administrative rights to make any changes. Also, think about whether the fix will cause a lot of downtime for the organization. You might need a quick temporary fix that you can do right away, and then do the permanent fix later when it won't bother as many people, such as after hours or on the weekend.

Make sure to get any needed approval or components for your plan. Some plans are simple, like replacing a network cable, and don't need approval from a higher-up. Others are more complex, like shutting down a server to install new memory. This type of step will need approval. Some hardware or software issues need resources that your department already has. Other times, you might not have what you need, and you'll have to order it. There might also be times when the software needs to be installed on the company server, and only the server admin can do that.
Identify Potential Effects

Think about what might happen when you fix the problem. For example, if you replace a network cable, make sure it's the same speed or faster than the original one, or the user might complain about a slow connection. This is easy to mess up because network cables have small print showing their speed, which can be hard to see. Another example is if you have to reinstall the operating system because it's corrupt, make sure to back up the user's data first to avoid making them upset.
Backup Important Data

This is one of the most important parts of tech work. If you drop a laptop and break the screen, it's disappointing, but the screen can be replaced. If you short out a system and need to replace the motherboard, it's another setback. While these are frustrating, they don't compare to the huge impact of losing data. If a user says their information is backed up, ask them to explain how and where it's backed up. Be very careful and back up the data if you have any doubt.
Implement the Solution

You followed all the steps and procedures; now it's time to fix the problem. It's important to solve a problem by making only one change at a time and seeing what happens. It can be tempting to try a lot of solutions at once, reboot the computer or network device, and hope everything is fixed. While this might work, the problem with this approach is that you won't know which action actually fixed the issue. By making one change at a time, you'll know what worked, which will help you and your team the next time a similar problem comes up.
Or Escalate the Issue

You probably won't be able to fix every problem. A junior tech, someone just starting in their career, might not have full access to some of the most critical systems. In these cases, you may need to ask a more experienced technician to help. Problems can range from software to operating systems to network hardware, creating a wide variety of issues and solutions.

In larger companies with bigger IT departments, some staff members have specialized roles, focusing on things like networks, voice over Internet protocol services (V oIP), or servers. You might look at an issue and realize it needs the expertise of someone in one of those roles.
Don't be ashamed if you can't solve the issue; the vastness of IT makes it nearly impossible for anyone to be an expert in all areas.
Confirm the Solution Works

Next, you need to test the results of your fix. This means making sure everything is working properly, both from your perspective and from the user's point of view. If the problem might happen again, you can take some extra steps to prevent it from coming back.
Confirm Functionality

You've fixed the problem and checked that everything is working as expected. Now, you should have the user work with the system to make sure the issue is fully resolved. Sometimes, users do things in unusual ways, which can make them think there's still a problem when it's really just a matter of training them on the right way to do things.

Have the user go through all their typical tasks, like printing, sending and receiving emails, and logging into the websites they use most often. Make sure they see that their system is no longer having issues. You should also watch for any new problems that might have come up because of the fix. Sometimes, fixing one problem can cause another. For example, you might fix a security problem, but in doing so, some users might no longer be able to access resources they used to.
Put in Preventative Measures if Needed

In addition, if any other steps can be taken to prevent the original problem from recurring, look to implement them as well. If, for example, a problem was an Ethernet cable that keeps falling out of the back of a printer, causing it to go offline. While it was easy to put back in place, why does it regularly come loose? On closer inspection, you see the clip on top of the RJ-45 cable end, which snaps into the port, is broken. Replacing the entire cable now will reduce the chance that the problem could happen again.
Document Your Findings
Finally, the issue is resolved! Before you finish up, you need to write down what happened.

Documenting your findings helps you remember what you did to fix the problem, making it easier to solve similar issues in the future. It also lets others see the steps you took and the solutions you found, which can be helpful for teamwork and training. Plus, good documentation can prevent repeated mistakes and save time by providing a reference for fixing recurring problems.
Add to the Knowledge Base

Effective documentation makes it easier for other technicians to troubleshoot similar problems in the future. While you work through a problem and solution, write down your actions step by step. Remember to include what you did and what happened, even if things didn't go as expected. This helps clearly show the steps you took. Also, if a fix is delayed because you need to order parts, make sure to document up to that point. Don't wait until the job is completely done, because you might forget some details.

Another reason to keep good documentation as you go through the process is to let others know what you have tried so far. This documentation is also helpful if your changes cause new problems. With good records of what you did, it's easier to undo your changes or adjust settings.
Explain in Detail

Provide as much detail as possible, especially about what it took to fix the problem. You might have tried several solutions before finding the right one. Mention the methods that didn't work and give the most detail about the fix that did. This documentation can be very helpful if the problem comes back months later. You'll be glad you wrote everything down, and it will feel good to have solved the problem.

blocks.text: Cloud computing has changed how people and businesses use technology. Instead of relying entirely on local hardware, cloud services let you store files, run applications, and access computing resources over the internet. Understanding cloud technology is essential because nearly every modern device and service depends on it in some way.

In this lesson, you will learn what cloud computing is and how it compares to on-premises solutions, explore the three main cloud service types (SaaS, PaaS, and IaaS), examine public, private, and hybrid deployment models, and compare popular cloud platforms like Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and Amazon Web Services.

One of the easiest ways to explain cloud services is by thinking about sharing the workload. In a regular client-server setup, companies handle their own servers, storage, and networking. They buy costly and complicated hardware, hire experts to manage it, and can't easily adjust as their business grows or changes. This is called on-premises management, and it's the traditional way of setting up and running systems and software. The equipment is kept in the same place as the business. Before cloud services, this was the only choice. Benefits to on-premises systems include lower long-term costs and complete control over the IT setup.
With cloud services, companies can let a cloud provider take care of some or all of these tasks.
Cloud Service Types

Cloud services can be defined by what they offer you. The simplest service is called Software as a Service (SaaS). This lets you use a program through your web browser over the Internet. A popular example is Gmail, which is part of Google Workspace. With Gmail, you can access your email and other tools that are stored on Google's servers. The cloud service provider (Google, in this case) takes care of the hardware, the operating system, and the software updates.

There are also bigger on-demand services, like Platform as a Service (PaaS). With PaaS, you get more advanced IT tools, including operating systems. PaaS is usually for developers and database administrators. They use the platform to create applications or database services needed by the company without having to build the platforms themselves. For example, a database administrator no longer has to request a server, install an operating system, and then install a database platform such as Microsoft SQL Server. Those tasks have all been offloaded to the cloud service provider. PaaS can also grow and change quickly, giving a stable development platform as needs change.

Another type of cloud service is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS). IaaS gives you physical equipment such as servers, routers, and storage. Big businesses often use IaaS because it can be cheaper than buying the equipment themselves. Having servers on-site requires a lot of support. Servers take up a lot of space, need reliable power, constant cooling, and physical security. All these needs mean high costs for businesses. By letting a cloud service provider handle these costs, businesses can save a lot of money and time. Popular IaaS providers are Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure.
Cloud Resource Deployments

All these services can be managed in different ways. One way is for a single organization to handle everything itself (an on-premises solution). Another way is to have a cloud service provider manage the services for many organizations (called a cloud deployment).
Public cloud deployment is open to anyone who wants to pay for it. A private cloud, on the other hand, is set up just for authorized users within an organization.
These two models can also be mixed into a hybrid solution. The hybrid deployment model combines both public and private for greater flexibility.
Cloud Computing

The term "cloud computing" basically refers to using somebody else's hardware over the internet to do computing tasks. Common uses of cloud technology include file storage, website hosting, web applications, social media, and gaming services. The following two tables summarize some of the benefits and drawbacks of cloud computing.
Table 31: Benefits of Cloud Computing
Benefit Discussion
Backup The cloud provides reliable backup solutions, so you won't lose your data if a local storage device fails.
Accessibility The cloud gives you access to your data on any device and from any location. All you need is the right application and an internet connection.
Collaboration Cloud-based applications give you the ability to share documents and collaborate with other people in creating and editing them.

Resource Pooling Many businesses want to expand their computing resources without purchasing and maintaining additional in-house hardware. For these companies, low-cost cloud hosting solutions are a great option.
Table 32: Drawbacks of Cloud Computing
Drawback Discussion
Privacy and Security
Concerns

Data files stored on the cloud are susceptible to hackers, who gain access to cloud storage devices or tap into data as it travels over the internet between your local device and the cloud. Nearly all cloud service providers use encryption for this reason.

Internet Connection Issues While storing your data on the cloud is a huge benefit when you need access from multiple devices, it's a big problem when your internet connection goes down. Without a local copy of files, your productivity may be completely dependent on the quality of your internet connection.
Drawback Discussion

Cloud Hosting Outages Even if your internet is up and running, you may be unable to access your files when the cloud service is down. Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and other cloud-hosting businesses work hard to avoid any downtime, but there will always be short periods of hardware or software failure. For this reason, you should keep an offline copy of any critically important files or applications.
Common Cloud Platforms

Many different companies offer cloud services, and each one has its own strengths. Some focus on everyday consumers who want to store photos and documents, while others serve businesses that need powerful infrastructure. Understanding what each platform offers helps you choose the right tools for your needs.

In most cases, the answer depends on the devices you already own and the software you already use. If you have an iPhone and a Mac, iCloud works automatically without any extra setup. If your school or employer uses Google Workspace, your documents and email are already there. If you rely on Word and Excel, Microsoft 365 keeps everything in sync through OneDrive.

Many people use more than one cloud platform at the same time. For example, you might store personal photos in iCloud, use Google Docs for school projects, and keep work files in OneDrive. The key is understanding what each platform does well so you can pick the right tool for each task.
