blocks.text: Storing files only on your computer means you could lose everything if the device is damaged, stolen, or hit by malware. Cloud storage solves this problem by keeping your files on remote servers that you can access from any device with an internet connection. Major providers like OneDrive, Google Drive, iCloud, and Dropbox offer automatic backups, file versioning, and easy sharing, all without requiring you to manage the hardware yourself.

In this lesson, you will learn what cloud storage is and how it works, compare popular cloud storage providers, explore the benefits and drawbacks of cloud versus local storage, and practice sharing and managing files through OneDrive. You will also learn how shared network folders work in a business environment, including how to set permissions and map network drives.
Cloud Storage

"The cloud" is an increasingly common way to talk about resources on the Internet. The idea of cloud storage is similar to the idea of renting a storage unit when you have more things than your house can hold. Cloud storage is renting space on another company's computer. Because high-speed Internet access has become so common in many places, the cloud has become a very popular storage option for both individuals and businesses.
Cloud Storage Benefits

Cloud storage offers several compelling benefits. One is elasticity, which means the storage resources can expand or contract based on your workload and business needs. If you find that you need to add storage, that is an easy shift. If you need less storage, you can make that change too, though you should check your contract for the agreed-upon details.

Another benefit is that if you need more space, the cloud provider can give it to you right away. This is called scalability. Cloud resources, including storage, can scale up easily and accommodate a business or organization's growth.

Beyond automatically saving your files, cloud storage keeps different versions of them, so you can go back to an earlier version if you change your mind about edits. For individual consumers, cloud storage costs are typically low, usually just a few dollars per month for tens of gigabytes of data.

Cloud storage also makes collaboration easy. You can easily share a file with someone else. You can choose different ways to share, from letting the person only view the file to giving them full editing rights.
Cloud Storage Providers

Many companies offer cloud services through their own and other companies', data centers. A data center is a dedicated location that holds thousands of servers. All the big tech companies have their own online storage. Apple provides iCloud, Google offers Drive, and Microsoft delivers OneDrive. Other companies like Dropbox and Box also compete in this space. The well-known providers focus on security, using encryption and advanced virus protection to keep threat actors away.
Screenshot reprinted with permission from Apple Inc.

Ransomware attacks can lock up files on your local computer, but strong firewalls protect files stored in the cloud from these threats. Cloud storage works closely with your operating system, so you can access your files just like they were in File Explorer or Finder. It appears as just another folder, but it includes automatic backups and access to your files from any computer with an Internet connection. Simply open a browser and log in to your cloud storage. Remote access and redundancy make it easy to keep your important files safe and secure.

Microsoft joined the cloud storage game later than others and needed to get people's attention. To do this, they first offered 25GB of free storage to their users. This service is now called OneDrive.
Cloud Storage Drawbacks

People don't often talk about how much it costs to use the cloud. It's great to have all the remote features and so much storage space, but cloud service providers charge a lot for this convenience. Some IT departments with limited budgets need to decide which files or resources should be in the cloud and which should stay on their own computers (often called "in-house"). The benefit of keeping things in-house is that it saves money.

Cloud computing has some environmental downsides. Data centers, which are the main part of cloud computing, use a lot of electricity to run servers and other equipment. This high energy use can lead to more carbon emissions, especially if the electricity comes from non-renewable sources. Data centers also need a lot of water to stay cool, which can be a problem in places where water is scarce or during droughts. Additionally, big data centers take up a lot of space, which can change how the land is used and disrupt local habitats. Building and running these centers can affect local ecosystems and wildlife.

To reduce these environmental problems, many cloud service providers are using renewable energy sources, making their data centers more energy-efficient, and adopting eco-friendly practices. However, the overall impact of cloud computing on the environment is still a big concern.
Shared Storage

On a home computer system, data is usually saved on a local storage device such as the system hard disk drive. But computers used in a business environment will likely use shared storage to make information more manageable.
To do this, the network administrator creates a shared folder on a server within the network.

Employees are then required to save all of their work-related files in the shared folder instead of on their computer's local hard disk. This makes it much easier for the administrator to manage, back up, and control access to the organization's data. Because the folder is shared, you can access it from your computer and save information to it just as if it were on a local storage device.

In order to access a shared folder, your user account must be granted access to it. Depending on how your workstation and server are configured, you may be required to provide a username and password to access the shared folder.
Several common shared folder management tasks are described in the following table:
Table 34: Windows File and Folder Management Tasks
Task Description
Share a Folder You can share existing folders or create new folders to share. To share a folder, complete the following steps: 1. In File Explorer, identify the folder to be shared.
2. Right-click the folder and then select Show more options.
3. Select Give access to > Specific people.
4. Select the user or group you want to share the folder with and then select Add.
5. In the Permission Level column, specify the level of access they'll have to the shared folder. Options include:

items: Read allows the user to open and view files, but not save any changes.
Read/Write allows the user to open files, view their contents, make changes, and save those changes.

blocks.text: 6. Select Share (the network path to the share should appear). This is the information you must provide to other users who want to connect to the shared folder. The network path consists of the following:

items: Two backslashes (\\)
The name of the computer
A backslash (\)
The name of the share or path to the folder

blocks.text: 7. Click Done.
Be very careful when sharing folders. Make sure the files in the folder contain information that you are comfortable sharing with other users.
Access Shared Folder To access a shared folder on the network, do the following: 1. Open File Explorer and select Network from the left pane.
2. Double-click the computer or network server where the shared folder resides.
3. Double-click the shared folder.
Map a Drive to a Shared
Folder
You can map a drive letter to a shared folder to enable faster access.
1. Browse to the shared folder in File Explorer.
2. Right-click the shared folder and then select Map Network Drive.
3. Select an unassigned drive letter to associate with the shared folder.
4. The network path to the share should automatically be entered for you.
5. Click Finish.
In File Explorer, the drive letter you specified now points to the shared folder on the network server.
Windows Cloud Storage
You can open and save files directly from within applications using OneDrive as a storage location.
Opening and Saving Files with OneDrive

Many applications, including Microsoft Office and other programs, let you open files from OneDrive or save files directly to OneDrive without leaving the application. This means you do not need to manually copy files into your OneDrive folder first.
To open a file from OneDrive in an application: 1. Within the application, select File > Open.
2. Select OneDrive.
3. Browse and select the file, then select Open.
To save a file to OneDrive from an application: 1. Within the application, select File > Save As.
2. Select OneDrive and browse to the desired folder.
3. If necessary, give the file a name.
4. Click Save.
If you originally opened the file from OneDrive, you can simply use File > Save to save changes back to the same location.
Common Cloud Storage Providers

Most major tech companies offer cloud storage as part of their services. While they all let you store files online, each provider differs in how files sync to your devices, how much storage you get for free, and what collaboration tools are included. Understanding these differences helps you choose the best option for your needs.
Storage Features by Provider
The following table compares the storage-specific features of popular cloud storage services, focusing on what matters most when choosing where to keep your files.
Table 35: Cloud Storage Provider Comparison

Service Free Storage Sync Behavior Collaboration Supported Platforms OneDrive 5 GB Built into Windows; Files On-Demand downloads only when opened Real-time co- editing in Office apps; share links with view or edit access Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Web Google Drive 15 GB (shared with Gmail and Photos) Google Drive for Desktop streams files or mirrors them locally Real-time co- editing in Docs, Sheets, Slides; commenting and suggesting modes Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, Web iCloud Drive 5 GB Automatic across Apple devices; Windows app available Share files and folders; real-time co-editing in Pages, Numbers, Keynote macOS, iOS, Windows, Web Service Free Storage Sync Behavior Collaboration Supported Platforms Dropbox 2 GB Smart Sync keeps files in the cloud until needed; selective sync for folders Shared folders, file requests, commenting, Dropbox Paper for documents Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, Web Choosing a Cloud Storage Service For most people, the best cloud storage service is the one that works with the devices and software they already use. If you work primarily on Windows and use Microsoft Office, OneDrive integrates seamlessly. If you use Google Workspace for school or work, Google Drive keeps your documents together. Apple users benefit from iCloud's automatic sync across iPhone, iPad, and Mac.

Many users rely on more than one service at the same time. You might keep school documents in Google Drive, personal backups in iCloud, and shared project files in Dropbox. The key is knowing what each service does best so you can organize your files effectively.
Cloud Storage vs. Local Storage

When deciding where to store your files, you have two main options: keeping them on your device (local storage) or saving them to the cloud. Each approach has strengths and weaknesses, and understanding the trade-offs helps you make smart decisions about where to put different types of files.
Comparing Cloud and Local Storage
The following table compares cloud storage and local storage across several important factors.
Table 36: Cloud Storage vs. Local Storage
Factor Cloud Storage Local Storage

Access Available from any device with an internet connection Only available on the device where the file is stored (or attached external drives) Internet Required Yes: files may be inaccessible without a connection (unless synced locally) No: files are always available regardless of connection Backup Automatic; multiple copies stored across data centers Manual; you must create your own backups to external drives or other media Sharing Easy: share links or grant access with a few clicks Difficult: must copy files to USB, email, or set up network shares Capacity Can be expanded by upgrading your plan (pay for more space) Limited to the physical drive size; expanding requires buying new hardware Security Protected by provider encryption and firewalls, but vulnerable to account breaches Physically secure if the device is safe, but vulnerable to theft, damage, or malware Cost Free tier available (limited); paid plans for more space One-time hardware cost; no ongoing fees
When to Use Each
In practice, most people use a combination of both. Here are some general guidelines:

items: Use cloud storage for files you need to access from multiple devices, share with others, or keep safely backed up, such as school assignments, work documents, and photos.
Use local storage for files you need to access quickly without internet, very large files like video projects, or sensitive documents you prefer to keep off the internet.
Use both for critical files, keep a local copy and a cloud backup so you are protected against device failure and internet outages.

What is Virtualization?
Virtualization technology has been available for decades. Early computers were very expensive,
with personal computer prices ranging from $440 to $9,875 (in US dollars) in the 1970s. With
virtualization, users could make their computers act like they had another, separate system
running on it at the same time. So instead of buying a new, separate computer for $1,500, you

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 2.6 Compare and contrast virtualization and cloud technologies.
3.3 Explain the purpose and proper use of software.

blocks.text: Virtualization lets a single physical computer run multiple operating systems at the same time, each in its own isolated virtual machine. This technology powers everything from server consolidation in data centers to safe testing environments on a desktop. Special software called a hypervisor manages how the computer's processor, memory, and storage are shared among these virtual machines.

In this lesson, you will learn what virtualization is and how it is used, explore the differences between Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors, understand how guest operating systems work inside virtual machines, and discover how remote desktop tools let you access and control computers from anywhere. You will also see how containers and virtual servers make IT infrastructure more efficient and secure.

Virtualization technology has been available for decades. Early computers were very expensive, with personal computer prices ranging from $440 to $9,875 (in US dollars) in the 1970s. With virtualization, users could make their computers act like they had another, separate system running on it at the same time. So instead of buying a new, separate computer for $1,500, you could spend $300 on components to get a second operating system running on the computer you already have!
At the time of writing, inflation and rising costs mean that the personal computer price range of $440 to $9,875 in the 1970s is equal to a price range of $3,100 up to $47,500 today.

When you use virtualization, you partition off a safe and separate space on your computer for the virtual machines (VMs). Virtual machines are sometimes called guests, and they are the computer systems that run commands, open programs, and save files. In other words, they do all the things a typical computer does. VMs do this within your original physical computer, often called a host.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: Imagine your computer is a large apartment building. Different families (operating systems, in this analogy) live in their own apartments (virtual machines) within the larger structure. Walls are separating the apartments from each other, and every family has their own home with everything they need. Things like a kitchen (CPU), a living room (memory), storage space (hard disk), and a door to the outside world (network link) are all available to each family.

Just like families within an apartment building can borrow a cup of sugar or chat in the hallways, virtual machines can communicate between themselves if they are connected through a network. In most situations, VMs are organized so that they don't share information directly with the host computer, as this type of connection can be a security risk.
Virtualization Uses

Virtualization is especially useful for servers. Servers are powerful computers that can manage a huge number of tasks at once. They can easily run more than one operating system without any loss of performance. They have so much capacity that they can divide up the memory and storage space so each operating system has its own little section to work in. This is one of the biggest advantages of virtualization: resources get used very efficiently. All that capacity on servers doesn't go to waste.
Virtualization software can also be used on desktop computers for various purposes. Some typical uses of desktop virtualization are:

items: Virtual labs: Used to create a research lab to analyze viruses. As the malware is contained within the guest OS, it cannot infect the researcher's computer or network.

Support legacy software applications: If the host computers have been upgraded, software may not work well with the new operating system. For example, Windows 7 could be installed, which can natively run older programs.

Development environment: Test software applications under different operating systems and resource constraints. This is a quick and easy way to run through new software to see if there are any issues.

Training: Lab environments can be set up so that students can practice using a live operating system and software without impacting the production environment. At the end of the lab, changes to the VM can be discarded, and the original environment is available again for the next student to use.

blocks.text: The presence of other guest operating systems can be completely transparent to any single OS.

Each OS "thinks" it’s working with its own CPU, memory, hard disk, and network link. However, the guest operating systems can be networked together, or they may be able to share data directly through the hypervisor (though this is not commonly done for security reasons).
Remote Desktop

A remote desktop connection lets you control a computer from a different location as if you were sitting in front of it. You see the remote computer's screen on your device, and your keyboard and mouse inputs are sent to the remote machine. This technology is widely used for IT support, working from home, and accessing virtual desktops hosted in data centers.
How Remote Desktop Works

Remote desktop uses a client-server model. The computer you want to control runs a remote desktop server (or host) service. You connect to it using a remote desktop client application on your local device. All communication between the two happens over a network connection, typically encrypted to keep your session secure.

When connected, the remote computer sends screen images to your device and receives your keyboard and mouse inputs in return. Files on the remote machine stay on the remote machine unless you specifically transfer them. This makes remote desktop useful for situations where sensitive data should not leave a secure network.
Common Remote Desktop Tools
Several remote desktop and remote support tools are available:

items: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP): Built into Windows Professional and Enterprise editions.

blocks.text: Lets you connect to another Windows computer over the network. The remote machine must have Remote Desktop enabled.

items: TeamViewer: A cross-platform tool that allows remote access and remote support without complex network configuration. The remote user installs TeamViewer and shares a session

blocks.text: ID and password.

items: Quick Assist (Windo ws): A built-in Windows tool for remote support. A helper generates a security code and shares it with the person who needs help, then connects to view or control their screen.
Chrome Remote Desktop: A free, browser-based option from Google that works across

blocks.text: Windows, macOS, Linux, and Chrome OS.

items: Virtual Network Computing (VNC): An open-source protocol that works across different operating systems. Popular implementations include RealVNC and TightVNC.

blocks.text: Remote Desktop Use Cases
Remote desktop technology serves several important purposes:

items: IT support: Technicians can troubleshoot and fix problems on a user's computer without being in the same room or even the same building. This is especially valuable for help desk teams supporting remote workers.
Working remotely: Employees can connect to their office workstation from home and access all their files, applications, and network resources as if they were on-site.

Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI): Organizations can host virtual desktops on centralized servers using hypervisors. Users connect to their virtual desktop remotely using a thin client or any device with a remote desktop client. This simplifies management because IT only needs to maintain the server-side virtual machines.

Server administration: System administrators manage servers that may be located in data centers far away. Remote desktop or SSH (Secur e Shell) connections let them configure, update, and monitor servers without physical access.

blocks.text: Security Considerations
Because remote desktop gives full control over a machine, securing the connection is critical:

items: Strong passwords: Remote access accounts should use complex passwords to prevent unauthorized access.
Multi-factor authentication (MF A): Adding a second verification step (like a phone code) makes it much harder for attackers to break in.
Encryption: Most remote desktop tools encrypt the connection so that screen data and keystrokes cannot be intercepted.
Firewall rules: Only allow remote desktop connections from trusted networks or through a

blocks.text: Virtual Private Network (VPN).

items: Disable when not needed: If you don't use remote desktop, turn it off. An open remote desktop port is a common target for attackers.

blocks.text: Hypervisors and Guest Operating Systems
Type 1 Hypervisors

A bare-metal hypervisor, also called a Type 1 hypervisor, is special software that works directly on a computer without needing Windows or any other operating system first. It's great because it lets virtual machines (VMs) run incredibly well without a lot of interference. Since there's no main operating system in the way, the computer can give out more power to the VMs. It's also safer because there's less chance for viruses or malicious software to get in.
Type 2 Hypervisors

On the other hand, a Type 2 hypervisor is similar to a regular program you run on your computer, like a game or a word processor. It needs the main operating system, like Windows or macOS, to work. It does a lot of the same things as Type 1, but it uses more of the computer's resources to get started.
You can virtualize Windows and Linux inside of each other, inside their own OS, or inside a macOS.
However, you can't virtualize the Apple macOS inside a virtual environment. Apple does not permit this; they want users to run their OS on their platform.
So what do real hypervisors look like? Here are a few you're likely to run into:

items: Hyper - V : This one is actually built right into certain versions of Windows (Pr o and Enterprise editions). It comes with a tool called Hyper-V Manager that lets you create, start, and stop virtual machines without installing anything extra. Even though it lives inside Windows,

blocks.text: Hyper-V itself acts like a Type 1 hypervisor under the hood.

items: VMware ESXi: This is a Type 1 hypervisor you'd find in big server rooms and data centers.

blocks.text: Companies use it to run dozens or even hundreds of virtual servers on a single powerful machine.

items: VirtualBox: A free Type 2 hypervisor that works on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It's a popular choice for students and hobbyists who want to experiment with different operating systems without any risk to their main computer.
VMware Workstation: Another Type 2 hypervisor, but geared more toward IT professionals who need to test software or set up practice labs on their desktops.

blocks.text: Guest Operating Systems

The guest operating system (OS) is the term for the operating system that runs inside the virtual environment. This might surprise you, but sometimes people need to use an older version of Windows for certain things. And when it comes to Linux, there are hundreds of versions, or "distros," that can be set up in these virtual machines.

What's most common, though, is putting several Linux or Windows servers inside one physical computer. This is handy because servers have a ton of power. They often have more than one CPU with multiple cores (which is like having more than one brain), a lot more memory than a typical computer, and more storage space as well. With virtualization, you can divide up this power among multiple guest operating systems. If you wanted, you could even have Windows running inside another Windows, kind of like Russian nesting dolls, where one fits inside the other.
Guest OS Uses

Let's try to understand why this is so great. Your computer can pretend to be many computers at once. Now, each pretend computer can do a different job. For example, one might keep all the office files together for you and your coworkers, another might keep track of all the printers, and a third might handle all the emails. These pretend computers can each use a different OS if a certain system is better for a certain thing, Windows Server on one and Linux Ubuntu on another, for example.

It's important to make clear that these computers don't affect each other. That's one huge advantage. If one gets a virus or stops working, it won't cause problems for the others. Each VM is isolated in its own space, so what happens in one doesn't affect the others.
Hardware and Virtual Machines (VMs)

The magic behind virtualization is done by the hypervisor. It's like the director of a play, telling everything where to go and what to do. The hypervisor can actually create new virtual central processing units (CPUs). Even though it's using the real CPU, the hypervisor divides it up so that many virtual guest computers can use the CPU at the same time. This division can happen with other parts of the computer system, such as with memory, for example.

For memory, the hypervisor divides out a portion of the real memory and assigns it to each virtual computer. And it does the same with storage, giving each virtual machine a slice of the real computer's hard drive to keep its files on. Sometimes, it even makes virtual graphics cards for high-end video graphics. The hypervisor also handles the connection of these virtual computers to networks and the Internet.

One benefit is how fluid everything can be. If one of the guest machines needs more storage space, the hypervisor can just assign more storage from the real computer's hard drive over to the guest machine. It's like having a backpack made of expandable material. You can keep stuffing books in there, and the backpack will keep stretching out.
Organizations and cloud storage providers try to use virtualization for their servers quite a lot.

Instead of having many separate servers, they make one big server pretend to be many smaller ones. Doing this takes some of the load off their IT workers and technicians. There's also less equipment in general in the network room, so they can use the space for other things. Less equipment means less generated heat. Heat is a natural enemy to computers; having a cooler temperature in the network room means the computers will run better and last longer.
Container Virtualization

Container virtualization is a lighter way to use a computer to run a lot of apps at the same time without them getting in each other's way. In this scenario, let's imagine that your computer is a house, and each app lives in its own room. It's a lot like regular virtualization, because even though they share the same house, there are walls between them. The difference is that containers are more flexible and don't need a whole computer system for each app or program, just enough to make the app work. So they don't take up much space, they work very fast, and you can easily move them from one computer to another. It's a leaner, more portable way to take advantage of virtualization.
Virtual Servers
You might not realize it, but a lot of websites you visit are actually running on virtual servers.
To you, it looks and feels the same as any other website. But using virtual servers has some benefits for the professionals who run the websites.

First, it saves them money. Instead of having to buy a bunch of physical machines, they can just have one machine act like many, and they don't end up spending as much on upkeep. It's also just easier overall when things aren't scattered everywhere, and it's all in one place. And the network administrators who manage all these complex operations love virtual servers because they make their jobs easier, too.

For those professional developers, virtual servers work great because they can test new apps and programs in a virtual, safe environment, so they don't mess up the whole system if something goes wrong. It's like having a sandbox to mess around in and then clean up and start over again. In fact, it actually is called a "sandbox" in the technological world.

Another benefit is that if a virus gets in, it won't spread to other parts of the computer system. It's confined to its own little virtual bubble. Also, fewer physical computers means less electricity being generated. That's not only good for saving money but also better for the planet!
So even though you might not see it, virtual servers are a big part of your everyday life on the internet.

6.2 Explain methods to secure devices and security best practices.

blocks.text: Every time you connect to the internet or install a new program, you are exposing your computer to potential threats. Malicious software, or malware, comes in many forms including viruses, worms, spyware, and ransomware. Each type behaves differently, but all of them can compromise your data, your privacy, or your ability to use your device.

You will learn about common types of malware and how they spread, and explore the security tools that help protect your devices. You will discover how firewalls filter network traffic, how anti-malware software detects and removes threats, and what steps you can take to reduce your risk of infection.
Malware and Spyware

Since the very beginning of the computer age, threat actors have been making harmful code to attack or to invade computers. Originally, when most of the computers in the world belonged to governments or to corporations, malicious software or malware evolved as another part of espionage and spying. Here are some of the common types of malware, or malicious content.
Virus

A virus is the worst kind of malware, intentionally designed to disrupt computer systems or networks. Viruses need users to get started, but once they are inside a system, they can spread between computers and corrupt both data and software. It's important to know that viruses can't actually break the computer's physical components, but they can make programs, and the computer's operating system stop functioning properly.

Viruses come in many varieties, and they can have different goals, including simple vandalism, financial gain, or disabling parts of an enemy nation's infrastructure. Some viruses can delete data, replacing the target files with code or information of their own. Some are designed to target specific types of programs, and others are designed to move through entire networks as quickly as possible.
The most famous of all virus infections, designed to damage Iran's nuclear program, is Stuxnet.

Discovered in 2010, this virus used several different types of code to disable machinery and to cover its tracks. The Stuxnet attack specifically targeted computers that were air-gapped, or separated from any network. This meant that the attackers had to introduce the virus without relying on someone clicking a link or downloading a file. They instead used USB or flash drives with the virus pre-installed, and placed the drives near the nuclear facilities. One or more employees eventually plugged the flash drives into the air-gapped computers, and Stuxnet was off and running. In this way, the attack used both a virus and social engineering to accomplish its goal Worms Worms are another type of malware that spreads over a network by themselves, without needing human intervention. A worm can make copies of itself to move from one computer to another, taking advantage of weak spots in the network. Within the past 25 years, there have been many serious worm infections, affecting millions of computers. Sometimes worms carry another type of malware, which may lock up data, steal sensitive information, or install backdoors or infect entire systems.
Spyware
Spyware is a type of software that tries to view and record what you do on your computer.

Users may inadvertently install spyware onto their computers because it often comes bundled with legitimate programs. Sometimes it can include a keylogger, which is a tool that records what you type, like your passwords and other credentials. This means that the threat actors who run the keylogger could steal your information.

Most of the time, people use spyware to make money by showing you annoying pop-up ads or banners. They do this by getting the malware into lots of computers, bundled with legitimate programs. Companies that sell things want lots of people to visit their website. More visitors could mean more sales. So, they pay for ads that help bring people to their site. You might see these ads as banners on different websites. Websites can charge money based on how many people see the ad or click on it to visit the company's site.

While it's not always illegal, there are many software programs designed just to show you more ads and pop-ups. If you click on these, the person who made the program gets paid by the company that's happy to have more people visiting their site.
Ransomware

Ransomware is a type of malware that locks you out of your own files or entire computer and demands a payment (ransom) to give you access back. It typically works by encrypting your files so you cannot open them. The attacker then displays a message demanding payment, usually in cryptocurrency like Bitcoin, in exchange for the decryption key.

Ransomware can arrive on your computer in several ways. The most common delivery method is through phishing emails that trick you into clicking a malicious link or opening an infected attachment. It can also spread through compromised websites, infected USB drives, or by exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in software.

Once ransomware activates, it works quickly. It may encrypt documents, photos, databases, and other important files within minutes. Some advanced versions can also spread across a network, locking down multiple computers in an organization at the same time. Victims typically see a ransom note on their screen with instructions for how to pay and a deadline, after which the attacker may threaten to delete the files permanently or increase the ransom amount.
Security experts and law enforcement agencies generally advise against paying the ransom.
There is no guarantee the attacker will actually restore your files, and paying encourages more attacks. Instead, the best defense against ransomware is prevention:

items: Keep regular backups: Store copies of important files on an external drive or cloud service that is not always connected to your computer. If ransomware strikes, you can restore your files from the backup.
Update your software: Install operating system and application updates promptly. Many ransomware attacks exploit known vulnerabilities that patches have already fixed.
Be cautious with email: Do not open attachments or click links from unknown senders. Even messages that appear to come from someone you know could be spoofed.
Use anti-malware software: Keep your anti-malware protection active and up to date so it can detect and block ransomware before it executes.

blocks.text: Security is the practice of controlling access to something important, like information or a place.

With computers occupying a large part of personal and professional life, keeping them safe from threats such as hacking and identity fraud is vitally important. Layers of security come from understanding industry standards, using common sense, and enforcing rules about who can do what with a given computer system.
In this lesson, you will explore the foundational concepts that keep computers and data safe.

You will learn about physical device security, security frameworks like the CIA Triad and NIST, how authentication and authorization control access, how encryption protects data in transit, and how accounting and tracking monitor what happens on a system.
Device Security

The most basic part of cybersecurity is controlling physical access to computers and network devices. If a threat actor gets physical access to a computer without permission, they can do a lot of harm to the entire system. Physically touching the computer means someone can begin to guess passwords, or steal a hard drive to get access to its data, among other attacks.
Computers are high-value targets for two different reasons:

items: Physical value: Some computers are expensive because they're made with expensive parts.

blocks.text: The computer is valuable for what it is.

items: Data value: Almost every computer stores data of some kind. The computer is valuable for what it holds.

blocks.text: People who work in cybersecurity also ensure the physical security of the computers and devices they look after, as part of their job role.
Equipment Locks

Hardware locks for computers and networking equipment have been around for decades. As computers became smaller and more mobile, it became easier for threat actors to walk away with sensitive equipment. These hardware locks can attach to any device. In some cases, the lock will keep the equipment in one place, and in other situations, a different type of lock will prevent unauthorized people from using the device, even if they are able to steal it.

Most laptops, except ultra-thin laptops, have a small hole on the side or back. This hole is made for a special kind of lock, called a Kensington lock. This lock looks similar to a bike lock and comes with a cable. You first wrap the flexible cable around something big and sturdy, like a pole, a handrail, or another anchor point. Then insert the cable through the laptop and into the locking mechanism, locking it with a code or a key.
The first company to make these locks was called Kensington. While many different manufacturers produce this type of device lock, most people just call the locks "Kensington locks.

While it might seem like very basic security measures, many times people steal things just because they see a chance. If a laptop is left sitting alone on a table, it's easy for someone to grab it and put it in their backpack. A locking cable around a laptop makes it much harder to steal. When theft requires bolt cutters, crime goes down.
Many organizations use these locks on other devices as well. Desktop computers, monitors, and projectors are all compatible with this type of cable-based lock.
USB Locks

You can also put a USB lock on an open USB port on a computer to stop users from using these ports. The lock is easy to install and will prevent unauthorized data transfers through the USB port. It can also stop the computer from booting up from a USB drive.
Other Physical Security

In addition to locking devices directly, cybersecurity professionals also help prevent theft in other ways. This usually involves keeping servers in one room where doors are locked, and not allowing unauthorized people into areas of critical operations.

"I was working for a client who had multiple spaces in an office tower, which also occupied several other companies. The client's server room was down the hallway on the same floor. While walking past the server room one day, I noticed that the server room door was propped open with a door stop. No one was in the server room, but the door was wide open. On a floor that not only housed my client, but also several other companies. I asked them why the server room door was propped open, and they told me it was because there was no ventilation in the room, so they kept the door open to keep the servers cool. I asked if they were concerned about some random person walking into the server room. They told me "Well, no one has done it so far." -- Greg C., security technician All employees have a role in cybersecurity. Companies should train every person to understand how they can help support security measures and how to confidently enforce the rules. Any person can ask people they don't know, or people without the right security badge, to prove they should be where they are. A lot of trouble can be stopped if people using computers know about common threats and take precautions to avoid them. Many businesses make sure their workers go through training often, so everyone knows about the newest threats.
Security Strategies

Most companies want to believe their computer networks are safe. They create user accounts, follow strict rules, and check for security issues. But sometimes, people try to break into these networks from both inside and outside the company. These attempts might be harmful, or just someone with computer skills wanting to see if they can get in. Because keeping information safe is so important, working in this part of technology requires a lot of focus, discipline, and a clear understanding of security concepts.

A cybersecurity framework guides the selection and configuration of devices and behaviors that keep a computer system secure. Frameworks are important because they stop an organization from building its security program in a vacuum, or from building the program on a foundation that fails to account for important security concepts.
Here are two commonly used strategies that many organizations use to guide their work in security.
The CIA Triad

The field of information security uses the CIA Triad as its primary principles of security control and management. For information and systems to be considered secure, they must have all three of these properties:

items: Confidentiality: The information can only be read by people explicitly authorized to access it.
Integrity: The information is stored and transferred as intended, and any modification is authorized.
Availability: The information is readily available and accessible to those authorized to view or modify it.

blocks.text: The triad can also be referred to as "AIC" to avoid confusion with the Central Intelligence Agency.

Nearly all organizations have information that should be kept confidential. For example, the president of a public company might receive the company's financial documents from the accountant, but they will not be publicly released for weeks. Other employees do not need to see the numbers before the release date. Keeping these numbers a secret from the other employees is an example of information confidentiality.

When the company accountant transmits the balance sheet to the company president, the numbers should not change. They should be the same numbers when they leave the accountant and when they arrive in the president's files. This is an example of information integrity.

If the president of the company needs to review the financials right away, she can easily and reliably access those documents. There's no barrier to her being able to open or to read those files. This is an example of information availability.

Some security models and researchers identify other properties of secure systems. The most important of these is non-repudiation. Non-repudiation means that a person cannot deny doing something, such as creating, modifying, or sending a resource. For example, a legal document, such as a person's will, must usually be witnessed when it is signed. If there is a dispute about whether the document was correctly completed, the witness can provide evidence that it was.

"A user clicked a link he should not have clicked. He ended up forwarding a phishing email to everyone in his address book. Clients, vendors and coworkers reported the phish. The user told his boss he did not click the link and did not forward any phish emails. I performed an eDiscovery search within Microsoft 365. The employee actually DID forward the phish email. I found evidence in his Sent Items folder. Ten minutes later, the same evidence was in his Deleted Items folder. The employee's lies were not credible. He lost to non-repudiation. The employee no longer works there." -- Mark A, cybersecurity consultant The NIST Cybersecurity Framework When we talk about keeping information safe, cybersecurity means making sure the computers and programs we use are secure. Information security and cybersecurity tasks can be grouped into five basic functions, following the framework developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIS T):

items: Identify: Develop security policies and capabilities. Evaluate risks, threats, and weak spots in the system and recommend security controls to reduce the risks.
Protect: Develop, install, operate, and retire IT hardware and software assets. Focus on security as a requirement of every stage of this operation's lifecycle.
Detect: Perform ongoing, proactive monitoring to be sure that controls are effective and capable of protecting against new types of threats.
Respond: Identify, analyze, contain, and eliminate threats to systems and data security.
Recover: Restore systems and data if other controls are unable to prevent attacks.

blocks.text: Where the CIA Triad is a collection of ideas about security, the NIST framework is something that companies can apply more actively to the work their employees do. Some companies choose to organize their cybersecurity departments around these five functions. They might have job roles that are only associated with the Protect function, for example. Other job roles focus specifically on the Recovery aspect of cybersecurity.
Authentication Factors
Authentication is the process of ensuring that each account is only operated by its proper user.
There are many different authentication technologies and methods. These different ways of authenticating a subject are referred to as factors.
Something You Know

This category includes anything that only the user should know. The typical example is the login credentials. Login credentials are the combination of a username and a password. The username is not typically a secret, because it's usually some combination of the user's first and last names, but the password must only be known to the account holder. Some other examples include:

items: Passphrase: A passphrase is a longer password comprising several words. This has the advantages of being more secure because of its length, and easier to remember.

blocks.text: "PurpleMonkeyDishwasher" will stay in most people's minds longer than " o x94T Y8~3qio7" will.

items: PIN: A Personal Identification Number (PIN) is a type of password you remember. It's also called a passcode, and it can contain both numbers and letters. Using a passcode is a fast and safe way to get into your device. Many people like to use passcodes because they're easy to remember.

Patterns: Devices with touchscreens can offer the option to use a pattern lock as another security measure. This allows the user to draw a predefined pattern on a grid of 3 columns and 3 rows of dots.

blocks.text: Another key idea in proving who you are by using things you know is the concept of Personally Identifiable Information (PII). This kind of proof is also helpful when you need to reset your account. For instance, PII is often used for security questions to check who you are when you call about your account. The person talking to you on the phone wants to make sure you are really you. For example, PII could be answers to questions like "What is your favorite movie?" "What street did you grow up on?" or "What is the name of your first-grade teacher?" Something You Have This category means that the account holder, or the person with permission, owns something unique that no one else has. There are several ways to authenticate a user based on something they have.

One way to prove who you are is to give each person a special hardware token. The most well-known one used to be the SecurID token. It creates a number code that matches a code on a server, which you need to enter to log in. The code changes about every 60 seconds. SecurID tokens were popular until smartphones became more common. Now, with authenticator apps, smartphones make it easier to use this kind of "something you have" authentication.
Something You Are
This category relies on something unique and virtually unchangeable about the user.

"Something you are" authentication means using a system that recognizes unique body features. Biometric authentication uses special traits each person has that can prove who they are. You can use many kinds of biometric information, such as fingerprints, retina or iris patterns in a person's eye, facial recognition, or even the way someone's voice sounds, to identify them.

When the system administrator creates the account, the user is there in person to have their unique body features, like fingerprints or eye patterns, scanned into the system. These scans are saved in the security system as a template. When the user wants to log in, the system checks the biometrics that the user provides and compares them to the saved template to make sure they match.

This is a fast and easy way to figure out who someone is. If the scans match, the person is allowed in. These unique features are very difficult for someone else to copy, which makes them an excellent part of the authentication process. Another good thing is that, unlike special security devices, it's hard to lose your own biometrics!

Windows 10 and 11 provide support for biometrics to authenticate you through something called Windows Hello. If your computer can use Windows Hello (if your laptop has the right camera or a fingerprint reader), you'll find this option in Account Settings. Your computer can remember your face, iris image, or fingerprint and use that to let you in. It's a nice way to get into your device without needing a password or PIN. Plus, once you're logged in, you can use your biometrics to sign in to websites or pay for things online.

The biggest issues with using biometrics are that some users find it intrusive and worry about their privacy. Also, setting up and keeping the system running can be more expensive than other authentication methods. Sometimes, biometrics can make mistakes, like not letting the right person in (false negatives) or letting the wrong person in by mistake (false positives).
Multifactor and Two-factor Authentication

Passwords alone are usually not strong enough to protect very important or high-risk applications like company networks or bank accounts. Any of the factors on this page can be a key part of two-factor authentication (2F A). Two-factor authentication adds an extra step to logging in, on top of using passwords.

Some situations require even more security, an authentication system that's as strong as possible. Implementing multi-factor authentication (MF A), using multiple authentication types, will increase the strength of the system. With two or more steps, it's much tougher for hackers to get into accounts and devices.
Single Sign-On

Single Sign-On (SSO) means that a user only has to authenticate to a system one time to gain access to all its resources. For example, with one set of login credentials on a Windows computer, a user will also seamlessly be logged into other Windows services, websites, and programs. This makes life easier because users don't have to remember lots of different logins, which can be tiring. It's handy because you don't have to keep track of many accounts, but there's a downside, too. If a hacker gets into your one account, they could get into everything else you have access to.
Authorization Factors
Authorization is the process of determining what rights, or permissions, users should have on each resource, such as a file or a program. Authorization also includes enforcing those rights.
Permissions

Every organization has a huge number of programs, files, and folders in its computer system. Even smaller companies create many files in the course of regular operations. Larger organizations have the added layer of different departments with different roles, such as Marketing and Finance. Each department has specific programs and files they work with to do their jobs, and they don't need to use or look at files or resources from other departments. A network administrator will set different permissions for those files, based on who needs to use them.
Permissions can vary between systems, but the IT industry broadly categorizes permissions into different types, like the ones listed here:

items: Read: A user or group of users can view or read the file, but that is all.
Write: A user or group of users can read the file, and can also modify or edit the file.
Execute: A user or group of users can run a program or script from the file.
Delete: A user or group of users can remove the file.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, a company may have a mission statement on how it will conduct its business.
Employees may want to review the document from time to time, but no one should change the mission statement. This document has "read-only" permissions.

Network administrators can also set permissions at different levels. For example, the company's brand directory, or entire set of files, could have one set of permissions, such as "read-only," to make sure that everyone in the company uses the same set of logos and colors. A company might also set specific permissions that apply only to a single folder or a small group of files.
Network administrators can also assign permissions to individual users or to groups of users.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, the entire Development team may need to read or to view the schedule for project A, but only the individual project manager should be able to edit or write to that schedule.

In other cases, an entire department has different levels of permission related to a directory, but members of other departments can't access that set of files at all. Financial and human resource files, containing sensitive information, fall into this category. Setting group permissions makes the IT department's job much simpler.
Least Privilege

In IT, there's a rule called least privilege. This rule means that a user only gets the access they need to do their job, and nothing more. You could think of it like keys to a building. Employees only get keys to the rooms they need to go into and are kept out of places they don't need.

This helps to reduce the risk of security breaches, simple mistakes that expose a network, or introducing software that may corrupt system data. The concept of least privilege makes IT management quite a bit easier.

When you give more people access or permissions on a computer or network, you're taking a bigger risk that someone might use those permissions in a way they shouldn't. The user could misuse that permission intentionally, or they could cause a problem by accident. To keep things safer, authorization policies make sure people only get the special access they really need, based on the concept of least privilege.

Think of it like an invite-only party. If you're not on the party's guest list, you can't come in. In the same way, access controls work by saying "no" to everyone unless there's a specific "yes" that lets them in. This is called implicit denial. If there's no clear rule that says you can have access, then the answer is automatically no.
Administrators and Standard Users

Some special accounts can do anything they want on the entire computer system. On Windows and Apple macOS, these accounts are called Administrators, and on Linux, they're called the Root user. Because these accounts can change anything on the computer, network administrators must be extremely careful when assigning these special user types.

Just below the Administrator, there's a type of account called a standard user. Standard users can still do their job tasks, such as opening files and using programs, but they can't add new software or modify important system settings. The goal for the standard user permission level is to let the workers do their jobs without needing to ask the IT department for help all the time, while also keeping the computer safe.

In many organizations, it's common to assign these standard permissions to people using the computers or workstations. This helps to limit changes from being made and lowers the risk of malicious events. For a virus to get into a computer or network, it has to run, just like any other program. That's why not allowing the installation of new programs is a key step in keeping things secure.
Accounting and Tracking

Accounting is the process of documenting user actions on the computer system. Accounting uses specialized software to log, or record, events that take place on the network. Events are things like sign-on attempts, software use, and file modification. When you log into a system that has this type of security logging software, that software will record how you logged in, what time you logged in, which programs and files you worked on (and at what times), and when you sign out. Accounting can keep track of different things like computer systems, people using the computer, files, and even remote connections.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, the resources could be the database programs the user opens in the course of their day-to-day work. This database generates monthly sales reports, and the user prints out these reports.
Another example is the history of websites visited while browsing the web. This allows the accounting system to track what users are doing within the system.
Windows Event Viewer can display many of these accounting functions.
Location Tracking
Location tracking uses technology to record the geographical location of a person or a device.

Different tracking systems use different methods to do this, including the Global Positioning System (GPS), cell towers, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi. People and companies use location tracking for many things, such as using a token to find where you left your cell phone, or for larger logistical systems like trucking companies.

Location tracking can also be used as a barrier to stop hackers from getting into computer systems. Geofencing is a security measure that tracks assets by drawing an invisible line around the specific physical place that holds them. If those important assets move outside the line, it sends a warning to the IT department that someone might have moved the company's equipment. This could mean someone stole something from the company.
Web Browser History

Browsers don't just remember the websites you go to; they also know where you're using the internet from. Are you at home, or are you somewhere else on vacation? There are actually some valid reasons to let your browser keep doing this, even if it seems intrusive. For example, if you're hungry and want to order a pizza, searching online will show you pizza places near you. You can choose if you want your location to be tracked or not by turning this setting on or off whenever you like.

When you travel to a different part of the world and try to log into common apps such as Gmail, your account might get flagged. This is because logging in from a location you've never been to, or don't typically go to, looks suspicious. This could look like someone else trying to get into your account. The site owners flag your account, or reach out to you through your cellphone or other backup method, to help stop anyone who shouldn't be getting into your account.

5.4 Explain basic data backup concepts.

blocks.text: Keeping a computer safe requires more than just being careful online. Security tools like antivirus software and firewalls work behind the scenes to block threats before they can cause damage. Understanding how these tools work, and how people can use them correctly, is an essential part of protecting any device or network.

In this lesson, you will learn how antivirus software detects and removes malware, how firewalls filter network traffic to block unauthorized access, and how layered security strategies like defense in depth protect organizations. You will also explore recovery options such as patching, System Restore, Safe Mode, and Reset This PC that help you fix problems when something goes wrong.
Antivirus Software

Antivirus scanners or antivirus software helps to identify and stop harmful attacks on your computer or network. It primarily works by using a list of known virus patterns, called definitions or signatures. Another way it works is through heuristic identification. This means the software looks for actions or behaviors that are similar to what viruses do and tries to block those actions.
What is Antivirus Software?

Antivirus software, also called security software, usually comes in two types. One type is a personal security suite, which protects just one computer. The other type is a network security suite, which protects many computers and is managed from a central server. Most antivirus software is made for Windows PCs and networks because most viruses target these systems. However, there is also antivirus software for Linux and for Apple's macOS. Some of the big companies that make antivirus software are Avast, Norton, AVG, Trend Micro, Sophos, Malwarebytes, and Bitdefender.

Some companies offer a basic free version of their antivirus software. This free version usually has the same main engine as the paid version, but doesn't have all the extra features. Corporate networks don't use the free versions, but it can be a good option for individuals. The most important thing is to install antivirus software on your computer and keep it updated.

If one antivirus program is good, then two must be better, right? Actually, that's not true. If you use two antivirus programs, they will conflict with each other and slow down your machine. It's best to stick with one good antivirus and malware program.

A good IT professional will use antivirus software to protect systems. Make sure you have these programs installed and updated. Remember, there's no such thing as 100% protection from every possible attack, so always be careful when you connect to the Internet.
Constant Vigilance

All antivirus software is set up for real-time scanning. Real-time scanning is a feature in antivirus software that constantly watches your computer for threats. It checks files, programs, and processes as you open or use them to make sure they are safe. If the software finds anything suspicious, it can block or remove the threat right away. This helps protect your computer from viruses, malware, and other harmful attacks as they happen.

Real-time scanning might make your computer a little slower, but it's an important part of keeping it safe from threats. Just as the software checks files as you use them, the software can also check system memory, email attachments, removable drives, and network drives for viruses. Many scanners can even find websites with harmful scripts or code. When setting up antivirus software, it's important to set the right exceptions, or rules. Scanning some system files and folders in real-time can cause performance issues.
In addition to real-time monitoring, you can set up scans to run at times that work best for you.
If your computer is busy all day, schedule scans at night when the system activity is lower.
You can choose to scan daily, weekly, or monthly. You can also decide whether to scan only important files or the entire system on your hard drive.
How Antivirus Software Works During an Attack

Malware such as worms can spread over networks. This means that once they get into a network, they will copy themselves to other computers. Therefore, if an attack happens, one of the first things you should do is disconnect the network. Taking a system off the network is a simple but effective way to stop the threat from spreading.

If a file has a virus, most of the time, antivirus software will find it and neutralize it. You can set up what the software should do when it finds malware during a scan. You can use antivirus software to try to remove the virus (called cleaning) or quarantine the file, in which the software blocks any attempt to open it. Think of quarantining like putting the bad software in a locked box.

The reason you would not want to permanently delete the file is that sometimes the antivirus software makes a mistake and thinks a safe file is a virus. This is called a false positive. The file might be needed by a legitimate system program. If, days later, you notice that an important program isn't working, it might be because the file is in quarantine. To fix this, you can take the file out of quarantine and put it back in the right folder.

Sometimes a virus can infect a computer so badly that the only way to fix it is to format the hard drive or erase everything on it completely and reinstall Windows. Ideally, you have backed up your data before starting this process.
Security Tools in Practice

The security devices, software, and practices are a very important part of keeping networks secure. Making sure that people use them correctly is just as important. The way people use security tools can affect cybersecurity in many ways, both good and bad.
Human Impact on Cybersecurity
When people use security tools correctly, they can make an organization much safer.
Automated tools can find, analyze, and fix security problems quickly, often much faster than a person could. This means that humans can spend more time focusing on complex problems.

However, if people use security tools incorrectly, they can create weaknesses. For example, a poorly configured firewall might let in unauthorized users. In another example, people can rely too much on automated tools, leading them to miss subtle signs of a security breach that the tool can't catch.

Having advanced security tools might make people feel too safe, causing them to ignore other important parts of cybersecurity, like training employees and making good policies. Without proper training and effective security policies, people might misuse or not fully use the tools.
Using Layered Security Methods

Network security must include the concept of layered security, or defense in depth. This refers to placing security controls throughout the network, so that there are many different kinds of ways to stop threats. Cybersecurity technicians enforce defense in depth with security tools and with policies that set out expectations for the way people behave. This includes behaviors like separation of duties and segmenting the network, in addition to requiring users to authenticate or prove who they are, using multiple authentication factors.

Separation of duties is a behavioral way to defend against insider threats, meaning abuse by people who are part of the organization or company. Any tasks that require multiple steps should be split between different people to prevent ethical conflicts or abuse of power.
Network segmentation is one way to restrict access to different areas of a company's network.

One example would be a company separating its Finance department files from the rest of the organization. Putting the financial information in its own zone, or network segment, makes it harder for threat actors to obtain that information.
Any security tool only as good as the person who uses it. Effective training, good policies, and strong security tools are all necessary to ensure the highest levels of cybersecurity.
Firewalls

Cybersecurity professionals use firewalls as part of defense in depth to establish a secure barrier at the network edge, where access attempts are most common. This type of security provides a good first chance to protect the network, but it can still be vulnerable to modern malware and insider threats. This is why using antivirus software and keeping up with software updates is so important.
What are Firewalls?

The basic function of a firewall is traffic filtering. Network communications, or traffic, flow across different areas of the network, out to the Internet, and back into the network from external sources. A firewall organizes this traffic according to a set of rules that let in or keep out different types of traffic. Simple firewalls use three criteria or rules when filtering data: 1. Source: Where did the traffic come from?
2. Destination: Where is the traffic going to?
3. Protocol: What transport protocol is the traffic using?
A firewall is an important part of any corporate network. Most home routers also feature a built-in firewall, which users can configure at a website portal.

Firewalls can be hardware devices or software programs. Hardware firewalls, which are dedicated appliances or devices, typically protect a whole network. A technician would install these firewalls at the edge of the network so that it can inspect all traffic that passes through it.

Software firewalls typically protect a single workstation or server. These firewalls are installed as a program or application on the computer and inspect only the traffic addressed to that computer, and nothing else.

A web application firewall helps protect web applications by filtering and monitoring traffic between a web application and the Internet. Web application firewalls can be deployed on the network, on a host, or by using a cloud-based firewall.
Using Firewalls

Different operating systems come with pre-installed firewalls. Windows computers will come to you with Windows Defender already installed, while macOS devices will include the macOS Firewall software. You can replace these applications if you prefer. Many people do, for reasons like increased security or because they prefer the way a different firewall works. It's best not to run two firewall applications at the same time, because they can conflict with each other.

You can set up any home firewall software to be used on either private or public networks. A private network would be a connection you trust, such as your home or office. Public networks include the local coffee shop, your public library, or an airport.
Recovery Options

Even with antivirus software and a firewall in place, there are situations where a computer might stop working correctly. A virus could slip through, a critical system file could become corrupted, or a bad software update could cause problems. When this happens, knowing how to recover your system is just as important as knowing how to protect it in the first place.
Patching and Updating

One of the best ways to keep a computer secure is to install software updates, also called patches, as soon as they are available. Software developers regularly release patches to fix security vulnerabilities that hackers could exploit. If you delay updates, your system remains exposed to known threats that attackers are actively trying to use.

Most modern operating systems, including Windows, macOS, and mobile platforms like iOS and Android, offer automatic updates. Automatic updates download and install patches in the background, often while the device is idle or restarting. Keeping automatic updates turned on is the easiest way to make sure your system has the latest protections.

In addition to operating system updates, it is important to keep all installed applications up to date. Web browsers, office programs, and media players all receive patches that fix bugs and close security holes. Many applications can check for updates on their own, but it is a good habit to check manually from time to time.
System Restore

Windows includes a feature called System Restore that can roll back the computer's system files and settings to an earlier point in time. The operating system automatically creates restore points before major changes, such as installing new software or drivers. If something goes wrong after a change, you can use System Restore to undo those changes without affecting your personal files, like documents, photos, or music.

System Restore is useful when a new program or update causes the computer to behave strangely. For example, if your computer starts freezing or showing errors right after you install a new driver, restoring to a point before that installation can fix the problem. To access System Restore, search for "Create a restore point" in the Windows search bar and follow the on-screen instructions.
System Restore does not remove personal files, but it will uninstall any programs or drivers that were added after the selected restore point.
Reset This PC

When a computer has a serious problem that System Restore cannot fix, Windows offers a more powerful option called Reset This PC. This feature reinstalls the Windows operating system while giving you the choice to keep or remove your personal files.

items: Keep my files: This option reinstalls Windows and removes all installed applications and settings, but preserves your personal files. You will need to reinstall your programs afterward.

Remove everything: This option erases all files, applications, and settings, returning the computer to a factory-like state. This is the best choice when selling or recycling a computer, or when a malware infection is too severe to clean.

blocks.text: You can find Reset This PC in Windows Settings under System > Recovery. Because this process is significant, make sure you have backed up any important files before starting.
Recovery Drives and Installation Media

Sometimes a computer is in such bad shape that it will not start up at all. In these cases, you need a way to repair or reinstall the operating system from an external source. A recovery drive is a USB flash drive that contains the tools needed to troubleshoot and restore Windows, even when the computer cannot boot on its own.

Creating a recovery drive ahead of time is a smart precaution. Windows has a built-in tool called Recovery Drive that walks you through the process. Once created, you can boot the computer from the USB drive and access recovery tools such as System Restore, Startup Repair, and Reset This PC.

Another option is to download Windows installation media from Microsoft's website. This lets you create a bootable USB drive or DVD that can be used to perform a clean installation of Windows. A clean installation erases everything on the system drive and installs a fresh copy of the operating system.
Safe Mode

Safe Mode is a special startup option that loads Windows with only the most basic drivers and services. This makes it useful for troubleshooting problems that prevent the computer from starting normally. In Safe Mode, you can remove a problematic program, update a driver, or run an antivirus scan without interference from malicious software.

To access Safe Mode in Windows 10 or 11, go to Settings > System > Recovery and select Restart now under Advanced startup. From the recovery menu, choose Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Settings, then restart the computer and select Safe Mode from the list.

If the computer cannot start Windows at all, it will usually enter the recovery environment automatically after two or three failed boot attempts. From there, you can access Safe Mode and other recovery tools.

leaving a network open?
How have wireless security standards evolved from WEP to WPA3, and which should you
use today?

Why should features like remote management and WPS be disabled on most home and small
