What is MAC address filtering, and why is it not sufficient as a standalone security measure?

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 6.5 Given a scenario, configure security settings for a small wireless network.

blocks.text: A wireless network is only as secure as its weakest setting. Many home and small office networks are vulnerable not because of sophisticated attacks, but because default settings were never changed and basic security features were left turned off. Understanding how to configure a router's security options is one of the most practical skills you can have as a technology user.

In this lesson, you will learn how wireless encryption protocols like WEP, WPA, WPA2, and WPA3 protect network traffic, how to secure a router by changing its default SSID and passwords, and how additional settings like firmware updates, disabling remote management and WPS, and MAC address filtering can strengthen your network's defenses.
Securing Small Wireless Networks

Securing a small home or office network means protecting both your digital data and your physical equipment. It's just as important to prevent people from stealing your computers as it is to encrypt your information.
Wireless Network Security

Another important thing to think about is the security of the network. Each new version or generation of Wi-Fi supports the same or better security protocols than the version before. This keeps your Internet better protected with each new standard.
A Wi-Fi network doesn't have to be encrypted, but there are risks if it's not. Without encryption, unwanted people can easily get into the network, see private information, or disrupt the network.

With encryption, which is set up automatically with wireless security, computers on the network are safe from tampering. Only people you invite can access the network, keeping everything private from outsiders. In public places, you might see an open network that doesn't need a password, making it easy to connect. However, this type of network only connects devices to the Internet and doesn't have other computer hardware on it, just the modem and router. While there is no hardware for threat actors to access, data flowing across this unsecured network can still be at risk.

Routers have a guest network option that you can turn on or off. If you want to let people use your internet, you can turn on the "guest" option. But make sure to set a password so random people can't get on your network and use up your bandwidth.

In order to keep others from viewing or intercepting your network activity, the industry added a security component to wireless transmissions. The first iteration of this encryption came out in 1997 and was called Wired Equivalent Privacy (WEP). It provided for either 64-bits or 128-bits of encryption. This first generation of security was easily hacked and is now what the industry calls "deprecated," or no longer used.

WEP limited users to using exactly 10 hexadecimal characters for the password. The password could not be any shorter or any longer than 10 characters. This limitation caused many people in the United States to use their phone number, a 10-digit long number of hexadecimal characters that they could easily remember. Of course, this ease of use also contributed to WEP's vulnerability.

The new standard, Wi-Fi Protected Access (WP A) came out in 2003 with improved 256-bit encryption. The industry has continued to improve security, which brought about WPA2, with the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) algorithm. Current protocols have evolved to include Wi-Fi Protected Access (WP A3), which includes different divisions for personal and business use, making it much safer. Most routers today support using WPA2 and WPA3 encryption.
Securing a Router

Aside from having strong security, it's a good idea to change the default Service Set Identifiers (SSIDs) and passwords that your router broadcasts. The SSID is what you see when you connect your mobile device to a Wi-Fi network. Sometimes, users might want to change the SSID for convenience. To do this, you need to use a smartphone app or a web browser to log into the wireless router. In the main menu, you'll see a box showing the current SSID. Just replace the text and apply the changes to start broadcasting the new SSID.

Remember, an SSID is one of the few things in computing that is case-sensitive. While today's Wi-Fi passwords have strong encryption, changing the Wi-Fi password is easy and follows similar steps to changing the SSID. Just erase the information in the password box and replace it with whatever you prefer. After making this change, all connected devices will need to reconnect.
Pre-Shared Key
A pre-shared key is a type of password used in offices to let users access a wireless network.

IT sets up the key when they configure the router or access point. Authorized users get the key so they can connect their devices. However, there's a risk with this method because the key might get shared with the wrong people.
Physical and Device Security

Make sure to keep all doors and closets locked to stop thieves from taking your computer equipment, and use cable locks for laptops when needed. In order to protect sensitive personal or company data, every computer should have a login password. The password should be strong enough to keep unauthorized people from getting in, but not so hard that it frustrates the user. Using biometrics, like fingerprint scanners on laptops, is another great way to make it easy for users to log in while keeping threat actors out.

Routers come with a built-in firewall, which will work for a basic network. But if you have a larger, more complex network, or you're worried about cyberattacks, you can upgrade your equipment. A standalone small office firewall can offer stronger protection. For example, an accounting office that prepares customers' taxes is at a higher risk because tax returns have a lot of personal information that hackers might want to steal. That type of office may want to add more levels of security to protect the sensitive information on their networks. These steps are crucial to keep a small office network safe from potential attacks.
Router Security Options

Setting up a strong Wi-Fi password and encryption is a great start, but routers have many other security settings that are just as important. Many of these settings are turned off or set to weak defaults when the router is brand new. Taking a few minutes to configure these options can make your home or small office network much harder to break into.
Changing Default Admin Credentials

Every router has an administration page where you can change its settings. To access this page, you open a web browser and type in the router's IP address, which is usually printed on a sticker on the bottom of the router. The problem is that most routers come with a default username and password, such as "admin" and "password." These defaults are well known and easy for attackers to guess.
One of the first things you should do after setting up a new router is change the admin username and password. Choose a strong password that is different from your Wi-Fi password.
If someone gains access to your router's admin page, they can change any setting, redirect your traffic, or even lock you out of your own network.
Updating Router Firmware

Routers run their own software, called firmware, that controls how the device operates. Just like computers and phones, routers need software updates to fix security vulnerabilities and improve performance. Router manufacturers release firmware updates periodically, but unlike most computers, routers usually do not update themselves automatically.

To check for firmware updates, log into the router's admin page and look for a section labeled "Firmware Update," "Software Update," or "Administration." Some newer routers do support automatic firmware updates, and turning this feature on is a good idea if it is available. Running outdated firmware is one of the most common security weaknesses in home and small office networks.
Disabling Remote Management and WPS

Remote management is a feature that lets someone access the router's admin page from outside the local network, over the Internet. While this might sound convenient, it also means that anyone on the Internet could try to log into your router. For most home and small office networks, remote management should be turned off.

Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is another feature found on many routers. WPS was designed to make it easier to connect devices to a wireless network by pressing a button on the router or entering a short PIN instead of typing the full Wi-Fi password. However, the WPS PIN is vulnerable to brute-force attacks, where an attacker tries every possible combination until the correct one is found. Because of this weakness, security experts recommend disabling WPS and using a strong Wi-Fi password instead.
MAC Address Filtering

Every network device, such as a laptop, phone, or tablet, has a unique identifier called a MAC address. Routers can use MAC address filtering to create a list of approved devices that are allowed to connect to the network. Any device not on the list will be blocked, even if it has the correct Wi-Fi password.

MAC address filtering adds an extra layer of security, but it is not foolproof. Advanced attackers can spoof, or fake, a MAC address to match one on the approved list. For this reason, MAC address filtering works best as one part of a larger security strategy rather than the only line of defense. It is most practical for small networks where the number of devices does not change often.

What is a Database?
Databases are everywhere, and most people use them every day.
On the way home from school or work, you stop by the grocery store. You scan your items at
the self-checkout, swipe your loyalty card, and pay with your debit card. Once you get home,
you go to your favorite pizza chain's website, place an order from their online menu, and pay
with your credit card. While you wait for the pizza to arrive, you check your favorite social
media platform and browse for a good movie on your video streaming service. In about an hour,
you have used seven databases without even thinking about it.

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 5.1 Explain the value of data and information.
5.2 Explain database concepts and the purpose of a database.
5.3 Compare and contrast various database structures.

blocks.text: Almost everything you do online depends on a database. Social media, banking, streaming services, and school systems all rely on databases to store, organize, and retrieve information quickly. Understanding how databases work gives you insight into the technology behind the apps and services you use every day.

In this lesson, you will learn what a database is, why organizations prefer databases over spreadsheets, and how data is structured within a database. You will also explore the differences between relational and non-relational databases.
Databases are everywhere, and most people use them every day.

On the way home from school or work, you stop by the grocery store. You scan your items at the self-checkout, swipe your loyalty card, and pay with your debit card. Once you get home, you go to your favorite pizza chain's website, place an order from their online menu, and pay with your credit card. While you wait for the pizza to arrive, you check your favorite social media platform and browse for a good movie on your video streaming service. In about an hour, you have used seven databases without even thinking about it.
The Importance of Databases

A database is a highly organized, multi-table digital storage system designed to hold information on a computer. You can store any information in the different tables within a database, including names, dates, files, pictures, transactions, comments, numbers, and more.
Data is vitally important for any group or business. By using databases to gather, store, and retrieve data, people and companies can use them to make smart choices and plan well for the future.

This is why databases are so important. Data is an important part of how businesses and organizations make their decisions, and databases are how those businesses organize that information. Without a way to organize the information and find the exact right pieces of information, the data just sits there. Databases provide a logical structure so people can actually use their data.
Database Characteristics
There are many kinds of databases, and this module will introduce you to each of them.
Each type of database uses different methods to organize data, and each has a different job.
However, most databases share these common features:

items: Centralized access: Multiple users can get into, or access, the database at the same time.

blocks.text: This allows people to use the data without waiting or taking turns.

items: Security: Databases include security measures to ensure only authorized users can access the data. Different users have different permission levels. For example, a top-level administrator can view and edit all the data, while lower-level users might only see records but not change or delete them.
Recovery: The information in a database is valuable, and losing it could cause significant damage to an organization. Databases are easy to back up, so database administrators

blocks.text: (DBAs) can restore the data if something goes wrong.

items: Scalability: Databases can store thousands, millions, or even billions of data points. Imagine trying to keep track of a billion rows on a spreadsheet. It would not be easy. Fortunately, a good database makes analyzing a million records just as easy as analyzing a few dozen.

blocks.text: Managing Databases

A database management system is a specific type of software that helps create and manage each database. It acts as an interface between the raw data in the database and the people who want to use or analyze it.

With a database management system, people can create, read, update, and delete data in real time. This means that the database stores any data changes immediately, and other users in the database can see those modifications right away. Database management systems allow every user to see the same data all at once.

The database management system decides the format and structure of the database and gives users the tools they need to work with the data. Microsoft Access, which comes with Microsoft Office 365, is the most popular consumer database management system. Larger organizations usually need a system with more features and security. Some of the most common ones are MySQL, Oracle Database, and Microsoft SQL Server.
Database vs. Spreadsheet

When you think about using databases, especially if you're new to their structure, you might think of them as overly complex. Why use database software if you're already familiar with spreadsheets such as Google Sheets or Excel, or simple comma-separated value (CSV) files?
The reason is that organizations of all kinds are generating more and more data every day.
Managing those data points and their relationships to each other is much simpler if you work within a database, not a spreadsheet.

Spreadsheets, also called flat file systems certainly have a role in managing information. They have a simple structure with rows and columns that are easy to understand and organize as you like. A spreadsheet works great for small to medium-sized sets of data, usually numbers, but it can also include words. They can be perfect for a single user or for a small group.
Benefits of Databases over Spreadsheets

While flat file systems help transfer information between systems or track sales orders, they don't always have enough functionality for what a company needs. Most of the time, databases are the solution. Here are some advantages of using a database over a flat file system:

items: Processing speed: Databases store billions of data points and let you quickly search for and retrieve a single record.
Backup and recovery: Databases back up information within seconds of adding it, making it easy to recover lost data through backup and replication.

Forced data types: Databases control and validate the information that users enter or provide. This control is called forced data entry. As an example, when you order a product online, the phone number field only accepts numbers, not letters. This is a situation where forced data entry helps ensure the data is as clean and accurate as possible.

Concurrent use: Databases allow many users to access the data at the same time without waiting. A database can support thousands or even millions of users at once. This is hard to do with a flat file system, which often locks a file when one person opens it, preventing others from using it. Online collaboration tools can help, but they usually limit the number of spreadsheet users, often to around 100.
Security: Databases ensure only authorized users can access the data.
Scalability: Databases can handle large volumes of data, and users can extend their capacity when needed by using external databases or data connections.

blocks.text: In short, databases offer faster processing, better backup and recovery, controlled data types, support for many users at once, and improved security compared to flat file systems.
Database Structure

In a database, an entity is a real-world thing that an organization uses. For example, a business considers each customer an entity. Similarly, a product that a business sells is another entity. An attribute provides a detail or characteristic of an entity. For instance, the customer's name and phone number are attributes of the customer. The name and price of a product are attributes of that product. A relationship connects two entities. When a business sells a product to a specific customer, that sale represents a relationship between two entities.
A database stores a collection of organized information on a computer. Organizations choose different kinds of databases based on the type of information they need to store.
Structured Data

Structured data divides information into clear, separate categories. For example, consider books in a library catalog. Each book is different, but they all share the same categories: title, author, publication date, and call number. This kind of information is easy to store in a structured table, where every book has a value for each category. This setup is ideal for a relational database. All data in a structured database follows a strict plan or outline and connects between tables.
Non-structured Data

Non-structured data is information that doesn't have a clear order or pattern. Think about having a bunch of different things about the US Civil War, like journals, newspapers, photographs, telegrams, and pamphlets. To keep all these different items organized, people often use something called eXtensible Markup Language (XML). XML is similar to HyperText Markup Language (HTML), which is used to create websites, but instead of showing how things should look, XML uses special tags and codes to give structure to the documents or items. This makes it easier to manage and find different types of data in a database.
Semi-structured Data

Semi-structured data falls between organized and unorganized. This type of data doesn't fit neatly into rows and columns like a table, but it still shares some common features. For example, when you classify different types of animals, every species has a scientific name, an average size, and a known life expectancy. However, you don't need to store information about a dog's wingspan, and you don't need to include a space for a frog's beak size.
A key/value pair database works best with semi-structured data. A key, also called a field, is a category of information. Some keys are the same for all items, but other keys can be different.
This type of database doesn't have a search option, so you need to know the key to find the information you need.
Relational and Non-Relational Databases

One common type of database is the relational database, which keeps data in several connected tables. Remember that spreadsheet programs use vertical columns and horizontal rows. But in databases, they are called fields and records. Rows are called records because all the information in a row goes together.

Records are unique. They collect information about only one entity. The entity in that record can be a type of vehicle, a specific piece of art, a single park in a national parks system, or a person. The record is always unique, even if the entity shares some data in common with other entities.

Because Michael Smith is a common name where you live, and more than one person with that name might work at your company, you need another way to find the person you're looking for.

Managing Relational Databases

A database is made up of many tables full of information, and some of that information can be located on more than one table. To show that there is a connection between tables, the software uses a primary key. Each table in a relational database has one field, and only one field, called the primary key field. This field's job is to give each record a unique identifier, such as the Employee ID in our example above.

A relational database management system (RDBMS) is software that lets users create, change, find, and manage the data stored in a database. These systems use Structured Query Language (SQL) is the standard language for working with data. You will explore primary keys, SQL, and relational database management in more detail in a later lesson.
Non-relational Databases

Not all data fits into strict fields and records. A non-relational database, also called NoSQL, which stands for "not only SQL", usually stores this kind of data. Unlike relational databases, these databases don't use traditional rows and columns. Instead, a non-relational database handles data in different formats, making it easier to organize semi-structured and unstructured data. They also use different query languages that are best for the specific types of data they store.

blocks.text: Now that you understand what a database is and why organizations use them, it's time to start working with one. In this lesson, you will learn how data gets into a database, whether by importing it from other sources or entering it manually using tools like forms. You will also explore how to use queries to find, add, and update information, and how to turn query results into easy-to-read reports.

You will also learn about where databases can be stored and accessed. Some databases run locally on a company's own servers, while others are hosted in the cloud. Each option has its own benefits for speed, security, and availability. By the end of this lesson, you will have hands-on experience managing data in Microsoft Access and writing simple SQL commands.
Working With a Database

When new learners start working with databases, it's important for them to understand some basic ideas and operations. Databases are used to store, find, and access lots of information, as you've learned. This topic will help you learn how to get started with those processes.
Import or Input Records

When you create a database, you need to first put data into the system. You can do this either by importing it from other sources, such as spreadsheets, forms, or other databases, or by typing it in manually.

Manually transferring your data from one source to another can be time-consuming. It can also expose your important data to the possibility of human error. For this reason, manual data entry is almost never your best available option.

Importing records can bring in large amounts of information very quickly and accurately, either to start a new database or to add to an existing one. People inside or outside the company can import data into the database.

One example of outside users entering data is when you shop online and enter your personal information as part of the transaction. You put your information into a series of fields for your name, email address, and shipping address at checkout. Those data points get added to the company's database.

As you enter personal information, you create a record and add it to the database. Each piece of information, like your first name or last name, is called a field. All the fields together make up a record, which is housed in a row. For example, everyone's first name goes into the first name field. Fields are like columns on a spreadsheet. A field describes one detail about each record in the database.
Queries

As you saw in the video, queries let you request specific data from a database. Beyond retrieving information, you can also use queries to manipulate data. People who work with databases will typically use the Structured Query Language (SQL). This language is important for managing databases, from simple commands to complicated requests involving many tables.

Queries can add or remove information from a database. For example, if a store customer buys two new pairs of shoes, database queries update the customer's record to show the new purchases. At the same time, another table that tracks product inventory will show fewer of those specific shoes. After the purchase, the customer remembers that their phone number changed recently and asks for it to be updated. A query then changes the phone number in the customer record.

Queries can also work with data from many different tables. In our shoe store example, the store manager wants a report on how many accounts are open at the Chicago location, and who is managing those accounts. The query checks both the customer account and account manager tables to get the results.

Reports

You can take the data you asked for in a query and change it into something easy to read and understand, called a report. Reports can look different depending on what you need. They give you easy-to-read summaries of the data, which could be shown in graphs or charts. You can base reports on tables, queries, or both.

As an example, imagine you are the manager of a shoe store. You keep track of things like shoe inventory, sales records, and customer accounts using a few different databases. Throughout the day, customers buy shoes, adding customer information and sales information to your databases and changing your shoe inventory database.

With our shoe store example, you can query your database and get reports of sales that you can sort in any way you want. You can find out how many sales the store had last month, or how many sales of children's shoes last month, or how many sales of children's size 3 shoes last month, or what the difference in total sales was last month compared to the same month last year.
You can see there are many ways to look at the data. If a full year of reports shows increased sales in December, you can see a pattern in buying habits and plan for next December.
Database Location and Access

Whether you're running a business, working on your education, or planning your next vacation, you need reliable information to make good decisions. Databases store a huge amount of data, in some cases more than you could ever use.

Servers play an important role because they store the database program and data. IT professionals make sure the data is available to everyone who needs it. The end user doesn't care where the data comes from; they just want it to be available when they need it. To save money, an organization might store the information on its own servers. For more flexibility and reliability, but at a higher cost, they might store the data in the cloud.
Offline vs Online Databases

An offline database can be used without an Internet connection. These are used when programs don't need Internet access. A big benefit of offline databases is that they reduce the risk of cyber attacks.

An online database is one that users can access over the Internet. This allows employees or customers of an organization to reach it from anywhere, not just a physical location. The main differences between online and offline databases are where the information is stored and how it's accessed.
Local Databases

Local access means putting the server on the company-owned network so employees at the office and those outside the local network can use it. It might also be an intranet, set up just for employees at one location. One benefit of local storage is that you can usually access the data a bit faster. The IT department controls the hardware and database setup completely. They also set up internal data security and firewalls to keep threat actors away from the database.
Cloud Databases

Cloud storage means putting the database and data online, hosted and managed by the cloud provider. You access the data over the Internet, either through a specific program or with a browser. The cloud provider takes over much of the management work from the local IT team.
Another benefit is that you can expect the data to be available 99.9% of the time, and you can quickly scale up to meet greater needs.

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 5.2 Explain database concepts and the purpose of a database.
5.3 Compare and contrast various database structures.

blocks.text: Relational databases are the most widely used type of database, and understanding how they work is essential for anyone who manages or interacts with data. A relational database organizes information into related tables, using a carefully designed schema to keep data structured, consistent, and easy to retrieve.

In this lesson, you will learn how to plan a database using schemas and data models, explore how tables use records, fields, and constraints to organize data, and see how primary and foreign keys link tables together. You will also tour Microsoft Access to see database objects like queries, forms, and reports in action, learn the basics of SQL for retrieving data, and explore how big data and NoSQL databases handle information that traditional tools cannot. Finally, you will examine specific types of NoSQL databases, including key-value and document databases.
Schema in a Relational Database

A database schema is the architecture of how a database is structured and organized. It defines how data is stored, how the relationships among data are managed, and how data can be accessed and manipulated.

Creating databases can be a complex process and often involves teams of people. Data modeling, or designing a schema, is a way to help programmers and others understand the complex flow of data within an organization. These models help organize tables of data and ensure consistency in things like naming conventions, default values, and security settings within the database. It's like a blueprint that an architect creates to show how everything should fit together. These models can also help you easily spot missing or duplicate data.

There are different kinds of data models, each serving a different purpose and having different levels of complexity. These include conceptual data models, logical data models, and physical data models.
Conceptual Data Models

Start by creating a conceptual data model. This is the simplest type of data model because it only focuses on high-level ideas. It answers the question of what a system contains. It provides an organized view of the data you need to support your business processes. It looks at the data being used but doesn't worry about how it's processed or its physical details.

This kind of model organizes and defines business ideas and rules. It shows what all the entities are, their attributes, and their relationships. You create it without considering hardware details like storage capacity. This model doesn't use primary or foreign keys. It can show that two entities are related, but it doesn't specify the attributes that connect them. These models are usually simpler and easier to read than other types.
Logical Data Models

A logical data model is more detailed than a conceptual model because it explains the data more thoroughly. It answers the question of how to structure a system, but it doesn't show how to implement the database with a specific database management system. It also doesn't consider the system's hardware.

This model aims to create a technical map of rules and data structures. It provides the foundation for building a physical data model. These models are more technical and can seem very complex to the average user. They can include primary keys, foreign keys, entity names, entity relationships, and attributes.
Physical Data Models

The physical data model is the most detailed type of data model. It shows you exactly how to set up a database using a specific database management system. It also includes technical details and performance needs for the hardware that will run the database. This model describes all the data needed for a particular project and provides enough information to actually build the database.
Tables in a Relational Database

As you saw in the videos, database tables use records (rows) and fields (columns) instead of the row-and-column terminology used in spreadsheets. Tables form the structure of the database, and some tables get their information from other tables.
Organizing Tables

The tables within a database work together by identifying specific data from key fields, and sharing that data between the tables. That specific data could be a field of text, numbers, or anything else that a table can hold. Most of the time, that field has the same name across both tables. In every situation, the shared field will be called either a primary key or a foreign key.
Primary and foreign keys are covered in more detail on the following page.

As you'll see in the Microsoft Access tour video, forms provide a convenient way for users to enter data into their tables, reducing the chances of data entry errors and preventing users from changing important settings.

A database's schema, its structure, is designed to stop fields from being left blank. This is called a NOT NULL constraint. It means that a value must be entered into the field whenever a new record is created. Essentially, constraints are rules about what can or cannot be entered.

Databases allow for constraints, or rules, to be applied to fields in tables. For example, you can add a rule to make sure an email address field is never empty. Another rule might require the format of a first name to always have a capital letter in it. You decide the type and format of the information to be entered. This helps avoid data inconsistency.
Primary and Foreign Keys
Primary keys give each record a unique identifier so you can tell records apart.
Employee Name Employee ID Site Client Account Status

Kai Garcia 13-4583209 Bedford Falls Bailey S&L Active Alex Lee 19-5634471 Waveland Stark Industries Suspended Michael Smith 23-719537 8 Atwater Stark Industries Active Joseph Deng 21-7 829299 Bedford Falls Bailey S&L Active Ahsoka Tano 21-6929371 Freeport Bailey S&L Active Michael Smith 19-3420155 Springfield Stark Industries Active Bill Hulbert 08-3228119 Waveland Bailey S&L Active Clark Addison 99-4501982 Waveland Stark Industries Suspended Michael Smith 13-3583285 Atwater Bailey S&L Active Michael Smith 19-4533356 Freeport Bailey S&L Suspended Primary Keys In this table, the Employee ID field is the primary key. As the video explained, a primary key gives each record a unique identifier. Primary keys are usually numbers, but they can be any unique value.

Beyond uniqueness, primary keys have important rules. They must be consistent and stay the same for the entire life of the database. They must also be unique, meaning no two records can have the same primary key. Additionally, there must always be a value for the primary key; it can't be left blank.
Foreign Keys

A foreign key is a field in one table that references the primary key of another table. This creates a link and relationship between different tables and their data, and helps keep the data accurate and consistent across related tables.

Account Holder Name Account Number (Pr imar y Key) Account Manager ID (F or eign Key) Sam Spade 137596 1001 Risha Patel 814418 1002 Joseph Deng 019346 1003 Kai Garcia 019820 1004 Supervisor Location Account Manager Account Manager ID (Pr imar y Key) Bill Hulbert Chicago Clark Anderson 1001 Riley Smith Atwater Alex Lee 1002 Bill Hulbert Chicago Ross Barnes 1003 Dan Osborne Newton Mary Hatch 1004 Relating Primary and Foreign Keys The relationship with a foreign key can take on a few different forms, including a one-to-one and a one-to-many relationship.

In a one-to-one relationship, one record in a table will be associated with only one record in another table. In a one-to-one relationship, the primary key in the first table is often the primary key in the other table as well.

Suppose when a student enrolls in school they are entered into the "tblStudents" table. The student record contains basic student information, like StudentID, date of birth, and other identifying information. Later, if a student is assigned to the gifted services team, a record will also be entered into the gifted entry table. The Student ID is the primary key for both the "tblStudents" table and the "tblGiftedEntry" table.

In a one-to-many relationship, a primary key is joined to a foreign key, meaning there is one record (in the table in which the key is primary) associated with multiple records in other tables (in which the key is foreign).

Suppose each time the student enters a new school year, you use their StudentID from the student information table to associate them with their new enrollment record in the "tblEnrollment" table. StudentID is a primary key in "tblStudents" but a foreign key in "tblEnrollment." That means you have one record for each student in "tblStudents," and you have as many enrollment records for that student as years they are enrolled.

If this student went to school for five years, you would have five records to represent each year they were enrolled. There can only be one record in "tblStudents" for a student, but an infinite number can exist for that same student in "tblEnrollment." This is a one-to-many relationship.
Database Terms
There are four primary database objects — tables, queries, forms, and reports. SQL commands like SELECT, WHERE, and LIKE let you find exactly the data you need.
The table below summarizes the key SQL concepts.
Table 37 : SQL Quick Reference
Term Description
SQL (Structur ed Query
Language)
SQL is a computer language used by most relational databases for creating queries. By using SQL, a database user can view, edit, delete, and create database records.
SELECT The SQL command used to retrieve data from a table. You can select specific fields (e.g., SELECT Title FROM Books) or the entire table using an asterisk (SELECT * FROM Books).
Term Description
WHERE A clause added to a SELECT command to filter results based on specific criteria (e.g., WHERE BookID=5).
LIKE A condition used with WHERE to search for patterns in text fields.
The percent sign (%) acts as a wildcard (e.g., WHERE Title LIKE '%Encyclopedia%').
Big Data Concepts

The video covered how big data is extracted, mined, and analyzed, and why ethical responsibility matters when working with large data sets. The table below highlights two additional concepts that distinguish conventional database tools from the newer approaches used with big data.
Table 38: Big Data Concepts
Concept Description

Conventional Database Tools Conventional database tools work well with structured data that are organized into relational databases and data warehouses. These tools are designed for Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMSs) and their use Structured Query Language (SQL) for querying and maintaining the databases. Traditional tools do not work well with big data, which requires query languages and other tools that are more flexible and dynamic.
NoSQL Because of the unstructured and complex nature of big data, we typically can't use SQL to query an organized collection of relational databases.

For this reason, the non-relational databases that arise from big data are often called NoSQL. NoSQL databases are sometimes called "Not only SQL" since the database structure stores data differently than a relational database and cannot rely only on SQL to access the data.
Key-Value Databases

A key-value database is a type of non-relational database. It stores data using a unique key that helps you find or save the matching value. To organize unstructured data, it uses key-value pairs. This means it shows data as a key with a value. The key is a unique identifier, like a number or a word, and the value can be any type of data.

This simple chart shows the basic structure of a key-value database. In this example, each key has only one corresponding value. The key is on the left and the value on the right. Notice that in this example the data stored in the Value column can be digits or words. You can store any data in the Value column.
Key Value
Weight 100 pounds Color Red Size Medium Year of Release 1982 Key-value databases handle lots of information that needs to be accessed quickly and often.

They have a flexible structure, so you can easily change how the data is set up. They also use a simple data model, making them easier to understand. Plus, they can grow quickly as the amount of data increases.

A key-value database lets you get data quickly, which is great for tasks where you need to access data often. These features make the database helpful for organizations. They use it as a cache layer in front of regular data to make apps run faster. For example, a key-value database can store scores and rankings for online games.
Document Databases

A good way to keep track of different resources is by using a document database, which is a type of non-relational database. Document databases manage and track data that doesn't fit into neat and orderly tables. This messy data can include nested files, arrays, and more. The file system on your computer is an example of a document database.

A document database differs from a traditional relational database because it can store multiple pieces of information in one field. In a relational database, this isn't possible. A document database stores data in flexible documents, like company inventory or blog posts. It is a type of NoSQL database that stores data as JSON or XML, which are two popular data formats. This approach is very different from the columns and rows used in a relational database.

Documents can have layers with different lists and complex data types, making it easier to show data in a natural way. Other important features include different ways to search the data and using data models that don't need strict organization. There's also flexibility, so data in the same collection can have different fields.

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 4.1 Compare and contrast programming language categories.

blocks.text: Nearly everything electronic runs on code, from the apps on your phone to the websites you visit every day. Code is a set of instructions written in a language that a computer can understand, and coding is the process of writing those instructions. Understanding how code works gives you a foundation for understanding the technology all around you.

In this lesson, you will learn what coding is and how it evolved from the earliest computer programs. You will explore the different types of programming languages, including compiled, interpreted, and assembly languages, and discover how web technologies like HTML, CSS, and JavaScript works together to create websites. You will also learn about object-oriented programming, query languages, runtime engines, and scripting functions.
Coding Overview

The videos above introduced what coding is and how computers follow step-by-step instructions. Coding has a long history. English mathematician Ada Lovelace created the first computer program in 1843 while working with Charles Babbage on his Analytical Engine designs. Lovelace's notes on the Engine are considered the first description of a computer program and software. While Babbage's designs were never built into an actual machine, they advanced the field of computing and changed ideas about what machines can do.
Coding Basics

At their most basic level, computers react to physical signals like positive and negative electric charges, which humans see as ones and zeros. Computer processors recognize certain patterns of ones and zeros as commands, which we call machine language or machine code.

Humans find this language very hard to understand because we are accustomed to letters and the decimal system for numbers, not binary. Luckily, modern developers don't work directly with machine language. They use programming languages instead, which make it much easier for humans to read and write instructions for computers.
What is a Programming Language?
A programming language is a system of notation that allows programmers to write code that a computing device can run.

Syntax in computer programming sets the rules for how to write the language. These rules include statements, symbols, capitalization, punctuation, and comments. Some computer languages, like Java and Python, are case-sensitive, so they treat uppercase and lowercase letters differently. For example, in Java, the variable "MyShoes" is different from "myshoes." Syntax and other characteristics help programmers collaborate because they can all "speak" the same language and understand each other's code.

When learning a programming language, you commonly start by writing a program that prints the words "Hello World" on the screen. In this case, "printing" means showing those words on the screen when the program runs, and doesn't have anything to do with putting ink on paper.
Here are some examples of how some programming languages print "Hello World" to the screen.

#include int main() { std::cout << "Hello World"; return 0; Python print("Hello World") Assembly Language SECTION .data ; initialised data section Msg: db "hello world", 10 ; message to print MsgLen: equ $ - Msg ; length of message SECTION .text ; code section global start start: ; printing message, use write() ; system call 4 syntax: ; user_ssize_t write(int fd, user_addr_t cbuf, user_size_t nbyte) push dword MsgLen ; length of message to print push dword Msg ; message to print push dword 1 ; FD of 1 for standard output sub esp, 4 ; OS/X requires extra 4 bytes after arguments mov eax, 4 ; 4 - write() system call int 80H ; perform system call add esp, 16 ; restore stack (16 bytes pushed: 3 * dword + 4) ; program exit, use sys_exit() push dword 0 ; exit value of 0 returned to the OS sub esp, 4 ; OS/X requires extra 4 bytes after arguments mov eax, 1 ; 1 - sys_exit() system call int 80H ; perform system call These examples show that each programming language has a different structure. When choosing a language, consider things like the platform you are targeting and which operating system (OS) that the platform runs on, the performance you need, and personal or organizational preferences. Programming languages fall into two categories: interpreted or compiled, also covered in this lesson.

You might have seen Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) and other markup languages, like eXtensible Markup Language (XML), grouped with programming languages. However, they are usually not considered programming languages for these reasons:

items: HTML doesn't make decisions or perform actions like a robot following commands. It simply tells the browser how things should look.
XML uses nested tags (similar to boxes sitting within boxes) to show how different pieces of information should fit together.

blocks.text: Compiled Languages
Compiled programs run fast and have full access to device hardware, but they are platform- specific and require porting to work on different systems.
Runtime Engines
Some languages, like C# (pronounced C-Shar p ) and Java, mix the ideas of compiling and interpreting to get the best of both worlds. These are called runtime code or runtime engines.

Think of it like building a model from a kit. Most of the hard work, like molding plastic and cutting metal, is done in the factory. When you get the kit home, you just need to put the pieces together and paint the model however you like.

Programs written in these languages follow a two-step process. First, the compiler converts them into a low-level language called bytecode. Then, a runtime engine translates the bytecode into the computer's machine language when the program runs. This is faster than a fully interpreted language but slower than a compiled executable. The key advantage is that bytecode can run on any computer that has the runtime engine installed.
Scripting Functions

People also call interpreted languages scripting languages. In addition to Python, JavaScript, Ruby, and Perl, many operating systems have their own scripting languages. For example, Windows includes PowerShell and Command Prompt, while Linux uses Bash. The Windows command line can run batch files, which are collections of commands that run one after another.

Windows PowerShell includes both a command-line shell and a scripting language called Windows PowerShell Integrated Scripting Environment (ISE). People often use PowerShell to perform administrative and management tasks. Sometimes, you can only complete these tasks using a PowerShell script.

To remember the difference between an interpreted and compiled language, think of an interpreter for spoken languages. Imagine someone speaking in a language you don't understand, and an interpreter next to them repeats what they say in your language. This real-time interpretation is similar to how an interpreted language works.
Interpreted Languages
Unlike compiled languages, interpreted programs don't turn source code into binary ahead of time. Instead, an interpreter runs the instructions in the source code each time the application launches.

Interpreted programs have the advantage of being platform-independent. This is often called portability; you can move a program from one system to another without changing the source code. Compiled programs, by contrast, must be rewritten and recompiled for each new platform.

The trade-off is speed and resource access. Interpreted languages are slower than compiled ones because the code is translated into machine language as it runs. They also have limited access to the system's hardware. Most applications you use through your web browser, including the labs in this course, are written in interpreted languages.
One benefit of interpreted languages is that debugging can be easier. Because the code runs line by line, errors show up right where the problem is, making them quicker to find and fix.
Assembly Language

Assembly language is one of the first human-readable computer languages. It is a low-level programming language that interacts directly with the computer's hardware, without using a compiler or interpreter.

Because assembly language is so close to machine language, code written in it is more efficient and runs faster than code written in higher-level languages. Assembly language allows direct access to hardware and is very specific to the processor and other components. You can write a program in assembly language for a specific system with known hardware.

Another capability, and also a challenge, is that assembly language allows direct memory access, letting you manipulate memory addresses. While programmers still use assembly language in some specialized areas, they more commonly use higher-level languages for most programming tasks.
Query Languages

Another type of language specializes in getting information from databases. Are called query languages, like Structured Query Language (SQL). They help you find specific data, show only what you are looking for, or present information in helpful ways.

Queries answer questions about data sets. For example, they tell you the greatest amount of a product in stock, how many orders the company had last week, or what the weather was like in January in your town.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: For example, if you want to learn more about your favorite movies, you can use the website IMDb. This is the Internet Movie Database, and it has millions of records about movies, TV shows, actors, directors, and producers. To get information about a specific topic, you type a search term on the home page. When you press enter, the website shows a page of results that match your search. You see the search page taking you directly to the results, but there's a lot more happening behind the scenes.

When you type a search term and press enter, the computer takes what you typed and translates it into a query language, like SQL. Then, it uses the query to search the database and find all the records that match your search. Once it has them, it organizes them into a nice-looking report and shows it on the screen. Using queries, you can turn the raw data in database tables into useful information to help you make informed decisions.

blocks.title: What you should be able to answer
items: Why is it important to plan a program before you start writing code?
What is a flowchart, and how do the different shapes represent steps in a program?
What is pseudocode, and how does it help a programmer organize their logic?
How do branching and looping control the flow of a program?
What are functions and procedures, and why do programmers use them?
What tools can you use to write and test code, and how do they differ?

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 4.4 Identify programming organizational techniques and logic concepts.
4.3 Explain the purpose and use of programming concepts.
4.1 Compare and contrast programming language categories.

blocks.text: Writing code is only part of programming. Before a single line is written, good programmers plan what their program should do and how it should work. This planning phase helps catch problems early, keeps the project organized, and makes the actual coding much smoother.

In this lesson, you will learn how to define the goals of a program, map out its logic using flowcharts, and write pseudocode to describe each step in plain language. You will also explore key programming concepts such as branching, looping, logical operators, and functions. Finally, you will look at the tools programmers use to write and test their code, including text editors, browser consoles, and integrated development environments (IDEs).
Define What the Program Should Do

Programmers use logic to tell a computer how and when to do certain tasks. They create the program, the system hardware sits in the middle, and the user interacts with the software on the other side. Whether a program is simple or complex, all programs instruct a system to follow a sequence of steps. The code could be for a computer, an IoT device, or even a car.

Programmers design and write their code by following several steps, including using flowcharts, branching, looping, algorithms, operators, procedures, and functions. Interestingly, some of the early work of creating a program doesn't always involve computers. The planning process can take time and shouldn't be rushed. Just like painting a room in your home involves a lot of prep work before actually putting paint on the wall, creating a well-thought-out program requires careful planning.

Say you want to create your own electronic version of the game Roshambo or Rock-Paper- Scissors. Before you start coding, decide what the program should do. The exact features of a program can be very different depending on your goals.

In this case, you want players to make a choice, and with your program, neither player's choice will be revealed until both have picked rock, paper, or scissors. Planning this program involves very little coding; you need to figure out all the variables, inputs, and outputs. How will the user interact with the program? What will they see on the screen? What are the different possible outcomes?

What is the difference between a script and a program? The key difference is in how they are executed. A script is a set of instructions that are interpreted by another program such as a scripting engine. In contrast, a program is compiled into machine code and executed directly by the computer's operating system. While scripts are typically used for automating specific tasks, programs are often more complex and can operate independently.
Map Out the Program Sequence

Any part of a programming sequence that can change (like input from a user) requires instructions for all possible changes. A flowchart helps you see how each step and variation fit together. Flowcharts show the flow (sequence) of logic in a program. One advantage of using flowcharts is that they make programming logic easier to understand, especially for people who are new to programming.

Sometimes computer programs start at the first line and run one line after another until they finish. Other times, the program needs to act differently based on what the user does or other situations. This is called branching and will be covered later.
Flowcharts use standardized shapes to help you see the decisions, actions, and order of steps the program takes. Some of the more common flowchart shapes include:

items: Oval: The start or end of a program.
Parallelogram: Input or output.
Diamond: Decisions answered with a Yes or a No.
Rectangle: Processes.
Arrow: The logical flow of the program.

blocks.text: You could use a flowchart for your Rock-Paper-Scissors program.
Digital Literacy Module 18: Telling Computers What to Do by Coding 438
Pseudocode

As your code gets more complex, it's a good idea to plan out what you want it to do before you start writing. This makes your ideas clearer, helps keep your code neat, and saves you time fixing mistakes later.

Before you start writing the code line by line, prepare pseudocode. Pseudocode is a simple way of describing what the code will do using plain language. Pseudocode aims to explain what the code will accomplish in a clear and easy-to-understand way. Another programmer should be able to read and follow it easily. After you finish the flowchart, create high-level pseudocode. It helps break big programs into smaller pieces. You can also use the same piece of pseudocode more than once.

Specific algorithms are an important part of a program and pseudocode. They provide step-by- step instructions to solve a problem. They include all the needed logic, like if-else statements, branches, and loops. Before you write them in code, you often show algorithms in flowcharts or pseudocode.
Pseudocode and Programming Constructs

Pseudocode is a way to write down six basic programming ideas or constructs always written in uppercase: SEQUENCE, WHILE, REPEA T -UNTIL, FOR, IF- THEN-ELSE, and CASE. These constructs, also known as keywords, help show how the steps of an algorithm are controlled.
1. SEQUENCE represents tasks that happen in a specific order, one after the other.
Steps in the SEQUENCE construct have their own keywords as well, including:

items: The Input step, which obtains data from another section of code or from a human: READ,

blocks.text: OBTAIN, GET

items: Output: PRINT, DISPLAY, SHOW
Compute: CALCULATE, COMPUTE, DETERMINE
Initialize: SET, INIT
Add: INCREMENT
Subtract: DECREMENT

blocks.text: 2. WHILE is a loop, or repeated section of code, with a condition at its beginning.
3. REPEA T -UNTIL is a loop with a condition at its ending.
4. FOR is a different way to loop a section of code.
5. IF- THEN-ELSE is a conditional statement that changes the flow of the directions or code.
6. CASE is a generalized form of the IF- THEN-ELSE construct.
Using Operators
Code has operators, just like math problems have symbols that tell you what to do with the numbers. Each coding language has its own operators. For pseudocode, you should know some basic operators.
Relational operators:

items: = and == mean "is equal to." This means it returns TRUE if both conditions are the same.
!= means "is not equal to." For example, a true statement would be "100 != 5"
> means "greater than." For example, a true statement would be "100 > 5"
< means "less than." A true statement would be "5 < 100"
>= means "greater than or equal to." A true statement would be either "100 >= 100" or "100
<= means "less than or equal to." A true statement would be either "5 <= 5" or "5 <= 50"

blocks.text: Explaining Your Code

When you write your code, it's very helpful to add comments that explain what each part of the code does. This way, you or a coworker can easily understand the code when you need to update or fix the program.

When adding comments, remember that if you want to add notes inside your code, you need to use a symbol that represents "comment." This symbol can vary depending on which programming language you end up using, but common symbols are the hash (#), an apostrophe ('), or double forward slashes (//). When it runs, the programming language ignores any lines within your code that begin with the comment symbol.
Working with Pseudocode

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: Imagine you’ve agreed to create a shopping cart for a friend starting an online business. Before you begin coding it, you can use pseudocode to decide how it should work. Pseudocode is a line-by-line description of what your program needs to do. Pseudocode is not a programming language; it is a way to represent code using English statements that are easy for a wide range of people to understand. It provides a good description of the steps and algorithms you need to implement in your program. Programmers translate pseudocode of the steps and algorithms they have designed into the programming language they are using to create their code.
Take a look at the pseudocode for the shopping cart we are writing for our friend.

When user clicks "Add to Cart": If user is logged in: Add item to cart Suggest similar items else: Redirect user to login page Our shopping cart pseudocode describes the steps the program needs to perform. It needs to watch for the user to click "Add to cart." When they do, it checks to see whether the user is logged in. If they aren’t, they get redirected to the login page.

Once the programmer has reviewed the steps defined in the pseudocode and determined that they are correct, the programmer translates the pseudocode to the programming language they are using and includes it in their program code.
Programming Tools

An important decision to make before writing code in JavaScript is what tool you will use to write your code. You could choose a simple text editor, the coding console in Google Chrome, or an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). Depending on the coding tasks you are doing will determine which coding environment you decide to use as you write a program.
Text Editors

A simple text editor like Notepad++ can be an easy environment to write simple programs in, but it lacks the helpful features and functions that other coding environments provide. For example, a simple text editor does not highlight the syntax in your code or identify syntax mistakes you might have made in your code, like missing a semicolon at the end of a line of code.
Console Editors

The coding console in Google Chrome is always available, easy to use, and there is nothing additional that you need to install if you have access to Google Chrome. The console is a good place to write and test simple programs because it will highlight different keywords, and the code can be directly run, which makes it easy to test that it's working. To access the coding console in Google Chrome, launch a Google browser, select the three vertical dots menu, select the More Tools menu option, and then select the Developer Tools menu option. In the Developer Tools panel, select the Console. In the console, you can write and run JavaScript code. To add additional lines of code to your program, press the Shift + Enter keys. When you have your program written, press Enter to run it.
Integrated Development Environments (IDEs)

IDE stands for Integrated Development Environment, and an IDE is a set of programming tools that work together to make it easier for a programmer to write code. An IDE helps you to more easily identify and correct coding errors and bugs by highlighting keywords, automatically adding closing parentheses and brackets, and allowing you to run the program to test it, including stopping the program at areas you want to test more deeply using markers called breakpoints. An IDE also allows many programmers to collaborate on the same programming project. For professional programmers, an IDE is an essential tool.IDEs provide many helpful features to make programming easier, such as:

items: A code editor
Auto-completion of coding syntax
Syntax highlighting and bug identification
Code execution displayed in a separate window
Organizing your code into project folders

blocks.title: What you should be able to answer
items: What is a variable, and how do constants differ from variables?
What are the fundamental data types, and how do integers, floats, characters, strings, and
Booleans differ?
How do arithmetic, relational, and logical operators transform data in a program?
What is the order of operations, and why does it matter when writing expressions?
How are Boolean operators like AND, OR, XOR, and NOT used to evaluate conditions?
What is a Variable in Program Code?
Computer programs often need to remember data to use later. For example, at a shoe store,
the number of shoes always changes. When customers buy shoes, the number goes down, and
when new shipments arrive, the number goes up. If we call a variable "Shoes," we can assign it
a number, and this number can change based on what happens.
A variable acts like a container that holds numbers, words, phrases, and other values. As
the name suggests, variables can change the values they hold. We call both variables and
constants identifiers, which are unique names given to something in the program. This is
important for how programs run.
In our simple shoe store example, we store the number of shoes in a variable called "Shoes."
The pseudocode might show that Shoes = 7. Using the equals sign, the program sets the value
of "Shoes" to be the number of shoes at the start of the day, which is 7 in this case. Later in the
code, the programmer types the name of the variable "Shoes" to get its value.

blocks.title: Objectives covered
items: 4.2 Identify fundamental data types and their characteristics.
4.4 Identify programming organizational techniques and logic concepts.

blocks.text: Programs need ways to store, organize, and manipulate information. Variables act as named containers that hold data while a program runs, and data types define what kind of information a variable can store, such as numbers, text, or true/false values. Understanding how to declare variables, choose the right data type, and apply operators to transform data is essential to writing functional code.
In this lesson, you will explore the fundamental data types used in programming and learn how arithmetic, relational, and logical operators work to compare and transform data.

Computer programs often need to remember data to use later. For example, at a shoe store, the number of shoes always changes. When customers buy shoes, the number goes down, and when new shipments arrive, the number goes up. If we call a variable "Shoes," we can assign it a number, and this number can change based on what happens.

A variable acts like a container that holds numbers, words, phrases, and other values. As the name suggests, variables can change the values they hold. We call both variables and constants identifiers, which are unique names given to something in the program. This is important for how programs run.

In our simple shoe store example, we store the number of shoes in a variable called "Shoes." The pseudocode might show that Shoes = 7. Using the equals sign, the program sets the value of "Shoes" to be the number of shoes at the start of the day, which is 7 in this case. Later in the code, the programmer types the name of the variable "Shoes" to get its value.

Variables can also store Boolean values. If a user logs into an account, the program tracks whether the user is signed in. When the user logs in, this variable stores the value true. When they log out, it changes to false.
Constants

Sometimes, a programmer wants to keep track of a value that never changes. For example, a physicist might want to keep track of the value of pi to fifteen decimal places. Because this value never changes, they use a constant. A constant is like a container that holds values, but unlike a variable, constants never change. Once they're set, they're set for good. With this constant, the physicist just types the name of the constant instead of the whole long number.
Data Types

Programmers use data types to tell a computer what type of data a variable is storing. Common data types are integer, floating point, character, string, and boolean. Programming languages use data types to tell a computer how much memory is needed to store variables and objects during code execution. Data types also define the ways that variables and objects can be used in programs. For example, two variables with the integer data type can be added together.
Variable Types
Variables store data values in programs and determine what kind of data they hold. Remember when you learned about numbering systems and how computers use binary numbers?

The ones and zeros create a map to ASCII and Unicode, which set the rules for how all computer characters are assigned. These same rules apply to programming languages. In these languages, you will find common types of variables, including the following:

items: Integers: Whole numbers, either positive or negative, without a decimal or fraction. Examples include 23, -7 , and 451.
Floating-point or float: Numbers that can have a decimal place or fractional part. Examples include 8.02, 99.999, and -1. 01.
Boolean: Variables that only store one of two logical values: True or False. Programmers often use them in logical operations.
String: A sequence of characters, like words or sentences. Examples include "Hello World,"
Character or Char: A variable that stores a single character, which could be a digit, letter, or symbol. Examples include '7', 'X', and '#'.

Array: A unique collection of values that must be of the same type and are accessed using an index. For example, in array [23 , 7 ,451], the value 23 is at index 0, 7 is at index 1, and 451 is at index 2.

blocks.text: Different programming languages might have extra types of variables or different versions of these basic types.

Programmers usually declare variables, define them with a specific data type, and give them a starting value at the beginning of the routine where they are used. Sometimes, you can use variables without declaring them first, but this can make the code harder to read and more likely to have mistakes.
Number Types

Understanding the different data types a computer program can use are important. This is especially true when you start writing your own programs (coding) or working with database systems. The central processing unit (CPU) and storage devices in a computer only process data as ones and zeros. These hardware parts don't know what the data means.

However, in programming, data types are very important because they determine what kind of operations you can do. For example, you can treat the characters "51" as a number and use it in addition and subtraction, or you can treat it as a text string (like a house number). If you store "51" as a string, you must convert it before using it in a math operation.
Different types of number values include:

items: Integers or int: Whole numbers like -7 , 23, or 65536. An integer data type uses 1 to 8 bytes of computer storage. They don't have a fraction or decimal place.

Floating-point numbers: Numbers that can have decimal fractions, like 4.1, 26.4, or 5.62. A floating-point number (or just "float") uses between 4 and 8 bytes of storage. A float can also store whole numbers (like 4 . 0). You use a float when you need more precision.
Fixed-point: Real numbers with a specific number of digits after the decimal point. They are common in financial calculations where accuracy is important, like $9.95.
Double: Similar to a float, but a double variable can store larger and more precise float numbers.

blocks.text: What the program needs determines the number type you choose. Most programming languages offer different number types to handle various situations.
Characters and Text

Programmers use characters and strings to represent and work with text data. A character includes anything you see on your computer keyboard, even the symbols in the corners. A string is more than one character and includes letters, numbers, or symbols. Programmers use them in the most popular programming languages. Here are the two types with examples:

items: Characters: A character (or char) is a single letter, symbol, or number. Examples include: a,

blocks.text: D, 7, $, @, #. Characters use one byte of storage. Note that when you enter a number as a character, you cannot do any math with it.

items: Strings: A string is a collection of characters. Examples include: XYZ, Hello world, Apartment

blocks.text: #101. There is no real limit on the storage a string can use. Usually, you define the string length when you set up the data type.

When you use single or double quotes to mark the start and end of a string ("Hello World"), the quotes are not part of the string itself. If you want to include a quote character (or other special character) inside a string, you have to use an escape character.

An escape character, usually \, placed in front of the quote, tells the program to include the quote in the output. For example, the string " John said \"Hello World\" then left." contains two single quotes, escaped using the backslash character (\). The output of that string would look like: John said "Hello World" then left.
Booleans and Logic
Boolean operations follow a format similar to binary numbers, a system of one of two states.
Their 1 or 0, however, represents either True or False.

Boolean operations compare two conditions to determine their state and make a decision on the outcome. The operations can be combined to make decisions on multiple conditions. They are fundamental building blocks of programming.

Boolean values are a special type of number that show if something is either TRUE or FALSE (using 1 or 0). They use just one bit of storage. You will use them for logical operators, which test multiple conditions at the same time.
Boolean Operators

items: AND: If both conditions are TRUE, the whole statement is considered TRUE.
OR: If either condition is TRUE, the whole statement is also considered TRUE.

X OR: If one condition is TRUE and the other condition is FALSE, the whole statement is considered TRUE. If both conditions are TRUE, the whole statement is considered FALSE. In other words, if the conditions are different from each other, this Boolean operator sees the statement as correct. If the conditions are the same (either TRUE- TRUE or F ALSE-F ALSE), then the statement is incorrect.
NO T : The whole statement is not TRUE.

blocks.text: Boolean Operators in Pseudocode

items: && (Logic al AND): If both conditions are TRUE, the whole statement is TRUE.
|| (Logic al OR): If either condition is TRUE, the whole statement is TRUE.
^ (Logic al X OR): If one condition is TRUE and the other condition is FALSE, the whole statement is considered TRUE. If both conditions are TRUE, the whole statement is considered FALSE.
! (Logic al NO T): The whole statement is not TRUE.

blocks.text: With Boolean values, true means something is correct, and false means something is incorrect.
Booleans are often used in conditional statements, like if-then statements. These statements check a condition to decide what part of the code to run next.
Data Operator

Here's a group of students playing a video game. As they play, computer program code instructs their computers on how to keep track of game data. Let's look at ways programming language code instructs computers how to work with data and operate on it.
Identifier Names

Identifier names are the names that a programmer gives to the constants and variables they create in their program code. Constants and variables are given descriptive names to make programs easier to read and write. When deciding on identifier names, it is a good programming practice to make the names meaningful and consistent. In the game example, variables could be created to keep track of the number of hearts, crowns, and score that a player earns. These variables could be called numberOfHearts, numberOfCrowns, and playerScore.
Assignment of Values

An assignment statement is used to set the initial value of a constant or variable, or reset the value of a variable. The assignment operator in JavaScript is an equals sign "=". For example, the value of the variable hearts could be set to 5 using the following command: hearts = 5; Relational Operators Here's a student taking an exam on a computer. The student answers each question on the exam, and the computer checks whether the student entered the correct answer or not. The computer uses this information to provide a score for the exam and to give feedback to the student on what questions they got right and what questions they missed. A programmer uses relational operators to instruct a computer how to make decisions to grade this exam. Relational operators are used by programmers to create conditional statements in their code to compare values and to take action depending on the results. Relational operators are also commonly used in branching and control statements like if statements, while loops, for loops, and switch statements, to control decisions a computer makes.
The relational operators are:

items: == is equal to. This means it returns TRUE if both conditions are the same.
!= is not equal to.
> greater than.
< less than.
>= greater than or equal to.
<= less than or equal to.

blocks.text: Often relational operators are used to create test conditions that control program flow and computer decisions. In our exam scoring example, let's say the answer to question 10 is D. If the student's response is D, the student gets a correct score on this question. If the student's response is not D, the student gets an incorrect score on this question.
Logical Operators

Every day, we make decisions and take actions based upon how we logically evaluate certain conditions. To determine if you are going to go to the beach, you could evaluate two conditions: Is it sunny outside? AND Is my homework done? AND is one of the logical operators and requires that both conditions must be true to act. So, it has to be sunny and your homework has to be done so that you can go to the beach. Common logical operators include AND, OR, XOR, and NOT. Logical operators are used by programmers to create decision-making statements in their code which compare multiple conditions and instruct a computer to act depending on the results. Logical operators are commonly used in branching and control statements, like if statements, while loops, for loops, and switch statements, to control actions a computer takes.
